exam: Expect four-option multiple choice items that ask for a number, the person responsible, the first step in a scenario, or a load chart result worked by hand. Wrong options are usually a real number applied to the wrong situation, the wrong role, or an answer with one step left out, so check each option against the exact condition in the question.
hard: There is a lot of ground to cover. Federal rules, industry practice, rigging, wire rope, signals and load chart arithmetic all come up together. The hardest part is matching numbers that sit close together and job titles that sound alike to the right rule, and working multi-step chart problems by hand without skipping a deduction. You also have to keep track of which statements are federal rules and which come from the manufacturer or industry practice.
mistakes: People study the rules and skip the load charts, but chart problems are a large share of the core exam and take hand practice. People treat industry practice as federal rule, so learn where each limit comes from. People assume the crane's name decides which rules apply, but coverage depends on what the machine does and the work it is doing. People memorize answers instead of the reasoning, and then miss the same idea when it comes back as a jobsite scenario. People read the question too fast and miss words like first, not or except.

summary: This course prepares you for the NCCCO Mobile Crane Operator written exams. It is built around the core exam that every mobile crane candidate takes, with practice in the style of the specialty and service truck crane exams. It is organized by exam domain and then by topic, so you can drill one skill at a time and see how the rules, the physics and the load chart fit together on a real lift. It is independent practice and is not affiliated with or endorsed by the certifying body or OSHA.
title: Mobile Crane Operator exam prep

exam: Items are four-option multiple choice. They cover rule values, who owes a duty, first-step scenarios, signal recognition and generic load chart calculations. Watch for words like gross, net, first, most likely and except, and for options that stop one step short of the right answer.
hard: You get a little under a minute per question, and load chart items take longer because you do every step by hand. Operations and Load Charts together make up more than half the exam, so weak chart skills cost a lot. Many items mix domains, like a power line scenario that also asks who is responsible.
mistakes: People spend too long on one chart problem, when they should flag it, move on and come back. People expect a calculator, but the core exam has none, so practice multiplication and division on paper. People think Load Charts just means reading a number off a table, but it also covers choosing the right chart, the next longer radius and boom length, and every deduction. People skim Technical Knowledge, but inspections, wire rope and rigging hardware carry a real share of the items.

summary: The core exam is the written test every mobile crane operator candidate takes, whatever crane type they certify on. It has 95 questions in 90 minutes with no calculator. The four domains are Site at 22 percent, Operations at 28 percent, Technical Knowledge at 23 percent and Load Charts at 27 percent. It checks that you know the rules, the machine and the chart well enough to run a lift safely on any mobile crane.
title: Mobile crane operator written exam, core (style)

exam: Expect jobsite scenarios that ask who is responsible for ground preparation or hazard information, what to do first at set-up, and how a support condition changes stability. Some items ask for a simple bearing-pressure or mat-area calculation, so watch the units in the question and the options.
hard: Ground duties are split among several parties, and the questions turn on exactly who owes what. Ground stability depends on things you can't see, like buried utilities, voids, fill and water, and on where the boom is pointed, because the load moves from one support to another as you swing. The bearing-pressure arithmetic is simple, but area and unit conversions trip people up without a calculator.
mistakes: People judge the ground by what they see on top, but voids, utilities, fill and water below the surface matter just as much. People think mats fix any ground, but mats only spread the load when they are sized and placed for the ground under them. People think the operator alone answers for ground conditions, but the controlling entity has duties to prepare the site and share what it knows about hazards below. People think power line precautions start once lifting begins, but they also apply during assembly, disassembly and travel. People convert square inches to square feet by dividing by the inches in a foot, when they should divide by the square inches in a square foot.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: Site covers the work before the first pick. That means judging ground stability above and below the surface, using mats and cribbing, watching for power lines during assembly and disassembly, traveling without a load, getting safely to the set-up spot, and controlling pinch and crush points. It also covers what the controlling entity owes on site conditions. It is 22 percent of the core exam, and most tip-overs and crush injuries start here.
title: Site

exam: Expect scenarios that ask what the operator does first or next, who has authority, and how a condition like wind, side load or deflection changes the lift. Some items test signal recognition and the steps after power line contact, so read for the order the question asks about.
hard: There are many subjects here, and each one has its own responsible person and its own exceptions. The physics questions reward knowing what really changes load moment and radius, like boom deflection, a swinging load, or a load released suddenly. Emergency items test the order of actions, and people pick a sensible action that comes in the wrong order.
mistakes: People think the operator keeps lifting until a supervisor stops the job, but the operator has authority to stop whenever safety is in doubt. People trust a failed operator aid or guess around it, but a malfunction calls for the alternative measures before work goes on. People think a little side load is harmless, but booms are built for vertical loads and can fail from side loading well below chart capacity. People take the radius from the unloaded boom, but the radius grows as the boom deflects under load. People think dynamic loading only means a dropped load, but a sudden loss of load can throw the boom backward. People think any signal the crew makes up will do, but new or non-standard signals are agreed on before the lift.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: Operations covers running the crane once it is set up. That includes leveling, verifying load weight, size and center of gravity, finding the radius, reeving, signals, power lines, tag lines, the fall zone, operator aids and safety devices, emergencies, dynamic and side loading, boom deflection, weather, attachments, the operator's authority to stop, and securing the crane. At 28 percent it is the largest domain on the core exam. It is where rule knowledge meets judgment in the seat.
title: Operations

exam: Expect items on which rule or standard applies, the meaning of a term, who performs an inspection and what is recorded, and when rope or rigging comes out of service. Watch for options that put a general industry term or interval into a construction question.
hard: Several sets of rules overlap. Construction rules, general industry rules and ASME B30 consensus standards cover similar ground with different wording, and people mix them up. Each inspection type has its own person and its own record, and the wire rope removal criteria change with the rope type. Protective devices for power lines each have limits that the questions like to test.
mistakes: People treat ASME B30 volumes as federal law, but they are consensus standards that sit alongside the federal rules. People assume one person does every inspection, but the required qualification changes with the inspection type. People think an insulating link or proximity alarm makes power line work safe by itself, but each device has limits and is only one layer of protection. People judge wire rope only by how it looks overall, but removal criteria include broken wire counts over a set length, kinks, crushing, corrosion and heat damage. People think a tagged sling or shackle is fine to use, but damaged hardware comes out of service whatever the tag says.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: Technical Knowledge covers the federal regulations and industry standards that govern mobile cranes, crane terminology, the functions and limits of cranes and attachments, and the inspection program. It also covers rigging hardware, wire rope and terminations, hook blocks and overhaul balls, electrical protective measures, instruments and gauges, and access, egress and fall protection. It is 23 percent of the core exam and is the knowledge base the other domains build on.
title: Technical Knowledge

exam: Expect generic charts with questions on gross or net capacity, whether a lift is allowed, the longest radius or boom length for a load, or the parts of line needed. The wording matters: gross versus net, loaded versus unloaded radius, and over the front versus over the side or rear.
hard: One chart problem stacks several steps: the right chart, the right work area, the next longer radius and boom length, the loaded radius, and then every deduction to get from gross to net. Skip any one of them and the wrong answer is usually sitting right there in the options. You do all of it by hand, so arithmetic slips cost as much as reading errors.
mistakes: People take the gross number straight off the chart, but net capacity is gross minus the block, rigging and any stowed or erected attachments. People round to the closest radius, but standard practice uses the next longer radius and boom length unless the chart says otherwise. People use the on-outrigger chart for an on-rubber setup, but the chart has to match the configuration and work area. People ignore the chart notes, but they say which values are structural limits and which are stability limits, and what to deduct. People forget parts of line, but a load can be within the chart and still be more than the reeving can carry.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: Load Charts covers chart terms, hand arithmetic, choosing the right chart for the crane's configuration, and reading rated capacity charts, range diagrams, work area charts, parts-of-line tables and boom angle limits. It also covers choosing the best configuration for a lift. It is 27 percent of the core exam, and every lift you make on the job starts with this skill.
title: Load Charts

exam: Expect questions worked from a manufacturer's chart: net capacity in a set configuration, maximum radius for a load, and line pull against rope capacity. Also expect type-specific scenarios on set-up, assembly and devices. Read every chart note the question points you to.
hard: Manufacturers' Load Charts is the biggest domain, and manufacturer charts have far more notes, configurations and deductions than the generic charts on the core exam. The calculator saves arithmetic time, but you still have to find the right page, line and note. Type-specific terms and devices differ between telescopic and lattice cranes.
mistakes: People think the calculator makes chart items easy, but most errors come from reading the wrong chart or missing a note. People study only general crane knowledge, but this exam asks about features of the specific crane type. People treat 60 minutes as plenty of time, but chart items with several pages of notes take time to work through. People skip the range and work area diagrams, but many items depend on them.

summary: The specialty exams test the crane type you certify on: telescopic fixed cab, telescopic swing cab or lattice boom. Each one has 28 questions in 60 minutes, and a calculator is allowed. The domains are Site at 23 percent, Operations at 23 percent, Technical Knowledge at 19 percent and Manufacturers' Load Charts at 35 percent. The questions are built on real manufacturer charts and type-specific equipment, so they go deeper than the core exam.
title: Mobile crane operator written exam, specialty (style; telescopic fixed cab, telescopic swing cab, lattice boom)

exam: Expect set-up scenarios for a given crane type: the next step in an assembly sequence, which outrigger position matches a chart, and what supporting materials a condition calls for. Watch for options that describe the right step for a different crane type.
hard: Assembly steps differ a lot between lattice booms, telescopic booms and their extensions or jibs, and the questions follow the manufacturer's sequence. Outrigger position decides which chart applies, so a set-up detail turns into a capacity question. Pin removal and boom support conditions are easy to blur.
mistakes: People think outriggers only need to be down, but their extended position decides which capacity chart you can use. People assume any jib or extension goes on the same way, but each type follows its own manufacturer procedure. People think a position sensor replaces looking, but you still confirm the setup matches the chart. People treat cribbing as a fix for any surface, but it has to be sound, sized and stacked for the load.

summary: Site on the specialty exam covers supporting materials like mats and cribbing, assembling and disassembling the boom for your crane type, outriggers, stabilizers and crawlers, and outrigger position sensors. It is 23 percent of the specialty exam. It goes from general ground knowledge to the set-up steps for one crane type.
title: Site

exam: Expect scenarios on which device does what, how a function can two-block the hook, and how operating on rubber or crawlers changes the lift. Read for the crane type the question names.
hard: Devices with similar names do different jobs, like a boom stop versus a boom hoist limiting device, or a jib stop versus a luffing jib limiting device. Pick and carry conditions change capacity and travel limits. On a telescopic crane, extending the boom can two-block the hook, which surprises people used to lattice cranes.
mistakes: People think a boom stop and a boom hoist limiting device are the same thing, but one is a physical stop and the other cuts power to the hoist. People think two-blocking only happens when hoisting up, but extending a telescopic boom or booming down a lattice boom can also cause it. People use the stationary chart for pick and carry, but pick and carry has its own capacities and conditions. People secure a lattice crane the same way as a telescopic one, but each follows its own shutdown procedure.

summary: Operations on the specialty exam covers working stationary on rubber, on outriggers and on crawlers, pick and carry, shutting down and securing, and the type-specific devices. Those include boom length indicators, boom hoist and luffing jib limiting devices, boom stops, brake locks, jib stops, power flow systems and approaching two-block on telescopic and lattice cranes. It is 23 percent of the specialty exam.
title: Operations

exam: Expect items on what a component does, an attachment's limits, and when a running or standing rope comes out of service. Watch for options that are right for the other crane type.
hard: Terms that mean one thing on a telescopic crane can mean something else, or nothing, on a lattice crane. Standing ropes have their own removal criteria, separate from running ropes, and people apply the wrong set.
mistakes: People apply running rope removal criteria to pendants, but standing ropes are judged by their own criteria. People think attachments are interchangeable across models, but only manufacturer-approved attachments go on a crane. People confuse similar component names across crane types, so learn the terms for your type.

summary: Technical Knowledge on the specialty exam covers the terms, functions, limits and attachments of your crane type, plus inspecting and replacing wire rope, including standing ropes like pendants. It is 19 percent of the specialty exam. It checks that you know your own machine, not just cranes in general.
title: Technical Knowledge

exam: Expect calculator-allowed items worked from a manufacturer's chart: net capacity in a set configuration, maximum radius for a given load, and the parts of line or line pull a lift needs. Watch whether the question asks for gross or net, and which configuration it names.
hard: A manufacturer's chart package runs several pages, and the right answer often depends on one note or one deduction table. Line pull limits and rope capacity are separate checks, and the lower one controls. Erection charts limit what you can do while the boom is being raised, apart from the lifting chart.
mistakes: People skip the chart notes, but they often hold the deduction or condition that changes the answer. People take the winch's maximum line pull as the rope's capacity, but the lower of line pull and rope safe working load controls. People read gross capacity as what they can hook, but net capacity takes off the block, rigging and attachments. People use the lifting chart while raising a long boom, but erection limits can apply first.

summary: Manufacturers' Load Charts covers reading a real manufacturer's chart package: notes, specifications, range and work area diagrams, erection charts and rated capacity charts. It also covers maximum radius, gross and net capacity in different configurations, and maximum line pull compared with the safe working load of the running rope. At 35 percent it is the largest specialty domain.
title: Manufacturers' Load Charts

exam: Expect four-option items on set-up, operating practice, inspections and reading a manufacturer's chart by hand. Scenarios often describe a field repair job and ask for the first or safest action.
hard: Operations dominates, so weak seat judgment costs more here than on the other exams. Service truck work happens on roadsides, in yards and next to equipment being repaired, where ground, traffic and power lines change from job to job. Chart work is done by hand from manufacturer charts.
mistakes: People think a small truck-mounted crane needs less care, but tip-overs, overloads and power line contacts happen on small cranes too. People skip the stabilizers for a quick lift, but the chart assumes the set-up it lists. People study only load charts, but Operations is the largest domain here. People expect a calculator, but this exam has none.

summary: The service truck crane exam is for operators of cranes mounted on service and mechanic trucks. It has 80 questions in 90 minutes with no calculator. The domains are Site at 17 percent, Operations at 45 percent, Technical Knowledge at 21 percent and Manufacturers' Load Charts at 17 percent. Operations carries almost half the exam, so it leans heavily on running the crane day to day.
title: Service truck crane operator written exam (style)

exam: Expect field scenarios asking where to set up, what to check first, and how a ground or overhead condition changes the job.
hard: Field sites change constantly, and soft shoulders, slopes and buried utilities are easy to miss. The truck's stabilizer setup decides its capacity, and a rushed setup is the usual cause of trouble.
mistakes: People park where the repair is and lift from there, but the truck goes where the ground and clearances allow. People think the truck's weight keeps it stable, but the stabilizers and level setup carry the load. People forget overhead lines in yards and on roadsides, but they are a leading hazard for truck-mounted cranes.

summary: Site on the service truck exam covers judging the ground, setting stabilizers and supporting materials, and spotting hazards like power lines, traffic and people where the truck parks to work. It is 17 percent of the service truck exam. A service truck often works wherever the broken equipment sits, so the site is rarely prepared for it.
title: Site

exam: Expect scenarios on the safest next action, how to respond to a malfunction, and when to stop a lift. Read carefully for who is operating and where they are standing.
hard: Many service truck lifts are done by one person who is both operator and rigger, which makes it easy to skip a check. Radio or remote controls let you move around, and that changes what you can see and where you stand.
mistakes: People think working alone means signals don't matter, but the operator still needs a clear view of the load or a signal person. People stand under or beside the load while running a remote, but you keep yourself out of the load path too. People leave the boom up and stabilizers out to save time, but the crane is stowed and secured before the truck moves.

summary: Operations on the service truck exam covers running the crane during field repair work: controls, load handling, signals, operator aids, emergencies and securing the crane for travel. At 45 percent it is by far the largest domain on the service truck exam.
title: Operations

exam: Expect items on terms, inspections, removal criteria and which rules apply to a described job.
hard: Coverage depends on the work being done, not just on the equipment, so the same truck can fall under different rules on different jobs. Inspection and rope criteria are the same ideas as on larger cranes, applied to smaller parts.
mistakes: People assume a service truck crane is always outside the crane rules, but coverage depends on the machine and the work it is doing. People skip the shift inspection on a small crane, but every crane gets inspected before use. People keep using worn hooks or rope because the loads are light, but removal criteria don't depend on load size.

summary: Technical Knowledge on the service truck exam covers the crane's components and limits, inspections, wire rope, rigging hardware and the rules that apply to service truck work. It is 21 percent of the service truck exam.
title: Technical Knowledge

exam: Expect chart items that ask whether a lift is allowed, the net capacity at a radius, or the reach for a given load. Watch the work area and stabilizer condition named in the question.
hard: Service truck charts often list capacity by boom extension and angle, with separate values for different stabilizer setups or areas around the truck. You do the arithmetic without a calculator.
mistakes: People read the over-the-rear value for a side lift, but capacity changes with the work area. People take the hook's listed capacity as net, but deductions for the hook and rigging still apply. People round the radius down, but standard practice uses the next longer radius unless the chart says otherwise.

summary: Manufacturers' Load Charts on the service truck exam covers reading the chart for a truck-mounted crane by hand: capacity at a radius and boom extension, stabilizer conditions and deductions. It is 17 percent of the service truck exam.
title: Manufacturers' Load Charts

exam: Expect short scenarios that ask whether a given machine and task fall under Subpart CC, which general-industry section applies, or who holds a duty. Watch for wording that pairs a covered machine with an excluded use, or an excluded machine with the exception that brings it back in.
hard: Coverage depends on what the machine can do and what work it is doing, not on its name, who owns it, or where the job is. The exclusion list is long, and many exclusions only apply to one use, like a mechanic's truck doing equipment repair or a gin pole erecting a communication tower. Citations nest letters and numbers, so 1926.1400(c)(9) is one specific exclusion, not the whole section.
mistakes: People pick the rule by the jobsite or the machine's label; what decides it is the type of equipment and whether the work is construction. People treat every exclusion as covering a whole type of machine; many exclusions apply only to a named use. People assume the equipment owner carries every duty; Subpart CC puts duties on the employer and on the controlling entity. People think a consensus standard is law on its own; it carries federal weight only where a rule adopts a named edition.

quotes.quote: This standard applies to power-operated equipment, when used in construction, that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load.
All sections of this subpart CC apply to the equipment covered by this standard unless specified otherwise.

summary: This part covers which federal crane rules apply to your work, what equipment they reach and leave out, and how to read a rule citation. Construction cranes fall under 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC. General industry has its own sections for overhead and gantry cranes, crawler, locomotive and truck cranes, and slings. Consensus standards like the ASME B30 volumes sit alongside the federal rules. Knowing which rule governs a job tells you who owes which duty and which limits apply.
title: The rules and who they cover

exam: Expect definition items, who-is-responsible items, and short jobsite scenarios where you pick the person who can lawfully do the task or clear the concern. Watch for answer choices that swap one defined role for another, or that slip in a requirement the rule does not have, like an annual retraining cycle or a mandatory rigging card.
hard: The defined roles sound alike. A competent person, a qualified person, a qualified rigger, a qualified evaluator and an A/D director each have their own definition. Certification, evaluation and training are three separate duties with separate records. Several numbers sit close together too: 5-year certificate terms, 3-year audits and accreditation reviews, a 180-day re-audit, and 15-minute trainee breaks.
mistakes: People treat a certification card as the whole story. The employer also has to evaluate the operator on the assigned equipment and train him. People mix up the competent person and the qualified person. Competent means spotting hazards plus having the authority to correct them; qualified means credentials or experience plus proven problem-solving. People think only the boss or the signal person can stop a lift. The operator obeys a stop signal from anyone, and he has the authority to stop for any safety concern. People assume every certificate travels with the operator. Only a certificate from an accredited testing organization is portable.

quotes.quote: General requirements for operators. The employer must ensure that each operator is trained, certified/licensed, and evaluated in accordance with this section before operating any equipment covered under subpart CC, except for the equipment listed in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.
Whenever there is a concern as to safety, the operator must have the authority to stop and refuse to handle loads until a qualified person has determined that safety has been assured.
The operator must obey a stop (or emergency stop) signal, irrespective of who gives it.

summary: This part covers who may do what around a crane: who operates, who trains and evaluates, who signals, who rigs, who directs assembly and disassembly, and who clears a safety stop. On a real job, most arguments after an incident come down to whether the right person was in the right role. Learn which job title matches which duty, because the exam tests that pairing over and over.
title: People, qualifications and authority

exam: Expect jobsite scenarios that ask which party is responsible, whether a set-up is acceptable, or what has to happen before operations begin. Some items ask for a number, such as a Table T travel clearance or a bearing pressure worked by hand. Read for words like only, before, all and except, because the answer usually depends on them.
hard: The rules split duties among several parties: the controlling entity, the operator's employer, the operator, the A/D director, and the employee walking into a hazard area. Questions turn on exactly who owes what. The exceptions are narrow and easy to stretch too far, like drainage in wetlands, J-hooks for wooden trusses, signs instead of barriers, and the few people allowed in the fall zone. The bearing-pressure math is simple, but area and unit conversions trip people up when there is no calculator.
mistakes: People think the operator has to provide the ground preparations; the controlling entity has to make sure they are provided. People think mats fix any ground; mats spread load, but the ground still has to be firm, drained and graded. People think the wetland exception relaxes everything; it removes only the drainage requirement. People think anyone working on the lift can stand in the fall zone; only the listed tasks allow it. People think the outrigger footprint marks the swing hazard; the counterweight can sweep well beyond it.

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be assembled or used unless ground conditions are firm, drained, and graded to a sufficient extent so that, in conjunction (if necessary) with the use of supporting materials, the equipment manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level of the equipment are met.
Ensure that ground preparations necessary to meet the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section are provided.
While the operator is not moving a suspended load, no employee must be within the fall zone, except for employees:

summary: This part covers everything that happens before the first pick: judging the ground, finding out what is buried under it, and knowing who has to prepare it. It also covers mats and cribbing, setting outriggers and leveling, barricading the swing radius, and keeping people out of the fall zone. Most crane tip-overs and crush injuries trace back to set-up, so this is where a lift is usually won or lost.
title: Site, ground and set-up

exam: Expect questions asking for a clearance distance by voltage, jobsite scenarios asking which option or measure meets the rule, questions about who confirms or who sets a distance, and questions about the first action after contact. Watch for the exact phrases "visibly grounded at the worksite," "maximum working radius," "working days," and "closer than."
hard: A lot of distances sit close together: the 20-foot trigger, the Table A values of 10, 15 and 20 feet, the Table T travel values of 4, 6, 10, 16 and 20 feet, the 10-foot barricade perimeter, and the 50-foot substitution over 350 kV. The other hard part is knowing who does what. The utility owner/operator confirms a line is deenergized and grounded and supplies the voltage. The utility or a qualified registered engineer sets distances over 1,000 kV and for work inside Table A. The employer is responsible for everything else.
mistakes: People apply Table A to travel; Table A is for operations, and Table T covers traveling with no load. People accept that a line is deenergized without checking for grounding; the line has to be visibly grounded at the worksite, and the utility owner/operator has to confirm it. People let an electrician, the operator or the controlling contractor confirm line status; only the utility owner/operator can. People treat a spotter as a way around choosing an option; a spotter is only one measure under Option (2) or (3). People think the operator should climb down after contact; the operator stays in the cab unless fire or another emergency forces them out.

quotes.quote: Determine if any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), if operated up to the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone, could get closer than 20 feet to a power line.

Power lines presumed energized. The employer must assume that all power lines are energized unless the utility owner/operator confirms that the power line has been and continues to be deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite.

summary: Power line contact kills crane operators and ground crews, so the federal rules lay out a fixed order of steps. You identify the work zone, check whether anything could get within 20 feet of a line, choose one of three options, and then put the encroachment measures in place. This part covers that order for operations and for assembly, plus Table A, lines over 350 kV, work closer than Table A, traveling with no load, transmitter towers, training, and what to do after contact.
title: Power lines

exam: Expect short jobsite scenarios that ask whether a signal person is required, who has to agree on signals and when, what the operator does when the radio goes quiet, and whose stop signal counts. Watch for answer choices that add a person who isn't named (supervisor, safety manager, rigger) or swap the trigger for something close but wrong.
hard: The rules sit close together and use similar wording. The trigger for a signal person is the operator's view of load travel and placement, not the boom tip or the outriggers. Two different people may stop a lift: only one person gives routine signals, but anyone may give a stop, and the operator has to obey it. Radio is a way of sending signals, not a signal type, and the agreement rules for non-standard hand signals and voice signals name slightly different groups and timing.
mistakes: People treat radio as a signal type; the types are hand, voice, audible and new, and radio is a means of transmission. People think only the assigned signal person can stop the crane; the operator has to obey a stop or emergency stop signal from anyone. People think two signalers are fine if they split functions or agree with each other; only one person gives signals at a time. People keep moving slowly when the radio cuts out; the operator has to safely stop until communication is back and a proper signal is given and understood. People think a signal person is needed whenever the boom tip is out of sight; the trigger is the point of operation, travel view, or a safety call by the operator or load handler.

quotes.quote: A signal person must be provided in each of the following situations:
Types of signals. Signals to operators must be by hand, voice, audible, or new signals.
Only one person may give signals to a crane/derrick at a time, except in circumstances covered by paragraph (j) of this section.
The operator must obey a stop (or emergency stop) signal, irrespective of who gives it.

summary: This topic covers how the operator and the signal person talk to each other: when a signal person has to be provided, the four signal types, Standard Method hand signals, voice and radio rules, and what happens when communication drops. Most crane accidents involving people on the ground come down to a missed or misread signal. On the job, every lift that isn't in full view of the operator runs on these rules.
title: Signals

exam: Expect a mix of short calculations done by hand, like beam weight, leg tension from an angle factor, D/d efficiency and net capacity after deductions, along with straight rule questions on inspection, removal criteria and who has to do the rigging. Read closely for whether an angle is measured from horizontal or vertical, which sling material is involved, and whether the question asks what the rule requires or what is good practice.
hard: Most of the trouble here comes from numbers that sit close together. The 5-degree vertical allowance, the 10-degree hook twist and the 15 percent throat opening get mixed up, and so do 10, 40 and 96 rope diameters and the 200 °F and 400 °F wire rope limits. The arithmetic also catches people: angle factors multiply the vertical share, D/d is diameter over diameter, and the CG moves toward the added weight. Some numbers are federal rules and some are industry practice, like choker reduction, D/d efficiency and the two-leg assumption, and you need to know which is which.
mistakes: People treat crane chart capacity as if it covers the rigging; every sling and fitting has its own rating, and the weakest one governs. People assume four legs share a rigid load; plan on two. People forget that the hook block and rigging count as part of the load. People apply one sling type's numbers to another, such as fiber core temperature limits to nonfiber core or braided-sling clear length to 6 × 19 slings. People think a damaged sling can be used carefully one more time; damaged slings come out of service immediately.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Each day before being used, the sling and all fastenings and attachments shall be inspected for damage or defects by a competent person designated by the employer.
Slings shall not be loaded in excess of their rated capacities.

summary: Rigging is everything between the hook and the load: the weight and center of gravity, the hitch, the sling angle, the hardware, edge protection, tag lines, and the inspection that keeps damaged gear out of service. The crane can be well within its chart and the lift can still fail at a sling, a shackle or a sharp edge. The operator stays responsible for knowing the load is within capacity, so a working grasp of rigging is part of running the crane.
title: Rigging

exam: Expect direct recall items on counts, percentages and intervals. Expect jobsite scenarios where you pick the category of a defect and what happens next. Expect short parts-of-line calculations with block weight included. Watch for the type of rope named in the stem, because it changes which number applies.
hard: There are a lot of numbers that sit close together. Broken-wire counts are different for running rope, rotation resistant rope and pendants. Running rope is counted per rope lay, but rotation resistant rope is counted over six and 30 rope diameters. The people involved also change from one inspection to the next: a competent person does the shift inspection, and a qualified person does the annual. Parts-of-line work adds arithmetic where the block weight and the rounding step are easy to get wrong.
mistakes: People use one broken-wire count for every rope; running, rotation resistant and standing ropes each have their own. People treat the maximum line pull on the hoist as the rope's rating; the lower of the two limits governs. People leave the hook block out of the parts-of-line total; the rope carries everything below the boom head. People think a qualified person does the shift inspection; it is a competent person, and the qualified person does the annual. People think a damaged rope can be spliced back to length; the rope can be cut to remove the damage, but splicing is prohibited.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: A competent person must begin a visual inspection prior to each shift the equipment is used, which must be completed before or during that shift.
Joining lengths of wire rope by splicing is prohibited.

summary: Wire rope is the part of the crane that wears out in normal use, so most of this topic is about knowing what the rope is made of, how it is reeved, how much it can carry, and when it has to come off. It covers construction and designations, rotation resistant types, reeving and parts of line, line pull, terminations, drum wraps, the shift, monthly and annual inspections, removal criteria, standing ropes and lubrication.
title: Wire rope

exam: Expect hand calculations on a small sample chart, plus rule questions on who sets ratings, where the charts are kept, front-area lifts and counterweight. Wrong options usually come from one skipped step, so when you check an answer, ask which step it left out.
hard: One chart problem stacks several steps: pick the right chart for the setup, the right area, the next longer radius and boom length, the loaded radius, and then every deduction. Skip any one step and you get a wrong answer that is usually sitting right there in the options. People also mix up gross and net capacity, and structural limits with stability limits.
mistakes: People treat gross capacity as the weight they can pick. Net capacity is gross minus the block, rigging and every other device on the hook. People interpolate or round to the nearest row. Unless a chart note says otherwise, use the next longer radius and the next longer boom length. People measure radius from the boom foot pin or an outrigger. Radius runs from the axis of rotation to the hoist line with the load on. People think a lift director or engineer can approve going past the chart. Rated capacity comes from the manufacturer, and the crane may not be run beyond it.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.
Rated capacity means the maximum working load permitted by the manufacturer under specified working conditions.

The procedures applicable to the operation of the equipment, including rated capacities (load charts), recommended operating speeds, special hazard warnings, instructions, and operator's manual, must be readily available in the cab at all times for use by the operator.

summary: The load chart tells you what the crane may lift in one specific setup, at a given boom length, radius and work area. Every lift starts with it, and most of the hand arithmetic on the core exam comes from this topic. The skills here cover chart terms, reading gross capacity, values that fall between rows and columns, deductions and net capacity, configuration and work area charts, jibs, range diagrams, parts of line, and the federal rules on rated capacity, charts in the cab and counterweight.
title: Load charts

exam: Expect jobsite scenarios asking what the operator does first, which person makes a decision, and whether a stated exception really applies. Watch for answer choices that sound careful but swap in the wrong threshold, the wrong timing or the wrong person.
hard: Many rules here turn on who is responsible: the operator, a competent person, a qualified person, or a registered professional engineer. The percentages sit close together (75 percent for weight verification, 90 percent of line pull for the brake test), and several rules have narrow exceptions with conditions that all have to be met. The physics questions reward knowing what really changes load moment and radius.
mistakes: People treat a supervisor's approval as permission to set a rule aside; most of these rules have no supervisor override. People mix up the competent person and the qualified person; each rule names one, and the exam checks which. People assume operator aids make judgment calls for them; the aids support the operator's judgment and do not replace it. People think lowering a load reduces load moment; only lowering the weight onto a support or bringing the radius in does that.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: This part covers how you run the crane once it is set up: following the manufacturer, staying within rated capacity, starting up, leaving the controls, tagging out, and handling side loads, travel, swing, dynamic loads and emergencies. Most real accidents come from operating choices made in the seat. On the exam, this is where rule knowledge meets jobsite judgment.
title: Operating the crane

exam: Expect who-is-responsible items, a wind-force multiplier you work out in your head, and jobsite scenarios about gusts, ice, storms and lightning. Watch the wording for competent versus qualified person, warning versus watch, and gust versus average wind.
hard: Three different parties show up here. The competent person adjusts for weather, the employer complies with manufacturer procedures, and a qualified person does the severe-service inspection after a possible overload or shock load. The wind physics is easy to get backward: force goes with speed squared, and wind is usually stronger at the boom tip than at the ground. The federal weather paragraph names only wind, ice and snow. Lightning and temperature are handled through the manual and accepted practice.
mistakes: People hand the weather call to the operator, signal person or controlling entity; the rule names the competent person. People think doubling the wind speed doubles the force; it gives about four times the force. People take a ground-level wind reading as the governing value; manufacturer limits usually refer to wind at or near the boom tip. People treat a broad storm watch as the trigger; the rule names a local storm warning. People wait for rain or nearby flashes before stopping for lightning; accepted practice is to stop when thunder is heard and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The competent person must adjust the equipment and/or operations to address the effect of wind, ice, and snow on equipment stability and rated capacity.
Storm warning. When a local storm warning has been issued, the competent person must determine whether it is necessary to implement manufacturer recommendations for securing the equipment.

summary: This part covers how wind, ice, snow, storms, lightning, temperature and wave action change what a crane can safely do. Weather doesn't change the numbers on the load chart, but it changes the conditions those numbers assume, so someone has to adjust the work or stop it. The federal rule puts wind, ice and snow adjustments and the storm-warning decision on the competent person. Wind limits, securing steps and cold-weather procedures come from the manufacturer.
title: Wind and weather

exam: Expect questions about who is responsible, what sets off a requirement, and what comes first on a jobsite during assembly or teardown. Read for words like immediately prior, partly or completely, in tension, and unavailable, because the right answer usually depends on them.
hard: Each duty belongs to one named person: the employer, the A/D director, a qualified person, a qualified rigger, a registered professional engineer, the operator, or the crew member. Mix them up and you miss the question. The pin rules turn on two conditions people blur: whether the pendants are in tension and how the boom is supported. Several triggers are events, not schedules, like testing the boom hoist brake each time you rely on it.
mistakes: People think the operator runs assembly; the A/D director directs it, and the director has to meet competent and qualified person criteria, alone or with qualified helpers. People think employer procedures let you ignore manufacturer prohibitions; prohibitions apply no matter which procedures you use. People think a pin can be backed out partway while pendants are loaded; no pin comes out, even partly, while the pendants are in tension. People think a test pick can stand in for the post-assembly inspection; the crane is not used until a qualified person's inspection shows it is configured to the criteria.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: When assembling or disassembling equipment (or attachments), the employer must comply with all applicable manufacturer prohibitions and must comply with either:
Assembly/disassembly must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person who is assisted by one or more qualified persons

summary: Assembly and disassembly is when a crane is at its weakest. It is partly built, often without a rated chart, and the crew is working in, on and under it. This topic covers choosing procedures, the A/D director and crew instructions, crew members out of the operator's view, staying out from under the boom when pins come out, specific hazards like blocking, center of gravity and backward stability, safe pin order, components and weights, capacity, rigging, outriggers, the post-assembly inspection, fall protection, and jibs.
title: Assembly and disassembly

exam: Expect items that ask which person does a given inspection, how often, how long the record is kept, and what a record has to contain. Scenario items describe a finding or an event, like a crack, a shock load or a crane back from storage, and ask what happens next. Watch the words competent and qualified, and watch for general industry terms dropped into a construction question.
hard: The hard part is keeping two lists straight: who does each inspection, and how long each record is kept. Shift and monthly inspections call for a competent person. Annual, post-assembly, modified, repaired, severe-service and idle-equipment inspections call for a qualified person. Monthly records are kept three months and annual records 12 months. The general industry rules use different words and intervals (frequent and periodic, one month idle), and people mix them into the construction rules.
mistakes: People treat competent person and qualified person as the same; the shift and monthly inspections name a competent person, and the annual, repair, modification, severe-service and idle inspections name a qualified person. People think the monthly record is kept until the next monthly; it is kept a minimum of three months, and the annual record a minimum of 12 months. People think operator certification makes someone the inspector; it does not by itself. People use the general industry one-month idle trigger on construction cranes; the construction rule is idle 3 months or more. People think the crane's owner or the controlling entity keeps the records; the employer that conducts the inspection does.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: A competent person must begin a visual inspection prior to each shift the equipment will be used, which must be completed before or during that shift.
This document must be retained for a minimum of three months.
In addition, at least every 12 months, the equipment must be inspected by a qualified person.
Upon completion of assembly, the equipment must be inspected by a qualified person to assure that it is configured in accordance with manufacturer equipment criteria.
Equipment that has been idle for 3 months or more must be inspected by a qualified person in accordance with the requirements of paragraph (e) (Monthly) of this section before initial use.

summary: This part covers every inspection a mobile crane goes through: shift, monthly, annual/comprehensive, post-assembly, after modifications or repairs, after severe service, and before use after sitting idle. For each one you need to know who does it, what it covers, and what gets written down. On the job, these inspections decide whether the crane runs today or gets tagged out.
title: Inspections

exam: Expect scenario items where a device fails and you pick the correct response, plus number items on repair days, capacity thresholds and manufacture dates. Read whether the device named is a safety device or an operational aid, and whether the crane is telescopic, lattice or articulating, before you look at the options.
hard: The hard part is keeping three groups apart: safety devices get no alternative measures and no repair window, Category I aids get temporary measures and 7 calendar days, and Category II aids get temporary measures and 30 calendar days. The manufacture dates are close and easy to swap, and the anti-two-block temporary measures differ by crane type by one word, and versus or. Exceptions are narrow and attach to one device only, so an exemption from one rule does not carry over to another.
mistakes: People treat a horn or level indicator like an operational aid and look for a temporary measure; safety devices allow no alternative measures. People swap the repair windows; Category I is 7 calendar days and Category II is 30 calendar days. People count working days or start the clock at the report; the clock runs in calendar days from when the deficiency occurs. People use the lattice boom mark-or-spotter measure on a telescopic crane; a telescopic crane needs the cable mark and a spotter when extending. People think an LMI replaces the boom angle or length indicator; each listed aid is its own requirement.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Alternative measures are not permitted to be used.
Operational aids listed in this paragraph that are not working properly must be repaired no later than 7 calendar days after the deficiency occurs.
Operational aids listed in this paragraph that are not working properly must be repaired no later than 30 calendar days after the deficiency occurs.

If a listed operational aid stops working properly during operations, the operator must safely stop operations until the temporary alternative measures are implemented or the device is again working properly.

summary: This part covers the devices that keep a crane inside its limits: the safety devices that must work before you run the crane, and the operational aids that warn you or take control of a function. You will learn which devices fall in which group, what you can do if one fails, how long the employer has to repair it, and how anti-two-block systems and load moment indicators work. On the job this decides whether you lift today, lift with a temporary measure, or park the crane.
title: Safety devices and operational aids

exam: Expect number-recall items where the wrong options are nearby values, short jobsite scenarios asking whether a step has to be repeated, and simple subtraction against half the chart capacity. Read for who is responsible (employer, qualified person, competent person or operator) and for trigger words like each shift, each jobsite and each new location.
hard: Many numbers sit close together. The crane is within one percent of level and the platform within 10 degrees of level. Platform and hardware are rated at five times, rotation resistant rope slings at ten times. The proof test is 125 percent with a five-minute hold, and the total load is 50 percent of rated capacity. The triggers are the other hard part: the trial lift comes before each shift, the proof test at each jobsite, and the pre-lift meeting at each new work location and for each newly assigned employee. Duties are also split between the employer, the qualified person and the competent person.
mistakes: People apply the 50 percent limit to the platform's rating. It applies to the crane's rated capacity for the radius and configuration, and the platform separately stays within its own rated capacity. People leave the hook, load line and rigging out of the total load, but they count. People mix up the trial lift and the proof test. The trial lift uses the unoccupied platform loaded to the anticipated liftweight; the proof test loads to 125 percent of the platform's rated capacity and holds five minutes. People accept cost or schedule as a reason to hoist workers. Only a showing that conventional access would be more hazardous or is not possible justifies it. People think the pre-lift meeting is held every shift. It is tied to each new work location and to newly assigned employees.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The use of equipment to hoist employees is prohibited except where the employer demonstrates that the erection, use, and dismantling of conventional means of reaching the work area, such as a personnel hoist, ladder, stairway, aerial lift, elevating work platform, or scaffold, would be more hazardous, or is not possible because of the project's structural design or worksite conditions.

Capacity: Use of suspended personnel platforms. The total load (with the platform loaded, including the hook, load line and rigging) must not exceed 50 percent of the rated capacity for the radius and configuration of the equipment, except during proof testing.
The trial lift must be performed immediately prior to each shift in which personnel will be hoisted.

At each jobsite, prior to hoisting employees on the personnel platform, and after any repair or modification, the platform and rigging must be proof tested to 125 percent of the platform's rated capacity.
Held prior to the trial lift at each new work location, and must be repeated for any employees newly assigned to the operation.

summary: Hoisting people with a crane is a last-resort operation. It has its own layer of rules on top of everything else in the crane standard. This part covers when it is allowed, crane setup and devices, platform and rigging criteria, the 50 percent capacity limit, the trial lift, the proof test, the pre-lift meeting, work practices, and the special cases such as drill shafts, pile driving and marine transfer. A missed step here puts people on the hook, not material.
title: Hoisting personnel

exam: Expect jobsite scenarios that ask who is responsible, what comes first, or whether a condition triggers a requirement, plus at least one load-share or chart calculation done by hand. Watch for answer choices that add a percentage, a job title or an exception the rule doesn't contain.
hard: The federal rules have a clear multiple-crane rule, but they don't define "critical lift." That label and its triggers come from company and project programs. People also mix up who plans, who directs and who attends the meeting, and they blur the fall zone with the space directly under the load.
mistakes: People think the federal rules define a critical lift; they don't, and the term comes from industry and company practice. People think a multiple-crane plan always needs an engineer; the qualified person decides whether engineering expertise is needed. People think the plan can come after a trial pick; planning comes before the operation begins. People think an essential worker may stand under a tilting panel; essential status opens the fall zone only, never the space directly under the load.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Plan development. Before beginning a crane/derrick operation in which more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load, the operation must be planned. The planning must meet the following requirements:

The multiple-crane/derrick lift must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person who is assisted by one or more qualified persons (lift director).
No employee must be directly under the load.

summary: This part covers lifts that need more than routine care. You'll work through the steps of an ordinary lift plan (weight, center of gravity, radius, chart, rigging, ground, clearances, people), the federal rule for lifts where more than one crane supports the load, how industry practice identifies and plans a critical lift, and how to keep people clear during tilt-up and tilt-down work. Most lifts that go wrong started with a wrong weight, a wrong radius, or a plan nobody explained to the crew.
title: Lift planning, critical and multiple-crane lifts

exam: Expect number items (walkway width, railing height, height triggers) and jobsite scenarios asking whether protection is required for a given boom type and task. Watch for "more than" versus "or more," lattice versus non-lattice, horizontal versus not, and which person (competent, qualified, operator, employer) holds a duty.
hard: The heights sit close together and the wording matters: more than 6 feet for general non-assembly work, 15 feet or more for walking a horizontal lattice boom, and more than 15 feet for assembly and disassembly. The walkway rule has its own numbers, a 12-inch minimum width and a 45-inch maximum railing height, and railings are not required at all. Anchorage rules split by system type and by person, with a competent person for apparently substantial parts and a qualified person for load-line tie-off.
mistakes: People think boom walkways need guardrails like a construction platform; railings are not required, and removable ones are prohibited. People use 6 feet for every boom; walking a horizontal lattice boom triggers protection at 15 feet or more. People think the hook is never a legal anchor; it is permitted when a qualified person has made the capacity determination, the operator is on site and informed, and no load is suspended. People believe only harnesses are allowed; the crane rule permits body belts or body harnesses. People assume the operator owns the training duty; the employer trains exposed employees.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The walkways must be at least 12 inches wide.

For non-assembly/disassembly work, the employer must provide and ensure the use of fall protection equipment for employees who are on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge more than 6 feet above a lower level as follows:
No load is suspended from the load line when the personal fall arrest system is anchored to the crane/derrick's hook (or other part of the load line).

summary: This part covers how people get on, off and around a crane without falling: boom walkways, steps and handholds, when fall protection is required, what you can anchor to, and the narrow conditions for tying off to the hook or load line. Most crane fall injuries happen during routine work like walking a boom or reaching a sheave, not during the lift. Knowing the triggers and who decides what keeps you and your crew off the ground the hard way.
title: Access, egress and fall protection

exam: Expect definition items, short scenarios about which device does what, and simple calculations like force from pressure and area or a load moment about the tipping axis. Read the wording closely for which crane type, which device, or which time limit the question names, because the wrong options are usually a neighboring term or number.
hard: Many terms sound alike but mean different things: boom stop versus boom hoist limiting device, jib stop versus luffing jib limiting device, pendants versus running rope, radius versus distance to the tipping axis. The numbers in this area sit close together, like 7 and 30 calendar days for repairs, or 30 and 120 days for modification requests. The stability ideas are hard because the crane tips about its outer supports, not about the center of rotation where radius is measured.
mistakes: People measure the load's lever arm from the center of rotation; for tipping it is measured from the tipping axis. People treat a boom stop and a boom hoist limiting device as the same thing; one is a physical stop against going over backward, the other cuts boom hoist power. People think a pressure relief valve holds a load; holding is the job of a check or holding valve. People assume any engineer or inspector can approve a crane modification; the rule sets a specific approval path that starts with the manufacturer.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: This part covers the machine itself: which crane types are which, what each component is called and does, how booms, jibs and extensions work, how hook blocks and hydraulics hold a load, how the operator's instruments warn you, and what the design rules and modification rules say. It also covers the physics of tipping: load moment, the tipping axis and backward stability. You need this to read a load chart correctly and to know when a crane is set up and equipped the way it was designed.
title: Crane types, components and design

exam: The core exam outline points to federal regulations, including 1910.180 and Subpart CC, and to specialty work such as barge operations, so floating cranes and general industry mobile cranes matter most here. Expect a number, or a scenario that asks which rule or limit applies. The other equipment types in this part are background, but their numbers make good distractors.
hard: The numbers sit close together across equipment types: wraps on the drum, list and trim degrees, wind speeds, manufacture cutoff dates, inspection intervals. The hard part is keeping each number tied to the right machine and the right condition. Many items also hinge on whether equipment is permanently installed or temporary, and whether it is a crane or a derrick.
mistakes: People assume the land mobile crane rules carry over unchanged to barges, tower cranes and derricks; each type has supplemental rules that change specific requirements. People mix general industry rules with construction rules; which one applies depends on the work and how the equipment is installed. People treat manufacture dates and installation dates as the same thing; the cutoffs are tied to when the equipment was made. People borrow a number from one equipment type for another, such as a derrick list limit for a crane on a barge.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: This part covers the supplemental rules for equipment other than the standard mobile crane setup: overhead and gantry cranes, crawler, locomotive and truck cranes in general industry, tower cranes, derricks, floating cranes and barges, sideboom cranes, small cranes, pile drivers and articulating cranes. Each type has its own numbers and its own exceptions to the general rules. Mobile operators run into these when they work in plants, on barges, or beside tower cranes and derricks.
title: Overhead, gantry, tower cranes, derricks and other equipment

exam: Items usually describe a machine and a task and ask whether Subpart CC applies, or offer a made-up condition as a reason it does not. Read for the three capabilities and construction use, and distrust answer options that add conditions such as ownership, location, boom type or load material.
hard: The list is examples, not a closed list, and the words in each item are the only conditions. A monorail crane has no rail-count, height or permanence condition. A service truck only needs a hoisting device, not hoisting as its main job. People also forget that attachments like augers, magnets and personnel platforms keep the equipment inside Subpart CC rather than moving it into some other rule.
mistakes: People think a service/mechanic truck is covered only if hoisting is its primary purpose, has a telescoping boom, or lifts steel; the listing just says a truck with a hoisting device. People think a monorail crane needs two rails, a ground track or a temporary rail; the rule simply names a crane on a monorail. People think attachments must hang from the load line, or must connect directly to the crane, or fall under their own separate scope; the rule covers equipment used with attachments whether crane-attached or suspended. People think the word industrial, indoor work, or rental status takes a carry-deck crane out of scope; it is expressly listed and is covered when doing construction work.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: This standard applies to power-operated equipment, when used in construction, that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load.
industrial cranes (such as carry-deck cranes); dedicated pile drivers; service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device; a crane on a monorail;

Such attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended include, but are not limited to: Hooks, magnets, grapples, clamshell buckets, orange peel buckets, concrete buckets, drag lines, personnel platforms, augers or drills and pile driving equipment.

summary: Subpart CC covers power-operated equipment used in construction that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load. The rule lists examples: mobile cranes of every kind, crawlers, articulating cranes, industrial and carry-deck cranes, service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device, a crane on a monorail, tower cranes, derricks, and more. It also covers that equipment when used with attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended. If the machine can do the three things and the work is construction, start from the position that it is covered.
title: Know what equipment Subpart CC covers

exam: Expect scenarios that sound like an exclusion but miss one word, such as the type of tower, the purpose of the truck work, or the hoisting method. Match each fact against the exact wording of the exclusion before choosing excluded.
hard: The use-based exclusions are narrow and the exam tests the edge. A gin pole on a wind turbine or water tank tower is not erecting a communication tower. A mechanic's truck setting a new pump or delivering material is not doing equipment repair. The hoisting exclusion names only a come-a-long or chainfall, so a powered winch or wire-rope drum does not qualify. The knuckle-boom delivery exclusion is lost when the crane holds material for attachment or handles prefabricated components or structural steel.
mistakes: People stretch the gin-pole exclusion to any tower; it names communication towers only, and the digger-derrick utility exclusion does not widen it. People treat installing new equipment, delivering material, or building a maintenance shop as maintenance work; the mechanic's-truck exclusion needs actual equipment maintenance or repair. People think any hoist mechanism counts; only a come-a-long or chainfall is named, not a hydraulic, electric or drum winch. People think an excavator becomes covered once it lifts a suspended load on slings; it stays excluded, with no bucket-contact or no-swing condition. People mix up the excavator exclusion with the forklift exclusion, which does have an exception for a hook or winch configuration.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Power shovels, excavators, wheel loaders, backhoes, loader backhoes, track loaders. This machinery is also excluded when used with chains, slings or other rigging to lift suspended loads.
Mechanic's truck with a hoisting device when used in activities related to equipment maintenance and repair.
Machinery that hoists by using a come-a-long or chainfall.
Gin poles when used for the erection of communication towers.
The material being handled by the articulating/knuckle-boom crane is a prefabricated component.

summary: Subpart CC lists machines and uses it does not cover. hard: The numbers sit close together. Certificates run 5 years. The testing organization's accreditation is reviewed at least every 3 years. An audited employer program is audited within 3 months of its start and at least every 3 years after that. If an audit finds a deficiency, the program is audited again within 180 days of the confirmation that it was fixed. Portability belongs only to the accredited-organization certificate, even though both certificate types run the same 5 years.
mistakes: People give operator certification a 1-year or 10-year term. Accredited and audited-program certificates are both valid for 5 years, and one year is the annual crane inspection interval. People borrow the 3-year number for the certificate. Three years is the accreditation review and the employer program re-audit interval. People think an audited program is re-audited every year or every 5 years. It is audited within 3 months of the start and at least every 3 years after. People think the 180-day window is a routine audit cycle. It applies only to the re-audit after a deficiency has been corrected. People assume every certificate is portable or that an auditor can transfer one.
