hard: The order is the hard part. The operator stops first, and the qualified person's determination comes afterward, before work resumes. The person who clears the concern is a qualified person, not whoever outranks the operator, not the controlling entity, and not a competent person by title. The authority covers any safety concern, not only overloads or wind.
mistakes: People think a superintendent, the controlling entity or a supervisor's written sign-off can clear the stop. The restart depends on a qualified person determining that safety has been assured. People swap in the competent person. This rule names a qualified person. People think stop signals, like directional signals, come only from the designated signal person or lift supervisors. A stop is obeyed from anyone, and no signal qualification is needed to give one. People limit the authority to overloads or high wind. Any safety concern counts. People think the operator needs a qualified person's approval before stopping. He stops first; the qualified person comes in afterward. People think lifting slowly over doubtful ground offsets the hazard. The operator can refuse the pick until the concern is resolved.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Whenever there is a concern as to safety, the operator must have the authority to stop and refuse to handle loads until a qualified person has determined that safety has been assured.
The operator must obey a stop (or emergency stop) signal, irrespective of who gives it.

summary: Whenever there is a concern about safety, the operator has the authority to stop and refuse to handle loads until a qualified person has determined that safety has been assured. Separately, the operator obeys a stop or emergency stop signal no matter who gives it. These two rules let the person at the controls stop first and sort it out after.
title: Apply the operator's authority and duty to stop

exam: Expect crew-composition scenarios asking whether a given arrangement can lawfully direct assembly or disassembly, and items asking whether a task like shortening a boom counts as disassembly. Read carefully for which person is competent and which is qualified; the answer often hinges on the direction of the assist.
hard: The competent person role cannot be dropped from the director. A qualified person helped by competent persons does not fit; it has to be the other way around. Disassembly includes partial dismantling, such as shortening a boom or substituting a component in the middle of a job. Operator certification and qualified rigger status are not the test for directing A/D.
mistakes: People reverse the roles and let a qualified person direct with competent persons helping. The director must be a competent person, assisted by qualified persons if he is not qualified himself. People think operator certification or qualified rigger status makes someone an A/D director. Neither one supplies the competent person criteria. People think a solo worker only needs to be qualified, or can use the assisted arrangement. Working alone, he has to meet both criteria himself. People think the director has to be a manager, hold a certain title, or have management countersign. The definition applies regardless of job title or management status. People think shortening a boom is routine reconfiguration, that only full teardown counts, or that using an assist crane decides it. Partial dismantling is disassembly, and it is defined by what is done to the crane.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Assembly/disassembly must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person who is assisted by one or more qualified persons (“A/D director”).

Where the assembly/disassembly is being performed by only one person, that person must meet the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. For purposes of this standard, that person is considered the A/D director.

A/D director (Assembly/Disassembly director) means an individual who meets this subpart's requirements for an A/D director, irrespective of the person's formal job title or whether the person is non-management or management personnel.
Dismantling includes partial dismantling (such as dismantling to shorten a boom or substitute a different component).

summary: Assembly and disassembly is directed by an A/D director. That is either one person who meets both the competent person and the qualified person criteria, or a competent person assisted by one or more qualified persons. If one person does the whole job alone, he has to meet both sets of criteria and is the A/D director. Job title and management status do not matter.
title: Know the A/D director's role

exam: Expect scenarios with a mechanic or inspector at the controls, asking whether the operation is allowed and under what condition. Watch for choices that require both routes together, or that name a supervisor who is not a qualifying operator.
hard: The two conditions are alternatives, not a pair; either one is enough. The familiarity route needs all four areas, operation, limitations, characteristics and hazards, for the equipment type, not just control layout or service history. Operation is limited to maintenance, inspection and verification functions, so production lifts are out. The qualified person requirement is about the repair work itself.
mistakes: People think a senior mechanic, an experienced inspector or the site superintendent can provide the direct supervision. The supervisor must be an operator who meets the operator qualification and certification requirements. People think knowing inspection paperwork, site orientation, or control layout and service history counts as equipment familiarity. Familiarity covers the operation, limitations, characteristics and hazards of the equipment type. People think direct supervision and familiarity are both required. Either one satisfies that condition. People think every inspector moving controls needs his own operator certification or site-supervisor approval. The familiarity route does not add those conditions. People think production-lift skill or knowing service intervals makes a mechanic qualified for repair work. He has to be a qualified person for the equipment and the repair tasks.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Maintenance, inspection and repair personnel are permitted to operate the equipment only where all of the following requirements are met:
The operation is limited to those functions necessary to perform maintenance, inspect the equipment, or verify its performance.
Operate the equipment under the direct supervision of an operator who meets the requirements of § 1926.1427 (Operator qualification and certification); or
Are familiar with the operation, limitations, characteristics and hazards associated with the type of equipment.
Maintenance and repair personnel must meet the definition of a qualified person with respect to the equipment and maintenance/repair tasks performed.

summary: Maintenance, inspection and repair personnel may operate the crane only for the functions needed to maintain it, inspect it or verify its performance. They also have to meet one of two conditions: work under the direct supervision of an operator who meets the operator qualification and certification section, or be familiar with the operation, limitations, characteristics and hazards of that type of equipment. Separately, maintenance and repair personnel must meet the qualified person definition for the equipment and the tasks they perform.
title: Know when maintenance and inspection personnel may operate

exam: Expect scenarios with a candidate who tests in another language or asks for verbal testing, asking what is allowed and what must be recorded. Watch for choices that swap the jobsite or employer language for the test language, or that replace the written literacy demonstration with something oral or practical.
hard: Verbal testing still depends on a written literacy demonstration, and an oral vocabulary check, a practical run or an employer's statement does not stand in for it. The manufacturer-procedures demonstration is tied to the class or type being sought, not the whole fleet and not to whatever machine he has run before. The language recorded is the language the test was actually given in, not the jobsite language or the candidate's first language.
mistakes: People think an oral vocabulary test, an operating demonstration or an employer's word covers the literacy piece. Verbal testing requires the candidate to pass a written demonstration of literacy relevant to the work. People tie the procedures demonstration to past experience, the employer's whole fleet, or machines with similar controls. It applies to the class or type of equipment for which he is seeking certification. People think the test has to be in English because the jobsite uses English, or in the candidate's native language. It may be in any language the candidate understands. People think recording the test language is optional, or that the employer's language goes on the documentation. The documentation has to note the language the test was given in. People forget the follow-on limit. The operator may run only equipment whose required manuals and load charts are in the language of the certification.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Tests under this section may be administered verbally, with answers given verbally, where the operator candidate:
Passes a written demonstration of literacy relevant to the work.
Demonstrates the ability to use the type of written manufacturer procedures applicable to the class/type of equipment for which the candidate is seeking certification.

Tests under this section may be administered in any language the operator candidate understands, and the operator's certification documentation must note the language in which the test was given. The operator is only permitted to operate equipment that is furnished with materials required by this subpart, such as operations manuals and load charts, that are written in the language of the certification.

summary: Operator tests may be given verbally, with verbal answers, if the candidate passes a written demonstration of literacy relevant to the work and shows he can use the type of written manufacturer procedures that apply to the class or type of equipment he is seeking certification for. Tests may be given in any language the candidate understands, and the certification documentation has to note the language of the test. The operator may then run only equipment whose required materials, such as operations manuals and load charts, are in the language of the certification.
title: Apply the language and literacy provisions

exam: Items ask which three words are in the definition, what the wetland exception covers, or whose specs set the standard. Scenarios give wet, soft or sloped ground and ask whether assembly can go ahead. Watch for answer choices that swap the definition's words with the operating rule's words.
hard: Two lists sit close together. The definition says slope, compaction and firmness, and the operating rule says firm, drained and graded. The benchmark is the manufacturer's specs for support and level, not an engineer's, a qualified person's or the controlling entity's opinion. The wetland exception removes drainage only, so grading, support and level still apply.
mistakes: People put drainage into the definition; the definition lists slope, compaction and firmness, and drainage comes from the operating rule. People add moisture or soil type to the definition; those affect support but are not the named factors. People think the wetland exception waives grading or the level spec; only drainage is waived. People think the rule covers only lifting; it says the crane cannot be assembled or used until the ground meets it. People think mats or close monitoring make up for bad ground; mats don't drain water, and the ground has to meet the requirement before assembly starts. People name an engineer or the controlling entity as the benchmark; the benchmark is the manufacturer's specs for support and degree of level.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: “Ground conditions” means the ability of the ground to support the equipment (including slope, compaction, and firmness).

The equipment must not be assembled or used unless ground conditions are firm, drained, and graded to a sufficient extent so that, in conjunction (if necessary) with the use of supporting materials, the equipment manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level of the equipment are met.
The requirement for the ground to be drained does not apply to marshes/wetlands.

summary: Ground conditions means how well the ground can support the crane, and the definition names slope, compaction and firmness. The operating rule says the crane cannot be assembled or used until the ground is firm, drained and graded well enough to meet the manufacturer's specs for support and level, with supporting materials if needed. Getting this wrong is how outriggers punch through and cranes go over.
title: Judge ground conditions as firm, drained and graded

exam: Expect scenarios where the operator spots a manhole, fresh fill or a buried tank and the question asks what happens next or who has to talk to whom. Some items ask for a utility color or whether a mat makes a spot over a void acceptable. Watch for the A/D director variation, where the A/D director's employer has the discussion instead.
hard: A solid-looking slab or a paved lot tells you nothing about a tank or void under it. A traffic rating covers spread-out wheel loads, not one outrigger carrying a large share of the crane and load. The duty to have the discussion falls on the employer of whoever made the finding, not on that person, and the other party is always the controlling entity. Utility paint colors come from the industry marking code, not from the crane rule.
mistakes: People put the discussion duty on the operator personally or on a competent person; it falls on the operator's employer, and the discussion is held with the controlling entity. People bring the manufacturer into it; the rule pairs the employer of the person who made the finding with the controlling entity. People think derating, a waiver or soil testing fixes inadequate ground; the rule calls for discussing ground preparations, with supporting materials if needed, until the ground meets the requirement. People think a mat can bridge a buried tank; a mat spreads load over only a few feet, and the tank top still carries the concentrated load. People mix up the marking colors; under the common industry code, red is electric, yellow is gas and oil, orange is communications, and green is sewer and storm drain.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Inform the user of the equipment and the operator of the location of hazards beneath the equipment set-up area (such as voids, tanks, utilities)

If the A/D director or the operator determines that ground conditions do not meet the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section, that person's employer must have a discussion with the controlling entity regarding the ground preparations that are needed so that, with the use of suitable supporting materials/devices (if necessary), the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section can be met.

summary: What you can't see is what drops a crane: voids, septic and fuel tanks, vaults, utility lines, old trenches and loose fill. The controlling entity has to tell the crane user and the operator about hazards beneath the set-up area that show up in its documents or that it otherwise knows about. If the operator or A/D director finds the ground isn't adequate, that person's employer has to discuss the needed ground preparations with the controlling entity.
title: Identify voids, tanks, utilities and loose fill

exam: Most items here ask who is responsible, often with several plausible employers in the answer choices. Others ask who has to be informed, or what happens when there is no controlling entity. Look for the phrase about authority at the site to make or arrange ground preparations.
hard: The test is authority over the site, not who owns the crane, employs the operator or owns the property. The disclosure goes to two named parties, the equipment user and the operator, not to the riggers or the signal person. It covers documents held at the site or off-site and hazards known some other way, and it does not wait for anyone to ask.
mistakes: People think the operator or the A/D director has to provide ground preparations; they can find the ground inadequate, but the controlling entity has to make sure preparations are provided. People assume the crane owner, the operator's employer or the property owner has the duty; it follows control of the site, or authority to make or arrange ground preparations when there is no controlling entity. People name the signal person, riggers or crane owner as the parties to be told; the rule names the equipment user and the operator. People think only documents kept on site count; the rule covers documents at the site or off-site. People think disclosure happens only on request; it is the controlling entity's own duty.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Ensure that ground preparations necessary to meet the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section are provided.

Inform the user of the equipment and the operator of the location of hazards beneath the equipment set-up area (such as voids, tanks, utilities) if those hazards are identified in documents (such as site drawings, as-built drawings, and soil analyses) that are in the possession of the controlling entity (whether at the site or off-site) or the hazards are otherwise known to that controlling entity.

If there is no controlling entity for the project, the requirement in paragraph (c)(1) of this section must be met by the employer that has authority at the site to make or arrange for ground preparations needed to meet paragraph (b) of this section.

Controlling entity means an employer that is a prime contractor, general contractor, construction manager or any other legal entity which has the overall responsibility for the construction of the project—its planning, quality and completion.

summary: The controlling entity is the prime contractor, general contractor, construction manager or other party with overall responsibility for the project. It has to make sure the ground preparations are provided, and it has to tell the equipment user and the operator about known hazards beneath the set-up area. If there is no controlling entity, the preparation duty falls on the employer with authority at the site to make or arrange ground preparations.
title: Know who must ensure and disclose ground conditions

exam: Items ask which item counts as a supporting material, where blocking can be placed, or what pressure results when a mat goes under a float. The calculations use round numbers you can work by hand. Check whether the stem gives the float area or the mat area, and use the one the load actually spreads over.
hard: Supporting materials work together with ground that is already firm, drained and graded. They don't replace any of those conditions. Crane parts like outrigger beams and counterweight aren't supporting materials, and compacted gravel is ground preparation, not a supporting material. The mat math depends on using the full contact area of the mat, not the float and not one side length.
mistakes: People count compacted gravel, outrigger beams or counterweight as supporting materials; supporting materials are separate items placed between the crane and the ground. People think mats take the place of drainage or that light loads or an engineered mat plan exempt the ground rule; the only drainage exception is marshes and wetlands, and there is no light-load exception. People swap in moisture, frost, soil type or bearing load for the definition's factors; the definition names slope, compaction and firmness. With 40,000 pounds on an 8-by-5-foot mat, people divide by 8, by the 4-square-foot float, or by half the mat; the load spreads over the full 40 square feet, which gives 1,000 pounds per square foot.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: “Supporting materials” means blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies (in marshes/wetlands), or similar supporting materials or devices.

Be placed only under the outrigger or stabilizer float/pad of the jack or, where the outrigger or stabilizer is designed without a jack, under the outer bearing surface of the extended outrigger or stabilizer beam.
Blocking (also referred to as “cribbing”) is wood or other material used to support equipment or a component and distribute loads to the ground.
The requirement for the ground to be drained does not apply to marshes/wetlands.

summary: Supporting materials are what go between the crane and the ground: blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies in wetlands, and similar devices. They spread the outrigger or track load over more area so the ground pressure drops. Outrigger blocking goes only under the float or pad, or under the outer bearing surface of the beam when there is no jack.
title: Use mats, blocking and cribbing correctly

exam: Expect a no-calculator problem: an outrigger load and a float or mat size, asking for pressure or the effect of a bigger mat. Wrong answers come from dividing by a side, using the wrong conversion, or multiplying. Write the area out first, then divide.
hard: Area is length times width, so doubling one side halves the pressure, and doubling both sides cuts it to one quarter. Square inches convert to square feet by 144, not 12 or 1,728. The total load doesn't change when you add a mat; only the pressure does. Questions about wetland ground sometimes slip in here, and only drainage is exempted.
mistakes: People divide by one side length or by the perimeter; 40,000 pounds on a 2-by-2-foot float is 40,000 divided by 4 square feet, or 10,000 pounds per square foot. People multiply load by area; pressure is load divided by area. People convert square inches with 12, 9 or 1,728; one square foot is 144 square inches. People think doubling both sides halves the pressure, or they count the change twice; the area goes up four times, so the pressure drops to one quarter. People think the same load on a bigger mat still has the same pressure; the force is the same, but the pressure falls. People think wetland ground is excused from firmness, grading or the level spec; only drainage is exempted, so support and level still have to meet the manufacturer's specs.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be assembled or used unless ground conditions are firm, drained, and graded to a sufficient extent so that, in conjunction (if necessary) with the use of supporting materials, the equipment manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level of the equipment are met.
The requirement for the ground to be drained does not apply to marshes/wetlands.

summary: Ground bearing pressure is the outrigger load divided by the contact area: pounds divided by square feet gives pounds per square foot. You compare it with what the ground can safely carry, and if it's too high, you add mat area until it isn't. This is physics plus arithmetic, worked by hand on the exam.
title: Compute outrigger ground bearing pressure (force over area)

exam: Scenarios describe a set-up, such as one beam at mid-extension, tires still loaded or a loose float, and ask whether it complies. Some items ask which component meets the holding-valve requirement. Watch for answers that sound like good engineering but skip the manufacturer's permission.
hard: Partial extension is allowed only when the manufacturer permits it and the load chart specifies it. A proportional derate or a qualified person's approval doesn't authorize it. Taking the weight off the wheels means all the wheels, not just the drive axle, and equal jack pressures don't prove it. The holding-valve requirement is about the jack itself, not about relief valves, gauges or shutoffs somewhere else in the circuit.
mistakes: People think a main relief valve, a pump-outlet shutoff or a pressure gauge meets the jack requirement; the jack has to have an integral holding device or check valve. People think a heavy float centered under the jack is good enough, or that floats need attaching only on slopes or with a load on the hook; floats have to be attached whenever they are used. People think a derate, a qualified person's approval or a tire-supported rating authorizes partial extension; it has to be permitted by the manufacturer's procedures and specified in the load chart. People think equal jack pressures or a derate allow the wheels to share the load, or that only the drive wheels must come up; the outriggers have to remove the equipment weight from the wheels.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The outriggers or stabilizers must be either fully extended or, if manufacturer procedures permit, deployed as specified in the load chart.

The outriggers must be set to remove the equipment weight from the wheels, except for locomotive cranes (see paragraph (q)(6) of this section for use of outriggers on locomotive cranes). This provision does not apply to stabilizers.
When outrigger floats are used, they must be attached to the outriggers. When stabilizer floats are used, they must be attached to the stabilizers.
Each outrigger or stabilizer must be visible to the operator or to a signal person during extension and setting.
Hydraulic outrigger jacks and hydraulic stabilizer jacks must have an integral holding device/check valve.

summary: When the load and radius call for outriggers, or any time you use them, they have to be fully extended, or set as specified in the load chart if the manufacturer's procedures permit. The outriggers have to take the crane's weight off the wheels, floats have to be attached, and each outrigger has to be visible to the operator or a signal person while it's extended and set. Hydraulic jacks need an integral holding device or check valve so they can't drift down under load.
title: Deploy outriggers and stabilizers per the manufacturer

exam: Items ask what the sensor measures, who does the temporary verification, and when. Expect answer choices that put the check after a trial lift or give it to another person. The word before carries the timing question.
hard: The sensor measures horizontal beam extension, not jack stroke, swing position or carrier level. The temporary duty belongs to the operator, not the inspector, the signal person or the controlling entity. The timing is before operations that need the outriggers begin, and a trial lift or first swing is already one of those operations.
mistakes: People confuse beam extension with vertical jack extension, upper rotation or carrier level; the requirement is horizontal beam extension. People hand the temporary verification to an inspector, a signal person or the controlling entity; it is the operator's duty. People think equal extension on all corners or full extension proves the set-up; the positions have to be correct under the manufacturer's procedures. People think stabilizers are exempt; the requirement names both outriggers and stabilizers. People verify after a trial lift, at the first swing or after a successful pick; verification comes before operations that need the outriggers begin.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Outrigger/stabilizer position (horizontal beam extension) sensor/monitor if the equipment has outriggers or stabilizers. Temporary alternative measures: The operator must verify that the position of the outriggers or stabilizers is correct (in accordance with manufacturer procedures) before beginning operations requiring outrigger or stabilizer deployment.

summary: Cranes with outriggers or stabilizers need a position sensor or monitor for horizontal beam extension. That matters because the load chart you read depends on how far the beams are out. If the sensor isn't working, the temporary alternative is that the operator verifies the positions are correct under the manufacturer's procedures before beginning any operation that requires the outriggers.
title: Know outrigger position sensor requirements

exam: Scenarios give a broken or missing level indicator, a crawler on mats, or a crane on a barge, and ask what is required. Others ask why being out of level reduces capacity. Watch the built-in versus removable wording.
hard: The two kinds of indicator are handled differently. A faulty built-in indicator is tagged out or removed, and a faulty removable one is removed. The only exemptions are portal cranes, derricks, floating cranes and land cranes on barges or other flotation. Mats, rough ground, slopes and truck carriers don't create an exemption.
mistakes: People tag out a faulty removable indicator; tagging out is an option only for a built-in one, and a removable one has to come off. People write up the defect and keep using the indicator, or wait for the next inspection; the faulty device has to be taken out of use now. People think mats count as flotation or that poor ground or a truck crane is exempt; land cranes need the indicator, and a slope makes it matter more. People think a lift director's hand level, a one-time survey or an inspection takes the place of the indicator; it has to be built into or available on the crane. People apply a mental correction for a faulty reading; that isn't allowed, and the error may not stay constant. People read capacity at the planned radius; read it at the actual radius where the load ends up.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must have a crane level indicator that is either built into the equipment or is available on the equipment.
If a built-in crane level indicator is not working properly, it must be tagged-out or removed. If a removable crane level indicator is not working properly, it must be removed.
This requirement does not apply to portal cranes, derricks, floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges, pontoons, vessels or other means of flotation.

summary: Load charts assume a level crane. Even a small tilt swings the load out past the charted radius when it hangs to the low side, and it puts side load on the boom, which cuts real capacity. The crane has to have a level indicator, either built in or available on the equipment, and a faulty one has to come out of service. Level can change during the shift as the ground settles, so you recheck it.
title: Level the crane and know why level matters

exam: Expect a jobsite description asking where barriers go, who has to tell the operator, or when the sign alternative is allowed. Items may give a counterweight tail swing that reaches past the outriggers. Look for the word both in the infeasibility exception.
hard: The barricade follows the counterweight's sweep, which often reaches past the outrigger and carrier footprint. The sign-and-marking alternative applies only when barriers are infeasible both on the ground and on the equipment. The duty to tell the operator belongs to the employee going in, who can ask someone else to relay it. Supervisory titles don't change that.
mistakes: People think only operators, signal persons or riggers need the training, or only people planning to enter; it covers every employee assigned to work on or near the equipment. People use hard ground placement, equipment interference or a short lift as the reason to skip barriers; the exception requires showing barriers are infeasible in both places. People put the entry notice on the lift director, a supervisor or the operator; the entering employee, or someone that employee instructs, has to make sure the operator knows. People set the barricade at the outrigger or carrier footprint or along the load path; it has to mark where the rotating superstructure can strike or crush.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Train each employee assigned to work on or near the equipment (“authorized personnel”) in how to recognize struck-by and pinch/crush hazard areas posed by the rotating superstructure.

Erect and maintain control lines, warning lines, railings or similar barriers to mark the boundaries of the hazard areas. Exception: When the employer can demonstrate that it is neither feasible to erect such barriers on the ground nor on the equipment, the hazard areas must be clearly marked by a combination of warning signs (such as “Danger—Swing/Crush Zone”) and high visibility markings on the equipment that identify the hazard areas. In addition, the employer must train each employee to understand what these markings signify.

Before an employee goes to a location in the hazard area that is out of view of the operator, the employee (or someone instructed by the employee) must ensure that the operator is informed that he/she is going to that location.

Where the operator knows that an employee went to a location covered by paragraph (a)(1) of this section, the operator must not rotate the superstructure until the operator is informed in accordance with a pre-arranged system of communication that the employee is in a safe position.

summary: Where the rotating superstructure could strike someone or pinch them against the crane or another object, the employer has to train the people working on or near the crane and put up barriers marking the hazard area. Control lines, warning lines, railings or similar barriers are the default. Before anyone goes into the area out of the operator's view, the operator has to be told, and the operator can't swing until the agreed system says the person is in a safe position.
title: Barricade the swing radius of the rotating superstructure

exam: Expect scenarios listing several workers near a suspended load and asking which one may be in the fall zone. Some items ask about hook type or who may rig the load. Match each worker's task against the exact listed exceptions.
hard: The zone reaches past the load's outline wherever falling material could reasonably travel, and it exists as soon as one end is off the ground. The listed exceptions are tasks, not job titles, so inspecting forms or sampling concrete next to a bucket doesn't qualify. The J-hook exception is for setting wooden trusses only. The rigger has to be qualified, and being a signal person, operator or supervisor doesn't make someone one.
mistakes: People think only fully suspended loads create a fall zone, or that controls start at lift-off; partially suspended materials count. People think the fall zone is only the area directly under the load; it extends wherever falling material could reasonably reach. People think anyone working on the concrete pour, checking tickets or taking samples can stand near the bucket; only the person operating the hopper or bucket is covered. People stretch the J-hook exception to steel joists, precast roof panels or any wood load; it covers setting wooden trusses only. People think a signal person, the operator or a supervisor can rig for fall-zone work because of their role; the materials have to be rigged by a qualified rigger.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Fall zone means the area (including but not limited to the area directly beneath the load) in which it is reasonably foreseeable that partially or completely suspended materials could fall in the event of an accident.
While the operator is not moving a suspended load, no employee must be within the fall zone, except for employees:
Operating a concrete hopper or concrete bucket.
Hooks with self-closing latches or their equivalent must be used. Exception: “J” hooks are permitted to be used for setting wooden trusses.
The materials must be rigged by a qualified rigger.

summary: The fall zone is the area where partially or completely suspended materials could reasonably fall in an accident, and it includes but isn't limited to the area directly beneath the load. While a load is suspended but not moving, nobody is allowed in it except people hooking, unhooking or guiding the load, making the initial attachment, or operating a concrete hopper or bucket. When people are in it for hooking, guiding or initial connection, the load has to be rigged against unintentional displacement by a qualified rigger, with self-closing latch hooks or their equivalent.
title: Define the fall zone and keep people out of it

exam: Scenarios name several people near a landing beam or a hanging load and ask who may stay. Some items test tilt-up rules or the J-hook exception. Focus on what each person is actually doing at that moment.
hard: Different rules apply when the load is stationary, when it's being landed, and during tilt-up or tilt-down. The test is the task the person is doing right now, not their rank or a related chore. Inspecting rope, checking outrigger pads or preparing the next set point doesn't count as hooking, guiding or receiving.
mistakes: People think inspecting hoist rope, checking outrigger pads or preparing for the next lift lets someone stand under a stationary load; those aren't listed exceptions. People think operator certification, signal-person designation or spotter duty qualifies someone to rig; the materials have to be rigged by a qualified rigger. People apply the J-hook exception to steel trusses, precast roof panels or any wooden member; it covers wooden trusses only. People think a foreman can stand in the zone to watch a beam land; only employees needed to receive the load are permitted. People count preparing the next location as receiving; it is not.

quotes.quote: Where available, hoisting routes that minimize the exposure of employees to hoisted loads must be used, to the extent consistent with public safety.
Engaged in hooking, unhooking or guiding a load;
Engaged in the initial attachment of the load to a component or structure; or
The materials being hoisted must be rigged to prevent unintentional displacement.
Receiving a load. Only employees needed to receive a load are permitted to be within the fall zone when a load is being landed.
No employee must be directly under the load.
Qualified rigger is a rigger who meets the criteria for a qualified person.

Hooking, unhooking, guiding and initial connection are allowed, with qualified rigging and latched hooks. During landing, only the people needed to receive the load can be in the zone. In tilt-up and tilt-down work, nobody can be directly under the load, and only essential people can be in the fall zone.
title: Apply the rules for hooking, guiding and receiving loads

exam: Scenarios describe a tight set-up next to a wall or a second machine and ask for the correct control or who has to inform the operator. Some answer choices offer spotters or horns as substitutes. Check whether the stem says barriers are feasible.
hard: The swing rule applies whenever a rotating superstructure creates a foreseeable strike or pinch hazard. It doesn't matter whether the upper is mounted permanently or temporarily, or what carrier it sits on. The fallback of signs plus high-visibility markings on the equipment applies only when barriers are infeasible on both the ground and the equipment. Spotters, horns, beacons and signs at the site gate don't substitute for it.
mistakes: People put the duty to tell the operator before entry on the signal person, the operator or a supervisor's approval; it belongs to the employee going in, who can ask someone to relay it, and the operator's duty is to hold the swing until the agreed all-clear. People think a spotter, alarms or entrance signs meet the exception; it calls for warning signs and high-visibility markings on the equipment, plus training. People think the rule covers only permanent or only temporary mounting, or only some carriers; it covers both kinds of mounting and turns on the hazard. People post a person in the pinch gap as a guard; that puts them in the hazard, and barriers keep people out. People use a horn, or the sign option, when barriers can be put up; barriers are required when they are feasible.

Erect and maintain control lines, warning lines, railings or similar barriers to mark the boundaries of the hazard areas. Exception: When the employer can demonstrate that it is neither feasible to erect such barriers on the ground nor on the equipment, the hazard areas must be clearly marked by a combination of warning signs (such as “Danger—Swing/Crush Zone”) and high visibility markings on the equipment that identify the hazard areas. In addition, the employer must train each employee to understand what these markings signify.

Before an employee goes to a location in the hazard area that is out of view of the operator, the employee (or someone instructed by the employee) must ensure that the operator is informed that he/she is going to that location.

The employer has to train each employee who works with the equipment to keep clear of holes, crush and pinch points, and the swing-radius hazards. Barriers are the default way to keep people out of those areas.

exam: Items give a voltage and ask for the travel clearance, or give a distance and ask whether a dedicated spotter is needed. Boundary voltages like 50 and 345 kV are a common trap. Separate the clearance question from the spotter question before you answer.
hard: Table T has its own bands: 4 feet up to 0.75 kV, 6 feet over 0.75 to 50, 10 feet over 50 to 345, 16 feet over 345 to 750, and 20 feet over 750 to 1,000. A voltage that sits exactly on a boundary stays in the lower band. The 20-foot spotter trigger is a separate requirement from the clearance. Traveling with a load falls under different rules, with a competent person supervising.
mistakes: People move a boundary voltage into the next band; exactly 50 kV needs 6 feet, and exactly 345 kV needs 10 feet. People use the lowest or highest band by habit; read the band that contains the line voltage. People treat 20 feet as the clearance for every line; it is the clearance only for lines over 750 to 1,000 kV, and it is also the dedicated-spotter trigger. People think the spotter trigger is 25 feet, or tie it to the band clearance; the spotter is required when any part will get closer than 20 feet. People think extra spotters or slower speed allow less clearance; at 500 kV the minimum is still 16 feet.

Speed and terrain have to be accounted for so bounce and sway don't break those clearances. If any part of the crane will get closer than 20 feet to the line, a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with the operator is required. At night or in poor visibility, the lines have to be lit or otherwise identified, and a safe travel path has to be identified and used.

exam: Scenarios place two cranes near each other and ask whether coordination is required and who sets it up. Watch whether the stem says there is or isn't a controlling entity. Small details like a tail swing or an outrigger inside the other radius decide the trigger.
hard: The trigger is any part of the crane, including an outrigger, counterweight or carrier, not just the boom or a load. It applies whether or not the cranes share a load or move at the same time. Responsibility depends on whether there is a controlling entity, not on crane size, who lifts first or who supplied the signal person.
mistakes: People give the duty to the biggest crane, the first operator or the signal person's employer; with a controlling entity present, the controlling entity sets up the system. People think coordination applies only to tandem lifts, simultaneous moves or crossing booms; any crane part within the other crane's working radius triggers it. People think separate loads or separate boom paths remove the need; an outrigger inside the other radius is enough. People think two schedules planned separately count as coordination; it has to be one system that coordinates the operations. With no controlling entity, people go by seniority, ownership or who does the inspections; the duty falls on the employer or employers operating the equipment.

quotes.quote: Where any part of a crane/derrick is within the working radius of another crane/derrick, the controlling entity must institute a system to coordinate operations. If there is no controlling entity, the employer (if there is only one employer operating the multiple pieces of equipment), or employers, must institute such a system.

summary: When any part of one crane is within another crane's working radius, a system to coordinate their operations is required. The controlling entity has to set it up. If there is no controlling entity, the employer operating the cranes sets it up, or the employers do it together if there are several. It keeps two machines from colliding or swinging into each other's loads.

exam: Expect scenarios with a crane next to a trench or on new fill, asking what has to happen first or who has to act. Answer choices often name plausible but wrong parties. Watch for the word assembled in the ground rule.
hard: The rule gives no set-back distance. A common practice is to stay back at least as far as the excavation is deep and to have a qualified person, often an engineer, decide anything closer or questionable, but that is practice, not a federal number. Fresh compacted backfill and a site next to an excavation get no drainage exception; only marshes and wetlands do. The ground rule covers assembly, so turning the boom another way or leaving off counterweight doesn't excuse ground you already know is bad.
mistakes: People give the discussion duty to a qualified person, the excavation supervisor or the operator personally; the operator's employer holds the discussion with the controlling entity. People think compaction, mats or excavation dewatering replace the drainage requirement; the only drainage exception is marshes and wetlands. People think the crane supplier, the earthwork contractor or the largest contractor automatically handles ground preparation; with no controlling entity, it goes to the employer with authority to make or arrange the preparations. People think ground support matters only once lifting starts; the rule bars assembly too. People think a favorable boom direction or a partial assembly excuses ground known to be inadequate; the ground has to meet the requirement before you go ahead.

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be assembled or used unless ground conditions are firm, drained, and graded to a sufficient extent so that, in conjunction (if necessary) with the use of supporting materials, the equipment manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level of the equipment are met.

If the A/D director or the operator determines that ground conditions do not meet the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section, that person's employer must have a discussion with the controlling entity regarding the ground preparations that are needed so that, with the use of suitable supporting materials/devices (if necessary), the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section can be met.

If there is no controlling entity for the project, the requirement in paragraph (c)(1) of this section must be met by the employer that has authority at the site to make or arrange for ground preparations needed to meet paragraph (b) of this section.

The ground rule still applies: firm, drained and graded enough to meet the manufacturer's support and level specs before assembly or use. When the operator or A/D director finds the support doubtful, that person's employer discusses the needed preparations with the controlling entity, and a qualified person often evaluates the set-back or the support.

exam: Items describe a boom position and ask which outrigger or track carries the most load, or which goes light first. Some ask whether a lift over the front of a truck crane is allowed. Picture where the combined center of gravity sits before you pick an answer.
hard: With the boom straight over the side, the two outriggers on that side share the load. Over a corner, one outrigger takes the most, and the one diagonally opposite goes light first as the crane nears tipping. On a crawler, the track on the boom side carries the most with a heavy load. Ground pressure under the tracks is even only when the center of gravity sits at the center of the footprint. A level crane isn't an evenly loaded crane.
mistakes: People assume over-the-corner lifts split the load like over-the-side lifts; over a corner, that one outrigger carries the most. People think the outrigger on the counterweight side carries the most with a load on the hook; the one diagonally opposite the boom carries the least and goes light first. People think a level crane is evenly loaded, or that long track contact evens out pressure; reactions shift toward the boom once the load swings off center. People think a front jack, full extension or a capacity percentage allows lifting over the front; only the manufacturer's permission does. People give the duty of passing on buried hazards to the crane owner or the A/D director, or mix up who informs and who is informed; the controlling entity informs the user and the operator.

quotes.quote: On wheel-mounted equipment, no loads must be lifted over the front area, except as permitted by the manufacturer.
Inform the user of the equipment and the operator of the location of hazards beneath the equipment set-up area (such as voids, tanks, utilities)

summary: As the boom swings and booms down with a load, the combined center of gravity moves toward the boom, and the outrigger or track under it picks up most of the load. That is physics, and it tells you where to put your best mats and which corner to watch. On wheel-mounted cranes, lifting over the front area isn't allowed unless the manufacturer permits it.
title: Which outrigger or track carries the most load as the boom swings and booms down

exam: Expect a scenario describing a site with planned lifts, followed by a question about where the work zone ends or what the boundary method requires. Watch for answer choices that use the planned radius or a working sector in place of the maximum working radius, and for choices that let a spotter or slow speed stand in for the prohibition.
hard: The full-circle method really means the full circle, out to the crane's maximum working radius. Planned picks, the current radius and the set-down point do not shrink it. The marked-boundary method only works if operation past the boundary is actually prohibited, and that prohibition covers all equipment operation, not just moving a load.
mistakes: People count only the working side or the planned lift sector; the full-circle method covers all 360 degrees, including the rear and the side away from the lifts. People set the edge at the planned radius, the current radius or the unloading point; it is the equipment's maximum working radius. People think the boundary limit applies only when a load is on the hook; it applies to any operation of the equipment. People think a signalperson watching, operating slowly or keeping the hook high makes crossing the boundary acceptable; none of these is an exception to the prohibition.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Demarcating boundaries (such as with flags, or a device such as a range limit device or range control warning device) and prohibiting the operator from operating the equipment past those boundaries, or
Defining the work zone as the area 360 degrees around the equipment, up to the equipment's maximum working radius.

summary: Before operations begin, the employer has to identify the work zone, because the power line check is made against that zone. There are two ways to do it. You can mark boundaries with flags or a range device and prohibit the operator from operating past them. Or you can define the zone as the full 360 degrees around the crane out to its maximum working radius.

exam: Expect a scenario giving the planned radius, the maximum radius and the distance to the line, followed by a question about whether an option is required. Read for "could get" and "maximum working radius." If the maximum reach comes within 20 feet, an option is required, no matter where the picks are planned.
hard: The check is about what could happen, not what is planned. The boom can swing and boom out farther than any planned pick. The trigger is 20 feet for lines up to 350 kV, and it does not change because some sites use a bigger buffer or because 10 feet is a familiar Table A number. Rigging and the load count, not just the boom tip.
mistakes: People use 10, 15 or 50 feet as the trigger; the federal trigger is closer than 20 feet (50 feet is a site buffer, not the rule). People base the check on the planned lift, the heaviest pick or the set-down points; the check uses the maximum working radius in the work zone. People use the longest radius anywhere on the load chart; the check uses the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone as rigged. People think a spotter alone covers the situation; once the crane could get within 20 feet, an option has to be chosen. People accept a site electrician, the controlling contractor, a lockout at a switch, or grounds at a substation as Option (1); it takes confirmation from the utility owner/operator that the line is visibly grounded at the worksite.

quotes.quote: Determine if any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), if operated up to the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone, could get closer than 20 feet to a power line.

If the crane is operated out to its maximum working radius in the work zone, could any part of the equipment, the load line or the load, including rigging, get closer than 20 feet to a power line? If the answer is yes, one of the three options has to be used before work starts.

exam: Expect questions asking which action satisfies a given option, or what has to be known before Option (3) can be used. Watch for answer choices with the right person but the wrong grounding location, or the right condition confirmed by the wrong person.
hard: Each option has its own required piece. Option (1) needs both the right source (the utility owner/operator) and the right condition (visibly grounded at the worksite). Option (2) uses exactly 20 feet. Option (3) starts with the voltage, because the voltage is what determines the Table A distance.
mistakes: People take confirmation for Option (1) from the controlling entity, a qualified person or the lift supervisor; it has to come from the utility owner/operator. People treat another open disconnect, grounding the crane, or keeping the outage going as the same as grounding; Option (1) needs the power line itself to be visibly grounded at the worksite. People use 10, 15 or 25 feet under Option (2); the Option (2) distance is 20 feet. People pick a Table A distance from line height, site dimensions or the crane's rated capacity; Option (3) starts with the line's voltage.

quotes.quote: Option (1)—Deenergize and ground. Confirm from the utility owner/operator that the power line has been deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite.

Option (2)—20 foot clearance. Ensure that no part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), gets closer than 20 feet to the power line by implementing the measures specified in paragraph (b) of this section.
Determine the line's voltage and the minimum approach distance permitted under Table A (see § 1926.1408).

Option (2): keep everything at least 20 feet away using the encroachment measures. Option (3): find out the line's voltage and keep everything outside the Table A distance, again using the encroachment measures.

exam: Expect a voltage followed by a question asking for the distance, often a voltage that sits right at the edge of a band. You may also see a question on the voltage deadline or on who sets the distance over 1,000 kV. Check whether the question is about Option (2) or Option (3) before choosing 20 feet.
hard: The top number of each band is included in that band, so 200 kV is a 15-foot line. Common distribution voltages such as 13.8 kV fall in the up-to-50 kV band. The 20-foot figure appears twice, once as the Option (2) distance and once as a Table A value, and people mix the two up. Above 1,000 kV there is no pattern to extend; a person sets the distance.
mistakes: People use 6 feet for a distribution line; 6 feet is a travel figure, and the smallest Table A value is 10 feet. People put 13.8 kV at 15 or 20 feet; it is 10 feet, and 115 kV is 15 feet. People set the warning line at 20 feet, or add a buffer, under Option (3); it goes at the Table A distance itself. People extend the table past 1,000 kV or leave it to the manufacturer or controlling entity; the utility owner/operator or a qualified registered PE sets it. People give the utility one, five or ten days to answer; it is two working days.

That covers the trigger check and the Option (2) clearance, for operations and for assembly. For lines over 1,000 kV, the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in transmission and distribution sets the clearance.

exam: Expect questions asking where the warning line goes for a given option, which item counts as the additional measure, and where the insulating link is installed. Read whether the scenario is operations or assembly, because the two lists are different.
hard: The warning line is mandatory for operations, and it does not count as the extra measure. If the operator cannot see the warning line, a dedicated spotter is required, plus one of the other measures. Assembly works differently: under the assembly rule, the warning line is one of the choices on the list, and the insulating link is not on that list.

People put the insulating link at the boom tip or in the reeving above the hook block; it goes between the end of the load line (or below) and the load. People treat the insulating link as a substitute for nonconductive tag lines; tag lines have to be nonconductive on their own. People count grounding the crane, line covers, or a second warning line as the extra measure; none of these is on the list.

quotes.quote: Conduct a planning meeting with the operator and the other workers who will be in the area of the equipment or load to review the location of the power line(s), and the steps that will be implemented to prevent encroachment/electrocution.
If tag lines are used, they must be non-conductive.

Erect and maintain an elevated warning line, barricade, or line of signs, in view of the operator, equipped with flags or similar high-visibility markings, at 20 feet from the power line (if using Option (2) of this section) or at the minimum approach distance under Table A (see § 1926.1408) (if using Option (3) of this section).

An insulating link/device, as defined in § 1926.1401, installed at a point between the end of the load line (or below) and the load.

exam: Expect a scenario where the spotter also handles a tag line or checks in only from time to time, followed by a question about what is wrong. Other questions ask which qualification a spotter needs. The right answer usually points to sole responsibility, continuous contact, or the signal person qualifications.
hard: "Dedicated" means the spotter does nothing else. Handling a tag line or rigging makes them no longer dedicated, whatever credentials they hold. The spotter watches everything that could reach the line, including the load and the hardware below the hook, not just the boom tip.
mistakes: People think a qualified rigger, a competent person or a certified operator qualifies as a spotter; the spotter has to meet the signal person qualifications. People watch only the boom or jib; the load line, the load and the rigging, including slings and shackles, have to stay clear too. People allow contact only at the start of a move, periodic check-ins, or contact only inside some distance; contact has to be continuous. People let the spotter handle a tag line, as long as it is nonconductive or the spotter is a rigger; any second job means they are no longer the dedicated spotter.

quotes.quote: Dedicated spotter (power lines): To be considered a dedicated spotter, the requirements of § 1926.1428 (Signal person qualifications) must be met and his/her sole responsibility is to watch the separation between the power line and the equipment, load line and load (including rigging and lifting accessories), and ensure through communication with the operator that the applicable minimum approach distance is not breached.

Their sole responsibility is to watch the separation between the power line and the equipment, load line, load and rigging, and to talk with the operator so the distance is never breached. They have to stay in continuous contact with the operator, have a visual aid such as a painted line, stanchions or line-of-sight landmarks, be positioned to judge the clearance, use communication equipment where needed, and give timely warnings. exam: Expect questions about who provides the voltage and how fast, and who has to presume lines are energized. Watch for "working days" versus "days" in the answer choices, and for answers that name the right condition but the wrong confirming party.

Answering a voltage request is not the same thing as confirming an outage. The confirmation has to cover the line staying deenergized and being visibly grounded at the worksite.
mistakes: People count calendar days, or think the utility has one or three days; it is two working days. People let an electrician, the operator or the controlling entity confirm the line is deenergized; only the utility owner/operator can. People assign the energized-presumption duty to the operator, the signal person or the utility; the rule assigns it to the employer. People treat a voltage reply, or an electrician's current reading, as outage confirmation; it is not. People treat a line's status as unknown until somebody measures it; the line is presumed energized.

quotes.quote: Voltage information. Where Option (3) of this section is used, the utility owner/operator of the power lines must provide the requested voltage information within two working days of the employer's request.

Power lines are presumed to be uninsulated unless the utility owner/operator or a registered engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution confirms that a line is insulated.

summary: Under Option (3), the voltage comes from the utility owner/operator, who has to provide it within two working days of the employer's request. Separately, the employer has to assume every power line is energized until the utility owner/operator confirms it has been, and continues to be, deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite. Lines are also presumed uninsulated unless the utility or a qualified registered engineer confirms they are insulated.
title: Get voltage from the utility; treat lines as energized until confirmed and grounded

exam: Expect a scenario giving the line height and the crane's maximum tip height at full extension and true vertical, followed by a question about whether work below the line is allowed. Read carefully: some answers reach the right yes or no for the wrong reason.
hard: The height test is vertical, measured against the plane of the line, and it is taken at the crane's highest possible reach: true vertical and full extension. Planned extension, working angle and working radius do not count. Deenergizing without visible grounding at the worksite does not meet the rule.
mistakes: People think notice of deenergizing is enough, or that grounds at a substation count; the line has to be visibly grounded at the worksite, and a voltage test does not replace that. People use 10 or 25 feet, the sag point, or a horizontal distance; the exception is more than 20 feet (or the Table A distance) vertically below the plane of the line. People measure with the boom stowed, at the planned extension, or at the working angle or radius; the test uses full extension at true vertical. People apply the general prohibition even when the crane's top at true vertical sits well below the line; when the exception is met, the prohibition does not apply.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: No part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) is allowed below a power line unless the employer has confirmed that the utility owner/operator has deenergized and (at the worksite) visibly grounded the power line, except where one of the exceptions in paragraph (d)(2) of this section applies.

For equipment with articulating or extensible booms: The uppermost part of the equipment, with the boom in the fully extended position, at true vertical, would be more than 20 feet below the plane of the power line or more than the Table A of this section minimum clearance distance below the plane of the power line.

Assembly/disassembly below power lines prohibited. No part of a crane/derrick, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), whether partially or fully assembled, is allowed below a power line unless the employer has confirmed that the utility owner/operator has deenergized and (at the worksite) visibly grounded the power line.

summary: No part of the equipment, load line or load may be below a power line unless the employer has confirmed that the utility owner/operator deenergized the line and visibly grounded it at the worksite. During operations there are exceptions. The main one: with the boom at true vertical, and fully extended if it is an extensible or articulating boom, the top of the equipment would be more than 20 feet, or more than the Table A distance, below the plane of the line. Assembly and disassembly below a line have no such height exception.
title: Know the limits on operating and assembling below power lines

exam: Expect questions about who has to attend the planning meeting, how many warnings are posted and where, and whether assembly can proceed below a line. Watch for answer choices that borrow the operations rules or the tower crane exception.
hard: The assembly check looks in the direction or area of assembly, not the full operating circle. The assembly list of measures is not the operations list: here the warning line is one of the choices, and the insulating link is not on the list. Overhead gantry and tower cranes are the only exception to the outside warnings, and mobile cranes are not exempt.
mistakes: People use 10, 15 or 50 feet as the assembly trigger; the check is closer than 20 feet. People give the utility five or ten days to provide the voltage; it is two working days. People reverse the warning counts, or require four outside; it is at least one in the cab and at least two outside, and a truck crane is not exempt. People leave the crew, the other workers in the area or the A/D director out of the meeting, or swap in the utility crew or the GC's foreman; the A/D director, operator, crew and others in the area attend. People think a spotter or an alarm allows assembly below a line; only deenergizing and visible grounding do.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Before assembling or disassembling equipment, the employer must determine if any part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) could get, in the direction or area of assembly/disassembly, closer than 20 feet to a power line during the assembly/disassembly process.

Conduct a planning meeting with the Assembly/Disassembly director (A/D director), operator, assembly/disassembly crew and the other workers who will be in the assembly/disassembly area to review the location of the power line(s) and the steps that will be implemented to prevent encroachment/electrocution.

Voltage information. Where Option (3) of this section is used, the utility owner/operator of the power lines must provide the requested voltage information within two working days of the employer's request.

Posting of electrocution warnings. There must be at least one electrocution hazard warning conspicuously posted in the cab so that it is in view of the operator and (except for overhead gantry and tower cranes) at least two on the outside of the equipment.

summary: Before assembly or disassembly, the employer checks whether any part of the equipment, load line or load could get closer than 20 feet to a power line in the direction or area of assembly. If so, the same three options apply. Under Option (2) or (3), the employer holds a planning meeting with the A/D director, the operator, the crew and the other workers in the area, uses only nonconductive tag lines, and adds at least one measure: a spotter, a proximity alarm, a range warning device, a range limiter, or an elevated warning line. Assembly below a line, or inside Table A, needs the line deenergized and visibly grounded. The crane also has to carry at least one electrocution warning in the cab and at least two on the outside.
title: Assemble and disassemble near power lines

exam: Expect questions asking which item is required for work inside Table A, who sets the distance, or what happens to reclosing. Expect a number question on the perimeter. Choose answers that keep the full list in place and put the authority with the utility or the qualified PE.
hard: This is a long all-of-the-following list, so the exam can test any single item on it. The 10-foot perimeter is measured from the equipment, and Table A has nothing to do with it. The insulating link does not protect the rigging below it, which is why the rigging also has to be nonconductive.
mistakes: People use 6 or 15 feet for the perimeter, or measure it from the line; it is at least 10 feet from the equipment, or as far as feasible where obstacles prevent that. People let the operator, spotter or a competent person set the clearance, or fall back on the Table A value; the line owner/operator or a registered PE qualified in transmission and distribution sets it. People think reclosing protects workers, only slow it down, or apply it only above some voltage; it has to be made inoperative where the design permits, on any line that has it. People think the insulating link or voltage-rated gloves cover the rigging; the rigging has to be nonconductive, and the glove substitute has expired. People accept a spotter who also calls stops part-time; the spotter has to be dedicated and in continuous contact.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The power line owner/operator or registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution determines the minimum clearance distance that must be maintained to prevent electrical contact in light of the on-site conditions.

If the power line is equipped with a device that automatically reenergizes the circuit in the event of a power line contact, before the work begins, the automatic reclosing feature of the circuit interrupting device must be made inoperative if the design of the device permits.
Nonconductive rigging if the rigging may be within the Table A of § 1926.1408 distance during the operation.
Barricades forming a perimeter at least 10 feet away from the equipment to prevent unauthorized personnel from entering the work area.
The person identified in accordance with this paragraph must direct the implementation of the procedures and must have the authority to stop work at any time to ensure safety.

summary: Operating closer than Table A to an energized line is prohibited unless every condition is met. The work has to be infeasible without breaching Table A, and deenergizing or relocating the line has to be infeasible after consulting the utility. The utility owner/operator or a qualified registered PE sets a site-specific clearance. A planning meeting sets procedures, which have to include: automatic reclosing disabled where the design permits, a dedicated spotter, an elevated warning line or barricade, an insulating link, nonconductive rigging, nonconductive tag lines, a barricaded perimeter at least 10 feet from the equipment, proper grounding, line hose or cover-up from the utility, and essential personnel only. The procedures are documented and kept on site, and one person directs them with authority to stop work.
title: Know the conditions for work closer than Table A

exam: Expect a voltage and a planned travel distance, followed by a question about whether the pass is allowed and whether a spotter is required. Many of these questions test the clearance and the spotter trigger together. Check whether the crane has a load, because a crane with a load is governed by the operating rules, not Table T.
hard: Two kinds of numbers live in this rule. The Table T clearances change with voltage. The spotter trigger is 20 feet for every voltage. A crane can legally pass at 15 feet from a 13.8 kV line, but only with a spotter. Bouncing over rough ground can raise the boom, which is why speed and terrain are part of the rule.
mistakes: People use 4 feet or 10 feet for a 25 kV line; it falls in the over 0.75 to 50 kV class, which is 6 feet. People treat 10 feet as one number for every line; 10 feet is only for over 50 to 345 kV. People put the spotter trigger at 10, 15 or 50 feet, or tie it to voltage; a spotter is required whenever equipment will be closer than 20 feet. People treat 20 feet as the required travel clearance for lower voltages; it is the spotter trigger, and the clearance for those lines comes from Table T. People let the controlling entity, the operator, the spotter or the manufacturer set the distance over 1,000 kV; the utility owner/operator or a qualified registered PE sets it.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: up to 0.75 | 4 over .75 to 50 | 6 over 50 to 345 | 10 over 345 to 750 | 16 Over 750 to 1,000 | 20
The boom/mast and boom/mast support system are lowered sufficiently to meet the requirements of this paragraph.

Dedicated spotter. If any part of the equipment while traveling will get closer than 20 feet to the power line, the employer must ensure that a dedicated spotter who is in continuous contact with the driver/operator is used.
The power lines are illuminated or another means of identifying the location of the lines is used.

summary: Traveling under or near a power line with no load uses Table T. Up to 0.75 kV the clearance is 4 feet. Over 0.75 to 50 kV it is 6 feet. Over 50 to 345 kV it is 10 feet. Over 345 to 750 kV it is 16 feet. Over 750 to 1,000 kV it is 20 feet. Over 1,000 kV, the utility or a qualified registered PE sets it. The boom has to be lowered enough, speed and terrain have to be considered, and a dedicated spotter is required if any part will get closer than 20 feet. At night or in poor visibility, the lines are illuminated or otherwise identified, and a safe path is used. Traveling with a load falls under the operating rules instead.
title: Travel under or near power lines with no load

exam: Expect a contact scenario followed by a question about the operator's first action, what the crew should do, or who can declare the line safe. Look for an emergency in the scenario, such as fire. Without one, the answer is to stay in the cab and keep everyone away.
hard: Things that look safe do not prove anything. Backing the boom off the line, seeing no arcing, or shutting off the engine does not de-energize the crane. Only the utility can confirm the line status. The jump-clear technique is for a real emergency, not a routine way out of the cab.
mistakes: People think separating from the line, seeing no arcing, or shutting off the engine makes it safe to climb down; the operator stays inside unless an emergency forces them out. People let the operator, the spotter or an electrical subcontractor declare the line dead; only the utility owner/operator can confirm. People think the danger is only at the contact point or only on the load; the crew has to avoid both the equipment and the load. People think a normal dismount, moving to another spot on the crane, or knowing the jump technique justifies leaving; with no emergency, the operator stays in the cab.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Information regarding the danger of electrocution from the operator simultaneously touching the equipment and the ground.
The importance to the operator's safety of remaining inside the cab except where there is an imminent danger of fire, explosion, or other emergency that necessitates leaving the cab.
The danger of the potentially energized zone around the equipment (step potential).
The need for crew in the area to avoid approaching or touching the equipment and the load.

summary: If the crane contacts a line, the operator stays in the cab unless fire, explosion or another emergency makes leaving necessary. The crew stays away and does not touch the equipment or the load. Touching the equipment and the ground at the same time completes a path to ground, and the ground around the crane can be energized (step potential). The line stays presumed energized until the utility owner/operator confirms otherwise. If the operator has to leave, common practice is to jump clear without touching the crane and ground together, land with feet together, and shuffle or hop away.
title: Respond to power line contact (operator stays on, others stay away)

exam: Expect questions about where the link is installed, how an alarm has to be set, or what governs how a device is used. Watch for answers that confuse warning before contact with preventing encroachment, and answers that treat any device as complete protection.
hard: An insulating link protects only what is below it. The boom, the load line above it, and conductive rigging can still be energized. A warning that comes too late does no good, because the operator needs time to stop the motion. In practice, range devices work on the boom or jib tip and do not track a swinging load.
mistakes: People think insulation at the boom head, the boom mounting or the winch counts as the link; it goes between the load-line end (or below) and the load. People think two devices, or a warning device paired with a limiter, or a spotter with every device, are required; the operations list requires at least one measure in addition to the warning line.
