People let operator preference, site rules or an inspector override how a device is used; it has to follow the manufacturer's procedures and conditions of use. People think a louder or repeated alarm fixes a late setting; the alarm has to give enough warning to prevent encroachment, not just warn before contact.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The limitations of an insulating link/device, proximity alarm, and range control (and similar) device, if used.
A proximity alarm set to give the operator sufficient warning to prevent encroachment.
An insulating link/device, as defined in § 1926.1401, installed at a point between the end of the load line (or below) and the load.
Insulating link/device means an insulating device listed, labeled, or accepted by a Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.7.

Devices originally designed by the manufacturer for use as: A safety device (see § 1926.1415), operational aid, or a means to prevent power line contact or electrocution, when used to comply with this section, must meet the manufacturer's procedures for use and conditions of use.

summary: Insulating links, proximity alarms and range devices help, but each one has limits, and the crew has to be trained on those limits. An insulating link has to be listed, labeled or accepted by a nationally recognized testing laboratory, and it goes between the end of the load line (or below) and the load. A proximity alarm or range warning device has to be set to warn early enough to prevent encroachment. A range limiter has to be set to prevent encroachment. Any of these devices used to comply has to follow the manufacturer's procedures and conditions of use.
title: Know the limits of insulating links, proximity alarms and range limiters

exam: Expect a tower scenario with the transmitter still on, followed by a question asking what is required. Watch for "or" in the rule, and for answers that apply power line clearance distances to a tower.
hard: The two precautions go together, and the only alternative to them is deenergizing the transmitter. The rule is triggered by induced charge, not by a fixed distance. It covers the load as well as the crane, and any boom type.
mistakes: People treat grounding and nonconductive tag lines as either/or, or think grounding makes a conductive tag line acceptable; both apply, and a tag line, if used, has to be nonconductive. People think the rule requires tag lines, or that bonding a tag line to ground is enough; tag lines are not required, but any tag line used has to be nonconductive. People limit the rule to one boom type, to metal loads, or to the boom and load line; it covers the equipment and the materials being handled. People think deenergizing is mandatory, or that a monitor or a fixed clearance satisfies the rule; deenergizing is one choice, and the other is the two precautions.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: When working near transmitter/communication towers where the equipment is close enough for an electrical charge to be induced in the equipment or materials being handled, the transmitter must be deenergized or the following precautions must be taken:
The equipment must be provided with an electrical ground.
If tag lines are used, they must be non-conductive.

summary: Near a transmitter or communication tower, a radio signal can induce an electrical charge in the crane or in the materials it is handling. When the equipment is close enough for that to happen, the transmitter has to be deenergized, or two precautions have to be taken: ground the equipment, and use only nonconductive tag lines if tag lines are used.
title: Handle induced current near transmitter towers

exam: Expect a question asking where the general industry crane rule sends you for overhead lines, or a scenario that says 1910.180 governs and then lists construction provisions as answer choices. The answer is the referral to 1910.333(c)(3).
hard: Paragraph (j) is only a pointer. It states no clearance, no voltage table and no travel distance. People reach for the construction crane rules or the industry operating and inspection standards they know better, even when the scenario says general industry applies.
mistakes: People point to the construction crane power line sections, or to industry operation or inspection chapters; 1910.180(j) refers to 1910.333(c)(3). People remember 1910.180(j) as a fixed-distance rule, a voltage table or a travel clearance; it states none of these and only refers to another section. People widen its subject to buried cables, telecom cables or electrical cabinets; it addresses overhead electric lines.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Operations near overhead lines. For operations near overhead electric lines, see § 1910.333(c)(3).

summary: The general industry crane rule, 1910.180, covers cranes used outside construction. For operations near overhead electric lines, its paragraph (j) does not give its own distances. It refers you to 1910.333(c)(3). Knowing which rule governs a lift tells you where to look for the overhead line requirements.
title: Know the general industry overhead line rule

exam: Expect questions asking who has to be trained, which item belongs in the training, or who can confirm a line is insulated or deenergized. Answers that narrow or widen the trained group, or that swap the confirming party, are the usual traps.
hard: The scope is narrower than everyone on site but wider than just the operator. It covers every crew member assigned to the equipment, such as riggers and tag line handlers. Two different presumptions are taught: energized and uninsulated. Each has a different list of parties who can confirm otherwise.
mistakes: People let the controlling entity's competent person, a site electrician or the crane owner confirm a line is insulated; only the utility owner/operator or a registered engineer qualified in transmission and distribution can, and no written survey is required. People accept a remote lockout, paperwork, or the operator's own test for deenergizing; the utility has to confirm the line stays deenergized and is visibly grounded at the worksite. People limit training to the operator, or to the operator and signal person, or extend it to every trade on site; it covers each operator and crew member assigned to the equipment. People think jumping clear, climbing down while holding the frame, or stepping onto outrigger pads is a safe exit with no emergency present; the operator stays in the cab, and pads and mats are not reliable insulation.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The employer must train each operator and crew member assigned to work with the equipment on all of the following:
Power lines are presumed to be energized unless the utility owner/operator confirms that the power line has been and continues to be deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite.

Power lines are presumed to be uninsulated unless the utility owner/operator or a registered engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution confirms that a line is insulated.
The procedures to be followed to properly ground equipment and the limitations of grounding.
Overhead powerlines. The employer must train each employee specified in § 1926.1408(g) and § 1926.1410(m) in the topics listed in § 1926.1408(g).

summary: The employer has to train each operator and each crew member assigned to work with the equipment on power line hazards. The training covers: what to do on contact (the danger of touching the equipment and the ground at once, staying in the cab, the safest way to evacuate, step potential, keeping the crew away, safe clearances); that lines are presumed energized unless the utility confirms they are deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite; that lines are presumed uninsulated unless the utility or a qualified registered engineer confirms otherwise; the limits of insulating links, alarms and range devices; and how to ground equipment and the limits of grounding.
title: Know what power line training must cover

exam: Items are usually scenarios: a description of what the operator can and cannot see, followed by whether a signal person is required and why. Read for exactly what is hidden: the load path and landing area count, while boom, supports and counterweight by themselves do not. Watch for choices that add an approval step to the operator's or load handler's call.
hard: The point of operation is defined narrowly as load travel and the placement area, so seeing the boom tip, the outriggers or even the load itself does not settle it. If the operator can see the tank but not where it sets down, a signal person is needed, and there is no exception for the final landing spot. The third trigger belongs to either the operator or the load handler alone; nobody has to agree with them or sign off.
mistakes: People take an obscured boom tip, outrigger or counterweight as the trigger; the stated trigger is the operator's view of load travel or the placement area, though a site safety concern can still call for a signal person. People think seeing the load is enough; the operator also has to see the area near or at placement, including the final support area. People think every pick-and-carry or reverse move needs signals; the travel trigger is an obstructed view in the actual direction of travel. People think the operator and load handler must agree, or that a supervisor or safety manager must approve; a determination by either one is enough. People think a wall is itself the trigger; it matters only because it hides the placement area.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The point of operation, meaning the load travel or the area near or at load placement, is not in full view of the operator.
When the equipment is traveling, the view in the direction of travel is obstructed.
Due to site specific safety concerns, either the operator or the person handling the load determines that it is necessary.

summary: A signal person has to be provided in three situations: the point of operation is not in full view of the operator, the view in the direction of travel is obstructed while the crane travels, or the operator or the person handling the load decides one is needed for site-specific safety reasons. The point of operation means the load travel or the area near or at load placement. Getting this right decides whether a blind pick goes ahead safely.
title: Know when a signal person must be provided

exam: Expect questions that show a hand signal description and ask what it means, plus scenarios on whether non-standard signals are allowed and who has to agree before the lift. Posting questions test the either-or wording, so watch for choices that demand both locations or accept a location away from the hoisting operation.
hard: The exception to the Standard Method depends on conditions, not on people: infeasibility, or an operation or attachment the Standard Method doesn't cover. Crew agreement, a lift director's approval, or a good demonstration does not create the exception. The posting rule gives two choices, so one location is enough, but an office, a file or a chart in someone's pocket is not posting. Directions are given from the operator's perspective, so a signal person's left and right have to be translated.
mistakes: People think unanimous agreement, a lift director's approval or a successful unloaded demonstration allows non-standard signals; they are allowed only when the Standard Method is infeasible or doesn't cover the operation. People swap in the lead rigger or site managers for the lift director, or leave out the signal person or the operator; the agreement is among the signal person, operator and lift director where there is one. People agree on signal meanings during a test movement, as the crane takes tension, or one at a time during the lift; agreement has to come before the operation. People think the chart has to be posted both on the crane and nearby; either location works. People think a chart in the office, in records, at the site entrance or carried by someone counts; it has to be on the equipment or conspicuously posted near the hoisting operation.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: When using hand signals, the Standard Method must be used (see appendix A of this subpart). Exception: Where use of the Standard Method for hand signals is infeasible, or where an operation or use of an attachment is not covered in the Standard Method, non-standard hand signals may be used in accordance with paragraph (c)(2) of this section.

Non-standard hand signals. When using non-standard hand signals, the signal person, operator, and lift director (where there is one) must contact each other prior to the operation and agree on the non-standard hand signals that will be used.
Hand signal charts must be either posted on the equipment or conspicuously posted in the vicinity of the hoisting operations.
All directions given to the operator by the signal person must be given from the operator's direction perspective.

summary: When hand signals are used, they have to be the Standard Method shown in Appendix A, for example stop as one arm extended palm down moving back and forth, emergency stop with both arms, and hoist with the forefinger up making small circles. Non-standard hand signals are allowed only where the Standard Method is infeasible or doesn't cover the operation or attachment, and then the signal person, operator and lift director (if there is one) agree on them before the operation. A hand signal chart has to be posted on the equipment or conspicuously near the hoisting operation.
title: Give and read the standard hand signals

exam: Questions ask you to pick the complete list of permitted signal types, to say who has to justify new signals and to what standard, or to choose a suitable method for a described site. Watch for lists that slip in radio or drop the new-signal category, and for wording like "superior" or "approved by" that raises or shifts the requirement.
hard: People mix up the signal type with the means of transmission: radio and video carry signals, they are not types. The new-signal bar is at least equal, not better, and the duty to show it sits with the employer. Suitability is judged on real conditions, so a plan written before anyone knew where the signal person would stand doesn't decide it.
mistakes: People list radio as a signal type; radio is a means of transmission, and the types are hand, voice, audible and new. People think hand signals are the only type allowed or always required; they are one option, and a signal the operator can't see doesn't suit the site. People treat flags and lights as standard types; they are new signals that need the employer's demonstration first. People put the new-signal duty on the operator, the signal person, the manufacturer, an agency or a crew sign-off; the employer makes the demonstration, with no pre-approval called for. People think new signals must be superior; they must be at least equally effective. People think horns are the only option for blind lifts; radio voice signals or video can also suit the site.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Types of signals. Signals to operators must be by hand, voice, audible, or new signals.
New signals. Signals other than hand, voice, or audible signals may be used where the employer demonstrates that:
The new signals provide at least equally effective communication as voice, audible, or Standard Method hand signals, or
The new signals comply with a national consensus standard that provides at least equally effective communication as voice, audible, or Standard Method hand signals.

Suitability. The signals used (hand, voice, audible, or new), and means of transmitting the signals to the operator (such as direct line of sight, video, radio, etc.), must be appropriate for the site conditions.

summary: Signals to the operator are by hand, voice, audible, or new signals. New signals are anything else, such as flags or lights, and may be used only where the employer demonstrates they communicate at least as effectively as voice, audible or Standard Method hand signals, or meet a national consensus standard that does. Both the signal type and the way it reaches the operator, such as line of sight, video or radio, have to suit the actual site conditions.
title: Choose hand, voice, audible or new signals

exam: Expect scenarios asking whether a radio setup complies: where and when it was tested, who else is on the channel, and how the operator hears it. Watch for answers that get the place right but the timing wrong, and for equipment that sounds like it belongs on the channel but isn't a crane or derrick.
hard: The test has two conditions that both have to be met: on site, and before operations begin. The dedicated channel has exactly two exceptions: multiple cranes or derricks and their signal persons sharing a channel to coordinate, and a crane on or next to railroad tracks coordinating with trains or other equipment on the same or adjacent tracks. Hands-free applies to the operator's reception, so a handheld or push-to-talk radio doesn't meet it, even within reach.
mistakes: People accept a yard test; the test has to be on site. People test after the first lift or only when a new signal person arrives; the test comes before operations begin. People think a handheld within reach, a push-to-talk radio or the operator's choice of device is fine; the operator's reception has to be hands-free. People let telehandlers, concrete pumps, other trades or site delivery traffic share the crane channel; the sharing exception covers cranes, derricks and signal persons only. People forget the railroad exception, or think it requires the trains to stop; it exists so the crane can be coordinated with moving trains or equipment on the same or adjacent tracks.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The device(s) used to transmit signals must be tested on site before beginning operations to ensure that the signal transmission is effective, clear, and reliable.
Signal transmission must be through a dedicated channel, except:
Multiple cranes/derricks and one or more signal persons may share a dedicated channel for the purpose of coordinating operations.

Where a crane is being operated on or adjacent to railroad tracks, and the actions of the crane operator need to be coordinated with the movement of other equipment or trains on the same or adjacent tracks.
The operator's reception of signals must be by a hands-free system.

summary: When signals go by radio, telephone or other electronic means, the devices have to be tested on site before operations begin to make sure transmission is effective, clear and reliable. Signals go over a dedicated channel, and the operator receives them hands-free. Steel, distance and other traffic on site can wreck a radio that worked fine in the yard, which is why the test happens where the work is.
title: Test and use radio signals on a dedicated channel, hands-free

exam: Expect items that give several spoken commands and ask which one is in correct order, and scenarios asking whether the crew has to meet again on voice signals. Watch for orders that look close but move the stop or the distance, and for triggers that sound sensible but aren't listed.
hard: The order is the whole point: the operator needs to know which motion before hearing how far, and the stop has to name the function. Once signals are agreed, there is no new meeting unless a worker is added or substituted, there is confusion, or a signal is changed. A new shift, moving the crane or changing the rigging is not on that list by itself.
mistakes: People give direction or distance first; the function and direction come first. People pair speed with the function; direction goes with the function, and distance and speed go together second. People put the stop in the middle or say a generic "all stop"; the last element names the function and then stop. People name a superintendent or riggers as part of the agreement, or brief the lift director afterward; the operator, signal person and lift director (if there is one) agree directly, beforehand. People think signals are re-agreed every shift, after relocation or after a rigging change; the triggers are a worker added or substituted, confusion, or a changed signal.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Prior to beginning operations, the operator, signal person and lift director (if there is one), must contact each other and agree on the voice signals that will be used. Once the voice signals are agreed upon, these workers need not meet again to discuss voice signals unless another worker is added or substituted, there is confusion about the voice signals, or a voice signal is to be changed.
Each voice signal must contain the following three elements, given in the following order: function (such as hoist, boom, etc.), direction; distance and/or speed; function, stop command.
The operator, signal person and lift director (if there is one), must be able to effectively communicate in the language used.

summary: Every voice signal has three elements in a fixed order: function and direction, then distance and/or speed, then function and stop. For example: "Hoist up, ten feet, slow, hoist stop." Before operations begin, the operator, signal person and lift director (if there is one) contact each other and agree on the voice signals, and all of them have to be able to communicate effectively in the language used.
title: Give voice signals with the three elements in order

exam: Expect scenarios where a second person starts signaling, or a bystander throws a stop, and you pick what the operator does. Watch for choices that sound careful, like slowing down, checking with the signal person or finishing the swing, which don't obey the stop.
hard: The two rules point in opposite directions, and that's the trick. Routine signals come from one person only, with no exception for split functions, matching instructions or a lead signaler. Stop signals can come from anyone, with no need for crew membership, supervisor status or confirmation from the assigned signal person. Obeying means stopping, not slowing down or finishing the current move.
mistakes: People think one person can call hoist while another calls swing, or that two signalers are fine if their signals match or a lead signaler oversees them; only one person gives routine signals at a time. People think a worker who spots a hazard should tell a supervisor or go through management, or alert the lift director instead of the operator; the stop or emergency stop signal goes to the operator or signal person. People think only the assigned signaler, the lift crew or supervisors can stop the crane, or that the assigned signaler has to confirm an outsider's stop; the operator obeys a stop from anyone. People slow down to ask for an explanation or finish the current movement first; the operator stops.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Only one person may give signals to a crane/derrick at a time, except in circumstances covered by paragraph (j) of this section.

Anyone who becomes aware of a safety problem must alert the operator or signal person by giving the stop or emergency stop signal. (Note: § 1926.1417(y) requires the operator to obey a stop or emergency stop signal).
The operator must obey a stop (or emergency stop) signal, irrespective of who gives it.

summary: Only one person gives signals to a crane at a time, so the operator never has to choose between two voices. The exception is a safety stop: anyone who becomes aware of a safety problem alerts the operator or signal person with a stop or emergency stop signal. The operator has to obey a stop or emergency stop signal no matter who gives it.
title: Apply one signaler at a time and anyone may stop

exam: Expect scenarios where the radio cuts out mid-swing or mid-landing and you choose the operator's next action, or where work is about to resume and you pick what has to happen first. Watch for responses that sound reasonable, like slowing down or completing the move, and for restart conditions that leave out a new signal.
hard: The stop applies to any interruption, at any time, with one function or several, with or without people nearby. Getting the radio back isn't enough to restart: a proper operating signal has to be given and understood after it's restored. For an operator-spotted safety problem, the agreement to resume is between the operator and the signal person, and nobody else stands in for either of them.
mistakes: People think the stop applies only to multiple-function moves, when people are near, or at startup; it applies to any interruption during operations needing signals. People finish the last instruction, reposition, or creep forward because they can partly see the landing; the operator safely stops. People restart on a clear-area report, a repeated earlier instruction or a repair confirmation; a proper signal has to be given and understood after communication returns. People let a supervisor or a qualified person stand in for the operator or the signal person on resuming after a safety problem; the operator and signal person have to agree it's resolved.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: During operations requiring signals, the ability to transmit signals between the operator and signal person must be maintained. If that ability is interrupted at any time, the operator must safely stop operations requiring signals until it is reestablished and a proper signal is given and understood.

If the operator becomes aware of a safety problem and needs to communicate with the signal person, the operator must safely stop operations. Operations must not resume until the operator and signal person agree that the problem has been resolved.

summary: During operations that need signals, the ability to send signals between operator and signal person has to be maintained the whole time. If it's interrupted, the operator safely stops those operations until communication is reestablished and a proper signal is given and understood. Separately, if the operator sees a safety problem and needs to talk to the signal person, the operator safely stops, and work resumes only when the operator and signal person agree the problem is resolved.
title: Stop when signals are interrupted

exam: Expect a set of spoken signals to two cranes and a question asking which one is correct, or a scenario asking who is responsible for identification. Watch the order of words in each choice: the crane's name has to come first.
hard: The identification goes before the motion command, because an operator who hears "swing left" may start moving before hearing whose signal it was. It goes on each signal, not once per lift and not only when switching cranes. The duty belongs to the signal person giving the signal. Alternatives are allowed, but only if they identify the crane as well as naming it does.
mistakes: People name the crane once per lift or only when switching cranes; under the naming method every signal carries its own identification. People name the crane after the command, or give the command first and then release it; the identification comes before the function and direction. People rely on "same crane"; that relies on memory and doesn't identify anything. People put the duty on the operator, the lift director or a qualified person; the signal person identifies the crane, though an operator repeating the call back is good practice. People think naming is the only method, or that alternatives need a written plan, approval or must be flags or hand signals; any equally effective method works.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Communication with multiple cranes/derricks. Where a signal person(s) is in communication with more than one crane/derrick, a system must be used for identifying the crane/derrick each signal is for, as follows:
for each signal, prior to giving the function/direction, the signal person must identify the crane/derrick the signal is for, or
must use an equally effective method of identifying which crane/derrick the signal is for.
Multiple cranes/derricks and one or more signal persons may share a dedicated channel for the purpose of coordinating operations.

summary: When a signal person talks to more than one crane, there has to be a system for identifying which crane each signal is for. The basic method is to name the crane before giving the function and direction, every signal, every time: "Crane two, swing left." An equally effective method may be used instead. Cranes and signal persons may share a dedicated radio channel to coordinate.
title: Communicate with multiple cranes

exam: Expect scenarios that describe a broken horn, built-in or removable, and ask the correct action, or describe where a spare horn is kept and ask whether the crane complies. Read for which kind of horn it is and exactly where the replacement sits.
hard: The built-in and removable cases have different fixes, and the exam swaps them. Built-in: tag out or remove. Removable: remove only, no tag-out. A removable horn has to meet both conditions at once, on the equipment and immediately available to the operator. A horn in the pickup, the trailer or the signal person's hand meets neither. The rule sets no repair deadline or grace period.
mistakes: People think the horn can sit at a separate station, on the site, in a pickup or trailer, or with the signal person; it has to be built in, or on the equipment and immediately available to the operator. People think only built-in horns count; a removable horn complies if it's on the equipment and immediately available. People think being on the equipment is enough for a removable horn; it also has to be immediately available to the operator. People wait for a repair deadline, a grace period or the next periodic inspection; a bad horn is dealt with now. People tag out a removable horn and leave it on the crane; a bad removable horn is removed, while a bad built-in horn may be tagged out or removed.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must have a horn that is either built into the equipment or is on the equipment and immediately available to the operator.
If a built-in horn is not working properly, it must be tagged-out or removed. If a removable horn is not working properly, it must be removed.

summary: The crane has to have a horn that is either built in, or on the equipment and immediately available to the operator. If a built-in horn isn't working properly, it is tagged out or removed. If a removable horn isn't working properly, it is removed. The horn is how the operator warns people on the ground, so a crane without a working one has no compliant horn.
title: Know the horn requirement

exam: Expect questions asking which list of signal types is complete, what to do with a faulty built-in or removable horn, and whether a described horn setup complies. Watch for answers that sound responsible, like documenting the defect or keeping a radio handy, but skip the actual tag-out or removal.
hard: You have to keep three things separate: signal types (hand, voice, audible, new), means of transmission (radio, video, line of sight), and the horn equipment rule. Flags and lights aren't listed types, so they fall under new signals. For a faulty horn, built-in means tag out or remove and removable means remove, and having a working backup or a radio doesn't cancel that.
mistakes: People apply remove-only to a built-in horn, or tag-out to a removable one; built-in may be tagged out or removed, and removable must be removed. People log the defect, wait for a repair deadline or rely on a backup horn; the faulty horn is still tagged out or removed. People treat a radio as a horn substitute or call radio and video signal types; they are means of transmission, and the types are hand, voice, audible and new. People call flags and lights listed types, or leave new signals off the list; flags and lights are new signals that need the employer's showing of equal effectiveness. People think removable horns are banned, or that one near the crane or with the signal person counts; a removable horn is fine if it's on the equipment and immediately available to the operator.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Types of signals. Signals to operators must be by hand, voice, audible, or new signals.
New signals. Signals other than hand, voice, or audible signals may be used where the employer demonstrates that:
The equipment must have a horn that is either built into the equipment or is on the equipment and immediately available to the operator.
If a built-in horn is not working properly, it must be tagged-out or removed. If a removable horn is not working properly, it must be removed.

summary: Audible signals, such as horn blasts, are one of the four permitted signal types along with hand, voice and new signals. In practice the crew agrees before the lift on what each sound means, so the operator and ground workers read it the same way. The horn itself has to be built into the crane, or on it and immediately available to the operator, and a faulty one has to be taken out of service.
title: Audible (horn) signals: what the rules require and when crews agree on meanings

exam: Look for a no-calculator beam weight problem where depth, length and pounds per foot are all listed as distractors. Also look for scenarios that give an indicator reading and several radii and ask whether the operator can proceed. Watch for the words longest radius and for answers that offer a workaround instead of verifying the weight.
hard: The 75 percent check is taken at the longest radius anywhere in the lift, not the pick radius and not automatically the set radius. Once the reading crosses 75 percent, being under 100 percent does not let you continue; the weight has to be verified first. The beam calculation is simple but easy to botch: in a designation like W12x50, the 12 is nominal depth in inches and the 50 is pounds per foot.
mistakes: People remember the trigger as 50, 85 or 90 percent; it is 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius. People take the check at the pick radius or the set radius; the rule uses the longest radius used anywhere in the lift, where capacity is lowest. People think a supervisor's signature or approval settles the weight; the weight itself has to be verified. People re-boom or reconfigure to duck under the trigger; once the reading is over 75 percent, the lift does not go ahead until the weight is verified. People multiply the 12 in W12x50 by the length or turn feet into inches; a 40 ft W12x50 weighs 40 × 50 = 2,000 lb.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The weight of the load must be determined from a source recognized by the industry (such as the load's manufacturer), or by a calculation method recognized by the industry (such as calculating a steel beam from measured dimensions and a known per foot weight), or by other equally reliable means. In addition, when requested by the operator, this information must be provided to the operator prior to the lift; or

The operator must begin hoisting the load to determine, using a load weighing device, load moment indicator, rated capacity indicator, or rated capacity limiter, if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used during the lift operation. If it does, the operator must not proceed with the lift until he/she verifies the weight of the load in accordance with paragraph (o)(3)(i) of this section.

summary: Before a lift the operator has to verify that the load is within the crane's rated capacity. One way is to get the weight from a source the industry recognizes, like the manufacturer, or calculate it a recognized way, like a steel beam's length times its weight per foot. The other way is to start hoisting and read a load weighing device, LMI, RCI or RCL. If that reading is over 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius of the lift, the operator stops until the weight is verified the first way.
title: Determine load weight from a recognized source or calculation

exam: Expect scenarios where a load tilts on liftoff and you pick the correct fix. Also expect questions on what the rule requires when the CG is uncertain. Wrong answers tend to offer crane motions, capacity derates or invented percentages in place of re-rigging or movement control.
hard: The geometric center and the CG are the same only when weight is evenly distributed, and many loads like pumps, valves and skids with motors are heavy at one end. Sling length and angle change leg tension, but they do not change where the CG ends up, which is under the hook. The rule's trigger is whether the stability method depends on the CG, not a capacity percentage, the number of legs or which crane is lifting.
mistakes: People assume the CG is in the middle of the load; it is there only if the weight is uniform. People think the attachment points or sling lengths set the CG; the weight distribution sets it, and the load hangs with the CG under the hook. People move the hook toward the high end to fix a tilt; the high end is the light end, so the hook has to move toward the low, heavy end. People think lifting higher or booming will level the load; neither changes the hook's position relative to the CG, so you set it down and re-rig. People think an unknown CG calls for derating or an engineer's calculation; the rule calls for measures that control dangerous movement.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The center of gravity of the load must be identified if that is necessary for the method used for maintaining stability.

Where there is insufficient information to accurately identify the center of gravity, measures designed to prevent unintended dangerous movement resulting from an inaccurate identification of the center of gravity must be used. (See Non-mandatory appendix B of this subpart for an example.)

summary: A freely hanging load always settles with its center of gravity directly under the hook. If the hook is not over the CG when the load lifts, the load swings or tilts until it is. Rigging so the hook sits over the CG gives you a level, stable pick. In the assembly and disassembly rules, the CG has to be identified when the method for keeping things stable depends on it, and if the CG cannot be pinned down accurately, you use measures that prevent dangerous movement in case the estimate is wrong.
title: Find the center of gravity and rig so the hook is over it

exam: Expect hitch identification from a description, questions comparing hitch capacities using a tag's vertical rating, and the five-degree vertical allowance. Read carefully for whether the basket legs are vertical or angled, since that decides whether doubling applies.
hard: The relative capacities are industry practice, not federal numbers. A vertical basket carries about twice the vertical rating because two parts share the load, a choker is usually rated around 75 percent of vertical because of the sharp bend at the choke, and ratings drop further when the choke angle is sharper than 120 degrees. A basket is named by having two parts under the load, not by the angle of its legs. A leg within five degrees of vertical counts as vertical; anything more needs an angle factor.
mistakes: People think any wrap under the load is a choker; a choker has one end passing through the eye on the other end. People call a doubled sling a bridle; a bridle is several separate legs gathered in one top fitting. People think the hitch does not affect capacity; the choker column on a tag is lower than the vertical column. People apply the choker reduction to a basket, or invent a 50 percent basket rule; a basket with vertical legs and an adequate bend is rated at twice vertical. People use 3, 10 or 15 degrees as the vertical allowance; it is five degrees or less from vertical.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Vertical hitch is a method of supporting a load by a single, vertical part or leg of the sling.
Choker hitch is a sling configuration with one end of the sling passing under the load and through an end attachment, handle or eye on the other end of the sling.
Basket hitch is a sling configuration whereby the sling is passed under the load and has both ends, end attachments, eyes or handles on the hook or a single master link.
provided that an angle of loading of five degrees or less from the vertical may be considered a vertical angle of loading

summary: The three basic hitches are the vertical hitch, the choker and the basket. A vertical hitch carries the load on one vertical part of the sling. A choker passes one end under the load and through the eye on the other end. A basket passes the sling under the load with both ends on the hook. The hitch you choose changes how much the same sling can carry, which is why sling tags list a rating for each hitch.
title: Choose vertical, choker or basket hitches and know their relative capacity

exam: Expect two-leg tension calculations with round numbers and a given or standard factor, plus questions about how tension changes as the angle flattens. Check whether the angle is measured from horizontal or vertical. Wrong answers usually come from skipping the factor, applying it to the whole load, or dividing instead of multiplying.
hard: The same factor can be described two ways: 60 degrees from horizontal is 30 degrees from vertical, and both give about 1.15. Check which reference the question uses before you pick a factor. Do the steps in order: split the load among the legs that carry it, then multiply each share by the factor. The factor is the reciprocal of the vertical fraction, so multiplying by 0.50 or 0.71 instead of dividing gets it backwards.
mistakes: People use 1.15 for a 30-degree angle from horizontal; at 30 degrees from horizontal the factor is 2.00, and 1.15 belongs to 60 degrees. People mix up the references; 60 degrees from vertical also needs 2.00. People use 1.41 for every angle; it applies only at 45 degrees. People multiply by the vertical fraction or divide by the factor; an 8,000 lb load on two legs with a 1.25 factor gives 4,000 × 1.25 = 5,000 lb per leg, not 3,200. People apply the factor to the whole load or skip it; split the load first, then multiply each share.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Angle of loading is the inclination of a leg or branch of a sling measured from the horizontal or vertical plane as shown in Fig. N-184-5; provided that an angle of loading of five degrees or less from the vertical may be considered a vertical angle of loading.

summary: When a sling leg leans away from vertical, it has to pull harder to hold up the same share of the load. Leg tension equals the leg's vertical share times the load angle factor. Measured from horizontal, the factors are about 1.15 at 60 degrees, 1.41 at 45 degrees and 2.00 at 30 degrees. This is physics, and it is why flat sling angles overload slings and fittings that look fine on paper.
title: Compute sling leg tension from sling angle (load angle factor)

exam: Expect questions on how many legs to count for a rigid load, why a four-leg table rating matches the three-leg rating, and what a slack leg tells you. Scenarios often show one leg slack and offer answers that add all four ratings.
hard: There are two separate ideas here and they get swapped. The table rating basis treats a four-leg bridle like three legs. The field assumption for a rigid load is two legs carrying the weight. Both are industry practice, not federal numbers. Adjusting one leg only changes which legs carry the load; an equalizing device is what actually makes legs share.
mistakes: People assume four legs share equally on a rigid load; a rigid load cannot flex to even out tension, so plan on two legs. People double the two-leg rating or add up all four leg ratings; the tables give the fourth leg no credit because it may carry nothing. People count three legs on a rigid load when one goes slack; the weight shifts mainly to the diagonal pair. People overcorrect and assume one leg carries everything; a balanced load settles until at least two legs carry it. People think shortening a leg guarantees four-way sharing; only an equalizing device does that.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Bridle wire rope sling is a sling composed of multiple wire rope legs with the top ends gathered in a fitting that goes over the lifting hook.

summary: A bridle is several sling legs gathered in one fitting over the hook. In theory four legs share a load equally. In practice small differences in leg length, lug height and CG location mean a rigid load ends up hanging on fewer legs. Many sling tables rate a four-leg bridle the same as three legs, and riggers plan rigid loads on two legs, usually a diagonal pair.
title: Know why only some legs of a multi-leg bridle carry the load

exam: Expect a quick ratio problem, such as a pin and rope diameter leading to an efficiency, and questions that offer clear-length or design-factor numbers as distractors. Check whether the problem gives a diameter or a radius before dividing.
hard: Use diameter on both sides of the ratio, never a radius. D/d is not the same as the federal minimum clear lengths of 10, 40 and 96 rope diameters, and it is not the 5 to 1 design factor. The efficiency table values are close together and easy to read off the wrong row.
mistakes: People use the pin's radius or the rope's radius; a 4-in pin under a 1-in rope is 4:1, which is about 75 percent. People read 65 or 75 percent for a 1:1 bend; 1:1 leaves only about half the strength. People think bending barely matters; the 91 percent figure applies only to a gentle 20:1 bend. People confuse D/d with the clear-length rules or the design factor; 10 and 40 diameters are minimum clear lengths, 96 is grommet circumference, 5 to 1 is a strength ratio, and the basket basis is 25:1. People treat every pin as the worst case; only a pin as thin as the rope gives 1:1.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: D/d is the diameter of the object a sling bends around divided by the diameter of the rope. Tight bends lose wire rope strength. As industry practice, approximate efficiencies are about 50 percent at 1:1, 65 percent at 2:1, 75 percent at 4:1 and about 91 percent at 20:1, and basket ratings for wire rope slings commonly assume a D/d of 25:1. Bending a sling around a small pin or a sharp corner can cut its strength well below the tag rating.
title: Apply D/d (bend diameter to rope diameter) to sling efficiency

exam: Expect photo-style or described scenarios asking which connection is correct or what is wrong with a setup, like a tip-loaded hook, a side-loaded eyebolt or a screw pin under a moving sling. Wrong answers tend to offer a substitute, like a latch, a nut, a bigger hook or a derate, in place of correcting the geometry.
hard: Several fixes look reasonable and do not work. A nut does not take the place of a shoulder. A latch does not fix a tip-loaded hook. A bigger hook does not fix a poor fit. The screw-pin shackle hazard is a pin that turns and loosens under load, not frequent removal and not the pin carrying load.
mistakes: People angle-load a plain eyebolt with the eye lined up; only a shouldered eyebolt, seated and aligned, takes angular load, at a reduced rating. People think tightening a nut acts as a shoulder; it does not give the same support. People turn the eye across the sling pull or split the difference; both bend the eye, so align it with the sling plane. People think a closed latch makes tip loading acceptable; the eye has to seat in the bowl. People think a higher-capacity hook or a guessed derate solves a poor fit; fix the connection geometry instead. People avoid screw-pin shackles for frequent rigging changes; that is a normal use, and the concern is the pin rotating under load.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Hooks with self-closing latches or their equivalent must be used. Exception: “J” hooks are permitted to be used for setting wooden trusses.

summary: Shackles, hooks, eyebolts and beams link the sling to the load and the hook, and each one has its own rating and its own right way to load it. These are industry practices from manufacturer and consensus guidance. Load a hook in the bowl, never on the tip. Use a bolt-type shackle where a sling or load could roll the pin. Load a plain eyebolt straight in line only, and align a shouldered eyebolt with the sling plane before any angular load. A spreader beam works in compression and a lifting beam works in bending. When workers are in the fall zone hooking or connecting, the federal rule calls for hooks with self-closing latches or the equivalent.
title: Use shackles, hooks, eyebolts, spreader and lifting beams correctly

exam: Expect short scenarios, like a rigger knotting a leg, a worker standing under a load at knee height, or a basket with the CG outside the slings, where you pick the rule being broken or the correct action. Watch for answers that add a condition the rule does not have.
hard: These rules have no thresholds, so watch for answers that add a height, a capacity percent or a condition that is not there. The crane chart limits the crane, not the sling, and each component has its own rating. Balance and capacity are separate problems: a strong enough basket still drops a load if the CG sits outside the baskets.
mistakes: People think the hazard starts at liftoff; the rule covers loads about to be lifted, and the moment the slings tighten and the load breaks free is one of the riskiest points. People add a height or percent-of-capacity threshold to the keep-clear rule; there is none. People shorten slings with knots, clips or twists; all are makeshift and prohibited, and kinked legs are prohibited too. People use the crane chart or a shackle rating as the sling's limit; the limit is the safe working load marked on the sling. People think a tag line or test lift fixes an unbalanced basket; the fix is to re-rig so the CG sits between the baskets.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Slings shall not be shortened with knots or bolts or other makeshift devices.
Sling legs shall not be kinked.
Slings used in a basket hitch shall have the loads balanced to prevent slippage.
All employees shall be kept clear of loads about to be lifted and of suspended loads.
Shock loading is prohibited.
A sling shall not be pulled from under a load when the load is resting on the sling.
Employers must not load a sling in excess of its recommended safe working load as prescribed by the sling manufacturer on the identification markings permanently affixed to the sling.

summary: The sling rules list the basic practices for every sling, every time. Do not use damaged slings. Do not shorten slings with knots, bolts or makeshift devices, and do not kink the legs. Do not exceed the rated capacity marked on the sling. Balance basket loads so they cannot slip. Pad sharp edges. Keep people clear of loads about to be lifted and of suspended loads. Keep hands out from between sling and load, do not shock load, and do not pull a sling out from under a resting load.
title: Apply the sling safe-operating practices

exam: Expect scenarios where a softener has shifted, or where a crew proposes a workaround like slower hoisting, a different hitch, a stronger sling or a wire rope swap, and you pick the correct action. The correct answer usually puts protection at the sharp edge before hoisting goes on.
hard: The rule has no trigger beyond a sharp edge touching the sling: no load percentage, no hitch type, no sling material and no visible damage first. Protection has to be at the edge itself. Padding on flat surfaces does nothing. If a softener slips out during the lift, stop and fix it before hoisting continues.
mistakes: People think light loads or spare capacity waive protection; the rule has no load threshold. People think only fiber or synthetic slings need it; the rule covers slings in general, wire rope and chain included. People wait for visible wear; protection comes before damage, not after. People add padding on the flat faces or change the hitch; neither helps if the sling still bears on the same sharp edge. People hoist slowly past a displaced softener, or think a sling that is not sliding is safe; a loaded sling on a bare edge needs protection before the lift continues.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Slings shall be padded or protected from the sharp edges of their loads.

Synthetic slings are protected from: Abrasive, sharp or acute edges, and configurations that could cause a reduction of the sling's rated capacity, such as distortion or localized compression. Note: Requirements for the protection of wire rope slings are contained in 29 CFR 1926.251(c)(9).

summary: A loaded sling pressed against a sharp edge can be cut or crushed in seconds. The rule says slings are to be padded or protected from the sharp edges of their loads. When rigging is used for crane assembly or disassembly, synthetic slings are also to be protected from abrasive, sharp or acute edges and from configurations that cause distortion or localized compression. Softeners, corner protectors and edge guards do this job.
title: Protect slings from sharp edges

exam: Expect questions about who inspects and when, broken-wire counts with close-together distractors, and scenarios where a sling is damaged mid-shift. Read whether the count is within one rope lay and whether the wires are scattered or in one strand.
hard: Two roles get mixed up: being the operator, rigger or signal person does not by itself make someone the inspector, who has to be both competent and designated. The daily inspection is the floor, so a pinch, a drop or a hard edge contact during the day calls for another look before the sling is reused. The 12-month maximum for a thorough periodic inspection is written for alloy chain slings, and lighter use does not stretch it.
mistakes: People think the operator, signal person or a qualified rigger is automatically the inspector; the inspector is a competent person designated by the employer. People use running-rope broken-wire counts or bump the single-strand count to six; sling removal is ten random or five in one strand, within one rope lay. People think the daily check covers the whole day; inspect again when an event like a pinch or crush happens. People substitute a test lift for that inspection; a test lift does not find damage. People treat six months as the universal limit or stretch to two years for light use; for alloy chain slings the periodic interval is set by service but never longer than 12 months.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Each day before being used, the sling and all fastenings and attachments shall be inspected for damage or defects by a competent person designated by the employer. Additional inspections shall be performed during sling use, where service conditions warrant. Damaged or defective slings shall be immediately removed from service.
Ten randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay, or five broken wires in one strand in one rope lay.
Wear or scraping of one-third the original diameter of outside individual wires.
Kinking, crushing, bird caging or any other damage resulting in distortion of the wire rope structure.

In addition to the inspection required by paragraph (d) of this section, a thorough periodic inspection of alloy steel chain slings in use shall be made on a regular basis, to be determined on the basis of (A) frequency of sling use; (B) severity of service conditions; (C) nature of lifts being made; and (D) experience gained on the service life of slings used in similar circumstances. Such inspections shall in no event be at intervals greater than once every 12 months.

summary: Each day before use, a competent person designated by the employer inspects every sling and all its fastenings and attachments for damage or defects. When service conditions call for it, more inspections are done during use, and damaged slings come out of service immediately. For wire rope slings, removal criteria include ten randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay or five broken wires in one strand in one lay, wear of one-third of outside wire diameter, kinking, crushing, bird caging, heat damage, damaged end attachments, bad hooks and corrosion.
title: Inspect slings daily and remove damaged ones

exam: Expect identification-list items with one entry swapped, interval questions, and hook removal numbers with reversed distractors. Also expect questions on who inspects versus who proof tests.
hard: The hook numbers get swapped: removal is for throat opening of more than 15 percent or twist of more than 10 degrees, and either one alone is enough. The fourth identification item is reach, not a serial number or a date. Proof testing of new or repaired slings is done by the sling manufacturer or an equivalent entity, but the periodic inspection is done by the employer's designated competent person.
mistakes: People name a proof-test certificate, purchase date or serial number as the missing ID item; the four items are size, grade, rated capacity and reach. People treat three or six months as the maximum, or allow two years for light use; the maximum is 12 months. People reverse the hook numbers or use one number for both; it is more than 15 percent opening or more than 10 degrees twist. People think the operator or a crew-picked rigger can do the thorough inspection; it is a competent person designated by the employer. People think the periodic inspection has to be done by the manufacturer; that is proof testing, not inspection.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Sling identification. Alloy steel chain slings shall have permanently affixed durable identification stating size, grade, rated capacity, and reach.
The employer shall make and maintain a record of the most recent month in which each alloy steel chain sling was thoroughly inspected, and shall make such record available for examination.

The thorough inspection of alloy steel chain slings shall be performed by a competent person designated by the employer, and shall include a thorough inspection for wear, defective welds, deformation and increase in length. Where such defects or deterioration are present, the sling shall be immediately removed from service.

Slings shall be removed from service if hooks are cracked, have been opened more than 15 percent of the normal throat opening measured at the narrowest point or twisted more than 10 degrees from the plane of the unbent hook.

Safe operating temperatures. Employers must permanently remove an alloy steel-chain slings from service if it is heated above 1000 degrees F. When exposed to service temperatures in excess of 600 degrees F, employers must reduce the maximum working-load limits permitted by the chain manufacturer in accordance with the chain or sling manufacturer's recommendations.

Proof testing. The employer shall ensure that before use, each new, repaired, or reconditioned alloy steel chain sling, including all welded components in the sling assembly, shall be proof tested by the sling manufacturer or equivalent entity, in accordance with paragraph 5.2 of the American Society of Testing and Materials Specification A391-65, which is incorporated by reference as specified in § 1910.6 (ANSI G61.1-1968). The employer shall retain a certificate of the proof test and shall make it available for examination.

summary: Alloy steel chain slings carry permanent identification stating size, grade, rated capacity and reach. Beyond the daily check, a competent person designated by the employer gives them a thorough periodic inspection for wear, defective welds, deformation and stretch. The interval depends on use and service but is never more than 12 months, and the employer keeps a record of the most recent month each sling was inspected. Chain slings come out of service if heated above 1000 °F, and the working load limit is reduced above 600 °F.
title: Know alloy chain sling rules

exam: Expect number-matching items where the distractors are the right numbers for a different sling type or core. Expect removal-condition questions that combine or reverse the hook criteria. Identify the sling construction and core type before you answer.
hard: The figures 10, 40 and 96 are each tied to a specific sling type and are easy to swap. The two temperatures belong to different cores: 200 °F means removal for fiber core, and 400 °F means follow the manufacturer for nonfiber core. Hook removal is opening over 15 percent or twist over 10 degrees, and either one is enough.
mistakes: People apply 400 °F, or a guess like 250 or 300 °F, to fiber core; fiber core is removed above 200 °F. People use 40 or 96 diameters, or an invented 20, for 6 × 19 and 6 × 37 slings; the minimum is 10. People think welded end attachments are proof tested at 1.25, 1.5 or 5 times rating; the rule is twice rated capacity, and 5 is a design factor. People think a hook has to be both opened and twisted before removal; either condition alone requires it, and no 30 percent allowance exists. People think an opened hook can be bent back; it has been overstressed and the sling comes out of service.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Sling use. Employers must use only wire-rope slings that have permanently affixed and legible identification markings as prescribed by the manufacturer, and that indicate the recommended safe working load for the type(s) of hitch(es) used, the angle upon which it is based, and the number of legs if more than one.
Cable laid and 6 × 19 and 6 × 37 slings shall have a minimum clear length of wire rope 10 times the component rope diameter between splices, sleeves or end fittings.
Braided slings shall have a minimum clear length of wire rope 40 times the component rope diameter between the loops or end fittings.
Cable laid grommets, strand laid grommets and endless slings shall have a minimum circumferential length of 96 times their body diameter.

Safe operating temperatures. Fiber core wire rope slings of all grades shall be permanently removed from service if they are exposed to temperatures in excess of 200 °F. When nonfiber core wire rope slings of any grade are used at temperatures above 400 °F or below minus 60 °F, recommendations of the sling manufacturer regarding use at that temperature shall be followed.

All welded end attachments shall not be used unless proof tested by the manufacturer or equivalent entity at twice their rated capacity prior to initial use. The employer shall retain a certificate of the proof test, and make it available for examination.
Hooks that have been opened more than 15 percent of the normal throat opening measured at the narrowest point or twisted more than 10 degrees from the plane of the unbent hook.

summary: Wire rope slings carry legible ID showing the safe working load for each hitch, the angle the rating is based on, and the number of legs if more than one. Minimum clear length between fittings is 10 rope diameters for cable laid, 6 × 19 and 6 × 37 slings and 40 for braided slings, and grommets and endless slings need a circumference of 96 body diameters. Fiber core slings exposed above 200 °F are permanently removed, while nonfiber core slings used above 400 °F or below minus 60 °F follow the sling manufacturer's recommendations. Welded end attachments are proof tested at twice rated capacity before first use.
title: Know wire rope sling rules (length, temperature, end attachments, removal)

exam: Expect items with one entry swapped, such as attachment method, tuck count, required ID items, or who may repair. Also expect environment scenarios pairing a web material with a chemical or a temperature. Note whether the sling is web or rope, and manila or synthetic.
hard: Tuck counts sit close together: manila eye splices take three tucks and short splices six, while synthetic eye splices take four and short splices eight. Web slings can be repaired by a qualified entity, but fiber rope slings cannot be repaired at all. Chemical limits split by material: nylon stays away from acids and phenolics, and polyester and polypropylene stay away from caustics.
mistakes: People think rivets, clamps or adhesive are fine if they reach full strength; stitching is the only permitted method. People use three, six or eight tucks for a synthetic eye splice; the minimum is four. People think a qualified rigger, supervisor or experienced operator can repair a web sling; only a sling manufacturer or equivalent entity can. People list diameter, length or manufacturing date as the missing ID item on a multi-leg fiber rope sling; the required item is the number of legs. People think a fiber rope sling can be repaired and returned to service; repaired or reconditioned fiber rope slings are prohibited.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Sling identification. Each sling shall be marked or coded to show the rated capacities for each type of hitch and type of synthetic web material.

Attachment of end fittings to webbing and formation of eyes. Stitching shall be the only method used to attach end fittings to webbing and to form eyes. The thread shall be in an even pattern and contain a sufficient number of stitches to develop the full breaking strength of the sling.
Synthetic web slings which are repaired shall not be used unless repaired by a sling manufacturer or an equivalent entity.

Each repaired sling shall be proof tested by the manufacturer or equivalent entity to twice the rated capacity prior to its return to service. The employer shall retain a certificate of the proof test and make it available for examination.

Sling use. Employers must use natural and synthetic fiber-rope slings that have permanently affixed and legible identification markings stating the rated capacity for the type(s) of hitch(es) used and the angle upon which it is based, type of fiber material, and the number of legs if more than one.
In manila rope, eye splices shall consist of at least three full tucks, and short splices shall consist of at least six full tucks, three on each side of the splice center line.
In synthetic fiber rope, eye splices shall consist of at least four full tucks, and short splices shall consist of at least eight full tucks, four on each side of the center line.
Repairs. Only fiber rope slings made from new rope shall be used. Use of repaired or reconditioned fiber rope slings is prohibited.

Safe operating temperatures. Synthetic web slings of polyester and nylon shall not be used at temperatures in excess of 180 °F. Polypropylene web slings shall not be used at temperatures in excess of 200 °F.
Nylon web slings shall not be used where fumes, vapors, sprays, mists or liquids of acids or phenolics are present.
Polyester and polypropylene web slings shall not be used where fumes, vapors, sprays, mists or liquids of caustics are present.

summary: Synthetic web slings are marked with rated capacities for each hitch and the web material. End fittings and eyes are attached by stitching only. Repairs are done only by a sling manufacturer or equivalent entity and proof tested to twice rated capacity. Fiber rope slings are marked with ratings per hitch, the angle the rating is based on, the fiber type and the number of legs if more than one. Synthetic rope eye splices take at least four full tucks, and repaired or reconditioned fiber rope slings are not used at all. Heat limits are 180 °F for nylon and polyester web, 200 °F for polypropylene web, and minus 20 to 180 °F for fiber rope without derating.
title: Know synthetic web and fiber rope sling rules

exam: Expect scenarios asking whether a line is required and what kind, plus power-line items about tag line material. Watch for answers that swap the trigger for alignment or visibility, or that offer observation or slower speed instead of a line.
hard: The trigger is narrow: hazardous rotation, not any rotation, not precise alignment and not poor visibility, though those can make a line useful as good practice. Either a tag line or a restraint line satisfies the rule, and you do not need both. Once the need is established, no substitute like slow hoisting or extra watching meets it. For non-conductive, the line itself has to be non-conductive; an insulated grip or grounding does not count.
mistakes: People think any possible rotation, alignment work or limited visibility triggers the requirement; the trigger is a line being needed to prevent hazardous rotation. People think only a hand-held tag line, or only a fixed restraint line, counts, or that both are needed; either one satisfies the rule. People substitute extra spotters, slow hoisting or a trial lift once the need is known; a tag or restraint line goes on. People think a conductive or grounded line, or an insulated handhold, is acceptable near power lines; the line has to be non-conductive.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: A tag or restraint line must be used if necessary to prevent rotation of the load that would be hazardous.
If tag lines are used, they must be non-conductive.

summary: A tag line or restraint line lets a worker control a load's rotation from a distance instead of grabbing the load. The rule requires a tag or restraint line when one is needed to prevent rotation that would be hazardous. Near power lines, the power-line provisions add that any tag line used is non-conductive.
title: Use tag lines and restraint lines

exam: Expect who-is-responsible items naming several roles, and scenarios with connectors or riggers in the fall zone where you pick the conditions that apply. Look for whether the lift is A/D or production with workers in the fall zone.
hard: A job title does not make someone a qualified rigger, whether that is A/D director, operator, signal person, supervisor or the worker hooking on, and neither does a competent person designation. Qualification is shown by knowledge, training and experience solving rigging problems. One class or general training is not automatically enough, and the federal rules do not require a specific rigger card, though a card can serve as evidence. Taglines do not remove the requirement while connectors are in the fall zone.
mistakes: People hand A/D rigging to the A/D director, the operator or a competent person; it goes to a qualified rigger. People think general training or one sling course makes someone qualified; qualification means showing the ability to solve rigging problems. People think a rigger card is mandatory; the federal rules require qualification, not certification, which is required of crane operators. People think the signal person or the worker hooking on is automatically qualified, or that supervising unqualified riggers is enough; the person doing the rigging has to be qualified. People think taglines replace the requirement when workers are in the fall zone; they do not.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The rigging work is done by a qualified rigger.

When employees are engaged in hooking, unhooking, or guiding the load, or in the initial connection of a load to a component or structure and are within the fall zone, all of the following criteria must be met:
The materials being hoisted must be rigged to prevent unintentional displacement.
The materials must be rigged by a qualified rigger.

summary: Two situations call specifically for a qualified rigger. One is rigging used for crane assembly or disassembly. The other is when workers are in the fall zone hooking, unhooking or guiding a load or making the initial connection; in that case the materials are also rigged to prevent unintentional displacement, and hooks with self-closing latches or the equivalent are used. What counts is whether the person doing the rigging is actually qualified, not their job title.
title: Know when a qualified rigger is required

exam: Expect a subtraction problem from a gross chart rating with the block and rigging listed separately, and who-is-responsible items. Read every listed weight and check whether the chart value is gross or net.
hard: Every deduction counts, and it is common to subtract the block and forget the slings, or the reverse. When the indicator method is used for verification, the 75 percent trigger is measured at the longest radius of the lift, not at pickup, at the start of swing or at an average radius. Others can supply weights, but verifying capacity stays with the operator.
mistakes: People treat gross chart capacity as payload; with a 12,000 lb rating, a 1,000 lb block and 500 lb of rigging, the payload limit is 10,500 lb. People subtract only the block or only the rigging; subtract both. People use 50 or 85 percent for the indicator trigger, or think only near-capacity loads need checking; verification kicks in above 75 percent. People check at the pickup radius, the start of swing or an average radius; the longest radius of the lift governs. People hand capacity verification to the rigger, signal person or supervisor; the rule puts that duty on the operator.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Load weight. The operator must verify that the load is within the rated capacity of the equipment by at least one of the following methods:

The operator must begin hoisting the load to determine, using a load weighing device, load moment indicator, rated capacity indicator, or rated capacity limiter, if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used during the lift operation. If it does, the operator must not proceed with the lift until he/she verifies the weight of the load in accordance with paragraph (o)(3)(i) of this section.
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

summary: The hook block, the overhaul ball and all the rigging below the boom tip count as part of the load on the crane. Load charts generally give gross capacity, so you subtract the block, the ball, slings, shackles and any spreader to find what is left for the payload, as the chart's notes direct. The operator is the one who has to verify the load is within rated capacity.
title: Use hook blocks and overhaul balls; know their weight counts

exam: Expect a moment problem with two or three parts and round numbers, and a two-leg share problem with the CG off-center. Answers built from averages, inverted ratios or the wrong direction are common, so check that your answer sits between the parts and closer to the heavy one.
hard: The shift goes toward the added weight, and you divide by the total weight, not the weight of one part. The leg-share rule feels backwards because each leg's share depends on the distance to the opposite leg. In the assembly and disassembly rules, the CG has to be identified when the stability method depends on it, not at some capacity percentage, and a load cell gives weight, not location.
mistakes: People average the positions, such as 10 and 16 ft, or divide by one part's weight; divide the total moment by the total weight. People shift the CG away from the added weight or invert the weight ratio; the combined CG moves toward the heavier addition by the distance times added weight over total weight. People think the far leg carries more; the near leg carries more. People assume vertical legs share equally or by their ratings; they share equally only when the CG is centered, and a rating is a limit, not a share. People think weighing the load locates the CG, or that an uncertain CG calls for a derate or a written calculation; the rule calls for measures that prevent unintended dangerous movement.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The center of gravity of the load must be identified if that is necessary for the method used for maintaining stability.

Where there is insufficient information to accurately identify the center of gravity, measures designed to prevent unintended dangerous movement resulting from an inaccurate identification of the center of gravity must be used. (See Non-mandatory appendix B of this subpart for an example.)

summary: To find the CG of a load made of parts, multiply each part's weight by its distance from a reference point, add the products, and divide by the total weight. For example, a 4,000 lb skid with its CG at 10 ft and a 2,000 lb pump at 16 ft give 64,000 ÷ 6,000, so the combined CG is at about 10.7 ft. Put another way, the CG shifts 6 ft × 2,000/6,000 = 2 ft toward the pump, landing at 12 ft. Correction: that shift method measures from the skid's own CG, so check the numbers in the problem and pick one method. For two vertical legs, each leg's share is the load times the distance from the CG to the other leg, divided by the span, so the leg nearer the CG carries more.
title: Locate the center of gravity of a composite or irregular load by moments; leg loads when the CG is off-center

exam: Items ask you to define a rope lay, name a rope part from a description, or count wires over the right length. Some items mix construction with inspection, for example a running rope with three broken wires in one strand in one lay. Read whether the rope is standard running rope, rotation resistant rope or a pendant before you choose a count.
hard: Strand lay and rope lay are two different things. Strand lay is wires going around the strand. Rope lay is one strand making a full turn around the whole rope, which is a longer distance. A crest-to-crest measurement is only part of a lay; on a six-strand rope it is about one-sixth. Core protrusion also changes category depending on whether the rope is standard or rotation resistant.
