mistakes: People measure from one crest to the next; one rope lay ends where the same strand comes back around. People use the strand lay for the count; broken wires are counted in one rope lay. People call six rope diameters a lay; that is the counting length for rotation resistant rope, and lay length depends on how the rope is built. People think steel core showing between strands is normal wear; in standard rope it is a Category I distortion, and in rotation resistant rope core protrusion is Category III. People call three broken wires in one strand a broken strand; that is a Category II wire count, and a broken strand means the whole strand has parted.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: In running wire ropes: Six randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay or three broken wires in one strand in one rope lay, where a rope lay is the length along the rope in which one strand makes a complete revolution around the rope.
Significant distortion of the wire rope structure such as kinking, crushing, unstranding, birdcaging, signs of core failure or steel core protrusion between the outer strands.
In rotation resistant wire rope, core protrusion or other distortion indicating core failure.
A broken strand.

summary: Wire rope is built from wires twisted into strands, and strands laid around a core. The lay is how the strands wind around the rope. You need these words because the inspection rules count broken wires per rope lay and per strand, and they sort core damage into categories. If you can't find a rope lay on a real rope, you can't do the count.
title: Name wire rope parts (wires, strands, core, lay)

exam: Expect number items: strand counts, the 5 and 3.5 design factors, and the 18 times D/d. Expect scenarios where a lift is repetitive or a single lift, and you decide whether the rope can be used. Watch for wording like "duty cycle," "repetitive" and "in writing."
hard: The type thresholds are easy to mix up: Type I has at least 15 outer strands, Type II at least 10, and Type III no more than nine. The normal design factor is 5 and the absolute floor is 3.5. Each has its own exceptions. Type I can go below 5 only with written approval from both the rope manufacturer and the equipment manufacturer. Types II and III can go below 5 only for non-duty-cycle, non-repetitive lifts, and only when per-lift conditions are met. On a boom hoist, the drum and all sheaves need at least 18 times the rope diameter.
mistakes: People give Type I the Type II count of 10 or the Type III count of nine; Type I needs at least 15 outer strands. People treat 5 as the absolute floor, or quote 4.0 or 3.0; 5 is the normal minimum and 3.5 is the floor for every type. People think inspecting before each lift makes repetitive work acceptable below a design factor of 5; Types II and III below 5 are barred from duty cycle and repetitive lifts. People use the ASME sheave value of 16 times, or round up to 20; for boom hoist use, the federal rule sets 18 times the nominal rope diameter. People forget the single-lift exception exists; Type II below 5 is allowed for a non-repetitive lift when a qualified person inspects the rope, dynamic effects are kept down, and the lift is recorded.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: It has at least 15 outer strands and comprises an assembly of at least three layers of strands laid helically over a center in two operations.
It has at least 10 outer strands and comprises an assembly of two or more layers of strands laid helically over a center in two or three operations.
It has no more than nine outer strands, and comprises an assembly of two layers of strands laid helically over a center in two operations.
Types II and III with an operating design factor of less than 5 must not be used for duty cycle or repetitive lifts.
Rotation resistant ropes (including Types I, II and III) must have an operating design factor of no less than 3.5.
Type I must have an operating design factor of no less than 5, except where the wire rope manufacturer and the equipment manufacturer approves the design factor, in writing.
Types II and III must have an operating design factor of no less than 5, except where the requirements of paragraph (e)(3) of this section are met.
In making this determination, more than one broken wire in any one rope lay must be considered a hazard.
The drum must provide a first layer rope pitch diameter of not less than 18 times the nominal diameter of the rope used.
except that the minimum pitch diameter for sheaves used in multiple rope reeving is 18 times the nominal diameter of the rope used (instead of the value of 16 specified in section 5-1.3.2(d)).

summary: Rotation resistant rope has layers of strands laid in opposite directions so the hook block doesn't spin on long single-part or high lifts. The rules split it into Types I, II and III by outer strand count, set design factors for each, and limit its use on boom hoists. It is less forgiving than standard rope, so it gets special attention during inspection.
title: Know rotation-resistant rope rules

exam: Items show a reeving sketch or description and ask how many parts are supporting the block. Others give a crane type and a rope type and ask whether it can be used for boom hoist reeving. Watch for answer choices that hand the decision to a person or a maintenance step; the rule does not allow either.
hard: To count parts of line, count every segment running between the boom head and the block. That includes the center segments and a dead end anchored at the block becket. The boom hoist rope limits look alike but work differently. The fiber core limit is a ban with one exception, derricks. The rotation resistant limit is a conditional allowance under (e)(4)(ii).
mistakes: People leave out the dead end at the block, or the inner segments; every segment between head and block holds up load and counts as a part. People think hydraulic cranes or crawlers are exempt from the fiber core boom hoist ban; the only exception is derricks. People think lubrication, the right diameter or a qualified person's approval makes fiber core boom hoist rope acceptable; none of those creates an exception. People think rotation resistant rope is banned from boom hoists; it is allowed when the (e)(4)(ii) conditions are met, and the derrick exception does not apply to it. People divide only the load by the parts; with a 36,000 lb load and 4,000 lb of block and rigging, the rope carries 40,000 lb.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Fiber core ropes must not be used for boom hoist reeving, except for derricks.
Rotation resistant ropes must be used for boom hoist reeving only where the requirements of paragraph (e)(4)(ii) of this section are met.
The employer must comply with all manufacturer procedures applicable to the operational functions of equipment, including its use with attachments.

summary: Reeving is the path the rope takes from the drum, over the boom head sheaves and through the hook block, and it follows the manufacturer's procedures. Parts of line are the rope segments that hold up the hook block. The rules also limit which rope can go on a boom hoist. Fiber core rope is out except on derricks, and rotation resistant rope is allowed only under added conditions.
title: Reeve to the manufacturer's procedures; count parts of line

exam: Expect a short no-calculator problem. You get a load, block and rigging weights, a hoist line pull and a rope allowable, and you find the minimum parts. Wrong answers usually leave out the block, use the higher limit, or round down. Check the total weight first, then the governing pull, then round up.
hard: The block weight is deducted from chart capacity and is also carried by the rope, so it belongs in both checks. The allowable pull is the lower of two limits, the drum and the rope, and you never average them. The answer always rounds up, even 4.1 becomes 5, and it doesn't have to be an even number.
mistakes: People leave the hook block and rigging out of the total; the rope parts carry them too. People use chart capacity instead of the actual suspended weight; parts are figured from what is really on the hook. People round 4.3 down to 4; a minimum always rounds up, and rounding down overloads every part. People use the drum rating when the rope is weaker, average the two, or treat the design factor as spare capacity; the lower limit governs and the design factor is already built in. People think reeving has to be even or add a spare part; odd parts are normal, and you only need the next whole number.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: This is the calculation that tells you how many parts of line you need. Add up everything hanging from the rope, which is the load plus the hook block and rigging. Divide that by the allowable line pull, and round up to the next whole part. The allowable line pull is the lower of the hoist's line pull and the rope's allowable load. If you get this wrong, every part is overloaded.
title: Compute parts of line from load and allowable line pull

exam: Expect items that give a hoist pull and a rope allowable and ask which one governs. Expect items about which drum layer gives the most pull, and about what the rope design basis is. Watch for choices that cite stall pull, job loads or a higher layer speed as the basis.
hard: Line pull is not one fixed number. At the same torque, pull is highest on the first layer and drops on each outer layer, while line speed goes up. The design-criteria rule covers all wire rope except rotation resistant rope, so it includes standing ropes and whip lines. Its reference point is the equipment's rated capacity, not hoist pull or the planned loads on one job.
mistakes: People think the hoist's 12,000 lb pull lets a rope rated at 10,000 lb carry 12,000 lb; the lower limit controls. People average the two limits to 11,000 lb; that is still 1,000 lb over the rope. People treat the design factor as capacity they can use; it covers wear and shock and is already in the allowable pull. People think pull peaks on the outer layer because speed is highest there; pull is torque divided by radius, so the outer layer gives the least pull. People think the design criteria cover only running ropes, or exempt auxiliary lines; everything except rotation resistant rope is covered, pendants and whip lines included.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Wire rope design criteria: Wire rope (other than rotation resistant rope) must comply with either Option (1) or Option (2) of this section, as follows:

Option (2). Wire rope must be designed to have, in relation to the equipment's rated capacity, a sufficient minimum breaking force and design factor so that compliance with the applicable inspection provisions in § 1926.1413 will be an effective means of preventing sudden rope failure.

summary: Maximum line pull is what the hoist can pull, and it changes with the drum layer. The rope's safe working load is what the rope is allowed to carry, based on its breaking strength and design factor. Both are limits, and the lower one governs. Under the federal rule, rope other than rotation resistant rope is designed against the equipment's rated capacity.
title: Distinguish maximum line pull from the rope's safe working load

exam: Expect scenarios showing a wedge socket with a clip and asking whether it is correct. Expect "whose instructions" items for socketing and seizing. Expect sequence items about cutting rope. Watch for wording like "live," "dead" and "before cutting."
hard: With a wedge socket, people want to clip the tail back to the live line. That is exactly what the rule bars, unless a device made for dead-ending in a wedge socket is used. For socketing, the instructions come from the rope or fitting manufacturer, not from the crane, boom, sheave or hook manufacturer. Seizing has a strict order: both sides first, then the cut.
mistakes: People put the clip on the loaded live end, or clip the live end and dead end together; ordinary clips go on the unloaded dead end only. People think more clips, a different spacing or flipping the clip fixes a live-end clip; the problem is which part of the rope the clip grips. People think the crane, boom or hook manufacturer sets the socketing method; it is the wire rope or fitting manufacturer. People seize only the side they keep, or seize during or after the cut; seizings go on each side before cutting starts.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Wire rope clips used in conjunction with wedge sockets must be attached to the unloaded dead end of the rope only, except that the use of devices specifically designed for dead-ending rope in a wedge socket is permitted.
Socketing must be done in the manner specified by the manufacturer of the wire rope or fitting.
Prior to cutting a wire rope, seizings must be placed on each side of the point to be cut.
The length and number of seizings must be in accordance with the wire rope manufacturer's instructions.

summary: A termination is how the rope end is fastened, for example with a wedge socket, a poured or swaged socket, or clips. The rules cover three points. Clips used with a wedge socket go on the unloaded dead end only. Socketing follows the instructions of the wire rope or fitting manufacturer. Seizings go on both sides of a cut before you cut. A bad termination can let go at full load.
title: Install wedge sockets, clips and sockets correctly

exam: Expect a direct number item and scenarios such as lowering into an excavation or lowering the boom with no load. Watch for choices that offer a common field number like three or five, or a person who supposedly waives the rule.
hard: The count is per drum. Wraps on one drum do nothing for another drum. The rule covers the boom hoist drum even when the hook is empty, because the boom's own weight loads that rope. It has no exception for limit devices, spotters, or assembly and disassembly.
mistakes: People think one wrap anchors the rope, or that three or five is the federal minimum; the minimum is two full wraps. People apply it only to the main load drum; it applies to the load drum and the boom drum, each on its own. People think a limit device or a spotter replaces the rule, or that the A/D director can waive it; none of those changes the minimum. People count wraps across drums; a full main drum does not help the whip drum doing the lowering. People link wraps to spooling, design factor or reverse bending; the wraps are there to protect the anchorage.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Neither the load nor the boom must be lowered below the point where less than two full wraps of rope remain on their respective drums.

summary: Neither the load nor the boom can be lowered past the point where fewer than two full wraps stay on its drum. The wraps take strain off the rope anchorage at the drum, which is not built to hold the full line pull by itself. This matters most on deep lowering, below-grade picks and boom-down work.
title: Keep at least two full wraps on the drum

exam: Expect "which category" items from a description of a defect. Expect broken-wire counts tied to the rope type, and "who and when" items about the shift check. Watch for "running," "rotation resistant" and "pendant" in the stem, and for "begin" versus "complete."
hard: The broken-wire counts depend on the rope. Running rope: six random wires in one lay, or three in one strand in one lay. Rotation resistant rope: two in six diameters, or four in 30 diameters. Pendants: more than two in a lay beyond the end connections, or more than one at an end connection. Diameter loss is more than 5 percent of nominal. The critical review items also need particular attention: rotation resistant rope, boom and luffing hoist rope at reverse bends, drum flange, crossover and pickup points, terminal ends, and rope at saddles and limited-travel sheaves.
mistakes: People use the rotation resistant count or the pendant count on standard running rope; running rope uses six per lay or three in one strand. People think the diameter limit is 10 percent, a fixed fraction of an inch, or measured against the rope's diameter at installation; it is more than 5 percent from nominal. People say a qualified person must do it, or only the operator, or that it must be finished before the shift; a competent person begins it before the shift and may finish during it. People put broken wires in Category I or Category III; visible broken wires are Category II.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: A competent person must begin a visual inspection prior to each shift the equipment is used, which must be completed before or during that shift.
Untwisting (opening) of wire rope or booming down is not required as part of this inspection.

In running wire ropes: Six randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay or three broken wires in one strand in one rope lay, where a rope lay is the length along the rope in which one strand makes a complete revolution around the rope.
In rotation resistant ropes: Two randomly distributed broken wires in six rope diameters or four randomly distributed broken wires in 30 rope diameters.
In pendants or standing wire ropes: More than two broken wires in one rope lay located in rope beyond end connections and/or more than one broken wire in a rope lay located at an end connection.
A diameter reduction of more than 5% from nominal diameter.
In rotation resistant wire rope, core protrusion or other distortion indicating core failure.

summary: Before each shift the crane is used, a competent person starts a visual check of the running and standing ropes likely to be used that shift. The check can be finished during the shift. You look for apparent deficiencies in three categories. Category I is distortion, corrosion, heat or arc damage, and end connection problems. Category II is broken-wire counts and diameter loss. Category III is core failure in rotation resistant rope, power line contact, and a broken strand. You don't have to open the rope or boom down for this check.
title: Do the shift wire rope inspection (category I, II, III deficiencies)

exam: Expect scenarios where you pick the next step or the person who decides. Expect items on what happens after cutting a rope, and a short broken-wire count to decide whether the rope comes off. Watch for the category named in the stem, and for answer choices that add an approval or a grace period.
hard: Only Category I gets a hazard call. Categories II and III stop use outright until one of the listed fixes is made. Cutting out damage is allowed, but splicing is not. After shortening, the drum must still hold two wraps with the load or boom at its lowest position. An alternate Category II criterion has to be approved in writing by the wire rope manufacturer for that specific rope.
mistakes: People apply the Category I hazard call to Category III, or wait for the next inspection; Category III stops use right away. People think a shortened rope can be spliced back to length; splicing is prohibited. People check the wraps with the hook at its highest position, or require three or five wraps; it is two wraps at the lowest position. People give the Category I hazard call to the operator, an engineer or the A/D director; the competent person makes it. People think the crane manufacturer, an engineer or the competent person can approve an alternate criterion; only the wire rope manufacturer can, in writing.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: If a deficiency in Category I (see paragraph (a)(2)(i) of this section) is identified, an immediate determination must be made by the competent person as to whether the deficiency constitutes a safety hazard.

The employer complies with the wire rope manufacturer's established criterion for removal from service or a different criterion that the wire rope manufacturer has approved in writing for that specific wire rope (see § 1926.1417),
If a deficiency in Category III is identified, operations involving use of the wire rope in question must be prohibited until:
Repair of wire rope that contacted an energized power line is also prohibited.
Joining lengths of wire rope by splicing is prohibited.
If a rope is shortened under this paragraph, the employer must ensure that the drum will still have two wraps of wire when the load and/or boom is in its lowest position.

Where a wire rope is required to be removed from service under this section, either the equipment (as a whole) or the hoist with that wire rope must be tagged-out, in accordance with § 1926.1417(f)(1), until the wire rope is repaired or replaced.

summary: This skill is what happens after a deficiency is found. For Category I, the competent person decides right away whether it is a safety hazard. If it is, the rope is out until it is replaced or the damage is cut out. Category II stops use until the rope meets the rope manufacturer's removal criterion or a written alternative, or is replaced, or the damage is cut out. Category III stops use until the rope is replaced or the damage is cut out, and rope that touched a power line can't be repaired. A rope removed from service is tagged out at the equipment or at that hoist.
title: Apply broken-wire and other removal criteria

exam: Expect interval and "who" items, plus scenarios about a deficiency flagged at the annual. Watch for the words "not feasible," "running" and "standing" when the extension is offered as an answer.
hard: The regular annual interval is 12 months. The extra 6 months applies only to running ropes, and only when the inspection is not feasible because of the setup or site. Standing ropes in that situation are inspected at disassembly. When the qualified person finds a deficiency, that person decides whether it is a hazard. If it is not a hazard but needs watching, it gets checked in every monthly inspection.
mistakes: People think the annual interval is 6, 18 or 24 months; it is at least every 12 months, and the extra 6 months is a conditional extension. People think an operator certification, site authority or the A/D director role is enough to do the annual; it takes a qualified person. People think the monthly is quarterly, set by hour meter, or done only after a report; it happens each month. People leave a monitored deficiency until the next annual, or wait for an operator report; it is checked monthly. People think every annual finding means replacement; if the qualified person finds it is not presently a hazard, it is monitored.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Each month an inspection must be conducted in accordance with paragraph (a) (shift inspection) of this section.
The inspection must include any deficiencies that the qualified person who conducts the annual inspection determines under paragraph (c)(3)(ii) of this section must be monitored.
At least every 12 months, wire ropes in use on equipment must be inspected by a qualified person in accordance with paragraph (a) of this section (shift inspection).
The inspection must be complete and thorough, covering the surface of the entire length of the wire ropes, with particular attention given to all of the following:
such inspections must be conducted as soon as it becomes feasible, but no longer than an additional 6 months for running ropes and, for standing ropes, at the time of disassembly.

If the qualified person determines that, though not presently a safety hazard, the deficiency needs to be monitored, the employer must ensure that the deficiency is checked in the monthly inspections.

summary: Each month, a shift-type rope inspection is done and documented. It also checks any deficiency the annual inspector flagged for monitoring, and the ropes aren't used until it shows no corrective action is needed. At least every 12 months, a qualified person inspects the full length of the ropes. That person pays particular attention to critical review items, normally hidden sections, reverse bends and rope over sheaves.
title: Know monthly and annual wire rope inspection duties

exam: Expect items on the pendant broken-wire count, where to look on standing ropes, the idle-rope trigger and record contents. Watch for answer choices that list extra record items or the wrong person.
hard: The pendant count is different from the running rope count. It is more than two broken wires in a lay beyond the end connections, or more than one at an end connection. The idle-rope trigger is a month, not a quarter or half a year. The record has only three items: date, the inspector's signature, and a rope identifier.
mistakes: People set the idle trigger at ten days, three months or six months; it is a month or more. People think the operator's routine check, an engineer or the manufacturer releases idle rope; an appointed or authorized person inspects it and approves further use. People think the record needs diameter readings, hours, length, load tests, the operator's name or the crane serial number; it needs the date, the inspector's signature and a rope identifier. People look hardest at mid-span, at drum sections or at wind exposure; the named wear points are equalizer sheaves, limited-travel sheaves and saddles.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: In pendants or standing wire ropes: More than two broken wires in one rope lay located in rope beyond end connections and/or more than one broken wire in a rope lay located at an end connection.
Particular care shall be taken to inspect ropes at these locations.
All rope which has been idle for a period of a month or more due to shutdown or storage of a crane on which it is installed shall be given a thorough inspection before it is used.
This inspection shall be for all types of deterioration and shall be performed by an appointed or authorized person whose approval shall be required for further use of the rope.

A certification record which includes the date of inspection, the signature of the person who performed the inspection, and an identifier for the rope which was inspected shall be prepared and kept readily available.

summary: Standing ropes, such as boom pendants, don't travel over a drum, so their wear concentrates where they sit on saddles, equalizer sheaves and other sheaves with limited travel. Pendants have their own broken-wire count. Under the general industry rules, rope that has sat idle for a month or more has to be thoroughly inspected before use. That inspection is done by an appointed or authorized person whose approval is needed, and it is recorded.
title: Inspect standing ropes and pendants

exam: Expect a direct question on what the rule bars, plus scenarios with a heavily coated rope where you pick the first step. Watch for answer choices that sound like good practice, such as matching the original lubricant, offered as the rule.
hard: The test in the rule is whether the lubricant hinders inspection. It is not whether the lubricant is listed in the manual, matches the original, has a certain base stock, or how often it has to be applied. In practice, lubricant soaks in best where the rope opens up as it bends. A straight, tight rope is closed up, and a slack rope does not open the way bending does.
mistakes: People think a lubricant is barred if it isn't in the manual or doesn't match the original; the ban is on lubricants that hinder inspection. People think the rule controls where the lubricant goes on; it controls the type. People think a heavy coating is better maintenance; a coating that hides the wires is prohibited no matter how much it protects. People think lubricant wicks down the rope from one end, or soaks in on a tight straight run; it gets in mostly where the rope bends. People replace a heavily coated rope at once, or put off dealing with it; first clean the rope and inspect it, then decide.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Rope lubricants that are of the type that hinder inspection must not be used.

summary: Lubrication slows internal wear and corrosion, but the rule is about inspection. A lubricant of a type that hinders inspection can't be used. If the coating hides the wires, nobody can count broken wires or see corrosion. In practice, a thin penetrating lubricant put on where the rope bends over a sheave or drum gets inside and still lets you see the wires.
title: Lubricate without hindering inspection

exam: Expect interval, person and record-content items, often with near-miss choices. Watch for wording like "at least once a month," "appointed or authorized" and "signature."
hard: The terms differ from the construction rules. Here it is an appointed or authorized person, not a competent or qualified person. The minimum interval is monthly, and more frequent inspection is fine. The record needs a signature, not just a typed name.
mistakes: People treat weekly as the minimum, or think quarterly or the annual crane inspection is enough; the minimum is monthly. People think an operator certification, a maintenance assignment or a rigging credential gives inspection authority; the inspector has to be appointed or authorized. People think the operator signs, or that a name entry or a rated strength works in the record; it takes the inspector's signature and a rope identifier. People think a sheave with little travel means little wear, or that lubrication replaces the inspection, or that limited travel means automatic rejection; these spots get particular care during inspection.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: A thorough inspection of all ropes in use shall be made at least once a month and a certification record which includes the date of inspection, the signature of the person who performed the inspection and an identifier for the ropes shall be prepared and kept on file where readily available.
All inspections shall be performed by an appointed or authorized person.
Heavy wear and/or broken wires may occur in sections in contact with equalizer sheaves or other sheaves where rope travel is limited, or with saddles.
Particular care shall be taken in the inspection of nonrotating rope.

summary: The general industry crane rules have their own rope inspection. Running ropes get a thorough inspection at least once a month, done by an appointed or authorized person. Each one is recorded with the date, the inspector's signature and an identifier for the ropes. The inspector watches for loss of strength: reduced diameter, broken or worn outside wires, end connection problems, and kinking or crushing. Ropes at equalizer sheaves, limited-travel sheaves and saddles, and nonrotating rope, get particular care.
title: Know the general industry rope inspection rules

exam: Expect decode items: what a given designation means, which lay is described, which core an abbreviation stands for, and which rotation resistant type a rope is. Read carefully whether a choice describes wire direction or strand direction.
hard: A classification covers a range of wire counts, not one exact construction. For example, 6x19 class includes several constructions, and wire counts above that range fall into 6x37 class. Lay has two parts. Right or left is which way the strands wind around the rope. Regular or Lang is whether the wires run opposite to the strands (regular) or the same way (Lang).
mistakes: People read 6x19 as one exact build; it is a class that includes several wire counts. People swap the numbers; the first number is the outer strands and the second is wires per strand. People call matching directions regular lay; when wires and strands go the same way it is Lang lay, and opposite is regular lay. People think IWRC is a solid steel center or the same as a wire strand core; it is a separate small wire rope made of strands, while FC is fiber core. People call 10 or 12 outer strands Type I, or count total strands; Type I needs at least 15 outer strands.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Selection of replacement wire rope must be in accordance with the recommendations of the wire rope manufacturer, the equipment manufacturer, or a qualified person.
It has at least 15 outer strands and comprises an assembly of at least three layers of strands laid helically over a center in two operations.
It has at least 10 outer strands and comprises an assembly of two or more layers of strands laid helically over a center in two or three operations.

summary: A rope designation tells you how it is built. The first number is the number of outer strands and the second is the wires per strand classification, as in 6x19 or 6x37. Next come the core (FC for fiber core, IWRC for independent wire rope core), the lay (right or left, regular or Lang) and the steel grade. Rotation resistant rope is classed as Type I, II or III by outer strand count. Replacement rope is chosen on the recommendation of the rope manufacturer, the equipment manufacturer or a qualified person.
title: Read a wire rope designation (classification, core, lay, grade, rotation-resistant type) and match it to the job

exam: Expect a part count with a dead end location, a per-part load calculation, and an item on what off-center reeving does to the block or boom. Watch for answer choices built from the wrong divisor or a missing block weight.
hard: Odd or even is what decides where the dead end goes, not how big the count is, and moving the dead end changes the count by one. The load on each part is the total weight below the boom head divided by the number of parts. The lead line to the drum is one of those parts. You divide by parts, not by sheaves.
mistakes: People reverse the rule; even parts end at the boom head and odd parts end at the hook block. People think the dead end location is a free choice; the geometry fixes it. People leave out block and rigging, count the lead line as an extra part, or divide by sheaves; 36,000 lb of load plus 4,000 lb of block on 4 parts gives 10,000 lb a part. People think strength, part count or a synthetic core makes fiber core rope acceptable on a boom hoist; only derricks are exempt. People think rotation resistant rope is banned from boom hoists, or limit it to derricks; it is allowed when the added (e)(4)(ii) requirements are met.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Fiber core ropes must not be used for boom hoist reeving, except for derricks.
Rotation resistant ropes must be used for boom hoist reeving only where the requirements of paragraph (e)(4)(ii) of this section are met.

summary: How you reeve the block changes how it hangs. Symmetrical reeving keeps the block level and centered. Off-center reeving can tilt the block, make it rotate, and put twist into the boom head. Where the dead end anchors follows from the part count: with an even number of parts it ends at the boom head, and with an odd number it ends at the hook block. The boom hoist rope limits on fiber core and rotation resistant rope still apply.
title: Symmetrical and off-center reeving, block rotation and boom twist, dead-end location

exam: Expect items on which layer gives the most pull or how pull changes as rope winds on. Expect D/d number recall and drum wrap minimums. Some items give a line pull chart by layer. Read which layer the rope is on before you take a value.
hard: Constant torque does not mean constant pull. Rope diameter stays the same, but the winding radius grows with each layer. The 18 times rule covers the drum's first layer and every sheave in the boom hoist reeving system, wherever it is mounted. It replaces the ASME value of 16 for multiple-part reeving sheaves.
mistakes: People think a larger radius gives more pull, or that the same torque means the same pull; at fixed torque, a bigger radius gives less pull. People think the winding radius stays fixed because the rope size does; each layer moves the rope farther out. People give the minimum as 16, 17 or 20 times; it is 18 times, and 20 just goes beyond it. People apply 18 times only to the lead sheave, only to boom-mounted sheaves or only to multiple-part reeving; it covers all sheaves in the boom hoist reeving system. People call three, four or five wraps the minimum; the federal minimum is two full wraps.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Neither the load nor the boom must be lowered below the point where less than two full wraps of rope remain on their respective drums.
The drum must provide a first layer rope pitch diameter of not less than 18 times the nominal diameter of the rope used.
All sheaves used in the boom hoist reeving system must have a rope pitch diameter of not less than 18 times the nominal diameter of the rope used.

summary: Line pull is drum torque divided by the radius where the rope sits. Each layer winds farther from the drum's center, so the first layer gives the most pull and outer layers give less. New rope is spooled tight and even, the flanges need clearance, and the rope must never drop below two full wraps on the drum. Bending over small drums and sheaves wears rope faster. When rotation resistant rope is used for boom hoist reeving, the drum and every sheave in that system need at least 18 times the rope diameter.
title: Line pull by drum layer, flange clearance, spooling new rope, sheave and drum D/d

exam: Expect items with a clip table where you read the count and torque for a rope size, and items on saddle orientation and wedge socket dead ends. Expect "where to look" items from the critical review list. Watch for answer choices that trade torque or turnback for clips.
hard: The clip count goes up with rope size, so there is no single number for all sizes. A common manufacturer table, for example, gives 3/4 inch rope 4 clips at 130 ft-lb with an 18 inch turnback. Torque, turnback and clip count are separate requirements, and one does not stand in for another. Every saddle goes on the live end; you don't alternate them.
mistakes: People clip a wedge socket tail to the live line, or think the right torque makes that acceptable; clips go on the unloaded dead end only. People put the saddle on the dead end, alternate the saddles, or set them by how the eye is turned; every saddle goes on the live end. People think three clips works for any size; three is the table value only for small ropes, and the count goes up with size. People over-torque to make up for a missing clip, or count the turnback in place of a clip; you need the full clip count, the table torque and the turnback together. People look for wear on long straight spans or the middle of the drum; the critical items are terminal ends, reverse bends on boom hoists, drum flange and crossover points, and limited-travel sheaves.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Wire rope clips used in conjunction with wedge sockets must be attached to the unloaded dead end of the rope only, except that the use of devices specifically designed for dead-ending rope in a wedge socket is permitted.
Wire rope at or near terminal ends.
Wire rope being used for boom hoists and luffing hoists, particularly at reverse bends.
Wire rope at flange points, crossover points and repetitive pickup points on drums.
Wire rope in contact with saddles, equalizer sheaves or other sheaves where rope travel is limited.

summary: For a clipped eye, the number of clips, the spacing, the turnback and the torque come from the clip manufacturer's table for that rope size. The standard practice is that the saddle goes on the live end and the U-bolt on the dead end. On a wedge socket, the federal rule allows clips on the unloaded dead end only, unless a device made for that job is used. Terminal ends are also a critical review item during inspection.
title: Wire rope clips: number, spacing and torque by manufacturer instruction; saddle on the live end; wedge socket dead end

exam: Expect definition questions: what radius is measured from, what counts as part of the load, and who sets rated capacity. Watch for the words gross and net, and for distractors that offer the foot pin or outrigger as the reference point.
hard: Radius and boom length are both in feet and both appear on the chart, but they are different things. Radius changes with boom angle even when the boom length stays the same. Radius is measured from the axis of rotation, not from the foot pin, an outrigger or the tipping edge. Also, the federal definition of load includes the block, slings and shackles, not only the piece you are picking.
mistakes: People measure radius from the boom foot pin, an outrigger float or the tipping axis. Chart radius starts at the axis of rotation. People read boom length as radius. Radius is horizontal and changes as the boom goes up or down. People assume the design margin covers the rigging or the load block. Both count as part of the load, along with every item hanging from the hoist line. People think a qualified person, an inspection, a load test or the LMI can set or raise a rating. Only the manufacturer sets rated capacity. People use the unloaded radius or average the radii over a lift. The loaded radius is longer, and capacity has to cover the longest radius the load reaches.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Rated capacity means the maximum working load permitted by the manufacturer under specified working conditions.

Load refers to the object(s) being hoisted and/or the weight of the object(s); both uses refer to the object(s) and the load-attaching equipment, such as, the load block, ropes, slings, shackles, and any other ancillary attachment.
Radius of the load is the horizontal distance from a projection of the axis of rotation to the rail support surface, before loading, to the center of vertical hoist line or tackle with load applied.

summary: Radius is the horizontal distance from the axis of rotation to the center of the hoist line, with the load applied. Boom length is measured along the boom, and it is a separate entry on the chart. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load for one specific configuration. Gross capacity is the chart number, and net capacity is what is left for the payload after the load-handling devices come off.
title: Use load chart terms (radius, boom length, rated capacity, gross, net)

exam: Typical items give a small chart, a boom length and a radius, then ask for gross capacity. The distractors are the values in the next column, the row above or the row below. Read the configuration and area headings before you read any number.
hard: The chart is a dense grid, and one row or column off gives a believable wrong number. When the radius falls between rows, the next longer radius governs, not the nearer one. The bold line on many charts separates structural ratings, above it at shorter radii, from stability ratings, below it at longer radii. It does not mark parts-of-line limits or ground conditions.
mistakes: People use the shorter listed radius or round to the nearest one. The next longer radius always governs. People interpolate between rows. Charts are not built for straight-line interpolation unless a note allows it. People read the wrong boom length column or the row next to the right one. Put your finger on the column and the row and confirm both before you read the number. People swap the zones. Structural strength governs above the bold line, and stability governs below it. People think the bold line shows reeving limits or ground bearing. Parts of line are in the notes, and ground support is checked separately.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

summary: Reading gross capacity means finding the boom length column that matches the crane, finding the radius row, and reading the number where they cross. That number is gross, and it still includes the block and rigging. It is the base for every net capacity and percent-of-capacity question.
title: Read gross capacity at a radius and boom length

exam: Expect a chart with a radius like 32 ft or 38 ft and options built from the shorter row, the longer row, an interpolated value and an average. Some items then ask whether a given load can be lifted, so finish the net capacity before you answer yes or no.
hard: The tempting move is to pick the closest row or to split the difference. Distance to a row does not matter. What matters is which side of the actual radius the row sits on. After you pick the right row, you still have to subtract the block and rigging to get net capacity.
mistakes: People round to the closest row. If the closest row is the shorter radius, its rating is too high. People interpolate or average adjacent rows. Unless a note allows it, that produces a number with no basis on the chart. People round boom length down. A longer boom carries more of its own weight, so go up to the next listed column. People pick the higher angle row. A higher angle means a shorter radius and a higher rating, so drop to the next lower angle. People stop at gross or subtract only the block. Subtract the rigging too. People cite a 75 percent threshold to pass or fail a load. That figure is a weight-verification trigger, not a capacity limit.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

summary: When the actual radius falls between two listed rows, you use the rating at the next longer radius. The same idea applies to boom length, where you go to the next longer column, and to boom angle charts, where you go to the next lower listed angle. Each choice lands on the more conservative rating.
title: Use the next longer radius when between rows

exam: Items give a boom length like 81 ft or 95 ft along with a radius, and they often quote the chart note. Options include the shorter column, an average and a four-cell average, so check which column and which row the note sends you to.
hard: You have to handle radius and boom length at the same time. That means the next longer radius row and the correct boom column, and getting only one of them right still gives a wrong answer. Read the exact note. 'Next longer length' and 'lower adjacent capacity' usually give the same number, but not always.
mistakes: People use the shorter boom column or round to the nearest length. The shorter column assumes less boom weight than you have out, so follow the note, which usually points to the next longer column. People average or interpolate the two columns. That is not allowed unless the note authorizes it. People always grab the longer column, even when the note asks for the lower adjacent rating. Read which rule the note gives. People invent an extra deduction for an in-between length. Apply only the deductions the chart lists. People round only the radius or only the boom correctly. Both have to be rounded the conservative way.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The employer must comply with all manufacturer procedures applicable to the operational functions of equipment, including its use with attachments.

summary: A telescopic boom is often run out to a length between two chart columns. The chart notes tell you how to read it. Most charts say to use the next longer boom column, and some say to use the lower of the two adjacent ratings. Either way you end up with the more conservative number for the boom you actually have out.
title: Handle a boom length between chart columns

exam: Expect a gross capacity plus a list of block, beam, sling and shackle weights, sometimes with a note saying one item is included. The distractors come from leaving out one item, counting one twice, or multiplying by the number of legs.
hard: Every device comes off once, and only once. Some charts say the block or certain items are already accounted for, so read the note before you subtract. A rigging assembly's stated weight is its total weight, however many legs it has.
mistakes: People leave out the hook block, the slings or the lifting beam. Every suspended device uses up chart capacity, even a beam that spreads the load. People deduct the block again when the chart note says it is already included. Deducting it twice understates net capacity. People multiply a four-leg assembly's total weight by four, or divide it by four. Deduct the full documented total once. People think load sharing between legs lowers the device weight on the crane. It does not. People subtract only part of the device weight. Add up every device group first, then subtract the total once.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Load refers to the object(s) being hoisted and/or the weight of the object(s); both uses refer to the object(s) and the load-attaching equipment, such as, the load block, ropes, slings, shackles, and any other ancillary attachment.
The weight of all auxiliary handling devices such as hoist blocks, hooks, and slings shall be considered a part of the load rating.

summary: Net capacity is gross capacity minus the weight of everything that hangs between the boom tip and the payload: the hook block or ball, slings, shackles, spreader or lifting beam, and any other device. What is left is what the payload itself may weigh. On the job, this is the number you compare to the load.
title: Compute net capacity (gross minus all load-handling devices)

exam: Items list a device with both a rating and a weight to see whether you pick the weight, and often add a jib stowed or erected note. Look for the word weight, or a tare figure, in the item, and ignore the capacity markings when you subtract.
hard: Rated hardware carries two numbers, its rating and its weight, and only the weight is deducted. Jib deductions depend on whether the jib is stowed or erected and on which line you are lifting with, so read the note for your exact setup. Being installed or certified does not make an item weightless.
mistakes: People deduct a block's rating or a sling's working load limit instead of its weight. The rating tells you what it can hold, and the deduction is what it weighs. People subtract the weight from the rating and call the difference a deduction. That number has nothing to do with the crane chart. People assume a block that stays on the crane, or certified rigging, is exempt. Its weight still hangs from the hoist line. People deduct a beam's payload rating, or the beam plus its maximum payload. Deduct only the beam's own weight. People leave out the block or the rigging. Subtract both.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Load refers to the object(s) being hoisted and/or the weight of the object(s); both uses refer to the object(s) and the load-attaching equipment, such as, the load block, ropes, slings, shackles, and any other ancillary attachment.
The employer must comply with all manufacturer procedures applicable to the operational functions of equipment, including its use with attachments.

summary: Deductions are the weights the chart says to subtract from gross capacity: the hook block or overhaul ball, rigging, and, depending on the chart notes, a jib that is stowed or erected, or other attachments. Getting them right is what turns a chart number into a payload number. The chart notes say which deductions apply in which setup.
title: Apply deductions (hook block, ball, jib stowed or erected, rigging)

exam: Expect setup scenarios: which chart applies, whether a mixed or partial extension is acceptable, who watches the outriggers, and what has to happen to the wheels. Wording such as 'approved by the lift director' or 'derated by 25 percent' signals a distractor.
hard: A mixed setup, with some beams full and some at mid, is only rated if the manufacturer's chart covers that arrangement. Taking weight off the wheels means all the wheels, not just lightening them. The person watching outriggers has to be the operator or a signal person, whatever anyone else's title is.
mistakes: People think an operator-chosen derate, a lift director's approval or a successful test lift makes a partial extension acceptable. The deployment has to be one the manufacturer allows and the chart specifies. People leave the carrier or the steering axle carrying some weight. The equipment weight comes off the wheels, with no axle excepted. People think the operator has to see every outrigger personally. A signal person can do it, but a supervisor or rigger does not count by title alone. People average two charts, or halve the full-extension rating, for a mid or mixed setup. Use the manufacturer's chart for a listed position, and set all beams to a listed position if the mix is not covered.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The outriggers or stabilizers must be either fully extended or, if manufacturer procedures permit, deployed as specified in the load chart.

The outriggers must be set to remove the equipment weight from the wheels, except for locomotive cranes (see paragraph (q)(6) of this section for use of outriggers on locomotive cranes). This provision does not apply to stabilizers.
Each outrigger or stabilizer must be visible to the operator or to a signal person during extension and setting.
When outrigger floats are used, they must be attached to the outriggers. When stabilizer floats are used, they must be attached to the stabilizers.

summary: Each support setup has its own chart: outriggers fully extended, outriggers at a marked mid-extension, on rubber, or crawler tracks at a given gauge. You use the chart that matches how the crane is actually set. Under the federal rules, outriggers are either fully extended or deployed as the load chart specifies when manufacturer procedures allow it. They are set to take the equipment weight off the wheels, and each one is watched by the operator or a signal person while it is extended and set.
title: Select the chart for the configuration (outriggers full, mid, on rubber, crawler)

exam: Expect scenarios asking who makes the travel determinations, what tire pressure to use, and whether a planned pick-and-carry is allowed. Watch for the difference between a manufacturer prohibition and site approval, and between competent person and qualified person.
hard: Three permissions get mixed up. The manufacturer decides whether travel with a load is allowed at all, and whether lifts over the front of a wheel-mounted crane are allowed. The competent person runs the travel within that permission. Tire pressure follows the crane manufacturer's on-rubber spec, not the tire sidewall maximum.
mistakes: People give the travel decisions to the rigger, the signal person or a qualified person. The rule names a competent person. People think soft tires spread the load or that more pressure is safer. Wrong pressure changes the deflection and stability the chart assumes, so keep the crane manufacturer's specified pressure. People treat the tire sidewall maximum as the spec. The crane manufacturer's pressure governs. People think a capacity margin, a site approval or a percentage derate allows travel the manufacturer prohibits. Nothing overrides that prohibition. People think travel with a load is banned for all cranes. It is allowed where the manufacturer permits it and the competent-person controls are in place.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Traveling with a load is prohibited if the practice is prohibited by the manufacturer.

A competent person supervises the operation, determines if it is necessary to reduce rated capacity, and makes determinations regarding load position, boom location, ground support, travel route, overhead obstructions, and speed of movement necessary to ensure safety.
For equipment with tires, tire pressure specified by the manufacturer is maintained.
On wheel-mounted equipment, no loads must be lifted over the front area, except as permitted by the manufacturer.

summary: On-rubber charts give much lower ratings than outrigger charts. They are often split into stationary and pick-and-carry columns, with limits on boom position and travel. Under the federal rules, traveling with a load is prohibited if the manufacturer prohibits it. Where it is allowed, a competent person supervises and makes the calls on rated capacity reduction, load position, boom location, ground support, travel route, overhead obstructions and speed, and tire pressure is kept at the manufacturer's spec.
title: Lift and pick-and-carry on rubber within chart limits

exam: Expect a jobsite scenario where someone wants to swing over the front of a truck crane, and the question is who can allow it or whether it can go ahead. Check the mounting type in the wording and look for manufacturer permission.
hard: The front-area rule names wheel-mounted equipment specifically. It is not a general rule for crawler, pedestal or rail-mounted cranes. A rating for one area says nothing about another area, even at the same radius. Only the manufacturer can open the front.
mistakes: People think a qualified person, engineer, lift director or the operator can approve an over-front lift. The exception depends only on manufacturer permission. People think outriggers automatically allow front lifts. Being on outriggers does not open the front area by itself. People carry a side or rear rating over to the front, or halve it as an informal derate. Neither creates permission. People think the front-area provision covers crawler, pedestal or rail-mounted cranes. It names wheel-mounted equipment. People think a lift that looks stable is acceptable. A judgment about tipping does not override the prohibition.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: On wheel-mounted equipment, no loads must be lifted over the front area, except as permitted by the manufacturer.

summary: The swing circle is divided into areas, commonly over the front, over the side and over the rear, and each can carry its own rating. The area boundaries come from the crane's support points. Under the federal rules, wheel-mounted equipment may not lift over the front area except as the manufacturer permits.
title: Know quadrants of operation and lifts over the front

exam: Typical items give a jib chart with 0, 15 and 30 degree columns and ask for net capacity at a stated offset. Watch for options built from the wrong offset column and for an option that stops at gross.
hard: Three angles are easy to confuse: the main boom angle, the jib's angle above horizontal, and the offset. Only offset picks the column. Jib radius is still measured from the axis of rotation, so it includes the main boom's reach, not just the jib's.
mistakes: People read the jib's angle above horizontal, the main boom angle, or the angle from vertical as the offset. Offset is measured from the main boom axis. People use the 0-degree or the next offset column instead of the one actually installed. Use the column for the installed offset. People measure jib radius from the heel pin, a support point, or the jib's own reach. Radius runs from the axis of rotation to the hoist line. People leave out the block or the rigging, or add them instead of subtracting. Both weights come off the gross jib rating. People treat the gross jib rating as the payload. Subtract the deductions first.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Load refers to the object(s) being hoisted and/or the weight of the object(s); both uses refer to the object(s) and the load-attaching equipment, such as, the load block, ropes, slings, shackles, and any other ancillary attachment.

summary: Jib and extension capacities are listed by jib length and offset, and usually by main boom angle or by radius. Offset is the angle between the jib and the centerline of the main boom. Ratings drop as offset increases. As with the main boom, you subtract the block or ball and the rigging from the jib rating to get the payload.
title: Read jib and extension capacities by offset

exam: Expect items asking for a boom angle or tip height read off a diagram at a given boom length and radius, or the shortest boom that clears an obstruction. Read the scales carefully, and remember the hook and rigging sit below the tip when height clearance is the question.
hard: Tip height is not hook height. The hook hangs below the tip by the block, the rigging and the rope paid out. Radius is still read from the axis of rotation, so heel pin offsets are already built into the diagram. As a matter of geometry, a boom gains height as its angle increases, and its full length points straight up only at 90 degrees.
mistakes: People think a steep working angle such as 60, 75 or 85 degrees gives the maximum geometric height. Only a vertical boom puts its whole length above the pivot. People measure radius from the heel pin, an outrigger or the front axle. The diagram's radius scale starts at the axis of rotation. People treat hook height and tip height as the same. Paying out rope moves the hook, not the tip. People think lowering the hook raises the tip, or that reeving changes tip height. With the boom held fixed, only the hook moves. People think procedures and charts can be kept with the signal person, in the site office or in an outside compartment. They have to be readily available in the cab.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The procedures applicable to the operation of the equipment, including rated capacities (load charts), recommended operating speeds, special hazard warnings, instructions, and operator's manual, must be readily available in the cab at all times for use by the operator.
Boom angle indicator means a device which measures the angle of the boom relative to horizontal.

summary: The range diagram, sometimes called the working range chart, plots boom length arcs, boom angle lines, a radius scale along the bottom and a height scale up the side. With it you can find the boom angle and tip height for a given boom length and radius, or the boom length you need to reach over an obstacle. It is a geometry tool. It does not show capacity.
title: Use the range diagram (radius, boom angle, tip height)

exam: Items often quote a note and ask how it changes the answer, or ask where the charts are kept and what the bold line means. Read every note in the item before you calculate, because one of them usually decides it.
hard: Notes often settle questions that look like plain arithmetic, such as whether the block is already deducted or whether you go to the next longer radius. The bold line usually splits structural ratings above it from stability ratings below it. Stability ratings are set as a percentage of tipping. The figures commonly taught from the consensus standard are 85 percent on outriggers and 75 percent on tires or crawlers, but the chart's own notes are what you go by.
mistakes: People think an office copy, a lift director's review or a carrier compartment is good enough. The charts belong in the cab at all times. People reverse the stability percentages or nudge them up or down. The commonly taught figures are 85 percent on outriggers and 75 percent on tires and crawlers. People swap the bold line zones, or think the line marks line pull or ground bearing. Structural governs above it, stability below it, and line pull and ground support are separate. People use the nearer, shorter radius, interpolate, or average. Unless the note allows otherwise, the next longer radius applies.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The employer must comply with all manufacturer procedures applicable to the operational functions of equipment, including its use with attachments.

The procedures applicable to the operation of the equipment, including rated capacities (load charts), recommended operating speeds, special hazard warnings, instructions, and operator's manual, must be readily available in the cab at all times for use by the operator.

Load rating chart. A substantial and durable rating chart with clearly legible letters and figures shall be provided with each crane and securely fixed to the crane cab in a location easily visible to the operator while seated at his control station.

summary: The notes are part of the chart, and they change how the numbers are read. They cover things like the support conditions the ratings assume, what has to be deducted, whether interpolation is allowed, which ratings are structural and which are based on stability, parts-of-line limits, and restrictions by area. Under the federal rules, the employer complies with the manufacturer's procedures, and the charts are kept readily available in the cab at all times.
title: Apply the chart notes

exam: Expect questions on which zone a chart value falls in and what failure it guards against, plus rule details such as least stable direction, 1 percent grade and what counts in the rating. Watch for percent versus degrees and for 'first wheel' versus 'half of the wheels.'
hard: The general industry rule sets stability ratings as a percentage of the tipping load, with the boom in the least stable direction for that mounting. For locomotive cranes it defines tipping as half the wheels farthest from the load leaving the rail, on track level within 1 percent grade. The rating covers the block, hooks and slings, not only the payload.
mistakes: People think tipping means every far-side wheel has lifted, or that the first wheel lifting is tipping. For locomotive cranes the rule says half of the wheels farthest from the load. People read 1 percent grade as 1 degree, or as half a percent or 2 percent. The rule says level within 1 percent grade. People think the margin is set in the strongest direction, always over the side, or in the direction the crane is usually used. It is set in the least stable direction. People think the rating is for the load alone, or for the load minus the block only, or that a flat percentage allowance covers rigging. Deduct the actual weights of the block and all rigging. People confuse boom angle limits with tipping. They are separate chart limits.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The margin of stability for determination of load ratings, with booms of stipulated lengths at stipulated working radii for the various types of crane mountings, is established by taking a percentage of the loads which will produce a condition of tipping or balance with the boom in the least stable direction, relative to the mounting. The load ratings shall not exceed the following percentages for cranes, with the indicated types of mounting under conditions stipulated in paragraphs (c)(1) (ii) and (iii) of this section.
Tipping with or without the use of outriggers occurs when half of the wheels farthest from the load leave the rail.
The crane shall be standing on track which is level within 1 percent grade.
The weight of all auxiliary handling devices such as hoist blocks, hooks, and slings shall be considered a part of the load rating.

summary: At short radii, ratings are usually limited by the strength of the boom and other components. At longer radii, they are usually limited by tipping. Many charts mark the change with a bold line. Structural overloads can fail with no warning of tipping, so how stable the crane feels tells you nothing in the structural zone.
title: Tell structural-strength limits from stability limits

exam: Expect a division problem: a hook load, often with the block included, and a permissible line pull, then the number of parts needed. Some items ask about hook speed or drum layers. Check that the block weight is in the load and round parts up.
hard: Hoist line pull and rope limit are two different numbers, and the lower one governs. Line pull is highest on the bottom drum layer and drops with each layer, because the same torque acts at a larger radius. More parts let the hook carry more, but the hook moves slower. Hook speed equals line speed divided by the number of parts.
mistakes: People think more rope on the drum means more pull. The outer layer gives the least pull and the most line speed. People think spooling quality sets the pull, or that line pull is one fixed number. It changes with every layer. People think hook speed equals line speed, or that fewer pounds per part makes the hook faster. Adding parts slows the hook in proportion, so going from 4 to 5 parts gives 4/5 of the old speed. People use the hoist's pull when the rope's limit is lower, or round the parts down. Use the lower limit and always round up. People apply the design factor again to a charted line pull. It is already built in. People cite a 2-to-1 strength ratio, a lay rule or a calendar replacement interval as the federal requirement. The rule given here only requires the rope to be compatible with the equipment.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Wire rope must be compatible with the safe functioning of the equipment.

summary: The parts-of-line or line pull table gives the permissible pull on a single line, which limits how much the hook can carry for a given reeving. Parts needed equals total hook load divided by permissible line pull, rounded up. Under the federal rules, the wire rope has to be compatible with the safe functioning of the equipment.
title: Use parts-of-line and line pull tables

exam: Expect volume or beam calculations done by hand and a question on acceptable ways to verify load weight. Watch for a wrong unit weight hidden in the options and for the phrase 'longest radius.'
hard: Keep volume and per-foot weights straight. Plate is a cubic foot divided by 12 for each inch of thickness. A beam's nominal depth is a size, not a multiplier. The rule's named example of a weight source is the load's manufacturer. The LMI method only works once the load is coming up, and its 75 percent check is taken at the longest radius.
mistakes: People use the steel, water or timber figure for concrete. Concrete is about 150 lb per cubic foot. People use 490 lb for 1-inch plate, or the concrete figure, or slip the decimal on 40.8. One-inch steel plate is about 40.8 lb per square foot. People multiply a beam's depth into the weight, so a 12-inch beam at 50 lb per ft over 40 ft is 2,000 lb, not 600 or 24,000. People name the trucking company, the rigging supplier or an in-lift reading as the rule's named source. The rule's example is the load's manufacturer, with the information given before the lift when the operator asks for it. People take the 75 percent check at the pick radius. It is taken at the longest radius that will be used.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Load weight. The operator must verify that the load is within the rated capacity of the equipment by at least one of the following methods:

The weight of the load must be determined from a source recognized by the industry (such as the load's manufacturer), or by a calculation method recognized by the industry (such as calculating a steel beam from measured dimensions and a known per foot weight), or by other equally reliable means. In addition, when requested by the operator, this information must be provided to the operator prior to the lift; or

The operator must begin hoisting the load to determine, using a load weighing device, load moment indicator, rated capacity indicator, or rated capacity limiter, if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used during the lift operation. If it does, the operator must not proceed with the lift until he/she verifies the weight of the load in accordance with paragraph (o)(3)(i) of this section.

summary: You often have to work out load weight from dimensions and unit weights. Common working figures are about 490 lb per cubic foot for steel, about 150 for concrete, 62.4 for fresh water and about 40 for dry timber. A square foot of 1-inch steel plate weighs about 40.8 lb, and a beam weighs its length times its pounds per foot. Under the federal rules, the operator verifies the load is within rated capacity either by an industry-recognized source or calculation, given to the operator before the lift on request, or by hoisting with a weighing device or LMI and stopping to verify the weight if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius of the lift.
title: Compute load weight from dimensions and unit weights

exam: Expect an arithmetic item where you add the piece, rigging and block and then find the percent, and a rule item on when, how and by whom the brake test is done. Watch whether the item gives line pull or chart capacity.
hard: The brake test is based on maximum line pull, not chart capacity, so you may have to compare the load per line against the hoist's line pull. The ratio goes load over capacity, never the other way. The test is a few inches up with the actual load, and the operator performs it.
mistakes: People base the brake test on chart capacity. It is based on maximum line pull. People use 75 percent as the trigger. The trigger is 90 percent or more of maximum line pull. People do the test at full height, with an empty hook, or a few feet up by just returning the lever to neutral. Lift the actual load a few inches and apply the brakes. People assign the test to the signal person, supervisor or rigger. The operator does it. People leave out the rigging or block, or one of them, from the load, or flip the ratio. Add every weight on the hook and divide load by capacity.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The operator must test the brakes each time a load that is 90% or more of the maximum line pull is handled by lifting the load a few inches and applying the brakes. In duty cycle and repetitive lifts where each lift is 90% or more of the maximum line pull, this requirement applies to the first lift but not to successive lifts.

summary: Percent of capacity is total hook load divided by capacity, times 100. The total includes the block and rigging. Under the federal rules, the operator tests the brakes each time a load of 90 percent or more of maximum line pull is handled, by lifting the load a few inches and applying the brakes. In duty-cycle or repetitive lifts at that level, only the first lift needs the test.
title: Compute percent of rated capacity (and the 90% brake test)

exam: Typical items give a payload, a block and rigging weight, and a column of ratings, then ask for the maximum radius. The options are the neighboring radii, so check one row beyond your answer to confirm it fails.
hard: The common slip is subtracting the block and rigging from the payload instead of adding them. Installed counterweight and the boom are part of the charted configuration, not deductions. The published rating is already the limit, so no extra stability factor is applied on top of it.
mistakes: People apply another 75 or 85 percent factor to the chart rating. The listed rating is the rated capacity, and the percentage was used in setting it, not in using it. People treat the margin between rating and tipping as usable capacity. Rated capacity is the limit. People deduct counterweight or boom weight. Those are part of the configuration, and the deductions are the block and rigging. People measure from the foot pin or the tipping edge, or use slant distance. Radius is horizontal from the rotation axis. People stop at the first radius that works, or leave out a deduction. Find the longest radius whose rating covers the full required gross.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.
Equipment must not be operated without the counterweight or ballast in place as specified by the manufacturer.

summary: To find the maximum radius for a load, work backward. Add the payload, block and rigging to get the gross capacity you need. Then go down the right boom length column to the longest radius whose rating still meets that number. This is how you decide how close the crane has to set up.
title: Find maximum radius for a given net load

exam: Expect scenarios: the display goes dark mid-lift, a file transfer fails, or the charts are in the office. Ask whether the ratings are still accessible in the cab, and choose the answer that follows from that.
hard: 'At all times' means the whole operation, not just setup or the first pick. The trigger for electronic failure is the rated capacities becoming inaccessible. A failure that leaves them accessible does not trigger it. Any form of the applicable ratings, paper included, restores operation.
mistakes: People think the charts only have to be on hand at setup, at the first hoist, or near capacity. The requirement is at all times. People think a site office, a signal person on the radio, or the access steps count. The charts have to be in the cab. People think any network, printer or download problem forces a shutdown. The trigger is ratings becoming inaccessible in the cab. People think paper backups are always required by this provision. It does not require them. People think an inspector's approval, a repair or a restart attempt has to come before using an applicable paper chart. The provision requires none of those once the ratings are available in another form.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The procedures applicable to the operation of the equipment, including rated capacities (load charts), recommended operating speeds, special hazard warnings, instructions, and operator's manual, must be readily available in the cab at all times for use by the operator.

Where rated capacities are available in the cab only in electronic form: In the event of a failure which makes the rated capacities inaccessible, the operator must immediately cease operations or follow safe shut-down procedures until the rated capacities (in electronic or other form) are available.
