summary: Under the federal rules, the load charts and the other operating procedures, including recommended speeds, special hazard warnings, instructions and the operator's manual, are kept readily available in the cab at all times for the operator. If the ratings exist in the cab only electronically and a failure makes them inaccessible, the operator immediately stops or follows safe shutdown procedures until the ratings are available again, electronically or in another form.
title: Keep load charts in the cab; handle electronic chart failure

exam: Expect scenarios where someone proposes extra counterweight or working with part of it removed, and the question is whether it is allowed or who could approve it. Check the crane type in the wording, because tower cranes are a deliberate trap.
hard: There are two limits, a missing-counterweight limit and a maximum limit, and neither can be approved away. The provision excludes tower cranes, including self-erecting, hammerhead and luffing-jib tower cranes. A mobile crane fitted with a luffing jib or tower attachment is still not a tower crane under the definitions.
mistakes: People think a lift director, a site engineering calculation, the operator or a lift plan can set or change the counterweight. The manufacturer's specification governs. People think a stability calculation or a strong-looking frame allows going over the maximum. The maximum stands regardless. People think a proportional derate or a shorter radius makes up for missing counterweight. Neither allows operating without the specified counterweight. People apply this provision to tower cranes. Tower cranes are covered elsewhere.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The following applies to equipment other than tower cranes:
Equipment must not be operated without the counterweight or ballast in place as specified by the manufacturer.
The maximum counterweight or ballast specified by the manufacturer for the equipment must not be exceeded.
Mobile cranes that are configured with luffing jib and/or tower attachments are not considered tower cranes under this section.

summary: Under the federal rules, equipment other than tower cranes is not operated without the counterweight or ballast in place as the manufacturer specifies, and the manufacturer's maximum counterweight or ballast is not exceeded. The chart you read assumes a specific counterweight, so the counterweight on the crane has to match the chart in use.
title: Use only the specified counterweight

exam: Expect recall items on the exact stipulations: the tipping definition, the grade limit, static testing and which code applies to which mounting. Watch for neighboring numbers and for answers that move the locomotive rules onto other cranes.
hard: The locomotive-crane details do not carry over to other mountings, which follow SAE J765. Ratings are built from static tipping tests, so they include no allowance for swing stops or hoisting dynamics. Those are left to the operator. The numbers are close together (1, 1.5, 2.5 percent), so learn the exact figure.
mistakes: People think tipping means every far wheel lifting, the first wheel lifting, or full weight transfer. The rule says half of the wheels farthest from the load leave the rail. People pick 0.5, 1.5 or 2.5 percent for track level. It is 1 percent grade. People apply the rail and track rules to crawler or truck cranes, or think each manufacturer's own method governs, or name B30.10. Those mountings follow SAE J765, and B30.10 covers hooks. People think the tests include line speed, swing stops or a worst-case dynamic stop. Tipping loads are applied under static conditions only.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The margin of stability for determination of load ratings, with booms of stipulated lengths at stipulated working radii for the various types of crane mountings, is established by taking a percentage of the loads which will produce a condition of tipping or balance with the boom in the least stable direction, relative to the mounting. The load ratings shall not exceed the following percentages for cranes, with the indicated types of mounting under conditions stipulated in paragraphs (c)(1) (ii) and (iii) of this section.
Tipping with or without the use of outriggers occurs when half of the wheels farthest from the load leave the rail.
The crane shall be standing on track which is level within 1 percent grade.
Tipping loads from which ratings are determined shall be applied under static conditions only, i.e., without dynamic effect of hoisting, lowering, or swinging.

Stipulations governing the application of the values in paragraph (c)(1)(i) of this section for crawler, truck, and wheel-mounted cranes shall be in accordance with Crane Load-Stability Test Code, Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) J765, which is incorporated by reference as specified in § 1910.6.

The effectiveness of these preceding stability factors will be influenced by such additional factors as freely suspended loads, track, wind, or ground conditions, condition and inflation of rubber tires, boom lengths, proper operating speeds for existing conditions, and, in general, careful and competent operation. All of these shall be taken into account by the user.

summary: The general industry crane rule sets stability-based ratings as a percentage of the tipping load, with the boom in the least stable direction. For locomotive cranes it spells out the conditions: tipping is when half of the wheels farthest from the load leave the rail, track is level within 1 percent grade, and tipping loads are applied statically. For crawler, truck and wheel-mounted cranes it refers to the SAE J765 test code. The user also has to take into account wind, ground, tire condition and inflation, speeds and careful operation.
title: Know general industry load rating limits (percent of tipping)

exam: Expect a scenario with a swing from one area into another and a chart giving different ratings for each, asking whether the lift works or what governs. Trace the whole swing path, not just the pick and set points.
hard: The boundaries are not fixed 45-degree sectors. Their angles depend on where the supports sit. The on-rubber boundaries, based on the axles and tires, do not apply on outriggers. Under the federal rules, wheel-mounted equipment does not lift over the front unless the manufacturer permits it, and a load-weight check never adds capacity.
mistakes: People think a lift director, full outrigger extension or a light load opens the front area. Only the manufacturer's permission does, and the 75 percent figure belongs to load-weight verification. People take that 75 percent check at the pickup radius, or use 50 or 85 percent. It is 75 percent at the longest radius that will be used. People draw the boundaries through the axles, the carrier corners, or at fixed 45 degrees while on outriggers. On outriggers, use the floats. People use only the pick-point rating or average two area ratings. Each area's own rating applies whenever the load is in it. People think verifying the weight allows a load over the area's rating. A known overload still cannot be lifted as planned.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: On wheel-mounted equipment, no loads must be lifted over the front area, except as permitted by the manufacturer.

The operator must begin hoisting the load to determine, using a load weighing device, load moment indicator, rated capacity indicator, or rated capacity limiter, if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used during the lift operation. If it does, the operator must not proceed with the lift until he/she verifies the weight of the load in accordance with paragraph (o)(3)(i) of this section.

summary: The work area diagram shows which areas around the crane are rated: over the side, over the rear, and over the front if the manufacturer rates it. It also shows where the boundaries fall. On outriggers, the boundary lines generally run from the center of rotation through the outrigger floats. If the load swings through more than one area, the lowest rating along the swing path governs that part of the lift.
title: Read a work area diagram: capacity by area, over-the-front and over-the-side zones

exam: Expect items giving unloaded and loaded angle readings and asking which row applies, and items on what to do when the angle indicator fails. Watch for options built on the unloaded reading or on the higher row.
hard: The loaded angle is lower than the unloaded angle. A reading taken before the slings go tight, or after the load lands, is the wrong reading. Dropping to the lower angle gives the longer radius and the lower rating. That runs opposite to the 'round up' habit used for radius.
mistakes: People use a previous setup's angle, an observer's estimate or the planned geometry instead of a measurement. The temporary alternative requires measuring with a device. People use the angle before the load is taken, after it is landed, or an average of the two. Use the loaded angle. People measure from vertical, from the slope of the ground, or from the rotation axis. Boom angle is measured from horizontal. People use the row for the unloaded reading, round the angle up, or average capacities. A loaded 43 degrees means the 40-degree row.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Boom angle or radius indicator. The equipment must have a boom angle or radius indicator readable from the operator's station. Temporary alternative measures: Radii or boom angle must be determined by measuring the radii or boom angle with a measuring device.
Boom angle indicator means a device which measures the angle of the boom relative to horizontal.

summary: Some charts and jib tables are read by boom angle, and many list a minimum angle. By chart practice, there is no capacity below the minimum angle. Boom angle is measured from horizontal and read with the load on, because the boom deflects and drops under load. Between listed angles, use the next lower listed angle. Under the federal rules, the crane has a boom angle or radius indicator readable from the operator's station, and as a temporary alternative the radius or angle is measured with a measuring device.
title: Use maximum and minimum boom angle data: no capacity below the minimum, loaded boom angle, the lower listed angle between rows

exam: Expect judgment items listing several setup positions or configurations, where you pick the one that works or the farthest position that still works. Do the chart reading for each option and reject any option that needs a configuration the manufacturer does not rate.
hard: Every choice has to land on a configuration the manufacturer actually rates. A mixed outrigger setup with no chart, extra counterweight, or ratings you split into zones yourself are not options. The deciding check is the rating at the longest radius the load will reach, read by the chart's rules with no interpolation.
mistakes: People run the 75 percent weight check at 85 percent, at 90 percent (a common LMI warning setting), or at the shortest or pick radius. The rule uses 75 percent at the longest radius used. People think a qualified person, a one-time exception or a small tolerance allows counterweight over the maximum. Any amount over the manufacturer's maximum is not allowed, and extra counterweight raises the risk of tipping backward. People rate a mixed outrigger setup by the majority of beams, make up zone ratings, or use the on-rubber chart while on outriggers. Use a manufacturer chart for the actual setup, which is limited by the least-extended beam where no mixed chart exists. People accept a small overload, add a margin the chart does not require, or interpolate to make a radius work. Rated capacity is the limit, read the chart's way.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.
The maximum counterweight or ballast specified by the manufacturer for the equipment must not be exceeded.
The outriggers or stabilizers must be either fully extended or, if manufacturer procedures permit, deployed as specified in the load chart.

The operator must begin hoisting the load to determine, using a load weighing device, load moment indicator, rated capacity indicator, or rated capacity limiter, if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used during the lift operation. If it does, the operator must not proceed with the lift until he/she verifies the weight of the load in accordance with paragraph (o)(3)(i) of this section.

summary: Getting the most usable capacity comes down to setup choices. Set up as close to the pick and the set as the site allows, use the shortest boom that reaches and clears, extend outriggers fully, run the counterweight the chart calls for without going over the manufacturer's maximum, and reeve enough parts of line. The best plan uses a listed chart configuration that covers the load at the longest radius of the lift.
title: Choose set-up position, boom length, counterweight, outrigger extension and parts of line for the most usable capacity

exam: Arithmetic shows up inside chart, load-weight and percent items rather than on its own. Do a rough estimate first. Options that are off by a factor of ten, or by a factor of two from the ton conversion, are common.
hard: Most errors come from units and zeros, not the math itself. A short ton is 2,000 lb. Inches divide by 12, not 10. Square units convert by the factor squared. Rounding should always land on the safe side, which means up for load weight and parts of line, and to the longer radius and lower rating for capacity.
mistakes: People divide by 1,000, multiply instead of divide, or use the 2,240 lb long ton. Pounds to short tons means dividing by 2,000. People write 9 inches as 0.09 ft or 0.9 ft. Nine inches is 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75 ft. People convert square yards to square feet with 3, add the sides, or work out the perimeter. One square yard is 3 × 3 = 9 sq ft. People drop or add a zero. Work 24 × 3 = 72, then put back the two zeros to get 7,200 lb. People halve a member's weight because it has two pick points. The crane still carries the whole weight.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: The exam is done without a calculator, so you need quick, reliable hand math: multiplying and dividing, percent, converting inches to feet, converting pounds to tons, area, and rounding in the safe direction. Most chart problems are a few additions and subtractions plus one multiplication or division. On the job, the same skills let you check a number before you trust it.
title: No-calculator arithmetic: multiplication and division, percent, feet and inches, pounds and tons, area, rounding in the safe direction

exam: Items usually give a scenario with a manual that exists or one that is missing and ask who develops the procedure or whether a workaround is allowed. Read for the word unavailable and for whether the subject is controls or capacity.
hard: There are two kinds of missing procedure, and each has its own author: controls go to a qualified person, capacity goes to the engineer. The whole fallback applies only when the manufacturer's procedures are unavailable, so it is never a way to override a manual that exists. If load charts are electronic only and the display fails, you stop or follow safe shutdown until the charts are available again.
mistakes: People think a qualified person can write capacity procedures; capacity procedures have to be developed and signed by a registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment. People think the engineer is needed for control procedures; a qualified person develops those. People think a competent person, the controlling entity or the operator writes missing procedures; none of them is named for that. People think a qualified person's approval, an engineer's signature, or close supervision can replace a manufacturer procedure that exists; the fallback only applies when the manufacturer's procedures are unavailable. People think being more careful than the manual counts as compliance, or that only the attachment's capacity chart matters; every applicable manufacturer step, including erection and use of the attachment, has to be followed. People think a thorough inspection establishes capacity; it does not.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The employer must comply with all manufacturer procedures applicable to the operational functions of equipment, including its use with attachments.
Where the manufacturer procedures are unavailable, the employer must develop and ensure compliance with all procedures necessary for the safe operation of the equipment and attachments.
Procedures for the operational controls must be developed by a qualified person.
Procedures related to the capacity of the equipment must be developed and signed by a registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment.
must be readily available in the cab at all times for use by the operator.
the operator must immediately cease operations or follow safe shut-down procedures until the rated capacities (in electronic or other form) are available.

summary: You follow every manufacturer procedure for the crane's operating functions, including when it is used with attachments. Only when the manufacturer's procedures are unavailable does the employer write its own: a qualified person writes procedures for the operational controls, and a registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment writes and signs anything about capacity. Load charts, operating speeds, hazard warnings and the operator's manual have to be readily available in the cab.
title: Follow manufacturer procedures and limits

exam: Expect a scenario with a call or task during operation and a choice of whether it is allowed. Ask yourself one question: is this signal communication? If not, the answer is to stop the activity or stop operating.
hard: The test is whether the activity diverts your attention, not whether it is work-related, hands-free or done with your hands still on the controls. The exception covers signal communications only, so a call about scheduling, weather or service advice does not fit it. The rule applies while you are operating, not to your whole shift or to just sitting in the cab.
mistakes: People think any work call is allowed; only signal communications fall under the exception, and planning, scheduling or service calls do not. People think hands-free use or keeping hands on the controls makes it fine; the activity still diverts attention. People think the rule covers only phones; it covers any practice or activity that diverts attention. People think it applies only while hoisting, or for the whole shift; it applies while you are actually operating. People think slowing the swing or having another worker watch excuses the distraction; it does not.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The operator must not engage in any practice or activity that diverts his/her attention while actually engaged in operating the equipment, such as the use of cellular phones (other than when used for signal communications).

summary: While you are actually operating, you may not do anything that takes your attention off the crane. A cell phone is the named example, and the only stated exception is using it for signal communications. One glance away at the wrong moment can put a load into a person or a structure.
title: Avoid distractions while operating

exam: Expect scenarios where the operator wants to step away and you pick whether that is allowed, or which missing condition makes it a violation. Check every condition and look closely at who is approving it and what the operator is doing meanwhile.
hard: All four conditions have to be met together, and people tend to remember two or three. An ordinary pause for signals, rigging adjustment or placement is part of normal lifting, so it does not qualify. The restraint list names crane functions, so carrier brakes or parking controls do not replace swing, telescope, boom hoist or outrigger restraint.
mistakes: People think the operator, the signal person or a rigger can approve leaving a suspended load; the competent person makes that call and puts the restraints in place. People think any pause qualifies; the hold has to be planned to last longer than normal lifting operations. People think setting the carrier brake or steering lock covers the restraints; the boom hoist, telescoping, load, swing and outrigger or stabilizer functions have to be restrained. People think doing paperwork close by, or having a signal person watch, is allowed; the operator stays adjacent and takes on no other duties. People think the competent person can waive a condition; no one can.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The operator must not leave the controls while the load is suspended, except where all of the following are met:
The operator remains adjacent to the equipment and is not engaged in any other duties.
The load is to be held suspended for a period of time exceeding normal lifting operations.
The competent person determines that it is safe to do so and implements measures necessary to restrain the boom hoist and telescoping, load, swing, and outrigger or stabilizer functions.
Barricades or caution lines, and notices, are erected to prevent all employees from entering the fall zone.
The operator shall not be permitted to leave his position at the controls while the load is suspended.

summary: The operator does not leave the controls with a load suspended. The construction rule has one narrow exception, and every condition has to be met: you stay adjacent to the crane with no other duties, the hold is longer than normal lifting operations, a competent person decides it is safe and restrains the boom hoist, telescoping, load, swing and outrigger or stabilizer functions, and the fall zone is barricaded with notices and kept empty. Light working gear over a non-entrance area is treated separately.
title: Secure the crane before leaving it; never leave a suspended load

exam: Items ask where the tag goes, who can remove it, or what the operator must confirm before starting a tagged crane. Watch whether the scenario takes out the whole crane or a single function, and count the conditions in the operator's verification.
hard: People blur the placement rule (cab for the whole crane, conspicuous position for one function) with the response rule, which covers tags on the equipment, the starting control or any other control. The operator's alternative takes two checks, not one. Removal is limited by authorization, not by who hung the tag.
mistakes: People think a tag anywhere visible on the crane is enough for a crane taken out of service; that tag goes in the cab. People use the cab tag when only one function is out, or the reverse; one function gets its own tag in a conspicuous position. People think a log entry or a tag saying the function is limited is enough; the tag has to say the function is out of service and is not to be used. People think only the person who hung the tag can remove it; any person authorized to remove it may. People think being qualified, being assigned to the crane, or holding a foreman's written order lets you start a tagged crane; it does not. People think a walk-around alone or an inspection satisfies the response rule; the operator verifies both conditions: no one in a dangerous position, and the crane repaired and working properly.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Where the employer has taken the equipment out of service, a tag must be placed in the cab stating that the equipment is out of service and is not to be used.
Where the employer has taken a function(s) out of service, a tag must be placed in a conspicuous position stating that the function is out of service and is not to be used.
the operator must not activate the switch or start the equipment until the sign has been removed by a person authorized to remove it, or until the operator has verified that:
No one is servicing, working on, or otherwise in a dangerous position on the machine.
The equipment has been repaired and is working properly.

summary: When the employer takes the whole crane out of service, a tag goes in the cab saying the equipment is out of service and not to be used. When only one function is out, a tag goes in a conspicuous position saying that function is out of service and not to be used. If you find a tag, you do not start the crane or use that control until an authorized person removes the tag, or until you have verified both that no one is working on or in danger around the machine and that it has been repaired and works properly.
title: Apply tag-out and respond to do-not-operate tags

exam: Expect timing items (when the check happens) and responsibility items (who does it), along with scenarios where someone is still near the machine. Watch for answers that move the deadline to just after startup.
hard: The deadline is before the engine starts, not at idle, warm-up or first crane motion. The rule says proper starting position, which is often neutral but is set for each control, not a blanket neutral. In practice the step that gets skipped is accounting for everyone, including mechanics and others outside the lifting crew.
mistakes: People do the check after the engine reaches idle, before warm-up, or before engaging hydraulics; it comes before starting the engine. People assign the check to the signal person, rigger or lift supervisor; they can help, but the operator verifies. People think every control goes to neutral; each control goes to its proper starting position. People think checking control locks, or leaving controls where they were at shutdown, is enough; you verify the starting positions. People think a warning shout, leaving hydraulics disengaged, or clearing only the riggers covers personnel; all personnel have to be confirmed clear.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Before starting the engine, the operator must verify that all controls are in the proper starting position and that all personnel are in the clear.

summary: Before you start the engine, you verify that every control is in its proper starting position and that all personnel are in the clear. A control left engaged or a mechanic under the deck can turn a routine startup into an injury. This duty belongs to the operator.
title: Check controls in neutral and people clear before starting

exam: Items ask who gets the report, in what form, and when the crew is told. Watch for choices that are right on one point (written) but wrong on another (wrong recipient or wrong timing).
hard: There are two duties held by two parties: the operator's written report, and the employer's shift-start notice. The report has to be written, prompt, and addressed to the designee, plus the next operator when shifts follow each other. The notice repeats every shift until the problem is resolved.
mistakes: People think a verbal report or a radio relay through the signal person is enough; the report is in writing to the designated person. People think a log entry for the next monthly inspection is fine; the report is prompt. People send the report to the annual inspector or the rental repair vendor; it goes to the designee and the next operator. People think the operator briefs all affected workers; that notice is the employer's job, and the employer, not the crane owner or a lift director, holds it. People think notice is a one-time, weekly, or end-of-shift event; it comes at the beginning of each shift.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The operator must, in writing, promptly inform the person designated by the employer to receive such information and, where there are successive shifts, to the next operator; and
The employer must notify all affected employees, at the beginning of each shift, of the necessary adjustments or repairs and all alternative measures.

summary: When the crane needs adjustment or repair, the operator promptly reports it in writing to the person the employer designated to receive it and, with successive shifts, to the next operator. The employer then notifies all affected employees at the beginning of each shift about the needed repairs and the alternative measures. This keeps the next crew from walking into a known problem.
title: Report needed adjustments and repairs

exam: Expect scenarios where an aid reads normal but something else is wrong, and you choose the operator's correct action. Distractor answers usually rely on the device, a test of the device, or a different device.
hard: An LMI can show a comfortable percentage while the crane is actually in trouble, for example when the setup entry is wrong or the footing is sinking. Knowing what the device measures (boom angle, length, pressure or load) and what it does not (ground support) is the core skill. A limit switch is a last line of defense, not a stop you run into on purpose.
mistakes: People put this duty on the lift director, signal person or a qualified person; the rule is about the operator's judgment. People think staying above a boom angle, warming the hydraulics, or a good anti-two-block test fixes an LMI with the wrong setup entered; only a correct setup does. People think boom angle is not sensed; it is a basic LMI input. People trust the LMI to prevent tipping on failing footing; it does not account for ground giving way, and moving slowly with a spotter or getting a lower percentage does not fix the support. People think a passed function test makes it fine to let the upper limit switch stop the hoist; the operator stops the hoist, and the switch is a backup.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Safety devices and operational aids must not be used as a substitute for the exercise of professional judgment by the operator.
The hoist limit switch which controls the upper limit of travel of the load block shall never be used as an operating control.

summary: Safety devices and operator aids such as the load moment indicator, anti-two-block and limit switches back you up; they do not replace your judgment. An LMI only knows what its sensors and its setup entry tell it, so a wrong configuration, soft ground or a failing switch can leave you with no protection. The operator's judgment is the one the rule protects.
title: Never use safety devices or aids as a substitute for judgment

exam: Items test the timing (before starting to lift), the location (drum and sheaves), and who decides re-spooling is needed. Physics items ask why tension jumps when slack is snatched.
hard: The check covers both the drum and the sheaves, and it happens as slack is removed, before you start to lift. A trial lift is already lifting. On the physics side, slack does not change the parts of line or the load weight; the spike comes from accelerating the load suddenly when the rope goes tight.
mistakes: People give this determination to the signal person, rigger or lift supervisor; the rule names the competent person. People verify seating during a trial lift, before swinging, before lowering, or once the load clears its supports; the verification comes before starting to lift. People recheck the drum and skip the sheaves; the rule covers both. People think slack changes mechanical advantage or the load's weight; neither changes, and the extra tension comes from sudden acceleration. People think taking up slack increases the radius; the spike is shock, not radius.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: If the competent person determines that there is a slack rope condition requiring re-spooling of the rope, it must be verified (before starting to lift) that the rope is seated on the drum and in the sheaves as the slack is removed.

summary: When the competent person determines that slack rope needs re-spooling, someone has to verify before lifting starts that the rope is seated on the drum and in the sheaves as the slack is taken out. Rope that jumps a sheave or piles up wrong on the drum can be crushed or cut under load. Separately, snatching a load out of slack creates a shock load.
title: Handle slack rope conditions

exam: Expect percentage threshold items, radius-selection scenarios with pickup, path and set points, and questions on acceptable weight sources. Read carefully for longest radius and before the lift.
hard: The 75 percent comparison uses the capacity at the longest radius of the whole lift, not the pickup or set radius. The 75 percent figure is a trigger for verification; rated capacity is still the limit. Weight information you request is due before the lift starts, and hoisting already counts as the lift.
mistakes: People use 50 or 85 percent as the trigger; the trigger is above 75 percent. People treat 75 percent as the operating limit; rated capacity is the limit, and above 75 percent you verify weight first. People take the check at the pickup radius, the destination radius or an average; it is taken at the longest radius that will be used. People think requested weight data can come once the load is up or before the swing; it is due before the lift. People accept a similar load's weight, the truck's payload rating or an eyeball estimate; use a recognized source, a recognized calculation, or equally reliable means.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.
The operator must not be required to operate the equipment in a manner that would violate paragraph (o)(1) of this section.
In addition, when requested by the operator, this information must be provided to the operator prior to the lift; or
if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used during the lift operation.

summary: The crane is not operated beyond its rated capacity, and the operator cannot be required to do so. You verify the load is within capacity one of two ways: get the weight from an industry-recognized source or calculation (provided before the lift if you ask), or begin hoisting with a load weighing device, LMI, rated capacity indicator or limiter. If that reading exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius used during the lift, you stop and verify the weight by the first method.
title: Never exceed rated capacity; verify load weight

exam: Expect setup scenarios with tight clearances and choices about what is covered, and questions about what to do after a strike. Watch for answers that manage the risk instead of removing the contact.
hard: People picture only the boom tip, but the counterweight sweeping past a parked truck counts too. Deflection has a vertical and a horizontal part, and both eat into clearance. A slow swing with a spotter still contacts the obstruction if the clearance is not there.
mistakes: People think only the tip, the boom or load-carrying members count; the boom and every other part of the equipment are covered, counterweight included. People think more cylinder pressure stiffens or raises the boom; loaded deflection moves the tip down and out. People forget either the outward or the downward movement; both happen. People think a spotter and a slow swing make a 6-inch clearance acceptable; the rule prohibits contact, so fix the clearance. People think swing-radius barricades satisfy this; barricades protect workers and do not stop the counterweight hitting something. People leave the evaluation of a struck boom to the operator, signal person or the next periodic inspection; good practice is a qualified person's evaluation before further use.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The boom or other parts of the equipment must not contact any obstruction.
The load does not contact any obstructions.

summary: No part of the crane may contact an obstruction: not the boom, the counterweight, the outriggers or the carrier. Under load the boom deflects, so the tip moves down and out, and clearances shrink. A boom that strikes something can hide damage, so in practice it gets reported and evaluated before the crane works again.
title: Keep the boom clear of obstructions

exam: Items describe a load needing to move a short distance and offer clever ways to drag it, or ask about the force on an angled line. The answer is to reposition so the hook is plumb over the load, or to use other equipment.
hard: No surface, roller, skid, boom length or direction makes dragging allowed. On the physics side, a tensioned line at an angle has a horizontal component that pulls the load toward the point under the boom tip and can start it swinging even when the upper is still. Overhead cranes in general industry have a separate side-pull provision; don't carry it over to mobile cranes.
mistakes: People think rollers, skids or a smooth floor make a sideways pull acceptable; the crane still may not drag or pull the load sideways. People think pulling in line with the boom, over the rear, or with a retracted boom is fine; none of these is an exception. People think pulling with boom retraction instead of the hoist changes things; it is still a sideways pull. People think slow motion and spare chart capacity permit it; they do not. People think hoisting only produces vertical force; an inclined line pulls sideways too, toward the suspension point, and can start a swing.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be used to drag or pull loads sideways.
Side loading of booms shall be limited to freely suspended loads. Cranes shall not be used for dragging loads sideways.

summary: The crane is not used to drag or pull loads sideways. Booms are built for vertical loads, and side force from an angled line can buckle a boom or upset the crane. In general industry, side loading of booms is limited to freely suspended loads.
title: Avoid side loading and dragging loads sideways

exam: Expect a scenario with a carrier type, a setup and a proposed approver, and you decide if the lift is allowed. Check the carrier type first, then whether the manufacturer, and only the manufacturer, permits it.
hard: The rule depends on the carrier type, not the setup, so full outriggers do not open the front area. The only exception is the manufacturer; there is no engineer, qualified person or supervisor alternative here. If the chart for that outrigger setup leaves out the front, there is no front rating to derate from.
mistakes: People think a qualified person, engineer, supervisor, controlling entity or lift plan can allow a front lift; only the manufacturer can. People think the rule applies only on rubber; it applies to wheel-mounted equipment in any setup. People think fully extended outriggers override the rule; they add no permission the manufacturer did not give. People think it covers only truck cranes, or includes crawlers; it covers all wheel-mounted equipment, and crawlers follow their own charts. People invent a reduced front value from the side rating; with no listed front permission, no derated number makes the lift allowed.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: On wheel-mounted equipment, no loads must be lifted over the front area, except as permitted by the manufacturer.
On truck-mounted cranes, no loads shall be lifted over the front area except as approved by the crane manufacturer.

summary: On wheel-mounted cranes, no loads are lifted over the front area unless the manufacturer permits it. That covers truck cranes, rough-terrain cranes and other wheeled carriers, on rubber or on outriggers. The load chart and working-area diagram show where the manufacturer allows lifting.
title: Know the over-the-front rule for wheel-mounted cranes

exam: Expect number items (the percentage, the height) and repetitive-lift scenarios asking which lift needs the test. Watch for line pull versus rated capacity in the wording.
hard: The number is 90 percent of maximum line pull, a hoist figure, not 75 percent of rated capacity. The height is a few inches, and the load has to be suspended. The repetitive-lift exception drops the test for successive lifts, not the first one.
mistakes: People use 75, 85, 95 or 100 percent as the trigger; it is 90 percent or more of maximum line pull. People test at a few feet or at travel height; it is a few inches. People apply the brakes while the load is still supported; the load has to be lifted. People test on every lift of a repetitive series, every other lift, or the last lift; it is the first lift only. People treat a pre-lift check as the test; the loaded test is still required.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The operator must test the brakes each time a load that is 90% or more of the maximum line pull is handled by lifting the load a few inches and applying the brakes.
In duty cycle and repetitive lifts where each lift is 90% or more of the maximum line pull, this requirement applies to the first lift but not to successive lifts.

summary: Each time you handle a load at 90 percent or more of the maximum line pull, you test the brakes by lifting the load a few inches and applying them. It proves the hoist brake will hold before the load is high enough to hurt anyone. In duty-cycle and repetitive lifts where each lift is at that level, the test is on the first lift only.
title: Test brakes on loads of 90% or more of the maximum line pull

exam: Items ask who supervises loaded travel, what that person decides, and what controls tire pressure. Watch for job titles standing in for the competent person.
hard: The competent person role is the key, and an operator, signal person or rigger fills it only if actually serving as the competent person. A required capacity reduction does not ban travel; it gets applied. Tire pressure comes from the crane manufacturer, not the sidewall and not the competent person.
mistakes: People think the operator, rigger or signal person decides travel conditions by default; a competent person does. People think a suspended load cannot be carried, or that only crawlers can pick and carry; both are allowed unless the manufacturer prohibits it. People think any derating means no travel; the competent person's reduction is applied. People think equal pressure in all tires, the sidewall maximum, or a number from the competent person is right; maintain the pressure the manufacturer specifies. People think a level route or crawler tracks remove the supervision requirement; they do not.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Traveling with a load is prohibited if the practice is prohibited by the manufacturer.

A competent person supervises the operation, determines if it is necessary to reduce rated capacity, and makes determinations regarding load position, boom location, ground support, travel route, overhead obstructions, and speed of movement necessary to ensure safety.
The determinations of the competent person required in paragraph (u)(2)(i) of this section are implemented.
For equipment with tires, tire pressure specified by the manufacturer is maintained.

summary: Pick and carry is prohibited if the manufacturer prohibits it. Where it is allowed, a competent person supervises, decides whether to reduce rated capacity, and makes the calls on load position, boom location, ground support, route, overhead obstructions and speed, and those calls are carried out. On tires, the manufacturer's specified tire pressure is maintained.
title: Travel with a load only as the manufacturer and a competent person allow

exam: Expect a speed-to-force ratio item that you can do in your head, and scenarios comparing start and stop techniques. Watch for answers that fix only half the motion.
hard: There is no listed rpm or percent; the limit is load control. Outward force goes up with the square of swing speed, so double the speed gives four times the force. The stop matters as much as the start: braking hard lets the load keep going.
mistakes: People look for a legal swing speed on the chart or a percent-of-chart trigger; the rule sets a performance limit, not a number. People think swing speed is left entirely to the operator; the operator judges it, but the load has to stay within controllable radius. People think radius is fixed by the boom tip, or that a pre-swing LMI reading still applies; an outswung load acts farther out. People think a brief outswing is harmless; brief dynamic overloads can tip a crane or damage the boom. People say doubling speed doubles, cubes or roughly 1.4 times the force; it is 2 × 2 = 4 times. People use taglines to stop a fast-moving heavy load; taglines guide and steady, and stopping a load that way endangers the crew.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Rotational speed of the equipment must be such that the load does not swing out beyond the radius at which it can be controlled.
A tag or restraint line must be used if necessary to prevent rotation of the load that would be hazardous.
When rotating the crane, sudden starts and stops shall be avoided.

summary: Swing speed has to be slow enough that the load does not swing out beyond the radius at which it can be controlled, and a tag or restraint line is used when load rotation would be hazardous. A load that swings out acts at a larger radius than the boom tip, which can overload or tip the crane. Smooth starts and stops are the main control.
title: Control swing speed so the load does not swing out

exam: Expect judgment items picking the action that creates or avoids shock, and stability items about a sudden release. Watch for words like abruptly, snatch and sudden.
hard: Shock loading is about suddenness, not about lifting or hoist speed itself; taking slack out slowly and then accelerating smoothly is fine. Load loss does not remove counterweight, it removes the load's forward moment, which can tip the crane backward. Static capacity margins do not excuse dynamic shocks.
mistakes: People think unused sling or crane capacity, or chain slings, make shock loading acceptable; shock loading is prohibited. People think any outward swing is a violation, or that a fixed fraction of swing speed is compliant; the test is control at the resulting radius. People think losing the load reduces the counterweight moment, or that less weight always means more stability; the load's forward moment disappears, and the crane can rebound rearward. People think fixed outrigger positions keep the moments constant; removing the load changes them at once. People think any lift, slack take-up or hoist acceleration counts as shock loading; abruptly taking up slack is the problem.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Shock loading is prohibited.
There is no sudden acceleration or deceleration of the moving load.
Rotational speed of the equipment must be such that the load does not swing out beyond the radius at which it can be controlled.

summary: Dynamic loading is extra force from motion: snatching a load out of slack, sudden starts and stops, fast swings, and the sudden loss of a load. Shock loading of slings is prohibited, and swing speed has to keep the load within controllable radius. Dropping a load suddenly removes its forward moment, so the crane can rebound backward.
title: Recognize shock loading, duty cycle and rapid loss of load

exam: Expect items asking which crane types need boom stops and conceptual items about which condition is least stable backward. Read whether the question asks about backward or forward stability.
hard: The exception depends on the boom type (hydraulic) or derricks, not the carrier, so lattice truck, crawler and pedestal cranes all need stops. At a steep angle, a suspended load ahead of the tipping edge actually helps backward stability. When a load releases suddenly, the counterweight has not changed; the load's forward balancing moment is what goes away.
mistakes: People think crawler, truck or pedestal mounting, or a fixed jib, exempts a lattice boom from boom stops; only derricks and hydraulic booms are excepted. People think a low boom angle is the least stable backward; a lower angle puts the boom's weight farther forward and helps resist backward tipping. People think a suspended load hurts stability in every direction; it adds forward moment against backward tipping, though forward limits still apply. People think load release increases the counterweight moment; the loss is in the load's forward moment. People think boom stretch on release adds forward moment; release relieves strain and the boom rebounds back.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Boom stops, except for derricks and hydraulic booms.
A crane with or without load shall not be traveled with the boom so high that it may bounce back over the cab.

summary: Backward stability is the crane's resistance to tipping over the rear, which is most at risk with the boom high, no load, and heavy counterweight. Boom stops are required, except on derricks and hydraulic booms, to keep a lattice boom from being pulled or bounced back over the cab. The crane is not traveled with the boom so high it may bounce back over the cab.
title: Understand backward stability and boom stops

exam: Expect radius-reference items, the direction of deflection, and no-calculator chart reads where the loaded radius lands between entries. Check what the chart notes say about radii between listed values.
hard: Radius starts at the axis of rotation, not the boom foot pin or an outrigger, and it is horizontal, not a diagonal. Deflection changes geometry without changing boom length or control settings. Common chart practice is to use the next longer listed radius when the actual radius falls between entries; don't round to the nearest or average.
mistakes: People measure radius from the boom foot pin or an outrigger; it is measured from the axis of rotation. People measure a sloped distance to the load; radius is horizontal. People think a loaded boom moves the tip inward, or that fixed boom length and controls mean a fixed radius; elastic bending moves the tip out. People think only load weight or telescoping raises load moment; any increase in radius raises it. People round 26 feet to the 25-foot entry, average two entries, or keep the capacity for the unloaded radius; chart practice is the next longer radius, here the 30-foot entry.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

summary: Under load, the boom bends, and on an elevated boom that moves the tip down and out. The working radius, measured horizontally from the axis of rotation to the hoist line, grows even though nobody touched the controls. A bigger radius means a bigger load moment and less capacity, so the loaded radius is what governs the chart.
title: Account for boom deflection increasing radius

exam: Items ask which indicator satisfies the rule, where it must be readable, and what to do when it fails. Simple geometry items check what radius means as the crane swings.
hard: It is an either/or: boom angle or radius indication, and a boom length indicator is not the alternative. The reading has to be readable from the operator's station, not from the ground or a platform. The temporary fix calls for actual measurement, not an estimate or an old record.
mistakes: People add a boom length indicator to the requirement or substitute one for boom angle; the requirement is boom angle or radius indication. People think both indicators are required; either one meets it. People think visibility to the signal person or from the ground or an access platform is enough; it has to be readable from the operator's station. People estimate radius by comparing to carrier length, use a past lift's record, or rely on an experienced person's eye; measure radius or boom angle with a measuring device. People think swinging changes the radius, or use the circle's diameter; swinging at the same reach keeps the same radius.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must have a boom angle or radius indicator readable from the operator's station.
Temporary alternative measures: Radii or boom angle must be determined by measuring the radii or boom angle with a measuring device.

summary: The crane has to have a boom angle indicator or a radius indicator you can read from the operator's station. If it is not working, the temporary alternative is to measure the radius or boom angle with a measuring device. Radius is the horizontal distance from the axis of rotation to the center of the hoist line.
title: Determine and verify radius

exam: Expect date items, lists of devices where you pick the one that does not count, and scenarios asking whether free fall is allowed. Check every listed condition before accepting an age-based exception.
hard: The date is October 31, 1984, and age alone never overrides the listed conditions. For backup devices, clutches and hydraulic motors do not count as brakes, but an internal static brake on a hydraulic drum does. Hydraulic boom cylinders and telescoping booms need integrally mounted holding devices, and a pressure test or remote valve does not substitute.
mistakes: People misremember the cutoff as July 31, the end of June, or later; it is October 31, 1984. People reject an internal static brake on a hydraulic drum; it is an accepted device, while clutches and hydraulic motors are not. People reject ratchet-and-pawl or secondary friction brakes; those are the listed examples. People think the secondary device has to engage automatically, or manually; either is allowed. People think the secondary device replaces the primary brake for lowering; it backs up the primary brake while the boom is held. People think a hose pressure test, a remote valve or a successful hold test meets the cylinder requirement; the holding device has to be integrally mounted.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: An employee is in the fall zone of the boom or load.
Lifting operations are taking place in a refinery or tank farm.
The equipment was manufactured prior to October 31, 1984; or

A secondary braking or locking device, which is manually or automatically engaged, to back-up the primary brake while the boom is held (such as a secondary friction brake or a ratchet and pawl device).
Hydraulic drums must have an integrally mounted holding device or internal static brake to prevent boom hoist movement in the event of hydraulic failure.
Neither clutches nor hydraulic motors must be considered brake or locking devices for purposes of this subpart.
Hydraulic boom cylinders must have an integrally mounted holding device.
Hydraulic telescoping booms must have an integrally mounted holding device to prevent the boom from retracting in the event of hydraulic failure.
An employee is directly under the load.

summary: A live boom, one designed to free fall, is prohibited when anyone is in the fall zone, someone is being hoisted, the load or boom is near power lines within the Table A distance, over an occupied shaft, over a cofferdam with people in the fall zone, or in a refinery or tank farm. Outside those conditions, a live boom is allowed only on equipment made before October 31, 1984, or on floating cranes and land cranes on vessels. Where live booms are prohibited, the boom hoist needs a secondary device, and load-line free fall is prohibited in similar listed conditions.
title: Know boom and load-line free fall prohibitions

exam: Expect scenarios with partial or extra counterweight and a proposed workaround, and you decide if operation is allowed. The answer almost always comes back to the manufacturer's specified configuration.
hard: The rule covers operating the crane at all, not just heavy lifts. Neither a reduced load nor a short radius makes up for missing counterweight, and a reduced load does not permit extra counterweight. Lattice crawlers, telescopic trucks and cranes with jibs are all non-tower equipment.
mistakes: People think having the counterweight on site is enough; it has to be in place as specified. People think it only matters for near-capacity lifts; it applies to operating the equipment. People think derating the load or working at short radius makes up for missing counterweight; it does not. People think a stationary lift, a lighter load or a good test lift allows exceeding the maximum counterweight; it does not. People think a lattice boom, telescopic boom or fixed jib puts the crane under the tower-crane provision; these are all non-tower equipment.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Equipment must not be operated without the counterweight or ballast in place as specified by the manufacturer.
The maximum counterweight or ballast specified by the manufacturer for the equipment must not be exceeded.

summary: Mobile cranes and other non-tower equipment are not operated without the counterweight or ballast in place as the manufacturer specifies, and the manufacturer's maximum counterweight is not exceeded. The chart you use assumes a specific counterweight, so missing weight means the wrong chart, and too much weight risks backward tipping and overstress. Tower cranes have their own section.
title: Run only with the specified counterweight or ballast

exam: Expect threshold wording items (less than versus or less), who inspects the rope, and where lifts get recorded. Watch for exceptions offered for a prohibited duty-cycle use.
hard: The threshold is less than 5, so a factor of exactly 5 is not in this prohibition. The duty-cycle ban has no inspection or approval exception. The records go in the monthly and annual inspection documents, not a daily log.
mistakes: People set the threshold at below 3, at 5 or less, or below 6; it is less than 5. People think the lift director, operator or a supervisor can inspect the rope by title; it has to be a qualified person, which an operator can be only if actually qualified. People record these lifts in a daily log or operating records; they go in the monthly and annual inspection documents. People think a good inspection, slower operation or the lift director's approval permits duty-cycle use below a factor of 5; nothing does.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Types II and III with an operating design factor of less than 5 must not be used for duty cycle or repetitive lifts.
A qualified person must inspect the rope in accordance with § 1926.1413(a).
Operations must be conducted in such a manner and at such speeds as to minimize dynamic effects.
Each lift made under § 1926.1414(e)(3) must be recorded in the monthly and annual inspection documents.

summary: Duty-cycle work, like clamshell, dragline or repetitive lifting, cycles the crane and rope over and over and builds heat and fatigue. Rotation-resistant rope (Types II and III) with an operating design factor below 5 may not be used for duty-cycle or repetitive lifts. For other lifts on that rope, a qualified person inspects the rope for each lift, the crane runs to minimize dynamic effects, and each lift is recorded in the monthly and annual inspection documents.
title: Know duty-cycle work limits

exam: Expect definition items on main versus auxiliary hoists, a number item on the platform winch, and scenarios asking whether a second line can be used. Watch for the exact exception named.
hard: Keep the whipline traits straight: lighter and faster. The other-line prohibition during personnel hoisting has one named exception, pile driving. The platform-winch limit is 500 pounds and also cannot exceed the winch or platform rating, whichever is lower.
mistakes: People think the whipline has more capacity because it is faster, or is slower because it is lighter, or reverse both; it is lighter capacity and higher speed. People think emergency rescue, proof testing or steel erection is the exception for other-line lifts during personnel hoisting; the named exception is pile driving. People apply 250, 750 or the 1,000-pound equipment rating to the platform winch; the ceiling is 500 pounds, within the winch and platform ratings. People think a separate signal person or spare capacity allows another-line lift during personnel hoisting; it does not.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The whipline (auxiliary hoist) is a separate hoist rope system of lighter load capacity and higher speed than provided by the main hoist.
No lifts must be made on any other of the equipment's load lines while personnel are being hoisted, except in pile driving operations.

Loads are permitted to be hoisted by such a winch while employees occupy the personnel platform only where the load on the winch line does not exceed 500 pounds and does not exceed the rated capacity of the winch and platform.

summary: Multi-drum cranes have a main hoist and an auxiliary hoist, or whipline, which has lighter capacity and higher speed. Each line has its own capacity limit, often set by parts of line and line pull, so the chart for one line does not cover the other. While personnel are being hoisted, no lifts are made on any other load line except in pile driving, with a 500-pound limit for factory-built boom-mounted platforms with their own winch.
title: Run multi-drum and main/auxiliary hoist operations

exam: Expect interval items, who-decides items, and trigger items about when a device is required. Read carefully for occupied and for external versus internal.
hard: The inspection intervals sit close: annual for the external vessel inspection, four years for the internal survey. Different people own different decisions: a competent person on wind, a qualified expert on capacity modification. Anti-two-block on these operations is required only for hoisting personnel or hoisting over an occupied cofferdam or shaft.
mistakes: People put the internal survey on an annual, three-year or five-year cycle; it is four years, and annual is the external inspection. People give the wind determination to the operator, the signal person or the capacity modifier; a competent person makes it. People think any hoisting over a shaft, alongside a vessel, or with a magnet or grapple triggers anti-two-block; it is required for personnel hoisting or hoisting over an occupied cofferdam or shaft. People think load charts for a crane with no cab and a movable station can be kept aboard, ashore or with a supervisor; they are posted on the equipment.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: A competent person must determine if wind is a factor that needs to be considered; if wind needs to be considered, a wind speed and direction indicator must be used.
An anti two-block device is required only when hoisting personnel or hoisting over an occupied cofferdam or shaft.
If the operator's station is moveable (such as with pendant-controlled equipment), the load charts are posted on the equipment.
The external portion of the barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of flotation used is inspected annually by a qualified person who has expertise with respect to vessels/flotation devices
Four-year: internal vessel/flotation device inspection. For each four-year inspection:

The rated capacity modification required in paragraph (n)(1) of this section is performed by the equipment manufacturer, or a qualified person who has expertise with respect to both land crane/derrick capacity and the stability of vessels/flotation devices.

summary: Cranes on barges and floating cranes face list, trim, wave action and wind that land charts do not account for. A land crane's rated capacity has to be reduced for those conditions by the manufacturer or a qualified person with both crane and vessel stability expertise, and the vessel itself is inspected each shift, monthly, annually on the outside, and every four years inside. Extra devices include a list and trim indicator, a positive house lock, and a wind indicator when a competent person decides wind matters.
title: Know the added rules for cranes on barges and floating cranes

exam: Expect physics items about when the hoist load peaks and rule items on the 75 percent check. Watch whether the scenario includes trapped water or drag.
hard: An LMI reading taken while the load is submerged understates what you will carry once it is clear of the water. The load's weight does not change; the upward help from the water does. The 75 percent comparison still uses the longest radius planned for the lift, which may be the landing or somewhere along the path.
mistakes: People use 50, 80 or 90 percent as the verification trigger; it is above 75 percent. People compare at the pickup radius, the break-out point or always the landing; use the longest radius that will be used. People think requested weight information can wait until the first swing, rigging or setup; it is due before the lift. People think water pressure adds downward load; losing buoyancy is what makes the hoist carry more. People think the peak is at the waterline; with no drag and no trapped water, the hoist load is greatest once the load is fully out of the water.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used during the lift operation.
In addition, when requested by the operator, this information must be provided to the operator prior to the lift; or

summary: A load coming out of water feels lighter while submerged because the water holds part of it up, and it can be held down by bottom suction or carry trapped water. As the load breaks the surface, buoyant support drops and the hoist takes the full weight, plus any water still inside. The 75 percent verification check and the before-the-lift weight information still apply.
title: Account for buoyancy, suction and water weight when lifting from water

exam: Expect a scenario after a malfunction asking the correct next step, who resolves the concern, and how the next shift is informed. Watch for answers that are right on timing but wrong on form or person.
hard: The paperwork duties after an emergency follow the repair rule: written, prompt, to the designee and the next operator, with the employer's shift-start notice. The person who clears a safety concern has to be qualified; a title is not enough. Emergency stop signals are obeyed no matter who gives them.
mistakes: People think prompt verbal notice or a shift handoff is enough; the operator's notice is written. People think reporting can wait for scheduled maintenance; it is prompt. People think the lift director, the assigned operator or a supervisor can clear the concern by title; a qualified person determines safety has been assured. People think a weekly briefing, a briefing tied to inspections, or notice after repairs are done covers the crew; affected employees are told at the beginning of each shift. People think a maintenance copy or asking someone to brief the next operator replaces written notice to that operator; it does not.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Whenever there is a concern as to safety, the operator must have the authority to stop and refuse to handle loads until a qualified person has determined that safety has been assured.
The operator must obey a stop (or emergency stop) signal, irrespective of who gives it.
The operator must, in writing, promptly inform the person designated by the employer to receive such information and, where there are successive shifts, to the next operator; and
The employer must notify all affected employees, at the beginning of each shift, of the necessary adjustments or repairs and all alternative measures.

summary: In an emergency (a control or travel failure, two-blocking, overload or fire) the first move is to stop safely, protect people, and put the load in a safe position if you can. Afterward, the repair goes in writing to the employer's designee and the next operator, and the crew hears about it at each shift start. Whenever there is a safety concern, the operator can stop and refuse loads until a qualified person decides safety is assured, and anyone's stop signal is obeyed.
title: Respond to control, travel, two-block, overload and fire emergencies

exam: Expect number items (30 versus 120 days) with careful wording about what the manufacturer did, and items about what form of approval counts. Identify which route the scenario is on before picking a number.
hard: There are fallback routes through a registered professional engineer, and each has its own timing. One applies if the manufacturer declines or fails to acknowledge or start review within 30 days. The other applies if the manufacturer agrees to review but does not finish within 120 days of receiving the detailed description. Approval alone is not enough; the operating documents have to match the change.
mistakes: People think an operator's notes of a phone call or witnessed verbal approval count; the manufacturer approves in writing. People think the owner's written statement substitutes; it has to be the manufacturer's approval. People use 15 or 60 days for nonresponse; it is 30 days, and it opens the engineer route, not immediate use. People apply 30 days to a manufacturer that agreed to review, or restart the clock at the agreement; that case is 120 days from when the detailed description was provided. People think an operator briefing, a filed approval letter, or waiting for the annual inspection takes care of the charts and manuals; the charts, procedures, manuals and decals are modified as necessary.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Modifications or additions which affect the capacity or safe operation of the equipment are prohibited except where the requirements of paragraphs (a)(1), (a)(2), (a)(3), (a)(4), or (a)(5) of this section are met.
The manufacturer approves the modifications/additions in writing.
The load charts, procedures, instruction manuals and instruction plates/tags/decals are modified as necessary to accord with the modification/addition.
but it declines to review the technical merits of the proposal or fails, within 30 days, to acknowledge the request or initiate the review, and all of the following are met:
but fails to complete the review of the proposal within 120 days of the date it was provided the detailed description of the proposed modification/addition
The employer must comply with all manufacturer procedures applicable to the operational functions of equipment, including its use with attachments.

summary: Attachments like hooks, magnets, buckets, augers and personnel platforms fall under the crane rules, and manufacturer procedures for their use are followed. Modifications or additions that affect capacity or safe operation are prohibited unless an approval route is met. The main route is the manufacturer's written approval, with charts, procedures, manuals and decals updated and the original safety factor kept.
title: Use only manufacturer-approved attachments

exam: Expect scenarios testing each condition of the suspended-load and working-gear exceptions, and who decides about storm securing. Find the one condition the scenario fails.
hard: Adjacent means right by the crane with no other duties; seeing it from a trailer or being on the radio does not count, and inspection paperwork is another duty. The working-gear exception compares to capacity as positioned, not maximum capacity, and the gear's weight has to be negligible, not just within capacity. Restraints do not satisfy the separate condition that the hold exceeds normal lifting operations.
mistakes: People give the hold determination to the signal person, rigger or controlling entity; it belongs to the competent person, who also implements the restraints. People think line of sight or radio contact equals adjacent; the operator stays adjacent. People think crane-related paperwork is allowed; any other duty breaks the exception. People compare gear weight to the crane's maximum capacity, or think within capacity means negligible; it is negligible relative to capacity as positioned. People think barricades let gear hang over a doorway; it has to be over an area other than an entrance or exit. People think restraints or adjacency alone make a routine pause acceptable; the hold also has to exceed normal lifting operations.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: When a local storm warning has been issued, the competent person must determine whether it is necessary to implement manufacturer recommendations for securing the equipment.
The operator remains adjacent to the equipment and is not engaged in any other duties.
The load is to be held suspended for a period of time exceeding normal lifting operations.
The competent person determines that it is safe to do so and implements measures necessary to restrain the boom hoist and telescoping, load, swing, and outrigger or stabilizer functions.

The provisions in § 1926.1417(e)(1) do not apply to working gear (such as slings, spreader bars, ladders, and welding machines) where the weight of the working gear is negligible relative to the lifting capacity of the equipment as positioned, and the working gear is suspended over an area other than an entrance or exit.

summary: Securing the crane at shutdown means landing the load, setting brakes and locks, restraining functions, and following manufacturer steps for the boom type, and when a local storm warning is issued, a competent person decides whether to apply the manufacturer's securing recommendations. If a load has to stay suspended, the construction exception requires all four conditions. Light working gear like slings or spreader bars can stay up if its weight is negligible compared with the crane's capacity as positioned and it hangs over an area other than an entrance or exit.
title: Shut down and secure lattice and telescopic cranes

exam: Expect number items (10 percent, two wraps) and scenarios on outrigger use and brake tests. A no-calculator chart comparison may ask whether a load exceeds the on-rubber rating.
hard: The 10 percent tolerance runs in each direction, not as a 20 percent window either way. Two full wraps is the floor for both the load drum and the boom drum. The brake test is per load, not per shift, and it does not change with setup or a heavier earlier lift.
mistakes: People treat 5 percent as the requirement or accept 15 percent uncertainty; the tolerance is plus or minus 10 percent. People read it as 20 percent either way; it is 10 percent either way. People use one, three or four wraps; the rule sets two full wraps on each drum. People think a shift-start brake test, an unchanged setup, or a heavier lift earlier covers the next near-rated load; each one gets the test. People think good tire pressure, a full-extension rating applied to partial extension, or a passed brake test allows a load above the without-outrigger rating; outriggers are required.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: No crane shall be loaded beyond the rated load, except for test purposes as provided in paragraph (e) of this section.

When loads which are limited by structural competence rather than by stability are to be handled, it shall be ascertained that the weight of the load has been determined within plus or minus 10 percent before it is lifted.
Neither the load nor the boom shall be lowered below the point where less than two full wraps of rope remain on their respective drums.
The operator shall test the brakes each time a load approaching the rated load is handled by raising it a few inches and applying the brakes.
Outriggers shall be used when the load to be handled at that particular radius exceeds the rated load without outriggers as given by the manufacturer for that crane.

summary: The general industry crane rule has its own load-handling list, and the exam pulls from it. No crane is loaded beyond rated load except for testing. For structurally limited loads, weight is known within plus or minus 10 percent before lifting, and neither load nor boom is lowered below two full wraps on its drum. Brakes are tested each time a near-rated load is handled, and outriggers are used when the load at that radius exceeds the without-outrigger rating.
title: Know the general industry load-handling rules

exam: Expect voltage-to-distance items from the travel table, spotter trigger items, and setup scenarios checking boom position and hook restraint. Read whether the crane is traveling with or without a load, since different rules apply.
hard: The travel table differs from the working clearance table, and its numbers sit close: 4 feet up to 0.75 kV, 6 feet over 0.75 to 50, 10 feet over 50 to 345, 16 feet over 345 to 750, and 20 feet over 750 to 1,000. The 20-foot spotter trigger is not voltage-based, even though 20 also appears in the table. A hook hanging low or held by the hoist brake can still swing.
mistakes: People use 10 or 16 feet for a 34.5 kV line; that band is 6 feet. People mix up the spotter trigger with the clearance table; the spotter trigger is closer than 20 feet regardless of voltage, while 6, 10 and 16 feet are table clearances. People think a high or low hook, or the hoist brake, counts as restraint; the empty hook is lashed or otherwise restrained. People angle the boom diagonally or sideways to see better or use open side space; the boom is carried in line with the direction of motion.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: up to 0.75 | 4 over .75 to 50 | 6 over 50 to 345 | 10 over 345 to 750 | 16 Over 750 to 1,000 | 20
The boom shall be carried in line with the direction of motion.
