The superstructure shall be secured against rotation, except when negotiating turns when there is an operator in the cab or the boom is supported on a dolly.
The empty hook shall be lashed or otherwise restrained so that it cannot swing freely.
A crane with or without load shall not be traveled with the boom so high that it may bounce back over the cab.

summary: Before you travel without a load, you set the boom in line with the direction of travel, lock the upper against rotation (except in turns under the stated conditions), restrain the empty hook so it cannot swing, keep the boom low enough that it cannot bounce back over the cab, and survey the route. Near power lines, travel clearance follows a separate travel table by voltage. When equipment will get within 20 feet of a line during travel, a dedicated spotter is part of the travel procedure.
title: Prepare to travel without a load: boom and jib position, swing lock, route survey, spotter

exam: Expect step-order scenarios after a malfunction and tag-placement items. Check the scope of what is out of service before picking a location.
hard: The tag depends on what was taken out of service: the whole crane gets a tag in the cab, a single function gets a tag in a conspicuous position. The report is prompt and written, not a conversation at shift end. Being the supervisor, the report recipient or the next operator does not make someone the qualified person.
mistakes: People think a verbal report, a weekly report cycle or a talk before leaving is enough; the report is prompt and in writing to the designee. People put a cab equipment tag on a single-function outage, or a function tag when the whole crane is out; match the tag to what was taken out of service. People write that the function is restricted or usable with approval; the tag says it is out of service and is not to be used. People keep the tag in a repair file, an office or on the access ladder; a function tag is in a conspicuous position and an equipment tag is in the cab. People think the lift supervisor, the report recipient or the next operator clears the concern by title; a qualified person does.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The operator must, in writing, promptly inform the person designated by the employer to receive such information and, where there are successive shifts, to the next operator; and
Where the employer has taken the equipment out of service, a tag must be placed in the cab stating that the equipment is out of service and is not to be used.
Where the employer has taken a function(s) out of service, a tag must be placed in a conspicuous position stating that the function is out of service and is not to be used.
Whenever there is a concern as to safety, the operator must have the authority to stop and refuse to handle loads until a qualified person has determined that safety has been assured.

summary: When a control, carrier or travel function misbehaves, stop the motion, get the load to a safe position if you can, and keep people clear. Then the operator reports the problem promptly in writing to the employer's designee and the next operator, and the employer tags out the equipment or just the bad function. Work resumes when a qualified person determines safety has been assured.
title: Respond to a control, carrier or travel malfunction: stop, secure the load, tag out, report

exam: Expect conceptual items asking which control action reduces load moment, and threshold and radius items on weight verification. Do the weight-times-radius comparison in your head.
hard: Lowering the hook without setting the load down changes height, not weight or radius, so the moment stays the same. Booming down lengthens the radius and increases moment, which is the instinctive wrong move on many cranes. Hoisting straight up does not shorten the radius either.
mistakes: People think the 75 percent trigger is 50 or 85 percent, or that verification waits for an actual overload; it begins above 75 percent, and exceeding rated capacity is prohibited. People check the pickup radius, the shortest radius or an average; use the longest planned radius. People think lowering the load or paying out rope reduces load moment; weight and radius are unchanged until a support takes the weight. People think booming down unloads the crane; going from 30 to 35 feet of radius raises the moment. People think hoisting reduces radius; it does not.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.
if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used during the lift operation.

summary: Load moment is load weight times horizontal radius. If you are overloaded, the functions that help are the ones that shorten the radius or put the weight onto a support; booming down or telescoping out make it worse. The crane is not operated beyond rated capacity, and above 75 percent at the longest planned radius you verify the weight before proceeding.
title: Respond to an overload: which functions reduce load moment and which increase it

exam: Expect identification items (which agent, which people, where the extinguisher goes) and emergency-sequence scenarios. Check whether the setting is construction or general industry.
hard: The two settings put the extinguisher in different places, and the exam can test which applies. The agent names are specific: dry chemical, not dry powder, wet chemical or pressurized water. The people who have to know the extinguisher are operating and maintenance personnel.
mistakes: People think the extinguisher has to be in the cab; construction calls for it on the equipment, accessible. People think a nearby fire station or an extinguisher on the service truck counts; it has to be on the crane. People substitute pressurized water, wet chemical or dry powder; the named types are carbon dioxide and dry chemical. People name the signal person, lift director or emergency responders as the second group; it is maintenance personnel alongside operating personnel. People read the general industry locations as cab-only, as the construction rule, or as both locations required; the cab or the vicinity of the crane is one choice or the other.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: If a fire starts on the crane, the usual sequence is to stop operations, land the load if you safely can, shut down, warn others and use the extinguisher only on a small fire you can safely fight. The crane rules call for an accessible fire extinguisher, with carbon dioxide and dry chemical named as the types, and operating and maintenance personnel familiar with its use and care. In construction the extinguisher is on the equipment; the general industry provision allows the cab or the crane's vicinity.
title: Respond to a fire on the crane; the fire extinguisher requirement

exam: Items ask who has to adjust operations for wind, ice or snow, or what the adjustment is meant to protect. Some ask for a wind-force multiplier when speed doubles, or where wind should be measured. Read for "competent" versus "qualified" and for the phrase "stability and rated capacity."
hard: The rule names one person and one effect: stability and rated capacity. Wrong answers usually name a nearby concern instead, like visibility, mat sizing or wear items. The physics trips people too. Wind pressure goes with speed squared, and wind usually gets stronger with height, so a ground reading tends to understate the wind at the tip.
mistakes: People give the weather duty to the qualified person, the controlling entity or the signal person; the rule names the competent person. People answer with visibility, snowmelt under the mats or cold-weather wear; the rule's stated concern is stability and rated capacity. People think twice the wind speed gives two, three or eight times the force; squaring the speed ratio of 2 gives about four times. People go by ground-level wind; manufacturer limits usually refer to wind at or near the boom tip, and wind generally increases with height. People think averaging readings fixes a reading taken at the wrong height; it hides gusts and still measures the wrong elevation.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The competent person must adjust the equipment and/or operations to address the effect of wind, ice, and snow on equipment stability and rated capacity.

summary: When wind, ice or snow affect stability or rated capacity, the competent person adjusts the equipment or the operation. That can mean lighter loads, a shorter boom or radius, a change in configuration, or stopping. It falls to the person on site who can spot changing conditions and has the authority to correct them.
title: Adjust or stop operations for wind, ice, snow and other weather

exam: Expect scenarios where a warning comes in during a job, with options asking who decides or what gets done next. Watch the wording for "local storm warning" versus a watch, and for answers that swap in the manufacturer's procedure with something improvised.
hard: Only a local storm warning triggers this rule. A broad watch, a set wind speed or a lightning distance does not. The duty is a decision about whether to use the manufacturer's securing recommendations. It is not an automatic boom-down, an evacuation order or a capacity derate. Securing means following the manual, not improvising.
mistakes: People give the storm-warning call to the operator, the qualified person or the controlling entity; the rule names the competent person. People treat a statewide watch, a fixed wind speed or lightning distance as the trigger; the rule names a local storm warning. People read the rule as "always lower the boom" or "evacuate the site"; it requires deciding whether the manufacturer's securing recommendations are needed. People leave the boom high and extended, set the brakes, or tie the boom to a structure; none of that is a manufacturer securing method, and a high, extended boom stays exposed to wind and can tip backward.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Storm warning. When a local storm warning has been issued, the competent person must determine whether it is necessary to implement manufacturer recommendations for securing the equipment.

summary: When a local storm warning is issued, the competent person decides whether to put the manufacturer's securing recommendations into effect. The securing steps come from the operator's manual, and many manuals call for retracting and lowering the boom. The operator carries out the steps once the call is made.
title: Follow manufacturer procedures on a storm warning

exam: Expect mental-math items on how force changes when wind speed or area changes, and scenarios with a load drifting out of plumb. Watch for answers that hold the radius fixed to the boom position, and for multipliers of 2, 3 or 8 when the right one is 4.
hard: Two variables act differently. Force goes up directly with projected area and with the square of wind speed. Load moment depends on where the load actually hangs, not where the boom points. In practice, load charts assume a freely suspended load hanging plumb, so wind-driven side loading and drift aren't accounted for in the chart.
mistakes: People think the assigned operator, qualified rigger or signal person owns the weather adjustment; the rule names the competent person. People think doubling wind speed doubles the force, or add the increase to the old force, or cube it; the force goes with speed squared, so it's about four times. People think a bigger area spreads the pressure out, or square the area; doubling the area doubles the force. People think steady wind means steady force; when the load turns a wider face into the wind, the force goes up. People think the radius holds as long as the boom doesn't move, or that an angled hoist line carries less weight; the full weight still hangs on the line and acts at the displaced, longer radius.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The competent person must adjust the equipment and/or operations to address the effect of wind, ice, and snow on equipment stability and rated capacity.

summary: Wind pushes on the boom and on the load's sail area. It can swing the load, side load the boom and reduce stability. A load blown out of plumb hangs at a longer radius than the boom position shows, so the crane is carrying more load moment than the operator may think. Large flat loads like panels and forms catch the most wind.
title: Understand wind on boom and load (sail area, swing, side load)

exam: Items ask you to read a direction in degrees, apply a gust limit to a set of readings, or name who has to comply with manufacturer procedures. Watch for "from" versus "toward" in direction items, and for the words gust, average and peak.
hard: The direction convention trips people. Wind "from the east" is traveling west and is reported as 90 degrees. When the instructions give a gust limit, the peak during the check governs, not the average or the reading right now. Doubling the wind speed gives about four times the force, so a limit that looks close can be well exceeded.
mistakes: People put the duty to follow manufacturer procedures on the controlling entity, the lift planner or the operator; the rule places it on the employer, while the operator applies the procedures. People mix up compass directions; wind from the west is 270, wind blowing toward the west comes from the east at 90, and wind blowing toward the north comes from the south at 180. People think doubling wind speed gives two, three or eight times the force; it gives four. People use the average wind, a low reading right now, or a lull to justify a lift; when the instructions set a gust limit, the measured gust governs.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The employer must comply with all manufacturer procedures applicable to the operational functions of equipment, including its use with attachments.

summary: A wind indicator, usually an anemometer mounted at or near the boom tip, shows the wind speed the manufacturer's limits refer to. Those limits vary by configuration and are often stated as gust speeds, and the employer has to follow the manufacturer's operating procedures. Wind direction is reported by where the wind comes from, in compass degrees: north is 360, east 90, south 180, west 270.
title: Read wind indicators and manufacturer wind limits

exam: Expect scenarios asking when work can resume after thunder, what an iced boom does to capacity, and which weather conditions the rule names. Watch for options that time the wait from the wrong event, or that treat practice as rule text.
hard: Keep the rule separate from practice: the paragraph names wind, ice and snow, not rain, fog or lightning. The lightning wait is timed from the last thunder, not from the last flash, the rain or the wind. Ice is a capacity problem, not just stiff controls, because load charts assume a clean boom.
mistakes: People give the weather duty to the rigger, signal person or crane owner; the rule names the competent person. People time the lightning wait from the last flash, the rain or the wind, or use 15 minutes; accepted practice is 30 minutes after the last thunder heard. People wait until lightning is close before stopping; lightning can strike miles ahead of a storm, so thunder is the signal to stop. People think the weather paragraph names fog, lightning or temperature; it names wind, ice and snow. People think load charts allow for ice or that a function test clears an iced boom; charts assume a clean boom, and ice adds weight and wind area that eat into capacity.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The competent person must adjust the equipment and/or operations to address the effect of wind, ice, and snow on equipment stability and rated capacity.

summary: The federal weather paragraph names wind, ice and snow, and makes adjusting for them the competent person's job. Lightning, cold and heat are handled through the manual and accepted safety practice. The widely used lightning practice is to stop when thunder is heard and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder. Ice adds weight and wind area to the boom. Cold and heat affect hydraulics, steel and the operator, so follow the manual's temperature procedures.
title: Handle lightning, cold and heat

exam: Expect scenarios like a gust or shock load during a lift, with options for what happens first and who inspects. Watch for "reasonable probability" versus "confirmed," and for answers that resume work on calmer weather or a test lift.
hard: The trigger is a reasonable probability. It doesn't take confirmed damage, visible damage or a measured overload, and not every remote possibility counts either. The inspection has to be done by a qualified person. The scope comes from the actual use or conditions, not from the next date on the inspection calendar.
mistakes: People wait for confirmed damage, visible evidence or a measured overload; a reasonable probability of damage triggers the requirements. People treat any conceivable possibility as the trigger; the rule says reasonable probability, judged by how severe the use or conditions were. People let the operator, a supervisor or any assigned mechanic do the inspection; it takes a qualified person, and a mechanic can do it only if qualified. People set the scope by the next scheduled inspection or the maintenance plan; the qualified person decides it from the severe use or conditions. People go back to work because the wind died down or a reduced-load trial lift went fine; neither replaces stopping and having a qualified person inspect.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Severe service. Where the severity of use/conditions is such that there is a reasonable probability of damage or excessive wear (such as loading that may have exceeded rated capacity, shock loading that may have exceeded rated capacity, prolonged exposure to a corrosive atmosphere), the employer must stop using the equipment and a qualified person must:
Inspect the equipment for structural damage to determine if the equipment can continue to be used safely.
In light of the use/conditions determine whether any items/conditions listed in paragraph (f) of this section need to be inspected; if so, the qualified person must inspect those items/conditions.

summary: When use or conditions make damage or excessive wear reasonably probable, the employer stops using the equipment. Examples are a load that may have gone over rated capacity, a shock load, or long exposure to a corrosive atmosphere. A qualified person then inspects for structural damage, decides what else needs inspecting given the conditions, and inspects it. Weather can set this off, for example a gust that shock-loads the boom or a load that swings into something.
title: Know when weather and use trigger severe-service inspection

exam: Questions usually give a jobsite where the employer wants to use its own procedures and ask what makes that allowed, who has to write them, or what still applies. Watch for answers that hand the job to someone by title, or that let employer procedures override a manufacturer prohibition.
hard: Employer procedures are not just a backup for when the manual is missing. They are an option the employer can choose if it can show they meet the requirements. Manufacturer prohibitions stay in force under both choices. Synthetic slings are an exception: if you use them in A/D rigging, you follow manufacturer procedures. Wire rope slings, alloy chain slings and spreader beams do not trigger that.
mistakes: People think choosing employer procedures turns manufacturer prohibitions into advice, or that a qualified person can waive them; the prohibitions apply under either choice. People think the operator, the inspector or a supervisor can write employer procedures because of their job; only a qualified person can develop them. People think employer procedures need the manufacturer's approval or the inspector's sign-off; what counts is the employer showing they meet the requirements. People think wire rope slings, chain slings or a spreader beam force manufacturer procedures; synthetic slings do.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: the employer must comply with all applicable manufacturer prohibitions and must comply with either:
Employer procedures may be used only where the employer can demonstrate that the procedures used meet the requirements in § 1926.1406.
The employer must follow manufacturer procedures when an employer uses synthetic slings during assembly or disassembly rigging.
Prevent unintended dangerous movement, and prevent collapse, of any part of the equipment.
Provide adequate support and stability of all parts of the equipment.
Position employees involved in the assembly/disassembly operation so that their exposure to unintended movement or collapse of part or all of the equipment is minimized.
Employer procedures must be developed by a qualified person.

summary: Every assembly or teardown follows one of two sets of procedures: the manufacturer's or the employer's. Either way, all applicable manufacturer prohibitions still apply. The employer can use its own procedures only if it can show they prevent unintended dangerous movement and collapse, give every part adequate support and stability, and position workers to keep their exposure low. A qualified person has to develop those procedures.
title: Choose manufacturer or employer A/D procedures

exam: Expect scenarios asking whether a setup can serve as the A/D director, when the review is due, whether the exception applies to a changed configuration, and which subject is missing from a crew briefing. Watch for the word immediately and for small configuration changes like a new jib or a different boom length.
hard: The two allowed setups are easy to blur. Two qualified persons with no competent person is not one of them. The review exception needs the same type and the same configuration, accessories included. Knowing the crane model is not enough. The review timing is immediately before assembly or disassembly begins, which may be later than shift start and earlier than the first pin goes in.
mistakes: People think an experienced operator or crew can stand in for the director's competent or qualified status; the director must meet the criteria directly or have qualified persons assisting. People think two qualified persons can replace the competent person; the director must be competent in either setup. People think a shift-start or planning-meeting review counts, or that the review can wait until the first pin or a changed step; it happens immediately before the operation begins. People think experience with the same crane type is enough to skip the review; it takes the same type and configuration, and a crew review does not replace the director's. People think covering capacities, signals or qualifications satisfies crew instructions; the crew must understand tasks, task hazards and hazardous locations, all three.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Assembly/disassembly must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person who is assisted by one or more qualified persons
Where the assembly/disassembly is being performed by only one person, that person must meet the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person.
Knowledge of procedures. The A/D director must understand the applicable assembly/disassembly procedures.

Review of procedures. The A/D director must review the applicable assembly/disassembly procedures immediately prior to the commencement of assembly/disassembly unless the A/D director understands the procedures and has applied them to the same type and configuration of equipment (including accessories, if any).
Before commencing assembly/disassembly operations, the A/D director must ensure that the crew members understand all of the following:
Their tasks.
The hazards associated with their tasks.
The hazardous positions/locations that they need to avoid.

During assembly/disassembly operations, before a crew member takes on a different task, or when adding new personnel during the operations, the requirements in paragraphs (d)(1)(i) through (d)(1)(iii) of this section must be met.

summary: The A/D director runs assembly and disassembly. That person meets both competent and qualified person criteria, or is a competent person assisted by one or more qualified persons. If one person does the whole job alone, that person has to meet both. The director understands the procedures and reviews them immediately before work starts, unless the director already understands them and has applied them to the same type and configuration of equipment. Before work starts, the director makes sure the crew understands their tasks, the hazards of those tasks, and the hazardous positions to avoid. This is repeated when someone changes tasks or a new person joins.
title: Know the A/D director's duties (supervision, review, crew instructions)

exam: Questions usually describe a crew member walking behind the counterweight or climbing onto the boom and ask who notifies whom, when, and what the operator may move. Watch for answers that limit the hold to one component or one direction of movement.
hard: The duty to notify belongs to the crew member who is going, not to the director or the signal person. The notice comes before going, not on arrival and not when work starts. The operator's hold covers any part of the equipment or load, in any direction. The rule calls for a pre-arranged system but does not name a method.
mistakes: People think the A/D director or signal person handles this notice, or that a work assignment counts as notice; the crew member going there informs the operator. People think it is fine to report after arriving or once work starts; the operator is told before the crew member goes. People think only the part being worked on, or only movement toward the worker or a change in radius, is off limits; no part of the equipment or load moves. People think the rule requires a radio channel, a written release or face-to-face clearance; it requires communication through the system arranged in advance.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Before a crew member goes to a location that is out of view of the operator and is either in, on, or under the equipment, or near the equipment (or load) where the crew member could be injured by movement of the equipment (or load), the crew member must inform the operator that he/she is going to that location.

Where the operator knows that a crew member went to a location covered by paragraph (e)(1) of this section, the operator must not move any part of the equipment (or load) until the operator is informed in accordance with a pre-arranged system of communication that the crew member is in a safe position.

summary: During A/D, crew members often go where the operator cannot see them: inside the carbody, on the boom, under the counterweight, beside the load. Before going to a spot out of the operator's view where crane or load movement could hurt them, the crew member tells the operator. When the operator knows someone went there, the operator does not move any part of the equipment or the load until told through a pre-arranged system that the person is in a safe position.
title: Protect crew members out of the operator's view

exam: Expect scenarios asking whether a worker may be under the boom during pin removal, who has to show the site constraint, and who sets the procedures. Read closely for whether another access route exists, because that usually decides it.
hard: The rule splits the duties: the employer shows the site really requires the exposure, and the A/D director carries out the procedures. It covers the whole time pins are being removed, not just the last one, and it covers jibs, other components and pin-like devices. The guidance example shows how it plays out. An assist crane supports the section, the far-side pins come out first from an aerial lift, then the basket moves out from under the boom before the near-side pins come out.
mistakes: People think the operator, inspector or signal person proves the exception; the employer does. People think the operator or a rigging supervisor carries out the exception procedures; the A/D director does. People think the rule covers only the main boom, literal pins, or the final connection; it covers the boom, jib, other components and similar devices for as long as pins are being removed. People think a spotter or a short exposure of a minute or so makes it acceptable; if there is side access, the exposure is a convenience, not a site necessity. Shorter exposure is required inside the exception but does not create one. People think every pin removal requires an assist crane; the rule's basic answer is to keep workers out from underneath.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: When pins (or similar devices) are being removed, employees must not be under the boom, jib, or other components, except where the requirements of paragraph (f)(2) of this section are met.

Exception. Where the employer demonstrates that site constraints require one or more employees to be under the boom, jib, or other components when pins (or similar devices) are being removed, the A/D director must implement procedures that minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize the duration and extent of exposure under the boom.

summary: When pins or similar devices are coming out, nobody stands under the boom, jib or other components. A released section can drop or kick without warning. The only exception is when the employer shows that site constraints require someone to be under there. Then the A/D director puts procedures in place that reduce the risk of unintended dangerous movement and keep exposure as short and as small as possible.
title: Keep people out from under the boom when pins come out

exam: Expect judgment scenarios: an unsymmetrical top section with an unknown CG, a crew about to rely on the boom hoist brake again, a short boom with full counterweight about to swing. Questions ask what the director does first or which hazard applies.
hard: The CG has to be identified only when the stability method depends on it. If you cannot pin it down, you use measures to prevent dangerous movement, like the guidance example of raising a section a few inches with everyone clear to see if it tips. The boom hoist brake test is tied to each time you will rely on the brake, which can happen many times in one shift. Backward stability is a real physics problem: with the boom short or off and the counterweight on, an empty hook gives the least forward moment, so the crane can tip back when swinging, traveling, or adding or removing components.
mistakes: People think one brake test per shift or per job covers it, or confuse it with periodic inspection; the brake is tested before each time you rely on it. People think the operator, controlling entity or rigger owns these hazards; the A/D director addresses them. People think the CG of every piece must always be found, or that a stenciled weight shows it; the CG is needed when the stability method depends on it, and a weight does not tell you where it is. People think only hook loads tip a crane and backward stability is only a travel issue; the counterweight can tip it back, and the check covers swinging, travel and attaching or removing components. People think a brake test deals with tipping backward; it only covers holding the boom.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Addressing specific hazards. The A/D director supervising the assembly/disassembly operation must address the hazards associated with the operation, which include:
Blocking material. The size, amount, condition and method of stacking the blocking must be sufficient to sustain the loads and maintain stability.

Verifying assist crane loads. When using an assist crane, the loads that will be imposed on the assist crane at each phase of assembly/disassembly must be verified in accordance with § 1926.1417(o)(3) before assembly/disassembly begins.
The center of gravity of the load must be identified if that is necessary for the method used for maintaining stability.

Where there is insufficient information to accurately identify the center of gravity, measures designed to prevent unintended dangerous movement resulting from an inaccurate identification of the center of gravity must be used.

Stability upon pin removal. The boom sections, boom suspension systems (such as gantry A-frames and jib struts), and components must be rigged or supported to maintain stability upon the removal of the pins.

Each time reliance is to be placed on the boom hoist brake to prevent boom movement during assembly/disassembly, the brake must be tested prior to such reliance to determine if it is sufficient to prevent boom movement.
Loss of backward stability. Backward stability before swinging the upperworks, travel, and when attaching or removing equipment components.

summary: The A/D director deals with a set list of hazards. Ground and site conditions. Blocking sized, stacked and placed to carry the load without damaging the boom. Assist crane loads verified before work begins. Suitable pick points. Center of gravity. Stability when pins come out. Pendants snagging on pins. Counterweights. Boom hoist brake failure. Loss of backward stability. Wind and weather. These are the reasons booms fall during teardown.
title: Address site, blocking, CG, boom support, pin and loss-of-backward-stability hazards

exam: Expect a teardown scenario that asks which pins can be removed now, or what has to happen before a given pin comes out. Watch for answers that offer partial withdrawal, reduced tension, or a support condition as a loophole.
hard: Every one of these rules says partly or completely. Backing a pin out to the taper or out of one plate counts as removal. Two different conditions apply: pendant tension, and the boom resting on its tip section. Learn which region of the boom each one protects. The cantilever rule covers top pins only, on the part ahead of the pendant attachments, until that piece is fully supported.
mistakes: People think a pin can be drifted partway out while it still bears, while one plate holds it, or once tension is cut in half; no pin comes out partly while the pendants are in tension. People think the rule covers only top pins, only bottom pins, or only the boom foot; it covers top and bottom pins across the whole region between the pendant attachments and the crane body. People think the resting-tip rule applies only on bare ground or only on cribbing; it covers the ground or any other support. People think lateral restraint makes withdrawal safe; restraining sideways movement does nothing to remove pendant tension.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: None of the pins in the pendants are to be removed (partly or completely) when the pendants are in tension.
None of the pins (top or bottom) on boom sections located between the pendant attachment points and the crane/derrick body are to be removed (partly or completely) when the pendants are in tension.

None of the pins (top or bottom) on boom sections located between the uppermost boom section and the crane/derrick body are to be removed (partly or completely) when the boom is being supported by the uppermost boom section resting on the ground (or other support).

None of the top pins on boom sections located on the cantilevered portion of the boom being removed (the portion being removed ahead of the pendant attachment points) are to be removed (partly or completely) until the cantilevered section to be removed is fully supported.

summary: Taking a lattice boom apart, including changing its length, follows a strict pin order that applies whether you use manufacturer or employer procedures. Pendant pins do not come out while the pendants are in tension. Boom section pins between the pendant attachment points and the crane body, top or bottom, do not come out while the pendants are in tension. With the boom supported by its uppermost section resting on the ground or other support, section pins between there and the crane body stay in. Top pins on a cantilevered section being removed stay in until that section is fully supported.
title: Remove boom and jib pins in a safe order

exam: Questions ask who sets a limit when the manual has none, whether a borrowed insert from another model is acceptable, or what to do with shipping pins. Watch for answers that treat a physical fit, a matching weight, or a later inspection as approval.
hard: An RPE comes in only when manufacturer data is unavailable. A qualified person, a competent person or the A/D director cannot fill that role. Readily available weights do not mean a specific marking method. Shipping hardware is kept, not thrown out, but leaving it loose on the boom creates a falling-object hazard once the boom goes up.
mistakes: People think the A/D director, a qualified person or a competent person can set the cantilever limit; without manufacturer data, an RPE determines it in writing. People think weights have to be stenciled on, or matter only for assist-crane picks or a controlling-entity lift plan; each component's weight has to be readily available. People think shipping pins can be thrown away, or left lying on a boom walkway; they are stowed or stored so they cannot fall. People think a boom insert that fits, matches in weight, or passes a test lift is approved; selection follows the manufacturer's specifications, and chord size, lacing and design loads differ between models.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Cantilevered boom sections. Manufacturer limitations on the maximum amount of boom supported only by cantilevering must not be exceeded. Where these are unavailable, a registered professional engineer familiar with the type of equipment involved must determine in writing this limitation, which must not be exceeded.
Weight of components. The weight of each of the components must be readily available.

Manufacturer instructions, prohibitions, limitations, and specifications. Where these are unavailable, a registered professional engineer familiar with the type of equipment involved must approve, in writing, the selection and configuration of components; or

Shipping pins. Reusable shipping pins, straps, links, and similar equipment must be removed. Once they are removed they must either be stowed or otherwise stored so that they do not present a falling object hazard.

summary: Components and configuration that affect capacity or safe operation follow the manufacturer's instructions, prohibitions, limitations and specifications. If those are unavailable, a registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment type approves the selection in writing. An approved modification is the other path. The weight of each component has to be readily available. Manufacturer limits on cantilevered boom are not exceeded, and without them an RPE sets the limit in writing. Reusable shipping pins, straps and links are removed and stowed or stored so they cannot fall.
title: Verify components, configuration, weights and shipping pins

exam: Expect a simple no-calculator comparison: section weight against the lug, sling and crane ratings, then pick the item that is exceeded or the action that is allowed. Watch for answers that add capacities together or point to the strongest piece instead of the weakest.
hard: The weakest rated piece in the load path governs. Ratings in series do not add up, and spare capacity in one part does not make up for an overloaded lug. The limits apply when a section is resting on blocking, while it is suspended, and before connections are secured. Proof-test loads and breaking strength are not working capacity.
mistakes: People think the limits apply only with an assist crane, only to suspended loads, or only after connections are made; they apply in all phases. People think a proof load or breaking strength is the allowable load; rated capacity governs. People think stability is the only limit; a component's rating can be reached first. People think a stronger sling, unused crane capacity, extra attachments or blocking can cover an overloaded lug; each piece stays within its own rating. For example, an 8,000-pound section on a lug rated 6,000 pounds is an overload no matter what the sling is rated.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Capacity limits. During all phases of assembly/disassembly, rated capacity limits for loads imposed on the equipment, equipment components (including rigging), lifting lugs and equipment accessories, must not be exceeded for the equipment being assembled/disassembled.

summary: During every phase of assembly and disassembly, the rated capacity of everything in the load path stays within limits: the crane, its components, the rigging, the lifting lugs and the accessories. A partly assembled crane can overload a lug or a sling long before it gets near tipping.
title: Stay within capacity during assembly

exam: Questions ask who may rig a boom section, whose instructions govern a synthetic sling, or what to do when webbing crosses a sharp chord edge. Watch for answers that swap in a different qualification or a different manufacturer.
hard: The rule is about who does the rigging, not who watches it or who is in charge. A competent person, the A/D director or a certified operator is not automatically a qualified rigger. For synthetic slings, the sling manufacturer is the source, not the crane manufacturer. Using synthetic slings also means following manufacturer A/D procedures.
mistakes: People think the A/D director, a competent person, a supervisor or a certified operator covers the rigging; the person doing it is a qualified rigger. People think synthetic slings are banned in A/D; they are allowed with protection and the sling manufacturer's requirements. People think the crane manufacturer or the rigger's own judgment sets how synthetic slings are used; the sling manufacturer does. People think extra capacity or more slings make up for a sharp edge; every sling touching a sharp edge needs protection. People think the synthetic sling paragraph also covers wire rope slings; wire rope protection is under 1926.251(c)(9).

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The rigging work is done by a qualified rigger.
Synthetic slings are protected from: Abrasive, sharp or acute edges, and configurations that could cause a reduction of the sling's rated capacity, such as distortion or localized compression.
Requirements for the protection of wire rope slings are contained in 29 CFR 1926.251(c)(9).
When synthetic slings are used, the synthetic sling manufacturer's instructions, limitations, specifications and recommendations must be followed.

summary: Rigging for assembly and disassembly is done by a qualified rigger, on top of the general rigging rules. Synthetic slings are allowed, but they have to be protected from abrasive, sharp or acute edges and from configurations that cut their capacity, like distortion or localized compression. You follow the synthetic sling manufacturer's instructions, limitations, specifications and recommendations. Wire rope sling protection is covered by a separate general rigging rule.
title: Rig A/D lifts with a qualified rigger and approved slings

exam: Expect setup scenarios: a tight site with one beam short, a loose float, an outrigger on the blind side. The question asks what is allowed or who can watch. Watch for answers that mix up the visibility rule with the extension rule.
hard: A partial extension is fine only if the manufacturer's procedures allow it and the load chart covers it. Staying under some percentage of capacity does not make it fine. The float, visibility and blocking rules name both outriggers and stabilizers. The removing-weight-from-the-wheels rule applies to outriggers only. A float set loosely under the pad, even centered, is not attached.
mistakes: People think a capacity margin or site approval allows a partial extension; the position has to be full extension or one the manufacturer allows and the chart covers. People think the float, visibility or blocking rules apply only to outriggers; they name stabilizers too. People think the operator has to see each outrigger personally, or that a rigger or the A/D director can watch it; the rule names the operator or a signal person. People think a centered loose float is fine, or that floats should be removed; floats that are used are attached, and blocking goes under the float or pad.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The outriggers or stabilizers must be either fully extended or, if manufacturer procedures permit, deployed as specified in the load chart.

The outriggers must be set to remove the equipment weight from the wheels, except for locomotive cranes (see paragraph (q)(6) of this section for use of outriggers on locomotive cranes). This provision does not apply to stabilizers.
When outrigger floats are used, they must be attached to the outriggers. When stabilizer floats are used, they must be attached to the stabilizers.
Each outrigger or stabilizer must be visible to the operator or to a signal person during extension and setting.

Be placed only under the outrigger or stabilizer float/pad of the jack or, where the outrigger or stabilizer is designed without a jack, under the outer bearing surface of the extended outrigger or stabilizer beam.

summary: Whenever outriggers or stabilizers are needed or used, they are either fully extended or, if manufacturer procedures allow, set as the load chart specifies. Outriggers are set to take the crane's weight off the wheels; that part does not apply to stabilizers. Floats that are used are attached. Each outrigger or stabilizer is visible to the operator or a signal person while it is being extended and set. Blocking goes only under the float or pad, or under the outer bearing surface of the beam if there is no jack.
title: Fully extend or set outriggers per the manufacturer

exam: Expect questions about who inspects, what the crane is checked against, what happens when the manual's criteria are missing, and whether a test pick is allowed first. Watch for wording that slips in a competent person or a different document.
hard: Keep the roles apart. The qualified person inspects and decides whether an RPE is needed. The employer makes sure the criteria get developed by the right person. The RPE comes in only when manufacturer criteria are missing and the qualified person says one is needed. The inspection checks against equipment criteria, not a lift plan, an old annual record or a crew checklist.
mistakes: People think a competent person or a certified operator can do this inspection; it takes a qualified person, and an operator can do it only if he also meets that standard. People think every post-assembly inspection needs an engineer; an RPE comes in only when criteria are unavailable and the qualified person decides one is needed. People think the lift plan, the annual record or an in-house checklist sets the standard; the manufacturer's equipment criteria do. People think the controlling entity, the employer or the operator decides whether an RPE is needed; the qualified person does. People think a shift inspection or a light test pick can come first; the crane is not used before this inspection.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Post-assembly inspection. Upon completion of assembly, the equipment must be inspected to ensure compliance with paragraph (m)(1) of this section (see § 1926.1412(c) for post-assembly inspection requirements).
Upon completion of assembly, the equipment must be inspected by a qualified person to assure that it is configured in accordance with manufacturer equipment criteria.

Determine if a registered professional engineer (RPE) familiar with the type of equipment involved is needed to develop criteria for the equipment configuration. If an RPE is not needed, the employer must ensure that the criteria are developed by the qualified person. If an RPE is needed, the employer must ensure that they are developed by an RPE.
Equipment must not be used until an inspection under this paragraph demonstrates that the equipment is configured in accordance with the applicable criteria.

summary: When assembly is finished, a qualified person inspects the crane to make sure it is configured to the manufacturer's equipment criteria. If those criteria are unavailable, the qualified person decides whether a registered professional engineer is needed to develop them. The employer makes sure the qualified person or the RPE develops them, and the qualified person then checks the crane against them. The crane is not used until this inspection shows it is configured correctly.
title: Inspect after assembly before use

exam: Expect questions that give a height and a location, like a worker on a boom section or on the deck, and ask whether fall protection is required. Also expect a question on the restraint anchorage factor. Watch for neighboring numbers and for locations close to the exception list.
hard: The A/D trigger is more than 15 feet, higher than the 6-foot trigger many workers know from other construction work. The exceptions are locations, not job titles, and the boom, jib and gantry are not among them. The twice-the-load test is for restraint anchorages. Personal fall arrest has its own rule: it can anchor to any apparently substantial part unless a competent person, by visual inspection, concludes the criteria would not be met.
mistakes: People apply 6 feet, 10 feet or 20 feet; the A/D trigger is an unprotected edge more than 15 feet above a lower level. People think boom, jib or gantry work is exempt; only the draw-works while running, the cab and the deck are excepted. People think fall protection is needed at any height during A/D; the rule sets a height trigger. People forget the deck exception, or tie it to a job title; it covers any worker on the deck. People give restraint anchorages a fixed pound rating, a factor of four, or an engineering analysis; the test is twice the maximum load the worker may impose.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: For assembly/disassembly work, the employer must provide and ensure the use of fall protection equipment for employees who are on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge more than 15 feet above a lower level, except when the employee is at or near draw-works (when the equipment is running), in the cab, or on the deck.

Personal fall arrest systems must be anchored to any apparently substantial part of the equipment unless a competent person, from a visual inspection, without an engineering analysis, would conclude that the criteria in § 1926.502(d)(15) would not be met.

Anchorages for fall restraint systems. Fall restraint systems must be anchored to any part of the equipment that is capable of withstanding twice the maximum load that an employee may impose on it during reasonably anticipated conditions of use.

summary: For assembly and disassembly, the employer provides fall protection and makes sure it is used when a worker is on a walking or working surface with an unprotected side or edge more than 15 feet above a lower level. The exceptions are at or near the draw-works while the equipment is running, in the cab, and on the deck. Fall restraint can be anchored to any part of the crane that can withstand twice the maximum load the worker could put on it under reasonably anticipated use.
title: Use fall protection during assembly and disassembly

exam: Expect scenarios like a jib borrowed from another model, a missing manual, or a manufacturer prohibition. The question asks who can approve, in what form, and when to inspect. Watch for the difference between unavailable instructions and instructions that prohibit.
hard: The RPE route applies only when manufacturer instructions are unavailable. If the manufacturer prohibits a jib or configuration, an engineer's approval on that route does not override it; only an approved modification is another path. Approval has to be in writing from an RPE. The post-assembly check is due when assembly is complete, not at the next monthly or annual inspection.
mistakes: People think a consensus standard or the owner's lift plan can authorize a jib configuration; selection follows the manufacturer or an approved modification. People think the A/D director, a qualified person or a competent person can approve a configuration when the manual is missing, sometimes just verbally; it takes an RPE, in writing. People think charts from another model, a jib whose pins fit, or a load test make it acceptable; none of those authorize a configuration the manufacturer does not allow. People think the RPE route applies even when the manual exists and prohibits the jib; it applies only when instructions are unavailable. People wait for the shift, monthly or annual inspection; the configuration is inspected upon completion of assembly.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Manufacturer instructions, prohibitions, limitations, and specifications. Where these are unavailable, a registered professional engineer familiar with the type of equipment involved must approve, in writing, the selection and configuration of components; or
Approved modifications that meet the requirements of § 1926.1434 (Equipment modifications).

Post-assembly inspection. Upon completion of assembly, the equipment must be inspected to ensure compliance with paragraph (m)(1) of this section (see § 1926.1412(c) for post-assembly inspection requirements).
Pile driving. Equipment used for pile driving must not have a jib attached during pile driving operations.
Jib stops (if a jib is attached), except for derricks.

summary: Jibs and boom extensions change capacity, so the jib you pick and how you rig it follow the manufacturer's instructions, prohibitions, limitations and specifications, or an approved modification. If manufacturer instructions are unavailable, a registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment approves the selection and configuration in writing. The configuration is inspected as soon as assembly is finished. Jib stops are one of the required safety devices when a jib is attached, and no jib stays attached during pile driving.
title: Erect and stow jibs and extensions

exam: Items ask who does the shift inspection, when it has to start, what is on the list, and what happens when something is found, such as a cracked cab window. Watch the wording on before versus during the shift, and on competent versus qualified. A choice that defers the decision to a later inspection or adds a workaround is usually the wrong one.
hard: The timing is easy to get wrong. The inspection has to begin before the shift, but it does not have to be finished before the shift, because some checks happen during trial operation. Booming down and taking parts apart are not part of it unless what you see or the trial operation calls for it. Findings are also reassessed as you watch the crane work during the shift. Safety device and operational aid problems follow their own rules, separate from the competent person's hazard call.
mistakes: People think a qualified person or a certified operator has to do it; the rule names a competent person, and an operator does it only when the operator is the competent person. People think the lift director owns the shift inspection; it belongs to the competent person. People think it has to be finished before the shift, or that it can start at the first lift or within some two-hour window; it has to begin before the shift and can be completed during it. People think the boom has to come down weekly or above some boom length; booming down depends only on what the visual check or trial operation shows. People think every deficiency removes the crane automatically, or that a signal person can work around a hazard; the competent person decides right away whether it is a hazard, and a hazard means out of service until it is corrected.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: A competent person must begin a visual inspection prior to each shift the equipment will be used, which must be completed before or during that shift.

Taking apart equipment components and booming down is not required as part of this inspection unless the results of the visual inspection or trial operation indicate that further investigation necessitating taking apart equipment components or booming down is needed.
Determinations made in conducting the inspection must be reassessed in light of observations made during operation.
Operator cab windows for significant cracks, breaks, or other deficiencies that would hamper the operator's view.
If the deficiency is determined to constitute a safety hazard, the equipment must be taken out of service until it has been corrected.

If any deficiency in paragraph (d)(1)(xiv) of this section (safety devices/operational aids) is identified, the action specified in §§ 1926.1415 and 1926.1416 must be taken prior to using the equipment.

summary: The shift inspection is a visual check by a competent person that starts before each shift the crane will be used. It can be finished before or during the shift. It covers controls, drive mechanisms, pressurized lines, hydraulic fluid level, hooks and latches, reeving, wire rope, electrical gear, tires, ground conditions, level, cab windows, rails when the crane travels on them, and safety devices. It is the check that catches settling outriggers, a leaking hose or a cracked hook before the first pick.
title: Do the shift inspection (competent person, visual, before each shift)

exam: Expect items on how long the monthly record is kept, what it has to contain, and who keeps it. Some choices look right but leave out one required piece, so read each one against the full list: items checked, results, name, signature, date. Watch for choices that mix up the three-month and 12-month numbers.
hard: The monthly is not a mini-annual. It follows the shift-inspection items, and the difference is the paperwork. The record contents are a short, exact list, and the hard part is spotting what is missing from a choice, like no signature, no date, or only the defects. For wire rope, the monthly also checks any deficiency the annual inspector flagged to be monitored.
mistakes: People think the record is kept only until the next monthly, or for 12 months; the minimum is three months. People think the record is only defects and hour meter readings, or a repair log; it has to show the items checked and the results, plus the inspector's name, signature and date. People think a supervisor signs or approves it; the signature is the person who did the inspection. People put the record duty on the controlling entity, the crane owner or the operator; it belongs to the employer that conducts the inspection. People think the monthly is an annual-type inspection, a recheck of old defects only, or includes a load test; it is the full shift-inspection scope, documented.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Each month the equipment is in service it must be inspected in accordance with paragraph (d) of this section (each shift).
Equipment must not be used until an inspection under this paragraph demonstrates that no corrective action under paragraphs (d)(2) and (3) of this section is required.
The following information must be documented and maintained by the employer that conducts the inspection:
The items checked and the results of the inspection.
The name and signature of the person who conducted the inspection and the date.
This document must be retained for a minimum of three months.
The inspection must include any deficiencies that the qualified person who conducts the annual inspection determines under paragraph (c)(3)(ii) of this section must be monitored.

summary: Each month the crane is in service, it gets an inspection with the same scope as the shift inspection, and this one gets written down. The record lists the items checked, the results, and the name and signature of the person who did it, plus the date. The employer that conducts the inspection keeps it for at least three months. The crane is not used until the monthly shows no corrective action is needed.
title: Do the monthly inspection and keep the record

exam: Items ask the interval, who does it, how long the record is kept, and whether a given part needs to be opened up. Scenarios may describe a qualified person finding a worn part that is not yet a hazard and ask what follows. Watch for choices that swap competent for qualified, or that use a near-miss number like nine months.
hard: The annual has different deficiency choices than the shift inspection. The qualified person decides whether a deficiency is a hazard now or something to watch in the monthly inspections. Disassembly is required as needed, which is neither a full teardown nor something you skip by running the function. The 12-month interval and the 12-month record are the same number for different things, and people slide the monthly's three months over to them.
mistakes: People think the interval is six months, nine months or quarterly; the rule is at least every 12 months, and inspecting more often is allowed but not what the rule sets. People think a competent person, a certified operator or the site supervisor can do it on that basis alone; it takes a qualified person. People think the record is kept 90 days, six months or three years; the minimum is 12 months. People think running a function can stand in for opening it up, or that an upcoming overhaul covers it; disassembly happens when it is needed to inspect the part. People think comprehensive means tearing down every assembly; it means disassembly as necessary.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: At least every 12 months the equipment must be inspected by a qualified person in accordance with paragraph (d) of this section (each shift)
Disassembly is required, as necessary, to complete the inspection.
This inspection must include functional testing to determine that the equipment as configured in the inspection is functioning properly.

If the qualified person determines that, though not presently a safety hazard, the deficiency needs to be monitored, the employer must ensure that the deficiency is checked in the monthly inspections.
Documentation of annual/comprehensive inspection. The following information must be documented, maintained, and retained for a minimum of 12 months, by the employer that conducts the inspection:

summary: At least every 12 months, a qualified person does the annual/comprehensive inspection. It includes everything on the shift list, plus a deep list: structure, welds, fasteners, sheaves, drums, pins and bearings, brakes and clutches, safety devices for accuracy, power plant, hoses, pumps, valves, cylinders, outrigger pads, electrical wiring, labels, seat, steps and guards. Parts get taken apart as needed to finish the job, and functional testing is part of it. The record is kept at least 12 months.
title: Do the annual/comprehensive inspection (qualified person)

exam: Scenario items describe a brake repair, a new safety device or a structural addition and ask who inspects, what it is checked against, or what testing is needed. Read whether the work is a repair or a modification first, because the answer depends on it. Choices with a load test percentage are wrong here.
hard: The two paths use different yardsticks. A modification is checked against its approval under § 1926.1434. A repair or adjustment is checked against manufacturer criteria. If those don't exist or don't apply, the qualified person decides whether an RPE is needed and the criteria come from the RPE or the qualified person. Testing for a repair covers the repaired parts and anything the repair may affect, not just the new part.
mistakes: People think a competent person or the operator can sign off; both paths call for a qualified person. People think an RPE is needed for every repair, or that the RPE does the inspection; an RPE comes in only on the repair path when manufacturer criteria are missing and the qualified person decides one is needed, and the inspector is still the qualified person. People check a modification against manufacturer repair criteria, or check a like-for-like repair against a modification approval; modifications go by the § 1926.1434 approval and repairs by manufacturer criteria. People use qualified-person criteria when manufacturer criteria exist; those fallback criteria apply only when manufacturer criteria are unavailable or inapplicable. People think acceptance means a rated-load or overload test; the rule calls for functional testing, and for repairs that covers the repaired parts and other affected components.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The inspection must assure that the modifications or additions have been done in accordance with the approval obtained pursuant to § 1926.1434 (Equipment modifications).
The inspection must include functional testing of the equipment.
The qualified person must determine if the repair/adjustment meets manufacturer equipment criteria (where applicable and available).
Determine if a registered professional engineer (RPE) is needed to develop criteria for the repair/adjustment.
The inspection must include functional testing of the repaired/adjusted parts and other components that may be affected by the repair/adjustment.

Equipment must not be used until an inspection under this paragraph demonstrates that the repair/adjustment meets the requirements of paragraph (b)(1)(i) of this section (or, where applicable, paragraph (b)(1)(ii) of this section).

summary: When a crane has a modification or addition that affects safe operation or capacity, or a repair or adjustment that relates to safe operation, a qualified person inspects it before first use. Examples are work on a safety device, a control system, the power plant, brakes, load-bearing structure, the load hook or an operating mechanism. Both paths include functional testing, and the crane stays parked until the inspection shows it meets the right criteria.
title: Inspect modified and repaired equipment before use

exam: Expect a jobsite scenario, like a load that shock-loaded or an overload, followed by what to do first or who decides. The right answer stops the crane and brings in a qualified person. Watch for choices that sound cautious, like derating or scheduling an early annual, but still keep the crane working.
hard: The trigger is a possibility, not proof. The words are 'may have exceeded rated capacity,' and one event is enough. The required action is to stop now, not to derate, write it down or move up the annual. A clean walkaround doesn't clear the crane, because cracked welds and bent members can be hard to see.
mistakes: People think the operator, a competent person or the lift supervisor can clear the crane; the rule names a qualified person. People think the crane can keep working at reduced capacity, or that logging it or moving up the annual is enough; use stops until the qualified person inspects. People wait for proof of an overload; 'may have exceeded' is the trigger. People invent a percentage threshold or count events; the line is rated capacity itself, and one shock load is enough. People treat no visible damage or a routine shift inspection as clearance; a qualified person's structural inspection is required.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Severe service. Where the severity of use/conditions is such that there is a reasonable probability of damage or excessive wear (such as loading that may have exceeded rated capacity, shock loading that may have exceeded rated capacity, prolonged exposure to a corrosive atmosphere), the employer must stop using the equipment and a qualified person must:
Inspect the equipment for structural damage to determine if the equipment can continue to be used safely.
In light of the use/conditions determine whether any items/conditions listed in paragraph (f) of this section need to be inspected; if so, the qualified person must inspect those items/conditions.
If a deficiency is found, the employer must follow the requirements in paragraphs (f)(4) through (6) of this section.

summary: Severe service means use or conditions that make damage or excessive wear reasonably likely. Examples are loading or shock loading that may have exceeded rated capacity, and long exposure to a corrosive atmosphere. When that happens, the employer stops using the crane and a qualified person inspects it for structural damage and decides whether to check annual-inspection items too. This is the rule that applies right after a dropped load, a two-block or an overload alarm you ran through.
title: Know when severe service requires more inspection

exam: Items give a time idle and ask whether an inspection is needed, who does it, and to what level. Read whether the question is about construction or general industry, because the numbers change. Watch for choices that get the person right but the level or timing wrong.
hard: Three sets of numbers sit close together: 3 months for construction, 1 and 6 months for general industry, and semiannual for standby cranes. The construction rule pairs a qualified person with the monthly-level criteria, which is an odd mix since a competent person normally does the monthly. And timing is before initial use, with no grace period.
mistakes: People use one month, six months or 12 months as the construction idle trigger; it is 3 months or more, and the one and six month numbers are general industry. People think a competent person or an operator's shift check covers it; the rule calls for a qualified person using the monthly criteria. People think it takes a full annual/comprehensive inspection; it points to the monthly criteria. People think a few days of use first is fine, or that the next scheduled monthly covers it; it happens before initial use. People think standby cranes need monthly, quarterly or annual inspection; the general industry minimum is at least semiannual, with more frequent checks advised in adverse environments.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Equipment not in regular use. Equipment that has been idle for 3 months or more must be inspected by a qualified person in accordance with the requirements of paragraph (e) (Monthly) of this section before initial use.

A crane which has been idle for a period of one month or more, but less than 6 months, shall be given an inspection conforming with requirements of paragraph (d)(3) of this section and paragraph (g)(2)(ii) of this section before placing in service.

A crane which has been idle for a period of six months shall be given a complete inspection conforming with requirements of paragraphs (d) (3) and (4) of this section and paragraph (g)(2)(ii) of this section before placing in service.

Standby cranes shall be inspected at least semiannually in accordance with requirements of paragraph (d)(3) of this section and paragraph (g)(2)(ii) of this section. Such cranes which are exposed to adverse environment should be inspected more frequently.

summary: Under the construction rule, a crane idle for 3 months or more gets inspected by a qualified person before its first use, using the monthly inspection criteria. The general industry crane rules are different: idle one month to under six months gets a frequent-inspection-level check, six months gets a complete inspection, and standby cranes are inspected at least semiannually. This matters any time a crane comes back from the yard or off a long standby.
title: Inspect equipment not in regular use

exam: Expect scenario items: a deficiency is found, then who decides, when, and what happens to the crane. The right answer usually has the right person making an immediate decision and the crane out of service if it is a hazard. Watch for answers that sound practical but delay, derate or work around the problem.
hard: Two things get blurred: who makes the call, and how fast. The decision is immediate, not at end of shift or before some later inspection. A hazard means out of service, not derated and not one more pick. The annual adds a third option, monitor it in the monthlies, and allows temporary alternative measures in limited cases that the shift rule doesn't give.
mistakes: People think a qualified person, the operator by default or the controlling entity makes the shift-inspection call; the competent person does, and the operator only if designated as the competent person. People let the decision wait until end of shift, the next lift, a 24-hour window or the next monthly; the determination is immediate. People derate the crane or make one more lift; a hazard means out of service until corrected. People think the annual includes an overload test, NDT, or testing at maximum boom length; the required element is functional testing of the crane as configured in the inspection. People defer a known hazard to a later inspection; it stays out of service until it is corrected.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: If any deficiency in paragraphs (d)(1)(i) through (xiii) of this section (or in additional inspection items required to be checked for specific types of equipment in accordance with other sections of this standard) is identified, an immediate determination must be made by the competent person as to whether the deficiency constitutes a safety hazard.
If the deficiency is determined to constitute a safety hazard, the equipment must be taken out of service until it has been corrected.

If any deficiency is identified, an immediate determination must be made by the qualified person as to whether the deficiency constitutes a safety hazard or, though not yet a safety hazard, needs to be monitored in the monthly inspections.

If the qualified person determines that a deficiency is a safety hazard, the equipment must be taken out of service until it has been corrected, except when temporary alternative measures are implemented as specified in § 1926.1416(d) or § 1926.1435(e). See § 1926.1417.
This inspection must include functional testing to determine that the equipment as configured in the inspection is functioning properly.
Where the employer has taken the equipment out of service, a tag must be placed in the cab stating that the equipment is out of service and is not to be used.

summary: When an inspection turns up a deficiency, someone has to decide right away whether it is a safety hazard. For shift and monthly inspections that is the competent person. For the annual, it is the qualified person, who can also flag a deficiency to be watched in the monthly inspections. A hazard takes the crane out of service until it is fixed, with a tag in the cab, and a function taken out of service gets a tag in a conspicuous spot.
title: Decide whether a deficiency is a safety hazard and act

exam: Items ask retention periods, who keeps the record, what goes on it, and who has to be able to see it. Some items describe a form and ask what is missing. Watch for answer choices that use the right number for the wrong record.
hard: The two retention numbers, three and 12 months, get swapped. The record duty follows the employer that did the inspection, not the owner, the operator's employer or the controlling entity, and on a multi-employer site those can all be different companies. Many forms carry extra fields like hour readings or supervisor sign-off, and people take those for federal requirements.
mistakes: People think each new monthly replaces the last record; the minimum is three months, so several monthly records stay on file. People use six months as a retention period; it isn't one, and the numbers are three months for monthly and 12 months for annual. People keep the annual record three months or 36 months, or until the next annual; the minimum is a fixed 12 months. People put the record duty on the controlling entity, the owner or the operator's employer; it belongs to the employer that conducted the inspection. People think the operator countersigns or a supervisor approves the record; the required signature is the inspector's. People think hour meter readings are required; the minimum contents are items checked, results, and the inspector's name, signature and date.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The following information must be documented and maintained by the employer that conducts the inspection:
The name and signature of the person who conducted the inspection and the date.
This document must be retained for a minimum of three months.
Documentation of annual/comprehensive inspection. The following information must be documented, maintained, and retained for a minimum of 12 months, by the employer that conducts the inspection:
All documents produced under this section must be available, during the applicable document retention period, to all persons who conduct inspections under this section.

summary: Monthly and annual inspections are documented with the items checked, the results, and the name and signature of the person who did the inspection, plus the date. The employer that conducts the inspection keeps them: monthly records at least three months, annual records at least 12 months. During that time, the records have to be available to everyone who conducts inspections on that crane, so the next inspector can see what was found and what is being watched.
title: Document inspections and keep records available
