exam: Items ask the interval range for frequent or periodic inspections, or the interval for a specific item or for a standby crane. Watch for choices that use the right range for the wrong class. When a question names a specific item, check whether it has its own interval.
hard: The two ranges touch at one month, so people slide them into each other. A specific interval written next to an item, like daily, overrides the general range for that item. The standby and idle provisions add their own intervals on top, such as at least semiannual for standby cranes.
mistakes: People stretch frequent inspections to weekly-to-quarterly or end them at quarterly; frequent is daily to monthly. People give frequent inspections the 1- to 12-month range; that range is periodic. People start the periodic range at three or six months, or set it at 12 to 24 months; the general periodic range is 1 to 12 months. People think standby cranes need monthly, quarterly or only annual inspection; the minimum is at least semiannual. People think a weekly maintenance visit, the general daily-to-monthly range, or a periodic inspection covers the daily items; hydraulic leakage and control maladjustment are checked daily.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Frequent inspection: Daily to monthly intervals.
Periodic inspection: 1- to 12-month intervals, or as specifically recommended by the manufacturer.
All control mechanisms for maladjustment interfering with proper operation: Daily.
Deterioration or leakage in air or hydraulic systems: Daily.

Standby cranes shall be inspected at least semiannually in accordance with requirements of paragraph (d)(3) of this section and paragraph (g)(2)(ii) of this section. Such cranes which are exposed to adverse environment should be inspected more frequently.

summary: The general industry crane rules split regular inspections into frequent and periodic. Frequent inspections run at daily to monthly intervals. Periodic inspections are complete inspections at 1- to 12-month intervals, or as the manufacturer specifically recommends. Some frequent items carry their own interval, such as daily checks of control mechanisms for maladjustment and of air or hydraulic systems for deterioration or leakage. Cranes that work outside construction, and test items that borrow these terms, use this vocabulary.
title: Know frequent vs periodic inspection in general industry

exam: Items give a measured opening or twist and ask whether the hook meets the removal criterion, or ask where the throat is measured. Read the units carefully, because the right number in the wrong unit is a common wrong choice. Watch for the words 'more than' in the question and the options.
hard: Two numbers sit close together and people swap them: 15 goes with percent of throat opening and 10 goes with degrees of twist. Both criteria say more than, so a hook exactly at the number is not past it, and a hook under it is not past it either. Opening and twist are judged separately and never added together.
mistakes: People put 10 with the opening and 15 with the twist; it is more than 15 percent throat opening and more than 10 degrees twist. People use 5 or 20 percent for opening, or 5 or 20 degrees for twist; those are not the criteria. People measure the bowl width, the latch pivot or the shank length; the throat opening is measured at its narrowest point. People reject a hook with an 8 percent opening or 6 degrees of twist on the numbers alone; neither meets the criterion, though a crack rejects a hook at any size. People add the percent and the degrees together; opening and twist are checked separately.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Hooks and latches for deformation, cracks, excessive wear, or damage such as from chemicals or heat.
Crane hooks with deformations or cracks. For hooks with cracks or having more than 15 percent in excess of normal throat opening or more than 10° twist from the plane of the unbent hook.
Hooks that have been opened more than 15 percent of the normal throat opening measured at the narrowest point or twisted more than 10 degrees from the plane of the unbent hook.

summary: Hooks and latches are on every shift inspection: look for deformation, cracks, excessive wear, and damage from chemicals or heat. The general industry rules give the numbers used to judge a bent hook: a throat opening more than 15 percent beyond normal, or a twist more than 10 degrees from the plane of the unbent hook. Any crack takes the hook out regardless of those numbers. The throat is measured at its narrowest point.
title: Inspect hooks (cracks, throat opening, twist)

exam: Items describe someone on a boom or deck and ask whether fall protection is needed, often with a boom type and height that sit near a threshold. Other items ask where a tag goes. Read the boom type, horizontal or not, and whether the person is moving or at a work station before picking a number.
hard: The 15-foot figure applies only to moving point to point on a horizontal lattice boom. Telescopic and other non-lattice booms use the 6-foot trigger whatever the boom angle. Tag location depends on whether the whole crane or one function is out of service. An operator who finds a tag on the starting controls does not start the crane until the tag is removed by someone authorized to remove it, or until the operator verifies no one is in a dangerous position and the crane is repaired.
mistakes: People use 4 feet, 10 feet or 20 feet as a trigger; the crane rule uses more than 6 feet, and 15 feet or more for point-to-point on a horizontal lattice boom. People apply the 15-foot figure to all boom work or to telescopic booms; it is only for moving point to point on a horizontal lattice boom. People think only work stations are covered; moving point to point is covered too. People think boom angle decides it on a non-lattice boom; non-lattice booms are covered horizontal or not. People hang the whole-crane tag at the defect, on the ladder or in a conspicuous spot; the equipment tag goes in the cab, and the conspicuous-position rule is for a single function.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: For non-assembly/disassembly work, the employer must provide and ensure the use of fall protection equipment for employees who are on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge more than 6 feet above a lower level as follows:
On non-lattice booms (whether horizontal or not horizontal).
On horizontal lattice booms where the fall distance is 15 feet or more.
While at a work station on any part of the equipment (including the boom, of any type), except when the employee is at or near draw-works (when the equipment is running), in the cab, or on the deck.
Where the employer has taken a function(s) out of service, a tag must be placed in a conspicuous position stating that the function is out of service and is not to be used.

If there is a warning (tag-out or maintenance/do not operate) sign on the equipment or starting control, the operator must not activate the switch or start the equipment until the sign has been removed by a person authorized to remove it, or until the operator has verified that:

summary: Inspecting a crane means climbing on it, so fall protection and tag-out apply to you. For work other than assembly and disassembly, fall protection is used on walking or working surfaces with an unprotected side or edge more than 6 feet above a lower level. That covers moving point to point on non-lattice booms, lattice booms that are not horizontal, and horizontal lattice booms where the fall distance is 15 feet or more. It also covers work stations, except at or near the draw-works with the crane running, in the cab, or on the deck. A crane taken out of service gets a tag in the cab, and a function taken out of service gets a tag in a conspicuous position.
title: Stay safe while inspecting (lockout, fall protection)

exam: Items ask a test-load percentage, who is responsible for a type of testing, at what stage it happens, or who can approve higher ratings. Watch for percentages that belong to a different crane type. Also watch for answers that put a manufacturer duty on someone at the jobsite.
hard: Keep each kind of test with the stage and the person it belongs to. Prototype testing is design work, production operational testing happens at final assembly, and field inspections use functional testing, not overload tests. The test-load ceilings differ by crane type: 110 percent of rated load at the selected radius for truck cranes, and 125 percent for overhead cranes. People mix them up.
mistakes: People cap a truck-crane rated-load test at 100, 125 or 150 percent; the ceiling is 110 percent of the rated load at the selected working radius, and 125 percent belongs to overhead cranes. People think the purchaser, the operator or the lift director does production operational testing; for a new crane supplied complete by one manufacturer, the manufacturer does it. People think tests of separate components, a later annual inspection or prototype approval can replace production testing; it is done on the production crane at final assembly. People think the owner, the lift director, an inspector or an engineer can approve ratings above the original; that approval comes from the manufacturer or final assembler. People think routine field inspections include a load test; they call for functional testing.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The inspection must include functional testing of the equipment.
The inspection must include functional testing of the repaired/adjusted parts and other components that may be affected by the repair/adjustment.
This inspection must include functional testing to determine that the equipment as configured in the inspection is functioning properly.

Prototype testing: mobile (including crawler and truck) and locomotive cranes manufactured on or after November 8, 2010 must meet the prototype testing requirements in Test Option A or Test Option B of this section.

summary: Testing comes in at several points. Mobile cranes are prototype tested by design, and production cranes are operationally tested by the manufacturer at final assembly. In the field, the post-modification, post-repair and annual inspections each include functional testing. Rated-load testing has its own limits on test load, and raising a crane's original load ratings takes the approval of the manufacturer or final assembler.
title: Know load and operational testing requirements

exam: Expect items that describe a crane type and setup and ask which device is required or which exception applies, and items asking what to do with a faulty built-in versus removable device. Watch the words built-in and removable, and check which device the exception in the options actually belongs to.
hard: Each exception belongs to one device only. Portal cranes, derricks and floating or barge-mounted equipment are exempt from the level indicator, not from boom stops. Hydraulic booms are exempt from boom stops, but a jib on that boom still needs jib stops, and only derricks are exempt from jib stops. A faulty built-in level indicator or horn may be tagged out or removed, while a faulty removable one must be removed.
mistakes: People think outriggers, mats or a level site make a level indicator unnecessary; only portal cranes, derricks and floating or flotation-mounted equipment are exempt, and rough-terrain and truck cranes are not. People apply the barge or portal exemption to boom stops; it covers only the level indicator. People think a hydraulic boom with a jib needs nothing; the boom is exempt from boom stops but the jib needs jib stops. People think tagging out fixes a faulty removable level indicator or horn; a removable device must be removed, because a tagged one could still be carried around and used. People look for a repair deadline on a safety device; the rule sets none and requires removal or tag-out of the bad device. People mix up rail stops with boom stops; rail clamps and stops are for equipment on rails, and only portal cranes are exempt from them.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must have a crane level indicator that is either built into the equipment or is available on the equipment.
If a built-in crane level indicator is not working properly, it must be tagged-out or removed. If a removable crane level indicator is not working properly, it must be removed.
This requirement does not apply to portal cranes, derricks, floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges, pontoons, vessels or other means of flotation.
Boom stops, except for derricks and hydraulic booms.
Jib stops (if a jib is attached), except for derricks.
Equipment with foot pedal brakes must have locks.
Equipment on rails must have rail clamps and rail stops, except for portal cranes.
The equipment must have a horn that is either built into the equipment or is on the equipment and immediately available to the operator.
If a built-in horn is not working properly, it must be tagged-out or removed. If a removable horn is not working properly, it must be removed.

summary: Safety devices are the short list every covered crane needs unless an exception says otherwise: a crane level indicator, boom stops, jib stops if a jib is attached, locks on foot pedal brakes, integral holding devices or check valves on hydraulic outrigger and stabilizer jacks, rail clamps and rail stops on rail-mounted equipment, and a horn. Each item has its own narrow exceptions. You check these before the shift because the crane cannot run without them.
title: Name the required safety devices

exam: Expect scenarios where the horn or level indicator quits mid-shift and you choose what happens next or who must act. Wrong options usually offer a reasonable-sounding substitute, a supervisor's approval or a repair deadline; the right answer is that the operator safely stops and the crane stays out of service until the device is fixed.
hard: Operational aids have temporary measures and repair windows, so people carry that habit over to safety devices, where it does not apply. The duty to stop sits with the operator, not the lift director, signal person or A/D director. Safely stopping means bringing the load to a safe position, not finishing the pick.
mistakes: People think a signal person, a hand-held air horn or another workaround can stand in for a failed horn; alternative measures are not permitted for safety devices. People think a supervisor or lift director can approve running anyway; no one can approve a substitute. People apply the Category I or II repair window; safety devices get no grace period. People think tagging and reporting the defect allows work to continue; the device has to work before operations begin or resume. People think only the devices needed for today's lifts must work; every listed device must be in proper working order. People think they should finish the lift first; the operator safely stops operations when the device fails.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Operations must not begin unless all of the devices listed in this section are in proper working order.
If a device stops working properly during operations, the operator must safely stop operations.
If any of the devices listed in this section are not in proper working order, the equipment must be taken out of service and operations must not resume until the device is again working properly.
Alternative measures are not permitted to be used.

summary: When a safety device fails, the answer is simple: do not start, and if you are already running, the operator safely stops operations. The crane comes out of service and stays out until the device works again. There is no temporary measure and no repair window for safety devices.
title: Stop when a safety device fails

exam: Expect a failed-aid scenario asking for the correct temporary measure, a deadline question, and date questions keyed to crane type. Identify the aid and the crane type first, then match the measure; watch for and versus or in the options.
hard: Each aid has its own temporary measure and its own manufacture date, and they sit close together: boom hoist limiting after December 16, 1969, anti-two-block on telescopic and lattice cranes after February 28, 1992, articulating cranes with a load hoist after December 31, 1999, and automatic-only prevention on lattice cranes and derricks after November 8, 2011. The anti-two-block measure on a telescopic crane is cable mark and spotter when extending; on lattice it is mark or spotter. A boom angle indicator is a measure for the boom hoist limiting device, not for anti-two-block.
mistakes: People use 14 days or a monthly window; the Category I deadline is 7 calendar days. People count working days from the report; the rule counts calendar days from when the deficiency occurs. People mix the dates, using December 16, 1969, December 31, 1999 or November 8, 2011 for a telescopic crane; telescopic cranes are covered after February 28, 1992. People think marine work is always exempt from anti-two-block; the lattice exception covers marine work only when it does not involve hoisting personnel, and precast setting or steel erection on the hook is not excepted. People use mark or spotter on a telescopic crane, or a spotter alone; a telescopic crane needs the cable mark and a spotter when extending. People offer a boom angle indicator or lowering the block by habit as the anti-two-block measure; that is not the listed measure.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Operational aids listed in this paragraph that are not working properly must be repaired no later than 7 calendar days after the deficiency occurs.

Exception: If the employer documents that it has ordered the necessary parts within 7 calendar days of the occurrence of the deficiency, the repair must be completed within 7 calendar days of receipt of the parts.
For equipment manufactured after December 16, 1969, a boom hoist limiting device is required.
Equipment with a luffing jib must have a luffing jib limiting device.

Temporary alternative measures: Clearly mark the cable (so that it can easily be seen by the operator) at a point that will give the operator sufficient time to stop the hoist to prevent two-blocking, and use a spotter when extending the boom.

Exception. The requirements in paragraphs (d)(3)(ii)(A) and (B) of this section do not apply to such lattice boom equipment when used for dragline, clamshell (grapple), magnet, drop ball, container handling, concrete bucket, marine operations that do not involve hoisting personnel, and pile driving work.

If a listed operational aid stops working properly during operations, the operator must safely stop operations until the temporary alternative measures are implemented or the device is again working properly.

summary: Category I operational aids are the boom hoist limiting device, the luffing jib limiting device and the anti-two-block device. If one fails, the operator safely stops until the listed temporary measure is in place, and the aid must be repaired within 7 calendar days of the deficiency, or within 7 days of receiving parts if the parts were ordered and documented within 7 days. These aids keep the boom from going over backward and the block from pulling into the tip.
title: Know Category I aids and their alternative measures

exam: Expect deadline questions, threshold questions that hinge on the word over, date questions, and scenarios asking what you do when the angle indicator or LMI quits. Check whether the number in an option is the repair deadline or the parts-order window.
hard: The 7-day figure shows up here too, but only as the window to order and document parts for the exception, not as the repair deadline. The load weighing requirement applies to equipment other than derricks and articulating cranes built after March 29, 2003 with a rated capacity over 6,000 pounds; over means exactly 6,000 does not qualify. The temporary measures call for actual measurement, not estimates or old readings.
mistakes: People take 7 days as the Category II repair deadline; 7 days is the parts-order window and the normal deadline is 30 calendar days. People use two or three weeks; the period is 30 calendar days. People use 2,000 or 10,000 pounds, or read over 6,000 as at least 6,000; the threshold is over 6,000 pounds. People use March 29, 2003, 2010 or 2014 for the drum rotation indicator; its cutoff is equipment built after November 8, 2011. People think an experienced eye, a remembered reading or another working aid replaces a failed angle or radius indicator; the radius or boom angle must be measured with a measuring device.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Operational aids listed in this paragraph that are not working properly must be repaired no later than 30 calendar days after the deficiency occurs.
Temporary alternative measures: Radii or boom angle must be determined by measuring the radii or boom angle with a measuring device.

Equipment (other than derricks and articulating cranes) manufactured after March 29, 2003 with a rated capacity over 6,000 pounds must have at least one of the following: load weighing device, load moment (or rated capacity) indicator, or load moment (or rated capacity) limiter.
The following devices are required on equipment manufactured after November 8, 2011:

Temporary alternative measures: The operator must verify that the position of the outriggers or stabilizers is correct (in accordance with manufacturer procedures) before beginning operations requiring outrigger or stabilizer deployment.
Hoist drum rotation indicator if the equipment has a hoist drum not visible from the operator's station.

summary: Category II operational aids are the boom angle or radius indicator, the jib angle indicator on a luffing jib, the boom length indicator on a telescopic boom, load weighing and similar devices, and, on equipment built after November 8, 2011, the outrigger or stabilizer position sensor and the hoist drum rotation indicator where the drum is not visible. The repair deadline is 30 calendar days, and each aid has a temporary measure. These aids give you the numbers you read the load chart with.
title: Know Category II aids and their alternative measures

exam: Expect date-counting scenarios: an aid fails on a given day, parts are ordered on another, and you pick the latest compliant repair date. Mark the day the deficiency occurred, count calendar days, and confirm the parts order fell inside 7 days before using the exception.
hard: The number 7 appears three times with different jobs: the Category I repair deadline, the parts-order window in both categories, and the time after parts arrive. The clock starts at the deficiency, not at the report, diagnosis, inspection or estimate. Calendar days include weekends and days the crane sits idle.
mistakes: People count working days or skip idle days; the rule uses calendar days. People swap the categories, giving Category I 30 days or Category II 7 days; Category I is 7 calendar days and Category II is 30 calendar days. People think the parts order can be placed any time within the 30-day repair period; it must be ordered and documented within 7 calendar days of the deficiency. People start the clock when the failure is reported, diagnosed, inspected or estimated; it starts when the deficiency occurs, so a Monday failure starts the clock on Monday.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Operational aids listed in this paragraph that are not working properly must be repaired no later than 7 calendar days after the deficiency occurs.

Exception: If the employer documents that it has ordered the necessary parts within 7 calendar days of the occurrence of the deficiency, the repair must be completed within 7 calendar days of receipt of the parts.
Operational aids listed in this paragraph that are not working properly must be repaired no later than 30 calendar days after the deficiency occurs.

Exception: If the employer documents that it has ordered the necessary parts within 7 calendar days of the occurrence of the deficiency, and the part is not received in time to complete the repair in 30 calendar days, the repair must be completed within 7 calendar days of receipt of the parts.

Operations must not begin unless the listed operational aids are in proper working order, except where an operational aid is being repaired the employer uses the specified temporary alternative measures.

summary: When an operational aid fails, the employer has a fixed time to fix it: 7 calendar days for Category I and 30 calendar days for Category II, counted from when the deficiency occurs. If parts are ordered and documented within 7 calendar days of the deficiency, the repair must be done within 7 calendar days of receiving the parts; for Category II, that exception applies when the part does not arrive in time to finish within 30 days. The crane runs on temporary measures only during that window.
title: Know repair deadlines (7 days Category I, 30 days Category II)

exam: Expect items giving a crane type, build year and kind of work, asking what device or temporary measure applies. Check three things in order: type, year, and whether the work is on the lattice exception list.
hard: A lattice crane built in 2005 may comply with a warning device alone, while one built in 2012 needs automatic prevention. The lattice exception list is specific: dragline, clamshell, magnet, drop ball, container handling, concrete bucket, pile driving, and marine work that does not hoist personnel. It applies only to lattice equipment. Temporary measures are for a required device that is out of service, not a substitute for having one.
mistakes: People apply the post-2011 automatic-only rule to an older lattice crane; a lattice crane built before that date may use a warning device that warns in time at every two-block point. People add a spotter to a working warning device; the rule does not require one. People treat cable marking or a spotter as permanent compliance; they are temporary measures while the device is repaired. People miss that concrete bucket, magnet, pile driving and drop ball work on lattice equipment is excepted, so no device is required for it at all. People use mark or spotter on a telescopic crane, drop the mark, or substitute slowing the hoist; a telescopic crane needs the clear cable mark and a spotter when extending the boom.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Telescopic boom cranes manufactured after February 28, 1992, must be equipped with a device which automatically prevents damage from contact between the load block, overhaul ball, or similar component, and the boom tip (or fixed upper block or similar component).

Lattice boom cranes manufactured after Feb 28, 1992, must be equipped with a device that either automatically prevents damage and load failure from contact between the load block, overhaul ball, or similar component, and the boom tip (or fixed upper block or similar component), or warns the operator in time for the operator to prevent two-blocking. The device must prevent such damage/failure or provide adequate warning for all points where two-blocking could occur.

Lattice boom cranes and derricks manufactured after November 8, 2011 must be equipped with a device which automatically prevents damage and load failure from contact between the load block, overhaul ball, or similar component, and the boom tip (or fixed upper block or similar component).

Exception. The requirements in paragraphs (d)(3)(ii)(A) and (B) of this section do not apply to such lattice boom equipment when used for dragline, clamshell (grapple), magnet, drop ball, container handling, concrete bucket, marine operations that do not involve hoisting personnel, and pile driving work.

Temporary alternative measures. Clearly mark the cable (so that it can easily be seen by the operator) at a point that will give the operator sufficient time to stop the hoist to prevent two-blocking, or use a spotter.

Articulating cranes manufactured after December 31, 1999, that are equipped with a load hoist must be equipped with a device that automatically prevents damage from contact between the load block, overhaul ball, or similar component, and the boom tip (or fixed upper block or similar component).

summary: The anti-two-block requirement depends on crane type and build date. Telescopic boom cranes built after February 28, 1992 need a device that automatically prevents damage; lattice boom cranes built after that date may have an automatic device or a warning device; lattice cranes and derricks built after November 8, 2011 need automatic prevention; articulating cranes with a load hoist built after December 31, 1999 need automatic prevention. Lattice equipment doing certain kinds of work is excepted.
title: Know anti-two-block requirements by crane type

exam: Expect judgment scenarios: the block is near the tip while you telescope, the device has failed, or you must pick the first action after a two-block warning. Watch for options that address only hoisting when the scenario involves extending the boom.
hard: Telescoping is the path people forget, since the hoist lever never moves. That is why a telescopic crane's temporary measure needs both the cable mark for hoisting and a spotter for boom extension. As a matter of practice, if the device trips or the block reaches the tip, stop applying power, let the line out or retract carefully, and have the rope and components checked before going on.
mistakes: People use December 31, 1999 or November 8, 2011, or the standard's effective date, for telescopic booms; telescopic cranes built after February 28, 1992 are covered. People read November 8, 2011 as the start of lattice coverage; lattice cranes are covered after February 28, 1992 and the 2011 date only changes the type of device required. People extend the lattice magnet or marine exceptions to telescopic cranes, to personnel hoisting from a barge, or to ordinary hook work with a block; none of those is excepted. People think a spotter replaces the cable mark on a telescopic boom, or that the spotter is tied to personnel lifts; the mark covers hoisting and the spotter covers any boom extension while the device is out.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Two blocking means a condition in which a component that is uppermost on the hoist line such as the load block, hook block, overhaul ball, or similar component, comes in contact with the boom tip, fixed upper block or similar component.

Temporary alternative measures: Clearly mark the cable (so that it can easily be seen by the operator) at a point that will give the operator sufficient time to stop the hoist to prevent two-blocking, and use a spotter when extending the boom.

Telescopic boom cranes manufactured after February 28, 1992, must be equipped with a device which automatically prevents damage from contact between the load block, overhaul ball, or similar component, and the boom tip (or fixed upper block or similar component).

Lattice boom cranes and derricks manufactured after November 8, 2011 must be equipped with a device which automatically prevents damage and load failure from contact between the load block, overhaul ball, or similar component, and the boom tip (or fixed upper block or similar component).

summary: Two-blocking is when the block or overhaul ball contacts the boom tip or upper block; that binds the system, and continued power can break the hoist rope or other parts and drop the load. On a telescopic boom it happens two ways: hoisting up, or telescoping out without paying out load line, which pulls the block toward the tip without touching the hoist control. Knowing both paths is what lets you prevent it.
title: Recognize and prevent two-blocking (telescoping and hoisting)

exam: Expect threshold and date questions, items asking which device satisfies the requirement, and scenarios where the LMI fails and you pick the temporary measure and its timing. Watch for the word over and for options that list an aid not on the list.
hard: The rule requires at least one of the listed devices, not all of them. If the device fails, the temporary measure is to determine the load weight from a source recognized by the industry, like the manufacturer, or by a recognized calculation, and give it to the operator before the lift. The LMI is only as good as its setup, so wrong configuration, parts-of-line or counterweight input gives you wrong percentages; that is practice, not a separate rule.
mistakes: People think a test pick, rigging tension or the swing can come before the weight is known; the weight goes to the operator before the lift. People think a boom angle, wind speed or drum rotation aid satisfies this requirement; only a load weighing device, LMI or limiter qualifies. People read over 6,000 pounds as at least 6,000 or use 2,000 pounds; the rated capacity must exceed 6,000 pounds. People think a limiter must be added to a working load weighing device, or that weighing and moment indication must be paired; one listed device is enough. People think temporary measures supplement a working device; they apply only while the device is being repaired.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Equipment (other than derricks and articulating cranes) manufactured after March 29, 2003 with a rated capacity over 6,000 pounds must have at least one of the following: load weighing device, load moment (or rated capacity) indicator, or load moment (or rated capacity) limiter.

Temporary alternative measures: The weight of the load must be determined from a source recognized by the industry (such as the load's manufacturer) or by a calculation method recognized by the industry (such as calculating a steel beam from measured dimensions and a known per foot weight).
This information must be provided to the operator prior to the lift.

Articulating cranes manufactured after November 8, 2011 must have at least one of the following: automatic overload prevention device, load weighing device, load moment (or rated capacity) indicator, or load moment (rated capacity) limiter.

summary: A load moment indicator senses the overturning moment, load times radius, compares it with rated capacity and shows you the percentage you are working at; a limiter also cuts the functions that make things worse, like hoisting up, telescoping out or booming down, while leaving the functions that reduce loading. Equipment other than derricks and articulating cranes, built after March 29, 2003 with a rated capacity over 6,000 pounds, must have a load weighing device, an LMI or a limiter. Articulating cranes built after November 8, 2011 have a parallel requirement that also allows an automatic overload prevention device.
title: Use load moment indicators, limiters and load weighing devices

exam: Expect scenarios where an indicator fails and you choose the acceptable temporary method, plus date questions and radius questions. Wrong options often sound experienced, like an estimate or a derate; pick the one that actually measures.
hard: Each indicator has its own temporary measure. Angle or radius is measured with a measuring device; jib angle means finding the main boom angle and then measuring; boom length uses measured marks on the boom, a calculation from angle and radius, or measuring the boom; a drum is marked so you can see it turn. As physics, the boom deflects under load and radius grows, so the loaded radius is what counts.
mistakes: People use 2010 or 2014 for the outrigger sensor and drum rotation indicator; the cutoff is equipment built after November 8, 2011. People think a boom angle indicator or an LMI replaces the boom length indicator; angle alone does not give length, and the LMI depends on correct length input. People invent a fixed-extension exemption; the only exception is when rated capacity does not depend on boom length. People estimate by eye, count sections, time the extension, or read the load chart for an angle; the rule requires measuring or one of the listed methods. People rely on a stored reading after the boom has moved, or derate the crane instead of measuring; neither is a listed measure.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must have a boom angle or radius indicator readable from the operator's station.
Temporary alternative measures: Radii or boom angle must be determined by measuring the radii or boom angle with a measuring device.
Temporary alternative measures: Radii or jib angle must be determined by ascertaining the main boom angle and then measuring the radii or jib angle with a measuring device.
Boom length indicator if the equipment has a telescopic boom, except where the rated capacity is independent of the boom length.
Mark the boom with measured marks to calculate boom length,
Calculate boom length from boom angle and radius measurements,
Measure the boom with a measuring device.
Temporary alternative measures: Mark the drum to indicate the rotation of the drum.

summary: The crane must have a boom angle or radius indicator you can read from the operator's station, a jib angle indicator if it has a luffing jib, and a boom length indicator if it has a telescopic boom, unless rated capacity does not depend on boom length. Equipment built after November 8, 2011 also needs an outrigger or stabilizer position sensor and a hoist drum rotation indicator where the drum cannot be seen. These readings are what you take into the load chart, and radius is checked from the center of rotation to the hook.
title: Use boom angle, radius, length, jib angle and drum rotation indicators

exam: Expect date questions, items asking how many temporary methods are needed, and items asking which indicator is an acceptable substitute. Watch for near-miss dates and for options that name the wrong kind of indicator.
hard: The temporary measures are alternatives, use at least one: a boom angle indicator, a clear mark on the boom hoist cable the operator can see, with mirrors or cameras if needed, or a mark a spotter can see in time to signal a stop. The December 16, 1969 date applies to the boom hoist device only, not to the luffing jib requirement. This device is different from boom stops, which physically keep the boom from going over backward.
mistakes: People move the cutoff to 1968, January 1, 1970 or the start of 1969; it is December 16, 1969. People think two or all three methods are needed; at least one is required, and combining them is allowed. People apply the 1969 date to the luffing jib, or tie the jib device to visibility or rated-capacity lifts; any equipment with a luffing jib must have the device. People name a boom length, load or crane level indicator as the substitute; the listed indicator is a boom angle indicator.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: For equipment manufactured after December 16, 1969, a boom hoist limiting device is required.
Temporary alternative measures (use at least one). One or more of the following methods must be used:
Use a boom angle indicator.

Clearly mark the boom hoist cable (so that it can easily be seen by the operator) at a point that will give the operator sufficient time to stop the hoist to keep the boom within the minimum allowable radius. In addition, install mirrors or remote video cameras and displays if necessary for the operator to see the mark.

If the equipment was manufactured on or before December 16, 1969, and is not equipped with a boom hoist limiting device, at least one of the measures in paragraphs (d)(1)(i)(A) through (C) of this section must be used.
Equipment with a luffing jib must have a luffing jib limiting device.

summary: A boom hoist limiting device cuts boom hoist power when the boom reaches a set operating angle and sets brakes or closes valves so the boom does not lower afterward. It is required on equipment built after December 16, 1969; older equipment without one uses at least one of the listed measures. A luffing jib must have a luffing jib limiting device, which works the same way on the jib.
title: Know boom hoist and luffing jib limiting devices

exam: Expect items asking what component keeps a jack or boom from dropping after a hose failure and where it is mounted, plus basic hydraulic questions about flow, pressure and relief valves. Look for the word integral and reject options that place the valve elsewhere in the circuit.
hard: Integral means mounted at the cylinder, so a hose break upstream does not let the jack or boom drop; a valve in the supply line, at the manifold, at the pump or in a hose does not meet that. As physics, a fixed-displacement pump moves a set volume per turn, so flow follows engine speed, while pressure rises with resistance up to the relief setting. Pump torque rises with pressure, and hydraulic power depends on both pressure and flow.
mistakes: People think a common supply-line valve, a manifold shutoff, a pump-mounted device, an in-line hose valve or a pressure relief valve provides the required holding protection; the rule calls for an integral holding device or check valve at the jacks and an integrally mounted holding device on the telescoping boom. People think stabilizer jacks are exempt; they are named in the rule. People think a passed static test replaces the required construction; it does not. People think two holding valves per jack are required; one integral holding device or check valve meets the rule. People think fixed displacement means fixed pressure, torque or power; only displacement per turn is fixed.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Hydraulic outrigger jacks and hydraulic stabilizer jacks must have an integral holding device/check valve.
Hydraulic telescoping booms must have an integrally mounted holding device to prevent the boom from retracting in the event of hydraulic failure.

summary: Power reaches the crane's functions through hydraulics, mechanical drives, or both: pumps push oil to cylinders and motors, while clutches, brakes and gear trains handle mechanical drives. Hold-in-place protection is built in by rule: hydraulic outrigger and stabilizer jacks must have an integral holding device or check valve, and hydraulic telescoping booms must have an integrally mounted holding device so the boom does not retract if hydraulics fail. Knowing how oil flow and pressure behave helps you read slow, weak or drifting functions.
title: Understand hydraulic and mechanical power flow and holding valves

exam: Items usually give a short jobsite story and ask whether hoisting personnel is allowed, or who has to justify it. Watch for options that offer cost, schedule or worker preference as the reason, and for drill-shaft diameters just above or below 8 feet.
hard: People blur exclusions and exceptions. Exclusions take work out of the general prohibition entirely, and there are only two: steel erection under subpart R, and routine personnel access to an underground worksite via shaft under the underground construction rules. The platform exceptions (drill shafts up to and including 8 feet in diameter, pile driving, marine transfer, and storage-tank, shaft and chimney work) still fall under the prohibition. They only change what the worker rides in.
mistakes: People put the demonstration on the operator, or on whoever inspected the platform. It is the employer's duty. People accept worker consent, cost savings or schedule pressure as justification, but none of these shows that conventional access is more hazardous or not possible. People think impossibility is the only route; showing that conventional access would be more hazardous is the other. People remember the drill-shaft limit as 6, 10 or 12 feet. The exception covers shafts up to and including 8 feet in diameter. People treat routine elevated access, the drill-shaft provision or the marine-transfer provision as exclusions from the prohibition. Those provisions are only exceptions to the platform requirement.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The use of equipment to hoist employees is prohibited except where the employer demonstrates that the erection, use, and dismantling of conventional means of reaching the work area, such as a personnel hoist, ladder, stairway, aerial lift, elevating work platform, or scaffold, would be more hazardous, or is not possible because of the project's structural design or worksite conditions.

This paragraph does not apply to work covered by subpart R (Steel Erection) of this part and also does not apply to routine personnel access to an underground worksite via shaft as covered by § 1926.800 (Underground Construction) of this part.
When using equipment to hoist employees, the employees must be in a personnel platform that meets the requirements of paragraph (e) of this section.
Into and out of drill shafts that are up to and including 8 feet in diameter (see paragraph (o) of this section for requirements for hoisting these employees).

summary: As a general rule, using a crane to hoist workers is prohibited. The employer can get past that only by demonstrating that putting up, using and taking down a conventional means of access (a personnel hoist, ladder, stairway, aerial lift, elevating work platform or scaffold) would be more hazardous, or is not possible because of the project's structural design or worksite conditions. Knowing this keeps a personnel basket from being treated as a convenience.
title: Know when hoisting personnel is permitted

exam: Expect number items on the level tolerance and the capacity percentage. Expect scenarios where one device is out of service or swapped for another, and you decide whether the lift can go ahead. Watch for wording like firm footing or conservative chart that tempts you to overlook a separate requirement.
hard: Each device has its own job, so one cannot stand in for another. A load moment indicator or a boom length indicator does not replace the boom hoist limiting device. The rule calls for equal extension, not full extension, and choosing a more conservative chart does not fix unequal outriggers. If a required device stops working, the operator safely stops, and work does not resume until the device is fixed; alternative measures are not permitted. When the occupied platform is in a stationary working position, the brakes and locking features are engaged.
mistakes: People remember the level tolerance as 0.5 or 1.5 percent. The limit is one percent, and firm footing does not excuse a 2.5 percent slope. People use 75 percent, 25 percent or the full chart. The personnel limit is 50 percent, applied once. People count a load moment indicator, a capacity display or a boom length indicator as the boom hoist limiting device, but that device is a separate requirement. People think a lower chart cures unequal outrigger extension. Every outrigger has to be extended the same amount. People think full extension is always required. The rule calls for equal, locked extension that follows the manufacturer's procedures and charts.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The equipment must be uniformly level, within one percent of level grade, and located on footing that a qualified person has determined to be sufficiently firm and stable.

Equipment with outriggers or stabilizers must have them all extended and locked. The amount of extension must be the same for all outriggers and stabilizers and in accordance with manufacturer procedures and load charts.

Capacity: Use of suspended personnel platforms. The total load (with the platform loaded, including the hook, load line and rigging) must not exceed 50 percent of the rated capacity for the radius and configuration of the equipment, except during proof testing.
A boom hoist limiting device.
Equipment with telescoping booms must be equipped with a device to indicate the boom's extended length clearly to the operator, or must have measuring marks on the boom.

Personnel hoisting operations must not begin unless the devices listed in this section are in proper working order. If a device stops working properly during such operations, the operator must safely stop operations. Personnel hoisting operations must not resume until the device is again working properly. Alternative measures are not permitted.

When the occupied personnel platform is in a stationary working position, the load and boom hoist brakes, swing brakes, and operator actuated secondary braking and locking features (such as pawls or dogs) or automatic secondary brakes must be engaged.

summary: Before anyone rides, the crane is uniformly level within one percent of level grade, on footing a qualified person has found firm and stable. All outriggers or stabilizers are extended and locked, each to the same amount, following the manufacturer's procedures and load charts. The required aids have to be working: a boom angle indicator and boom hoist limiting device on variable-angle booms, a length indicator or measuring marks on telescoping booms, anti two-block, and controlled load lowering. The total load stays within 50 percent of rated capacity for the radius and configuration.
title: Set up equipment for personnel hoisting (level, outriggers, aids)

exam: Items test the 10-degree, five-times and 1/2-inch numbers, with nearby values as the wrong options, and ask who designs the platform or who welds it. On strength items, check that the right option counts the platform weight once and multiplies only the intended load.
hard: The strength formula is easy to garble. The platform's own weight is counted once, and the five-times factor applies only to the maximum intended load. The enclosure covers at least the zone from the toeboard to the mid-rail, in solid material or expanded metal with openings no greater than 1/2 inch. Gates do not swing outward unless the platform is too small for an inward swing, as with a one-person platform, and they have a device that prevents accidental opening.
mistakes: People pick 5 or 15 degrees, or apply the limit only at the working angle. The platform stays within 10 degrees of level regardless of boom angle. People use two times, multiply the platform weight too, or leave the weight out. The platform supports its own weight plus at least five times the maximum intended load. People think the enclosure runs up to the top rail. It runs at least from the toeboard to the mid-rail. People allow 1-inch mesh, but openings can be no greater than 1/2 inch. People name a state-licensed engineer, the certified welder or the rigger as the designer. The rule calls for a qualified person familiar with structural design.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: A qualified person familiar with structural design must design the personnel platform and attachment/suspension system used for hoisting personnel.
The system used to connect the personnel platform to the equipment must allow the platform to remain within 10 degrees of level, regardless of boom angle.

The personnel platform itself (excluding the guardrail system and personal fall arrest system anchorages), must be capable of supporting, without failure, its own weight and at least five times the maximum intended load.
All welding of the personnel platform and its components must be performed by a certified welder familiar with the weld grades, types and material specified in the platform design.
must be enclosed at least from the toeboard to mid-rail with either solid construction material or expanded metal having openings no greater than 1/2 inch (1.27 cm)
Be equipped with a device that prevents accidental opening.
The weight of the platform and its rated capacity must be conspicuously posted on the platform with a plate or other permanent marking.

summary: The personnel platform is an engineered structure. A qualified person familiar with structural design designs the platform and its attachment and suspension system. A certified welder familiar with the weld grades, types and material in the design does the welding. The platform supports its own weight plus at least five times the maximum intended load, stays within 10 degrees of level regardless of boom angle, and carries a plate or other permanent marking showing its weight and rated capacity.
title: Know personnel platform design and marking criteria

exam: Expect a no-calculator arithmetic item. You are given the chart capacity, platform weight, riders, tools and rigging, and you decide whether the lift is within limits or how much more can be added. Watch for options built from skipping the rigging weight or using the wrong percentage, and check both the crane limit and the platform limit.
hard: The step people skip is adding the hook, load line and rigging to the loaded platform before comparing against half the chart. Example: the chart gives 6,000 pounds at the radius, so the limit is 3,000. A loaded platform of 2,500 plus 300 of hook, line and rigging makes 2,800, which leaves 200 pounds. The 50 percent cut applies to the crane rating, not to the platform's plate, and unused crane capacity never raises the platform's rating.
mistakes: People halve the crane rating twice, or use 75 percent or the full chart. Take 50 percent of the crane rating, once. People halve the platform's marked rating, or invent a 75 percent platform derating. The platform limit is simply its rated capacity. People think spare crane capacity lets the platform carry more than its rating, and it does not. People treat the unoccupied trial lift, a stationary hold or the first occupied lift as exempt from the 50 percent limit. Only proof testing is excepted. People subtract only the loaded platform and get 500 pounds left in the example above. With the hook, line and rigging counted, only 200 pounds remain.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Capacity: Use of suspended personnel platforms. The total load (with the platform loaded, including the hook, load line and rigging) must not exceed 50 percent of the rated capacity for the radius and configuration of the equipment, except during proof testing.
The personnel platform must not be loaded in excess of its rated capacity.
The number of employees occupying the personnel platform must not exceed the maximum number the platform was designed to hold or the number required to perform the work, whichever is less.
Personnel platforms must be used only for employees, their tools, and the materials necessary to do their work.

summary: Two separate limits apply at the same time. The total suspended load (the loaded platform plus the hook, load line and rigging) stays within 50 percent of the crane's rated capacity for the radius and configuration, except during proof testing. The platform itself is never loaded past its own rated capacity. The number of riders is whichever is less: the most the platform was designed to hold, or the number needed to do the work.
title: Load the platform within its rated capacity and the 50% rule

exam: Items describe a piece of hardware or a sling and ask whether it is acceptable, or which strength factor applies. Watch for rotation resistant rope in the stem, which moves the answer from five to ten times, and for a latch described in a way that sounds secure but does not lock.
hard: An ordinary spring latch keeps a sling from slipping out, but it is not a locking closure. The two strength factors sit side by side: five for hardware and hooks, ten for rotation resistant rope slings. Each bridle leg connects to a master link or shackle so the load divides evenly among the legs. Bridle rigging that has been used for anything other than hoisting personnel is out.
mistakes: People accept a spring latch, sling tension or a load-activated closure as a locking hook. The hook has to close and lock, eliminating the throat opening. People substitute abrasion sleeves, extra clips or a master link for a thimble. Wire rope sling eyes are fabricated with thimbles. People use four or five times for rotation resistant rope slings, or double it to twenty. The requirement is at least ten times. People think screw-pin shackles are banned for personnel. Screw-type alloy anchor shackles are allowed when the pin is secured against accidental removal, and retightening the pin or turning it a certain way does not count as securing it.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Of a type that can be closed and locked, eliminating the throat opening.
Closed and locked when attached.
Of the screw type, with the screw pin secured from accidental removal.

Rigging hardware (including wire rope, shackles, rings, master links, and other rigging hardware) and hooks must be capable of supporting, without failure, at least five times the maximum intended load applied or transmitted to that component. Where rotation resistant rope is used, the slings must be capable of supporting without failure at least ten times the maximum intended load.
Eyes in wire rope slings must be fabricated with thimbles.
The bridles and associated rigging must not have been used for any purpose other than hoisting personnel.

summary: The connection between the hoist line and the platform has to be positive and strong. Hooks are a type that can be closed and locked, eliminating the throat opening, and they are closed and locked when attached. Shackles used in place of hooks are alloy anchor type, with either a bolt, nut and retaining pin in place, or a screw pin secured against accidental removal. Rigging hardware and hooks support at least five times the maximum intended load, rotation resistant rope slings at least ten times. Wire rope sling eyes have thimbles, and the bridle is used only for hoisting personnel.
title: Rig personnel platforms correctly

exam: Expect scenarios like a second shift starting, the crane being moved, the route changing, or several landings, where you decide whether a new trial lift is needed and how to run it. Also watch for who checks and inspects: it is the competent person.
hard: Timing is the trap. The trial lift is made immediately before each shift in which personnel will be hoisted. It is repeated when the crane is moved and set up in a new location or returned to a previously used one, and when the lift route changes, unless the competent person finds the new route adds no new safety factors. With several stops from one setup, you run either individual trials or one sequential trial, using the same method you will use for the people. The occupied check, raising the platform a few inches before each lift, is a separate step.
mistakes: People load the trial to the platform's rated capacity, or to half of something. The minimum is the anticipated liftweight. People call the occupied check a few inches off the boarding spot the trial lift. The trial lift is unoccupied. People think a weekly or daily trial, or an unchanged setup, is enough. The trial comes immediately before each shift that hoists personnel. People apply 75 percent, 25 percent or full rated capacity. The lift stays within 50 percent. People think reaching the highest stop covers the lower ones, or that order does not matter. The trial reaches and positions at each location, in the same method and sequence as the personnel lift.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: A trial lift with the unoccupied personnel platform loaded at least to the anticipated liftweight must be made from ground level, or any other location where employees will enter the platform, to each location at which the platform is to be hoisted and positioned.
the method selected must be the same as the method that will be used to hoist the personnel.
The trial lift must be performed immediately prior to each shift in which personnel will be hoisted.
The equipment is moved and set up in a new location or returned to a previously used location.
The lift will not exceed 50 percent of the equipment's rated capacity at any time during the lift.
Conduct a visual inspection of the equipment, base support or ground, and personnel platform, to determine whether the trial lift has exposed any defect or problem or produced any adverse effect.
The platform must be hoisted a few inches with the personnel and materials/tools on board and inspected by a competent person to ensure that it is secure and properly balanced.

summary: Before anyone rides, the unoccupied platform, loaded at least to the anticipated liftweight, is run from the boarding location to each place it will be hoisted and positioned. This proves the setup, route and radius with no one aboard. The competent person confirms the aids are working, nothing interferes, the lift stays within 50 percent of rated capacity the whole time, and the radius is accurately determined. Right after the trial, the competent person inspects the crane, ground and platform and confirms the test weight has been removed.
title: Run the trial lift and inspection

exam: Expect number items on the test percentage and hold time, and scenarios where the platform arrives at a new site or comes back from a repair. Watch for options that swap the competent person for another job title.
hard: The proof test and the trial lift are different tests, though they may be done at the same time. The proof test loads to 125 percent of the platform rating; the trial lift loads to at least the anticipated liftweight. The proof test is the one exception to the 50 percent capacity limit, but in practice the crane still has to handle the test load within its chart. The jobsite trigger applies even when nothing looks damaged and nothing has changed.
mistakes: People test at rated capacity, at 110 percent or at 150 percent. The proof load is 125 percent of the platform's rated capacity. People hold for two, ten or fifteen minutes. The minimum hold is five minutes. People let the certified operator, the lift supervisor or the rigger pass the test. The inspection and the pass decision belong to a competent person. People skip the test at a new jobsite because the platform was inspected, shows no transport damage, or has the same configuration. A proof test is required at each jobsite.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: At each jobsite, prior to hoisting employees on the personnel platform, and after any repair or modification, the platform and rigging must be proof tested to 125 percent of the platform's rated capacity. The proof test may be done concurrently with the trial lift.
The platform must be lowered by controlled load lowering, braked, and held in a suspended position for a minimum of five minutes with the test load evenly distributed on the platform.
After proof testing, a competent person must inspect the platform and rigging to determine if the test has been passed.
Personnel hoisting must not be conducted until the competent person determines that the platform and rigging have successfully passed the proof test.

summary: The platform and rigging are proof tested to 125 percent of the platform's rated capacity at each jobsite before employees are hoisted, and after any repair or modification. The test load is evenly distributed, and the platform is lowered by controlled load lowering, braked, and held suspended for at least five minutes. A competent person then inspects the platform and rigging and decides whether the test was passed. No one is hoisted until it has been.
title: Run the proof test

exam: Expect number items on wind and the winch cap, and scenarios asking whether the operator can step away, whether a rider can lean out, or what has to happen before someone steps off onto a structure. Watch for wording about where the wind is measured and whether gusts count.
hard: Wind over 20 mph, sustained or gusts, measured at the platform, does not stop the lift by itself. It requires a qualified person to decide whether lifting is unsafe, and if it is, the lift does not start or is ended. If the platform has its own controls, the crane operator still stays at a set of controls with boom and swing functions. No lifts are made on other load lines during personnel hoisting, except in pile driving, and a factory platform winch is limited to 500 pounds and to the winch and platform ratings.
mistakes: People use 15 or 30 mph, measure wind at the cab, or ignore gusts. The trigger is over 20 mph, sustained or gusts, at the platform. People take the winch rating as the limit, or think 1,000, 1,500 or 2,000 pounds is allowed. The winch line is capped at 500 pounds while the platform is occupied. People think the operator only has to be at the controls while the platform moves, or that radio contact with a rider is enough. At all times while the platform is occupied, the operator is at controls that include boom and swing, on site and in view. People forget the exceptions to keeping the body inside, or think signaling is banned. Reaching out is allowed when needed to position the platform or to act as signal person. People confuse those exceptions with the tie-off rule, which is about entering or exiting a platform that is not landed.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Hoisting of the personnel platform must be performed in a slow, controlled, cautious manner, with no sudden movements of the equipment or the platform.

Keep all parts of the body inside the platform during raising, lowering, and horizontal movement. This provision does not apply to an occupant of the platform when necessary to position the platform or while performing the duties of a signal person.

Before employees exit or enter a hoisted personnel platform that is not landed, the platform must be secured to the structure where the work is to be performed, unless the employer can demonstrate that securing to the structure would create a greater hazard.

Platforms without controls. Where the platform is not equipped with controls, the equipment operator must remain at the equipment controls, on site, and in view of the equipment, at all times while the platform is occupied.
The equipment operator must be at a set of equipment controls that include boom and swing functions of the equipment, and must be on site and in view of the equipment.

Wind. When wind speed (sustained or gusts) exceeds 20 mph at the personnel platform, a qualified person must determine if, in light of the wind conditions, it is not safe to lift personnel. If it is not, the lifting operation must not begin (or, if already in progress, must be terminated).
Except over water, employees occupying the personnel platform must be provided and use a personal fall arrest system. The system must be attached to a structural member within the personnel platform.
No lifts must be made on any other of the equipment's load lines while personnel are being hoisted, except in pile driving operations.

Loads are permitted to be hoisted by such a winch while employees occupy the personnel platform only where the load on the winch line does not exceed 500 pounds and does not exceed the rated capacity of the winch and platform.

summary: While people are aboard, the crane moves slowly and smoothly with no sudden movements. Riders keep their bodies inside, stay off the rails and toeboard, and do not pull the platform out of plumb. Before anyone steps on or off a platform that is not landed, the platform is secured to the structure, unless the employer can show that tying off would be the greater hazard. The operator stays at the controls, on site and in view of the crane the whole time the platform is occupied. Riders wear personal fall arrest attached inside the platform, except over water.
title: Follow personnel-hoisting work practices

exam: Items list attendees and ask who is required, or describe a change on site (new location, new worker, new shift, re-rigging) and ask whether a new meeting is needed. Watch the order of events: meeting first, then the trial lift.
hard: The meeting has two triggers, and neither is a shift or a day. One is each new work location, with the meeting held before the trial lift there. The other is any employee newly assigned to the operation. Everyone on the required list attends; a talk with the operator alone does not count.
mistakes: People tie the meeting to each shift or each day. It is tied to each new work location and to newly assigned employees, so an unchanged crew at an unchanged location does not repeat it daily. People hold it after the trial lift; it comes before. People think one meeting covers the whole project, or that an unchanged crew carries it to a new location. Each new location gets its own meeting before its trial lift. People add the safety manager, the rigger or the equipment owner to the required list. The listed attendees are the operator, the signal person if used, the hoisted employees and the person responsible for the task. People accept a coworker's informal briefing for a new hand. The meeting is repeated for the newly assigned employee.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Held to review the applicable requirements of this section and the procedures that will be followed.
Attended by the equipment operator, signal person (if used for the lift), employees to be hoisted, and the person responsible for the task to be performed.
Held prior to the trial lift at each new work location, and must be repeated for any employees newly assigned to the operation.

summary: The pre-lift meeting gets everyone involved on the same plan before people leave the ground. It reviews the personnel-hoisting requirements and the procedures that will be followed. The attendees are the operator, the signal person if one is used, the employees to be hoisted, and the person responsible for the task.
title: Hold the pre-lift meeting

exam: Expect scenario items naming a drill shaft, a pile-driving job, a marine transfer or a tank job, and asking where the signal person stands, where the harness attaches, or what flotation device is needed. Read the case named in the stem first, because the attachment answer changes with it.
hard: Where the harness attaches changes from case to case. In a drill shaft it is attached independent of the crane. In pile driving it is independently attached to the lower load block or overhaul ball. In tank, shaft and chimney work it is attached independent of the crane, unless there is no adequate structure, in which case it goes to the block or ball. In a drill shaft with a chair, the signal person is stationed at the shaft opening. In pile driving, anti two-block is not required. Instead, the cable is marked, and lattice booms use a mark or a spotter, while telescopic booms use both.
mistakes: People station the drill-shaft signal person beside the operator, at the bottom, or watching the winch. The station is at the shaft opening. People use four, six or ten times for the chair. It supports its own weight plus at least five times the maximum intended load. People accept a recreational flotation device, or one picked by the lift director or the vessel captain. It has to be U.S. Coast Guard approved for industrial use. People carry the pile-driving attachment to the block or ball into a drill shaft. There the harness is attached independent of the crane. People count a separate line to the chair suspension, or a tie to the boom tip, as independent, but both are still part of the crane.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Hoisting personnel within 20 feet of a power line that is up to 350 kV, and hoisting personnel within 50 feet of a power line that is over 350 kV, is prohibited, except for work covered by subpart V of this part (Power Transmission and Distribution).
A signal person must be stationed at the shaft opening.
The employee must use personal fall protection equipment, including a full body harness, attached independent of the crane/derrick.
The boatswain's chair itself (excluding the personal fall arrest system anchorages), must be capable of supporting, without failure, its own weight and at least five times the maximum intended load.
No more than one person must be hoisted at a time.
The employee must use personal fall protection equipment, including a full body harness, independently attached to the lower load block or overhaul ball.

For telescopic boom cranes: Clearly mark the cable (so that it can be easily seen by the operator) at a point that will give the operator sufficient time to stop the hoist to prevent two-blocking, and use a spotter who is in direct communication with the operator to inform the operator when this point is reached.
Each employee must wear a U.S. Coast Guard personal flotation device approved for industrial use.
When there is no adequate structure for attachment of personal fall arrest equipment as required in § 1926.502(d)(15), the attachment must be to the lower load block or overhaul ball.

summary: Some personnel hoisting follows its own rules. Hoisting personnel is prohibited within 20 feet of a power line up to 350 kV and within 50 feet of a line over 350 kV, except for power transmission and distribution work. Drill shafts up to and including 8 feet in diameter, pile driving, and storage-tank, shaft and chimney work can use a boatswain's chair, which supports its own weight plus at least five times the maximum intended load and carries one person at a time. Marine transfer can use a marine-hoisted personnel transfer device, with each worker in a U.S. Coast Guard personal flotation device approved for industrial use.
title: Know the power line, drill shaft, pile driving, marine and tank cases

exam: Expect radius and capacity questions where the load swings out past the pick or set point, and ground-condition scenarios that offer mats, pavement or frozen ground as exceptions. Read for the words "longest radius" and for which verification method the scenario actually uses.
hard: The 75 percent trigger is measured against capacity at the longest radius that will be used, not at the pick or the set. That number sits close to others people remember, like an indicator warning near 90 percent or the 85 percent tipping margin commonly built into outrigger charts. The drainage exception covers only marshes and wetlands, and mats don't waive drainage.
mistakes: People use half capacity as the trigger; the rule's trigger is 75 percent of maximum rated capacity at the longest radius used. People confuse the trigger with the 85 percent stability margin on outrigger charts or the indicator warning near 90 percent; neither is the verification trigger, and a load between 75 and 90 percent has to be verified before the lift goes on. People check capacity at the pick radius, the landing radius, or an average of the two; the longest radius used during the lift governs. People think mats, pavement or frozen ground get around drainage; only marshes and wetlands are exempt. People treat a visual estimate, the feel of the crane, or a supervisor's signature as weight verification; you need an industry-recognized source, a recognized calculation, or a weighing device or indicator.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The weight of the load must be determined from a source recognized by the industry (such as the load's manufacturer), or by a calculation method recognized by the industry (such as calculating a steel beam from measured dimensions and a known per foot weight), or by other equally reliable means. In addition, when requested by the operator, this information must be provided to the operator prior to the lift; or

The operator must begin hoisting the load to determine, using a load weighing device, load moment indicator, rated capacity indicator, or rated capacity limiter, if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used during the lift operation. If it does, the operator must not proceed with the lift until he/she verifies the weight of the load in accordance with paragraph (o)(3)(i) of this section.

The equipment must not be assembled or used unless ground conditions are firm, drained, and graded to a sufficient extent so that, in conjunction (if necessary) with the use of supporting materials, the equipment manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level of the equipment are met. The requirement for the ground to be drained does not apply to marshes/wetlands.
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

summary: Every lift plan starts with the same checks: the load's weight and center of gravity, the radius at every point of the lift, the chart capacity at the worst of those radii, rigging weight and fit, ground support, clearances, and where people will be. The operator has to verify the load is within rated capacity, either from a reliable weight source or by hoisting and reading a weighing device or indicator against the 75 percent trigger. Ground has to be firm, drained and graded well enough to meet the manufacturer's support and level specifications.
title: Plan a lift (weight, CG, radius, chart, rigging, ground, clearances, people)

exam: Expect judgment scenarios that describe a load, a site and a consequence and ask whether the lift needs special planning, plus multi-crane questions about who may develop the plan and when engineering is brought in. Be wary of choices that state a fixed percentage or call a project classification a federal rule.
hard: The hard part is separating company or project triggers from federal requirements. A lift can be light on the chart and still be critical because of what happens if the load is damaged. On the multi-crane side, people confuse a competent person with a qualified person and assume an engineer or a capacity percentage is built into the rule.
mistakes: People think low chart use makes a lift ordinary; losing an essential, irreplaceable item can make a light lift critical. People think only shared loads are critical; a single-crane lift can need critical planning because of the consequences. People quote a universal capacity threshold such as 25 percent; there isn't one, and company percentages vary. People think operator certification or competent-person designation qualifies someone to write a multi-crane plan; the plan developer has to be a qualified person.
