People think every multi-crane plan needs an engineer, or that a percentage or a third crane triggers one; the qualified person decides when engineering expertise is needed. People treat a trial pick, or waiting until both cranes take weight, as coming before planning; the trial is part of the operation, so the plan comes first.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The plan must be developed by a qualified person.
Where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided.

Plan development. Before beginning a crane/derrick operation in which more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load, the operation must be planned. The planning must meet the following requirements:

summary: The federal rules don't define "critical lift." In industry practice it means a lift where failure would have serious consequences, so it gets a written plan, a review and sign-offs. Common triggers in company programs include a high share of chart capacity, more than one crane, lifting personnel, work near power lines or over occupied areas, and loads that are irreplaceable or very costly to damage. The one federal planning rule that does apply here is the one for lifts where more than one crane supports the load, which needs a plan by a qualified person before the operation begins.
title: Recognize a lift that needs a written critical-lift plan (industry practice)

exam: Expect scenarios like a tailing pick, a vessel upend or a handoff between cranes, asking when planning has to happen, who may write the plan, or what triggers engineering. Watch for wording that delays planning to "after the trial" or "once the load is clear."
hard: The trigger is shared support, not lift duration, and not the moment the load leaves the ground. A tailing pick or a short transfer between cranes counts. The engineering trigger is the qualified person's judgment, not an unequal split, a percentage of capacity, or the number of cranes.
mistakes: People think the senior operator, the site superintendent or the signal person is automatically qualified to plan; the developer has to be a qualified person, whatever the role. People treat a trial lift or trial handoff as something to plan around afterward; it involves shared support, so it has to be planned first. People think planning starts once the load clears its supports or once balance is confirmed; it comes before the operation begins. People think a brief overlap is exempt; any time two cranes support the load, the rule applies. People think an unequal split, a capacity percentage, or just using two cranes requires engineering; the qualified person decides whether engineering expertise is needed. People think the receiving crane's own lift plan covers the transfer; the plan has to cover the operation with both cranes supporting the load.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Plan development. Before beginning a crane/derrick operation in which more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load, the operation must be planned. The planning must meet the following requirements:
The plan must be developed by a qualified person.
The plan must be designed to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met.
Where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided.

summary: Any time more than one crane will support the load, even briefly during a handoff, the operation has to be planned before it begins. A qualified person develops the plan, and the plan has to make sure every requirement of the crane rules is met for each crane. If the qualified person decides engineering expertise is needed, the employer has to provide it. In practice the plan covers load weight and center of gravity, each crane's share at every stage, radii, rigging, ground, travel or swing, and how the cranes and signals will be coordinated.
title: Develop a multiple-crane lift plan

exam: Expect "who may direct this lift" items that describe a person's credentials, and "who must attend" or "who runs the meeting" items. Check each choice against both allowed arrangements, and watch for choices that leave out ground crew.
hard: There are two allowed arrangements, and people tend to remember only one or get the roles backwards. A qualified person alone isn't enough to direct, and the competent person is the one who directs with qualified help, not the other way around. The meeting audience is everyone involved in the work, not just the crane crew or management.
mistakes: People think a qualified person alone, even one with a rigging credential, can direct; the director also has to meet the competent-person criteria, or be a competent person with qualified help. People reverse the roles; the competent person directs with qualified help. People think matching crane models or a written plan removes the need for qualified assistance; the rule has no such exceptions. People think the job falls to a role like the operator, the signal person or the safety manager; whoever directs has to meet the criteria, and the plan review belongs to the lift director. People think the meeting covers only crane control people, or that management sign-off or crew experience can stand in for it; all workers involved have to attend the review of that specific plan.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The multiple-crane/derrick lift must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person who is assisted by one or more qualified persons (lift director).
The lift director must review the plan in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation.

summary: A multiple-crane lift is run by a lift director. That's either one person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or a competent person assisted by one or more qualified persons. Before the lift, the lift director reviews the plan in a meeting with every worker who will be involved: operators, signal persons, riggers, tag-line handlers and anyone else on the operation.
title: Implement a multiple-crane lift

exam: Expect a hand calculation with round numbers that asks for one crane's share, with wrong choices built from swapped distances, an even split, or the wrong divisor. Check that your two answers add up to the total before you pick.
hard: The crane nearer the center of gravity carries more, which feels backwards to many people. The step that gets skipped is using the opposite distance and the full span, then checking that the two shares add up to the total. In this skill the arithmetic comes with planning questions about who writes the plan and who attends the meeting.
mistakes: People multiply by a crane's own distance to the center of gravity, which swaps the shares; use the distance to the other crane. People think the far crane carries more; the near crane carries more. People assume an even split; that holds only when the center of gravity is midway between the pick points. People divide by one distance instead of the full span; divide by the full span so the shares add up to the total weight. People think a bigger crane takes more of the load; geometry sets the share, not capacity. People think an engineer always writes the plan, or that the controlling entity or the lift director does; a qualified person develops it and decides whether engineering expertise is needed. People think the plan review is only for the crane crew, the planner or management; it's held with all workers involved, riggers and tag-line workers included.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The plan must be developed by a qualified person.
Where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided.
The lift director must review the plan in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation.

summary: When two cranes lift one beam, each hook's share comes from where the center of gravity sits between the pick points. Each crane's share equals the total weight times the distance from the center of gravity to the other crane, divided by the full span. Take a 20,000 lb beam with pick points 40 ft apart and the center of gravity 10 ft from crane A and 30 ft from crane B. Crane A carries 20,000 times 30 over 40, which is 15,000 lb, and crane B carries 5,000 lb. Add rigging weight to each hook, and remember the shares shift if the beam tilts or the hooks move.
title: Compute load share for two cranes on a beam

exam: Expect panel-erection scenarios that name a worker, a task and a position, and ask whether that worker may be there or which free fall restriction applies. Read carefully whether the item says "fall zone" or "directly under the load," and whether infeasibility has been shown.
hard: There are two separate limits: the fall zone, which opens to essential workers, and the space directly under the load, which never opens. Being essential takes both a listed task and a showing that the task can't be done from outside. The free fall rules key off different areas, with boom free fall tied to the fall zone and load line free fall tied to being directly under the load.
mistakes: People think guiding the load or installing bracing allows someone under the load; it allows them into the fall zone only. People treat any safety task as essential, like inspecting rigging or watching the crane's outriggers; only the three listed tasks count. People think a supervisor's title makes them essential; only the task and the infeasibility showing count. People forget the infeasibility condition, or add conditions the rule doesn't have, like a signal person standing beside the guiders. People attach the load line free fall ban to the fall zone or the swing radius; it applies when an employee is directly under the load, and boom free fall is the one tied to the fall zone.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: No employee must be directly under the load.

Only employees essential to the operation are permitted in the fall zone (but not directly under the load). An employee is essential to the operation if the employee is conducting one of the following operations and the employer can demonstrate it is infeasible for the employee to perform that operation from outside the fall zone: (1) Physically guide the load; (2) closely monitor and give instructions regarding the load's movement; or (3) either detach it from or initially attach it to another component or structure (such as, but not limited to, making an initial connection or installing bracing). Note: Boom free fall is prohibited when an employee is in the fall zone of the boom or load, and load line free fall is prohibited when an employee is directly under the load; see § 1926.1426.

summary: During tilt-up and tilt-down work, such as standing or lowering wall panels, no employee may be directly under the load. Only essential employees may be in the fall zone, and never under the load. An employee counts as essential only when doing one of three tasks and the employer can show it's infeasible to do it from outside the fall zone. The three tasks are physically guiding the load, closely monitoring and giving instructions about its movement, and initially attaching or detaching it, for example making an initial connection or installing bracing.
title: Keep clear during tilt-up and tilt-down

exam: Items ask for the walkway width, the railing height limit, or the profile that triggers a walkway, often with neighboring numbers as distractors. Scenario items describe a pendant-supported boom or a removable rail and ask whether a railing is allowed, so read whether the question asks for a minimum, a maximum, or whether anything is required at all.
hard: Several familiar construction numbers, 42-inch top rails, 18-inch walking surfaces, 16-inch ladder rungs, sit right next to the crane numbers and pull people off. The 45-inch railing figure is a ceiling, not a requirement, and railings are prohibited outright if pendants could snag them or if they are the removable kind set up at each assembly. The 6-foot walkway trigger is a boom profile dimension, not a fall height, and it applies only to lattice booms made after the 2011 date.
mistakes: People pick 16, 18 or 24 inches for walkway width; the minimum is 12 inches. People apply the 42-inch construction top-rail height, or its 39-inch low tolerance, to booms; boom walkway railings are not required and may be no more than 45 inches where allowed. People read 45 inches as a minimum height; it is only a maximum, and no railing is required. People set the walkway trigger at 4, 8 or 10 feet; it is a vertical profile of 6 feet or more. People suggest removable railings as a fix; railings designed to go on and off at each assembly are prohibited, as are any a pendant rope or bar could snag. People apply the general construction guardrail rule to cranes; that section does not apply to this equipment.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Equipment manufactured after November 8, 2011 with lattice booms must be equipped with walkways on the boom(s) if the vertical profile of the boom (from cord centerline to cord centerline) is 6 or more feet.
The walkways must be at least 12 inches wide.
Not required.
Prohibited on booms supported by pendant ropes or bars if the guardrails/railings/attachments could be snagged by the ropes or bars.
Prohibited if of the removable type (designed to be installed and removed each time the boom is assembled/disassembled).
Where not prohibited, guardrails or railings may be of any height up to, but not more than, 45 inches.
Section 1926.502(b) does not apply to equipment covered by this subpart.
The employer must maintain in good condition originally-equipped steps, handholds, ladders and guardrails/railings/grabrails.

Walking/stepping surfaces, except for crawler treads, must have slip-resistant features/properties (such as diamond plate metal, strategically placed grip tape, expanded metal, or slip-resistant paint).

summary: Lattice-boom cranes built after November 8, 2011 need a walkway on the boom when the boom's vertical profile, measured chord centerline to chord centerline, is 6 feet or more. Walkways are at least 12 inches wide, and railings along them are optional, limited and sometimes banned. Separately, the employer keeps original steps, handholds, ladders and rails in good condition, and newer machines provide safe access to the operator stations with slip-resistant stepping surfaces.
title: Know walkway, step, handhold and guardrail requirements

exam: Scenario items give a boom type, its orientation, the task and a height, and ask whether protection is required. Read carefully for lattice or non-lattice, horizontal or not, walking or working at a station, and whether the person is in the cab or on the deck.
hard: The 6-foot trigger and the 15-foot horizontal-lattice exception get swapped: the exception is only for lattice booms lying horizontal, so a telescopic boom stays at 6 feet whether it is up or down. The work-station rule has its own exceptions, at or near running draw-works, in the cab, or on the deck. People also forget the walk itself is covered, not just the spot where the work happens.
mistakes: People use 4 feet from general industry; this crane rule uses more than 6 feet. People invent a 10- or 20-foot trigger; the numbers are more than 6 feet generally and 15 feet or more for walking a horizontal lattice boom. People apply 15 feet to a lowered telescopic boom; it is non-lattice, so the 6-foot trigger applies. People think walking a lowered boom is exempt; point-to-point travel is specifically covered. People believe belts are banned or that arrest and restraint need different body wear; either a belt or a harness may be used in both. People think only work stations count; walking on a non-lattice boom above 6 feet needs protection during the walk.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: For non-assembly/disassembly work, the employer must provide and ensure the use of fall protection equipment for employees who are on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge more than 6 feet above a lower level as follows:
On non-lattice booms (whether horizontal or not horizontal).
On lattice booms that are not horizontal.
On horizontal lattice booms where the fall distance is 15 feet or more.
While at a work station on any part of the equipment (including the boom, of any type), except when the employee is at or near draw-works (when the equipment is running), in the cab, or on the deck.
Either body belts or body harnesses must be used in personal fall arrest and fall restraint systems.

summary: For work other than assembly and disassembly, the employer provides and ensures use of fall protection when an employee is on a surface with an unprotected side or edge more than 6 feet above a lower level. That covers walking point-to-point on non-lattice booms and on lattice booms that are not horizontal, walking a horizontal lattice boom only when the fall is 15 feet or more, and any work station on the equipment. Body belts or harnesses may be used, with components meeting the general fall arrest criteria.
title: Know when fall protection is required (non-assembly work)

exam: Expect "who determines" items that offer competent person, qualified person, operator and A/D director as choices, and items asking for the restraint anchorage factor. Load-line scenarios often leave out one of the three conditions, so check each one before answering.
hard: Two different people make two different calls: a competent person looks at the crane's structure, and a qualified person determines the set-up and rated capacity for load-line tie-off. Restraint uses its own twice-the-maximum-load test, not the fall arrest criteria. For the load line, all three conditions must be met: the qualified person's determination, the operator on site and informed, and no load on the line.
mistakes: People think an engineering analysis is needed to use a crane part as an anchor; the competent person decides by visual inspection without one. People believe only manufacturer-labeled or inspection-listed points are allowed; any apparently substantial part qualifies. People use a factor of three, or body weight plus tools, for restraint anchors; it is twice the maximum load the employee may impose. People apply fall arrest criteria or hook capacity to restraint; those belong to arrest systems and load-line tie-off. People assign the load-line determination to the operator, a competent person or the assembly/disassembly director; it belongs to a qualified person, and the operator only needs to be on site and informed. People forget the load line must be empty while someone is tied to it.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Personal fall arrest systems must be anchored to any apparently substantial part of the equipment unless a competent person, from a visual inspection, without an engineering analysis, would conclude that the criteria in § 1926.502(d)(15) would not be met.

Attachable anchor devices (portable anchor devices that are attached to the equipment) must meet the anchorage criteria in § 1926.502(d)(15) for personal fall arrest systems and § 1926.502(e)(2) for positioning device systems.

Anchorages for fall restraint systems. Fall restraint systems must be anchored to any part of the equipment that is capable of withstanding twice the maximum load that an employee may impose on it during reasonably anticipated conditions of use.
A qualified person has determined that the set-up and rated capacity of the crane/derrick (including the hook, load line and rigging) meets or exceeds the requirements in § 1926.502(d)(15).
The equipment operator must be at the work site and informed that the equipment is being used for this purpose.
No load is suspended from the load line when the personal fall arrest system is anchored to the crane/derrick's hook (or other part of the load line).

summary: Personal fall arrest and positioning systems are anchored to any apparently substantial part of the crane unless a competent person, from a visual inspection and without an engineering analysis, concludes it would not meet the anchorage criteria. Fall restraint anchors to any part able to withstand twice the maximum load the employee may impose. Tying a fall arrest system to the hook or load line is allowed only under three conditions that all apply together.
title: Use acceptable anchorages and the load-line rule

exam: Scenario items describe an inspector or mechanic at a given height on a given boom and ask whether protection is required, or ask who must train or protect that worker. Watch for exact-threshold heights, assembly versus maintenance work, and walking versus working at a station.
hard: The wording decides close cases: more than 6 feet means exactly 6 feet does not trigger, while 15 feet or more on a horizontal lattice boom includes exactly 15 feet, and assembly work uses more than 15 feet. An inspector moving between check points is walking point-to-point, not sitting at a station, so the boom-type rules apply to the walk. The duty belongs to the worker's employer, not the operator, the controlling entity, or the crane owner just because of their role.
mistakes: People apply 6 feet to walking a horizontal lattice boom; that travel triggers at 15 feet or more. People think the 15-foot travel rule starts above 15; it includes exactly 15 feet. People recall 4, 5, 8 or 20 feet; the figures are more than 6 feet for work stations and general exposure, and 15 feet or more for horizontal lattice travel. People think exactly 6 feet triggers protection; the rule says more than 6 feet. People think a telescopic crane needs protection at any height; the more-than-6-foot threshold still applies. People hand the duty to the operator, the controlling entity or the owner; it rests with the exposed employee's employer.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: For non-assembly/disassembly work, the employer must provide and ensure the use of fall protection equipment for employees who are on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge more than 6 feet above a lower level as follows:
On non-lattice booms (whether horizontal or not horizontal).
On horizontal lattice booms where the fall distance is 15 feet or more.
While at a work station on any part of the equipment (including the boom, of any type), except when the employee is at or near draw-works (when the equipment is running), in the cab, or on the deck.

For assembly/disassembly work, the employer must provide and ensure the use of fall protection equipment for employees who are on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge more than 15 feet above a lower level, except when the employee is at or near draw-works (when the equipment is running), in the cab, or on the deck.
Training. The employer must train each employee who may be exposed to fall hazards while on, or hoisted by, equipment covered by this subpart on all of the following:

summary: Inspection and maintenance put people on booms, decks and machinery at height, and the non-assembly fall protection rules cover that work: more than 6 feet generally, 15 feet or more when walking a horizontal lattice boom. Assembly and disassembly has its own trigger of more than 15 feet. The employer of the exposed worker provides the equipment, ensures it is used, and trains every employee who may be exposed to fall hazards on or hoisted by the crane.
title: Protect workers during maintenance and inspection at height

exam: Items give a short description of a machine or worksite and ask which type it is or whether it is covered. Watch for the one defining word, such as vertical only, permanent attachment, or the configuration in use.
hard: The definitions turn on one feature each, and the wrong answers usually borrow a feature from a neighboring type. A mobile crane is defined by a lattice or telescopic boom moved over the road, a sideboom by vertical-only boom and hook movement, and a floating crane by its marine design with permanent attachment, not by where it happens to work. Multi-purpose machines are covered only in the hook configuration.
mistakes: People assume every crane swings; a sideboom crane's boom or hook moves vertically only, with no slewing and no trolley motion. People call any truck-carried boom a mobile crane; folding, pin-connected members make it an articulating crane, while the mobile crane definition names lattice and hydraulic telescopic booms. People mix in tower crane parts; a fixed horizontal jib on a mast is tower crane construction. People call a land crane on a barge a floating crane because it works over water, is tied down for a long job, or has barge charts; floating means designed for marine use by permanent attachment. People think a machine sold as a forklift is never covered, or reverse the configurations; with forks it is not covered, with a hook jib or winch it is.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Mobile crane means a lifting device incorporating a cable suspended latticed boom or hydraulic telescopic boom designed to be moved between operating locations by transport over the road.
The boom or hook can be lifted or lowered in a vertical direction only.
Articulating crane means a crane whose boom consists of a series of folding, pin connected structural members, typically manipulated to extend or retract by power from hydraulic cylinders.
Floating cranes/derricks means equipment designed by the manufacturer (or employer) for marine use by permanent attachment to a barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of flotation.
When configured with the forks/tongs, it is not covered by this subpart.

summary: This skill is telling crane types apart by how they are built and how they move: mobile, crawler, articulating, tower, sideboom, floating, and multi-purpose machines. The type decides which rules apply and what the machine can and cannot do. A wrong classification leads to the wrong chart, the wrong rules, or the wrong expectations about motion.
title: Identify crane types and their typical limits

exam: Expect definition and function items: which device stops the boom from toppling backward, what the boom hoist limiting device does, where crossover points occur. The wrong options usually describe a real part, just not the one asked about.
hard: Several parts do jobs that sound alike. A boom stop physically keeps the boom from going over backward, while a boom hoist limiting device cuts boom hoist power and holds the boom from lowering. On a drum, crossover points happen at each flange where the rope climbs to the next layer, not in the middle of the barrel. Tower crane terms flip the mobile crane meaning: a fixed horizontal structure is a jib, a luffing one is a boom.
mistakes: People call a tower crane's fixed trolley jib a boom; on a tower crane it is a boom only if it moves up and down, and the mast is the vertical tower. People count a layer change at one flange only; it happens at each flange the rope reaches, and the lead-off point is a different thing. People think the boom hoist limiting device moves the boom back or cuts load hoist and swing; it only stops boom hoist power and sets brakes or closes valves. People confuse that device with the boom stop, which is a separate physical stop. People think pendants carry the hook load or set the boom angle; pendants are fixed-length members that hold up the boom tip, while the boom hoist rope changes the angle and the load hangs on the load line.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Boom (tower cranes): On tower cranes, if the “boom” (i.e., principal horizontal structure) is fixed, it is referred to as a jib; if it is moveable up and down, it is referred to as a boom.
This takes place at each flange of the drum as the rope is spooled onto the drum, reaches the flange, and begins to wrap back in the opposite direction.

This type of device disengages boom hoist power when the boom reaches a predetermined operating angle. It also sets brakes or closes valves to prevent the boom from lowering after power is disengaged.
These devices restrict the boom from moving above a certain maximum angle and toppling over backward.
Boom suspension system means a system of pendants, running ropes, sheaves, and other hardware which supports the boom tip and controls the boom angle.

summary: This skill is naming the parts of the crane and knowing what each one does: boom, jib, mast, pendants, sheaves, drums, outriggers, the swing bearing, and the safety devices on the boom. You talk about these parts with riggers, mechanics and inspectors, and the inspection and operating rules are written in these terms.
title: Name crane components (boom, jib, sheaves, drums, outriggers, swing bearing)

exam: Expect items that ask which device does a job on a jib, or a scenario with a jib attached that asks what the length indicator shows. Watch for the words fixed, luffing, stop and limiting device, since each pairs with a different job.
hard: The jib stop and the luffing jib limiting device are separate, just as the boom stop and the boom hoist limiting device are. The jib stop rule covers fixed jibs too, not only powered ones. A boom length indicator may show only the permanent boom, so with a jib pinned on, the length you read is not the total length, and it is never height or radius.
mistakes: People think a jib backstop guards against low angles or side wind; it stops the jib from going too high and tipping backward. People think a jib stop prevents two-blocking; anti-two-block devices do that. People think only luffing jibs need a stop or that the limiting device replaces it; the jib stop covers fixed and luffing jibs, and a luffing jib has both. People mix up the kick-out on the main boom, or an operator-set range control device, with the jib's own angle limit. People read the boom length markings as boom-plus-jib length, tip height or radius; ruled markings show the permanent boom, and height and radius change with boom angle and offset.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Jib stop (also referred to as a jib backstop), is the same type of device as a boom stop but is for a fixed or luffing jib.
Jib stops (if a jib is attached), except for derricks.
Luffing jib limiting device is similar to a boom hoist limiting device, except that it limits the movement of the luffing jib.
Range control limit device is a device that can be set by an equipment operator to limit movement of the boom or jib tip to a plane or multiple planes.

Boom length indicator indicates the length of the permanent part of the boom (such as ruled markings on the boom) or, as in some computerized systems, the length of the boom with extensions/attachments.

summary: This skill covers jibs and boom extensions: fixed and luffing jibs, offset angles, and the devices that protect them. A jib changes your length, height, radius and capacity, and it brings its own stops and limits. Reading the chart for a jib setup means knowing what the boom length indicator does and does not tell you.
title: Know jib and extension types and offsets

exam: Expect a simple force calculation done by hand, pressure times area, and items on which valve holds a load or which part protects an outrigger jack. Watch for options that name a real valve in the wrong place in the circuit.
hard: Pressure and flow do different jobs and are easy to swap. The relief valve limits pressure and so limits force; it does not hold a load or set speed. A pilot-operated holding valve stays seated under load until enough pilot pressure opens it, so losing pump flow does not let the load drop.
mistakes: People think a pressure relief valve, a control valve in neutral, or a check valve at the pump protects an outrigger jack; the jack needs its own integral holding device or check valve. People think the relief setting or reservoir size sets cylinder speed; speed is incoming flow divided by piston area. People think losing pump flow or opening the return path releases a holding valve; it stays closed without enough pilot pressure. People read a pressure gauge as total force or divide by area; force is pressure times area, so 2,000 psi on 10 square inches is 20,000 lb. People think a double-acting cylinder halves its force; with little rod-end pressure, extension force is still pressure times area.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Hydraulic outrigger jacks and hydraulic stabilizer jacks must have an integral holding device/check valve.
Hydraulic load hoists. Hydraulic drums must have an integrally mounted holding device or internal static brake to prevent load hoist movement in the event of hydraulic failure.
Hydraulic relief valve settings specified by the manufacturer.

summary: This skill is how hydraulic pressure, flow and valves move and hold a crane. Pressure times piston area gives force; flow divided by piston area gives speed. Holding valves and check valves keep cylinders and drums from moving when a line or pump fails, which is what keeps a load or outrigger in place.
title: Understand hydraulic systems and holding valves

exam: Expect number items on the 30 and 7 calendar-day periods, and scenarios where an aid has failed and you pick the correct temporary measure. Watch whether the question asks for the order deadline or the repair deadline.
hard: The repair timing has two numbers that sit close together. The normal deadline is 30 calendar days; the exception applies only if parts are ordered within 7 calendar days and documented, and then the repair is due within 7 calendar days of receiving the parts. Each failed aid also has its own temporary alternative, and an estimate or an old reading does not count as one.
mistakes: People use 7 days as the repair deadline or 30 days as the ordering deadline; ordering is within 7 calendar days, normal repair within 30. People guess 14 or 21 days; neither is in the rule. People think the outrigger position monitor senses jack travel, hydraulic pressure or float load; it senses horizontal beam extension. People think a known boom length, the last stored reading, or a signal person's eyeball is good enough when the angle or radius indicator fails; radius or boom angle has to be measured with a measuring device.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Category II operational aids and alternative measures. Operational aids listed in this paragraph that are not working properly must be repaired no later than 30 calendar days after the deficiency occurs. Exception: If the employer documents that it has ordered the necessary parts within 7 calendar days of the occurrence of the deficiency, and the part is not received in time to complete the repair in 30 calendar days, the repair must be completed within 7 calendar days of receipt of the parts. See § 1926.1417(j) for additional requirements.

Boom angle or radius indicator. The equipment must have a boom angle or radius indicator readable from the operator's station. Temporary alternative measures: Radii or boom angle must be determined by measuring the radii or boom angle with a measuring device.

Outrigger/stabilizer position (horizontal beam extension) sensor/monitor if the equipment has outriggers or stabilizers. Temporary alternative measures: The operator must verify that the position of the outriggers or stabilizers is correct (in accordance with manufacturer procedures) before beginning operations requiring outrigger or stabilizer deployment.

summary: This skill covers the operator aids that tell you boom angle or radius, boom length, outrigger position, drum rotation and load, and what to do when one fails. The rules set repair deadlines for these aids and spell out the temporary measures you use until the repair is done.
title: Read instruments and gauges

exam: Expect short number and direction items about cab features and block markings, and a scenario about a light block that will not overhaul the line. Watch for options that swap one marking or direction for its neighbor.
hard: The items are specific and the wrong answers are close: 250 pounds for a cab roof workstation, outward for swinging doors next to the operator, rearward for sliding operator doors. The hook block has to overhaul the line from the highest hook position for the boom or jib length and parts of line in use, which is a design condition, not your planned working range.
mistakes: People pick 200 or 300 pounds, or double the value, for the cab roof; the rule says 250 pounds without permanent distortion. People think rope size, test date or hook size can stand in for the block's weight marking; blocks are marked with rated capacity and weight. People reverse the door directions; swinging doors next to the operator open outward and sliding operator doors open rearward. People count the payload toward overhauling the line; the block alone has to overhaul it, from the highest hook position. People think the block must overhaul for every possible configuration; it is for the lengths and parts of line in use.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The following requirements apply to equipment that has a manufacturer-rated hoisting/lifting capacity of more than 2,000 pounds.
Areas of the cab roof that serve as a workstation for rigging, maintenance or other equipment-related tasks must be capable of supporting 250 pounds without permanent distortion.
Hook and ball assemblies and load blocks must be marked with their rated capacity and weight.

Cab doors (swinging, sliding) must be designed to prevent inadvertent opening or closing while traveling or operating the machine. Swinging doors adjacent to the operator must open outward. Sliding operator doors must open rearward.

Load hooks (including latched and unlatched types), ball assemblies and load blocks must be of sufficient weight to overhaul the line from the highest hook position for boom or boom and jib lengths and the number of parts of the line in use.
An accessible fire extinguisher must be on the equipment.

summary: This skill covers what the rules require the crane to have as built: load chart information in the cab, hook and block markings, hook latches, cab doors, windows, roof strength, guards, a fire extinguisher and hydraulic holding devices. These apply to equipment rated over 2,000 pounds. You check many of them during inspection and setup.
title: Know design, construction and testing requirements

exam: Expect scenarios where a manufacturer is silent, slow or unavailable and you pick what happens next, plus number items on 30 and 120 days. Watch for options that put the right action with the wrong person.
hard: The time limits sit close together: 30 days if the manufacturer never acknowledges the request or starts the review, 120 days if it agreed to review but did not finish. The fallback approver is a registered professional engineer who is also qualified for that equipment, not just any engineer, inspector or operator. Approval and keeping the original safety factor are two separate conditions.
mistakes: People think a derate or a written approval lets the safety factor drop; the original safety factor is never reduced either way. People think a capacity increase demands a higher safety factor; the rule only forbids reducing it. People apply 120 days to a manufacturer that never answered, or pick 60 or 90 days; an unanswered request runs 30 days. People think any professional engineer, a certified operator, or an inspector can approve; it has to be a registered professional engineer qualified for the equipment. People treat an inspector's acceptance, a logged phone call or the operator's okay as manufacturer approval; it has to be written approval from the manufacturer.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Modifications or additions which affect the capacity or safe operation of the equipment are prohibited except where the requirements of paragraphs (a)(1), (a)(2), (a)(3), (a)(4), or (a)(5) of this section are met.
The manufacturer approves the modifications/additions in writing.
The original safety factor of the equipment is not reduced.

Manufacturer refusal to review request. The manufacturer is provided a detailed description of the proposed modification/addition, is asked to approve the modification/addition, but it declines to review the technical merits of the proposal or fails, within 30 days, to acknowledge the request or initiate the review, and all of the following are met:
A registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to the equipment involved:

Manufacturer does not complete the review within 120 days of the request. The manufacturer is provided a detailed description of the proposed modification/addition, is asked to approve the modification/addition, agrees to review the technical merits of the proposal, but fails to complete the review of the proposal within 120 days of the date it was provided the detailed description of the proposed modification/addition, and the requirements of paragraphs (a)(2)(i) and (ii) of this section are met.

summary: This skill is knowing when a crane can be changed in a way that affects capacity or safe operation. The default is no; the rule allows it only through set paths, starting with the manufacturer's written approval. Charts, manuals and decals have to be updated, and the original safety factor cannot go down.
title: Know when modifications are allowed

exam: Expect a hand calculation of a load moment about the tipping axis and items on the locomotive crane tipping definition and track level. Read whether a distance given is from the center of rotation or from the tipping axis before you multiply.
hard: Radius is measured from the center of rotation, but the crane tips about its outer supports, so the load's arm is radius minus the distance from the center of rotation to the tipping axis. For locomotive cranes the tipping condition and track level are defined in the rule, and the numbers sit close together. Ratings are based on the worst direction, not the front or an average.
mistakes: People use the full radius as the lever arm; with a 40 ft radius and the tipping axis 10 ft out, the arm is 40 − 10 = 30 ft. People add the axis distance or use the 10 ft as the load's arm; it is subtracted and belongs to the crane's side. People think a rail crane tips when one wheel or all far wheels lift, or when outrigger floats lift; tipping is when half of the wheels farthest from the load leave the rail. People pick 0.5, 1.5 or 2.5 percent for the track; the stipulation is level within 1 percent grade. People think ratings use over the front or an average direction, or mix stability and structural limits; stability ratings come from the tipping load in the least stable direction.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The margin of stability for determination of load ratings, with booms of stipulated lengths at stipulated working radii for the various types of crane mountings, is established by taking a percentage of the loads which will produce a condition of tipping or balance with the boom in the least stable direction, relative to the mounting.
Tipping with or without the use of outriggers occurs when half of the wheels farthest from the load leave the rail.
The crane shall be standing on track which is level within 1 percent grade.
The equipment must not be operated in excess of its rated capacity.

summary: This skill is the arithmetic of tipping. Load moment is the load times its horizontal distance from the tipping axis; the stabilizing moment is the crane's weight and counterweight times their distance on the other side. As radius grows, the load's arm grows and the same load makes more overturning moment, which is why capacity falls with radius. Stability-based ratings are set as a percentage of the tipping load in the least stable direction.
title: Compute load moment and stabilizing moment about the tipping axis; why capacity falls with radius

exam: Expect setup scenarios that ask where the tipping axis is, and why the chart shows less capacity over the side. Watch for wheel-mounted cranes and the word front, and for options naming a person who cannot approve the lift.
hard: The tipping line moves with the setup and with swing direction, and it is never at the center of rotation. Over the side of a truck crane the tipping line is closer than over the rear, so stability-based ratings drop over the side. Lifting over the front of a wheel-mounted crane is off limits unless the manufacturer permits it, whatever the load size.
mistakes: People put the tipping line at the center of rotation; that is only where radius is measured from. People use the tire line when the crane is on outriggers, or the beam boxes; on outriggers the line runs through the floats. People use the track shoe edge for a crawler side lift, or the idler for a side lift; ratings commonly take the track centerline for side lifts, and the idler or tumbler is for over-the-end lifts. People think setting a front jack, a lift plan, a qualified person or a small load allows a lift over the front; only the manufacturer can permit it. People blame lower side ratings on boom deflection or frame twist, or think side floats carry less load; at stability-governed radii the shorter tipping distance is the reason, and the side floats carry more.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: On wheel-mounted equipment, no loads must be lifted over the front area, except as permitted by the manufacturer.
Caution or warnings relative to limitations on equipment and operating procedures, including an indication of the least stable direction.
Alternate ratings for use and nonuse of option equipment which affects rated capacities, such as outriggers, stabilizers, and extra counterweights.

summary: This skill is finding the line the crane would tip over for each setup. On outriggers it runs through the floats; on rubber it runs through the tires; on crawlers it is commonly taken at the track centerline for side lifts and near the idler or tumbler for lifts over the end. The distance from the center of rotation to that line changes as you swing, which is why charts rate quadrants differently.
title: Locate the tipping axis on outriggers, on rubber and on crawlers; why capacity differs by quadrant

exam: Expect questions on which conditions make backward tipping most likely, what happens on a sudden release of load, and which cranes need boom stops. Watch for options that mix up forward capacity with backward stability.
hard: Weight acts straight down, so its moment depends on horizontal distance from the tipping edge, not height. Raising the boom pulls the boom's center of gravity rearward even though the total weight is the same. When the load drops off, the crane's own center of gravity does not move; what disappears is the load's forward moment.
mistakes: People apply the boom stop requirement to hydraulic booms or to derricks; both are excepted, and truck or rough-terrain carrier does not change that. People use the height of the boom's weight as its lever arm; the arm is horizontal, and it shrinks as the boom rises. People think a shorter radius helps everywhere; it helps forward capacity but cuts the boom's forward balancing leverage against rearward tipping. People think raising the boom moves the counterweight or adds weight; it only moves where the boom's weight sits. People think losing the load shifts the crane's own center of gravity; the payload was never part of it, and the change is the lost forward moment.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Boom stops, except for derricks and hydraulic booms.
Loss of backward stability. Backward stability before swinging the upperworks, travel, and when attaching or removing equipment components.
Section 5-1.2 (“Stability (Backward and Forward)”).

summary: This skill is about the crane tipping backward over its counterweight. With a high boom angle, a short boom and no load, the boom's weight sits closer to the rear and gives little forward balance against the counterweight. A sudden loss of load removes the forward moment at once, which can rock the crane and whip the boom back, so boom stops and backward stability matter most in these conditions and during assembly.
title: How the crane's own center of gravity moves rearward (high boom angle, short boom, no load) and what a rapid loss of load does

exam: Expect definition items on pendants and boom length, and assembly scenarios that ask when the brake is tested or what must happen before pins come out. Watch for interval words like shift or daily that sound reasonable but do not match the trigger.
hard: Pendants are fixed-length wire or bar members, not running rope and not chain. Boom length is the length of the boom, not telescope stroke or horizontal reach, and the length indicator may not include a jib. During assembly and disassembly, the brake test is tied to each time you rely on the brake, and sections have to be stable the moment the pins come out.
mistakes: People list chain as a pendant type; the recognized types are wire and bar. People call a running rope a pendant; running rope moves over sheaves or drums, while a wire pendant is a fixed length with end fittings. People test the boom hoist brake once a shift, once a day, or only when operators change; it is tested each time you will rely on it during assembly or disassembly. People read boom length as stroke past the base or as reach, or assume the indicator counts the jib. People support only the boom foot, wait for the section to settle, or just clear the area; the sections have to be rigged or supported to stay stable when the pins are removed.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Pendants includes both wire and bar types.
Running wire rope means a wire rope that moves over sheaves or drums.

Boom hoist brake failure. Each time reliance is to be placed on the boom hoist brake to prevent boom movement during assembly/disassembly, the brake must be tested prior to such reliance to determine if it is sufficient to prevent boom movement. If it is not sufficient, a boom hoist pawl, other locking device/back-up braking device, or another method of preventing dangerous movement of the boom (such as blocking or using an assist crane) from a boom hoist brake failure must be used.

Stability upon pin removal. The boom sections, boom suspension systems (such as gantry A-frames and jib struts), and components must be rigged or supported to maintain stability upon the removal of the pins.
The sequence and procedure for extending and retracting the telescopic boom section.

summary: This skill covers how booms are built and handled: telescopic sections and their extend sequence, lattice sections held up by pendants, and jibs and offsets. Telescopic charts depend on the right section sequence and travel. Lattice booms bring assembly and disassembly hazards like pin removal and reliance on the boom hoist brake.
title: Telescopic sections and telescoping sequence, lattice sections and pendants, jib types and offset

exam: Expect a scenario with a warning light or abnormal reading that asks for the right action, and items on who gets written notice and the 30 and 7 calendar-day periods. Watch for options that sound productive, like finishing the pick first.
hard: The repair clock counts calendar days and starts when the deficiency occurs. The 7-day numbers are the parts-ordering window and the time allowed after delayed parts arrive, not the main deadline. The reporting duty is split: the operator gives written notice to the designated person and the next operator, and the employer briefs affected workers at each shift.
mistakes: People use 7 days as the repair deadline, count working days, or tie repairs to the annual inspection; the basic deadline is 30 calendar days from the deficiency. People restart the 30 days when parts arrive or count 7 days from the end of the 30; after a documented delay the repair is due within 7 calendar days of receiving the parts. People report verbally to the lift director, or think a tag replaces the report; the operator reports in writing to the person the employer designated and to the next operator. People think the employer's shift briefing covers the operator's duty; both are required. People finish the lift on zero oil pressure, call it normal, tap the gauge, or push through an overheat; land the load, shut down and find the cause.

quotes.quote: Category II operational aids and alternative measures. Operational aids listed in this paragraph that are not working properly must be repaired no later than 30 calendar days after the deficiency occurs. Exception: If the employer documents that it has ordered the necessary parts within 7 calendar days of the occurrence of the deficiency, and the part is not received in time to complete the repair in 30 calendar days, the repair must be completed within 7 calendar days of receipt of the parts. See § 1926.1417(j) for additional requirements.
The operator must, in writing, promptly inform the person designated by the employer to receive such information and, where there are successive shifts, to the next operator; and
The employer must notify all affected employees, at the beginning of each shift, of the necessary adjustments or repairs and all alternative measures.

summary: This skill is reading engine and hydraulic gauges and warning lights and acting on what they show. A zero oil pressure or a red-zone temperature at working speed is a real fault, and good practice is to land the load and shut down. When something needs repair, the operator reports it in writing, and failed operator aids have set repair deadlines.
title: Read engine and hydraulic gauges and warning lights; act on abnormal readings

exam: Expect number items on strand counts, hook deformation and design factors, plus scenarios about swivels, latches and a block that will not overhaul. Watch for swapped pairs of numbers and for options that move an exception to the wrong rope type or person.
hard: Rotation-resistant rope comes in three types with close strand counts: Type I has at least 15 outer strands and at least three layers, Type II at least 10 outer strands, and Type III only limited resistance. The hook limits are also easy to swap: 15 percent throat opening and 10 degrees of twist from the plane of the unbent hook. Design factors for rotation-resistant rope are normally 5, with 3.5 as the floor.
mistakes: People give Type II the Type I or Type III construction, or invent a 12-strand cutoff; Type II starts at 10 outer strands and Type I at 15. People swap the hook limits or use 5 degrees; the limits are 15 percent throat opening and 10 degrees twist. People think written approval or per-lift logging allows a design factor below 3.5, or that a qualified person can approve 4; 3.5 is the floor, and the written approval exception applies only to Type I. People think Type I rope binds a swivel or that counter-lay creates torque; Type I makes little torque, counter-lay cancels torque, and standard rope with no counter-laid layer is what spins a swivel. People think hooks can run without latches whenever convenient; that takes a qualified person's determination and preplanned routes that keep people out of the fall zone.

quotes.quote: Load hooks (including latched and unlatched types), ball assemblies and load blocks must be of sufficient weight to overhaul the line from the highest hook position for boom or boom and jib lengths and the number of parts of the line in use.
Hook and ball assemblies and load blocks must be marked with their rated capacity and weight.
Hooks must be equipped with latches, except where the requirements of paragraph (d)(4)(ii) of this section are met.
A qualified person has determined that it is safer to hoist and place the load without latches (or with the latches removed/tied-back).
Routes for the loads are pre-planned to ensure that no employee is required to work in the fall zone except for employees necessary for the hooking or unhooking of the load.
The latch must close the throat opening and be designed to retain slings or other lifting devices/accessories in the hook when the rigging apparatus is slack.

summary: This skill is choosing between a multi-sheave block and an overhaul ball, reeving the block to the parts of line the load needs, and pairing swivels with the right rope. It also covers hook latches, block markings and when a hook is too deformed to use. A light block that cannot overhaul the line, or a swivel on the wrong rope, causes real trouble on the job.
title: Choose block or overhaul ball, match block sheaves to parts of line, swivels with rotation-resistant rope, latches and hook loading

exam: This is not on the core exam outline, so treat it as background. Practice items ask for a number (clearance, brake percent, pedal force) or give a crane with two hoists and ask how they are marked. Read for the braking type and the direction of the clearance.
hard: Clearance is 3 inches overhead and 2 inches laterally, and people swap the two. Holding brake torque depends on the setup: 125 percent of full load hoisting torque with control braking other than mechanical, 100 percent with mechanical control braking, and 100 percent each when there are two holding brakes. The 70 pound foot brake limit and the 200 pound guard load are easy to confuse.
mistakes: People reverse the clearances; it is 3 inches overhead and 2 inches laterally. People use the same clearance both ways or use the lateral figure overhead; overhead needs the larger 3 inches. People apply 100 percent to a single holding brake with electrical control braking; that setup needs 125 percent, not 150 or 200 percent. People think a foot brake can need 100 pounds of force; 70 pounds is the most it may need to develop rated brake torque, and 200 pounds is the guard strength figure. People think markings on the bridge or the controls are enough for a crane with more than one hoist; each hoist carries its own rating on the hoist or its load block, legible from the floor.

quotes.quote: Minimum clearance of 3 inches overhead and 2 inches laterally shall be provided and maintained between crane and obstructions
125 percent when used with a control braking means other than mechanical.
100 percent when used in conjunction with a mechanical control braking means.
100 percent each if two holding brakes are provided.
Foot-operated brakes shall not require an applied force of more than 70 pounds to develop manufacturer's rated brake torque.
Each guard shall be capable of supporting without permanent distortion the weight of a 200-pound person unless the guard is located where it is impossible for a person to step on it.

Rated load marking. The rated load of the crane shall be plainly marked on each side of the crane, and if the crane has more than one hoisting unit, each hoist shall have its rated load marked on it or its load block and this marking shall be clearly legible from the ground or floor.

summary: In general industry, overhead and gantry cranes have their own design and equipment rules. These cover clearance from obstructions, holding brake torque, foot brake force, guard strength and rated load markings. If you run or work around plant bridge cranes, these are the basics that keep the crane and the people below it safe.
title: Know overhead and gantry crane requirements (general industry)

exam: This is not on the core exam outline, so treat it as background. Practice items give an interval and ask which classification it is, or describe an idle or standby crane and ask what inspection it needs. Watch for daily versus monthly on specific items and for the 6 month split on idle cranes.
hard: The two ranges overlap at monthly, so people swap them. Some frequent items are fixed at daily, such as operating mechanisms and air or hydraulic system leaks. Hooks and hoist chains get a daily visual check plus a monthly check with a certification record. Idle cranes split at 6 months: idle 1 month to under 6 months needs the frequent inspection, and idle over 6 months needs the complete inspection, while standby cranes are inspected at least semi-annually.
mistakes: People say frequent inspection is weekly to monthly; it runs daily to monthly. People give monthly to yearly as the frequent range; that is roughly the periodic range, which is 1 to 12 months. People start the periodic range at 3 or 6 months, or end it at 6 months; it spans 1 to 12 months. People set standby inspection at monthly, quarterly or annually; the rule says at least semi-annually. People think a monthly interval or an overhaul schedule covers hydraulic leaks; air and hydraulic system leaks and deterioration are checked daily. People think there is a separate inspection before every lift; the rule says daily, plus watching for defects during operation.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: Frequent inspection—Daily to monthly intervals.
Periodic inspection—1 to 12-month intervals.
Deterioration or leakage in lines, tanks, valves, drain pumps, and other parts of air or hydraulic systems. Daily.
All functional operating mechanisms for maladjustment interfering with proper operation. Daily.

A crane which has been idle for a period of 1 month or more, but less than 6 months, shall be given an inspection conforming with requirements of paragraph (j)(2) of this section and paragraph (m)(2) of this section before placing in service.

A crane which has been idle for a period of over 6 months shall be given a complete inspection conforming with requirements of paragraphs (j) (2) and (3) of this section and paragraph (m)(2) of this section before placing in service.
Standby cranes shall be inspected at least semi-annually in accordance with requirements of paragraph (j)(2) of this section and paragraph (m)(2) of this section.

summary: Overhead cranes in regular service get two kinds of inspection. Frequent inspections run daily to monthly, and periodic inspections run every 1 to 12 months, depending on activity, severity of service and environment. Idle and standby cranes have their own triggers. Knowing which items are daily checks is what catches a leak or a bad mechanism before it fails.
title: Inspect overhead cranes (frequent, periodic, idle)

exam: This is not on the core exam outline, but the same ideas show up in mobile crane items. Practice items ask for the wrap count, the timing and load condition for the limit switch test, who runs a multi-crane lift, or the right order of steps. Watch for words like daily versus each shift and light load versus no load.
hard: The order matters. The hook goes over the load before hoisting starts, not while the load is coming up. The limit switch test is per operator shift and under no load, and people loosen either part. The brake test is tied to each load approaching rated load, not to the shift.
mistakes: People think one wrap on the drum is enough, or that three or four are the minimum; the load is not lowered below two full wraps. People test the upper limit switch once a day, weekly, or with a light load; it is tried out under no load at the beginning of each operator's shift. People let each operator direct their own crane on a tandem lift, or give the job to the bigger crane or split it between supervisors; one qualified responsible person is in charge of the whole operation. People think a tag line makes up for an offset hook, or line the hook up after or while lifting; the hook is brought over the load before hoisting starts so the load does not swing. People use the upper limit switch to stop the hook in normal work; it is never used as an operating control.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

quotes.quote: The load shall not be lowered below the point where less than two full wraps of rope remain on the hoisting drum.
At the beginning of each operator's shift, the upper limit switch of each hoist shall be tried out under no load.
The hoist limit switch which controls the upper limit of travel of the load block shall never be used as an operating control.

When two or more cranes are used to lift a load one qualified responsible person shall be in charge of the operation. He shall analyze the operation and instruct all personnel involved in the proper positioning, rigging of the load, and the movements to be made.
The hook shall be brought over the load in such a manner as to prevent swinging.
The operator shall test the brakes each time a load approaching the rated load is handled. The brakes shall be tested by raising the load a few inches and applying the brakes.

summary: These are the load handling rules for overhead cranes: how you attach, start and move a load, and the checks you run each shift. They overlap with good mobile crane practice. Keep two full wraps on the drum, test the upper limit switch with no load at the start of each shift, center the hook before you hoist, and put one person in charge when two cranes share a load.
title: Handle loads with overhead cranes

exam: The core outline lists federal regulations, including Subpart CC, so expect items that name a crane setup and ask which rule or paragraph applies. Read closely for permanently installed versus temporary, and manufacture date versus installation date. Wrong options often take the right idea and apply it to the other branch.
hard: There are two branches, (a) for permanently installed and (b) for not permanently installed, and each has its own carve-outs. In the temporary branch, the general industry definitions apply except that hoist and load take their Subpart CC meanings. The general industry design paragraph (b)(2) applies only to cranes manufactured before September 19, 2001, and cranes made on or after that date use the listed ASME B30.2-2005 sections instead.
mistakes: People say paragraph (b)(2) or another paragraph such as (e)(1) is excluded for permanently installed cranes; for those cranes, (b)(1) is the only one removed. People apply the hoist and load definitions carve-out to permanently installed cranes; it applies only to equipment that is not permanently installed. People swap in crane or bridge as the redefined term; only hoist and load change. People use the installation date or reverse the date; the test is manufacture date, and cranes made before September 19, 2001 get (b)(2) while newer ones get the ASME sections. People think construction use brings in all of Subpart CC; only the listed sections apply. People put a rail-mounted temporary crane under the tower crane section, or use the permanent installation paragraph for it; it falls under (b).

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: Overhead and gantry cranes used in construction fall under 1926.1438, which sends you to different rules depending on whether the crane is permanently installed in a facility or not. A permanently installed crane follows the general industry overhead crane section, except for its application paragraph (b)(1). A crane that is not permanently installed follows a listed set of Subpart CC sections plus listed parts of the general industry section, and some of those depend on the manufacture date.
title: Know when 1926.1438 applies to overhead cranes in construction

exam: This section is named in the core outline. Expect number items (wraps, grade), scenario items about when a brake test is needed, and load-chart style items comparing a load to the with and without outrigger ratings at a given radius. Watch for words like each, approaching and fully extended.
hard: The ratings are tied to conditions. For locomotive cranes the track is level within 1 percent grade, and a rating without outriggers is only good when you are not using outriggers. The brake test is triggered by each load approaching rated load, not by the shift or a setup change. Two full wraps stay on each respective drum.
mistakes: People treat three or four wraps as the minimum, or think one wrap is fine because the rope is anchored; the minimum is two full wraps on each drum. People accept a 2, 3 or 5 percent grade for locomotive crane ratings; the condition is level within 1 percent. People test brakes once a shift, only after a setup change, or once for a batch of identical loads; each load approaching rated load gets its own test. People think a good brake test or locked travel brakes raise the capacity without outriggers; neither changes the chart. If the load is over the rating without outriggers, the fix is to set the outriggers and use that rating, not to get a bigger crane.
