Truck and wheel mounted without outriggers or using outriggers fully extended | 85

summary: The general industry section 1910.180 covers crawler, locomotive, truck and wheel-mounted cranes used outside construction. It sets load ratings as a percentage of tipping load by mounting type, along with drum wrap, track level, brake test and outrigger conditions. If you run a mobile crane in a plant, rail yard or yard operation, this is your rulebook.
title: Know 1910.180 for crawler, locomotive and truck cranes

exam: This is not on the core exam outline, so treat it as background. Practice items ask for the plumb ratio, the wrap count, who designs or verifies something, or the correct temporary measure for a failed device. Match each measure to the device it belongs to.
hard: When the manufacturer is silent, the tower is plumb to 1:500, about 1 inch in 40 feet. The drum device protects the last 2 wraps. The roles are split: the manufacturer or a registered professional engineer designs the foundation, the A/D director checks that it was built to the design, and a qualified person verifies plumb. The temporary measures for each failed device are different and get mixed up.
mistakes: People use 1:1000, 1:250 or a slope tolerance for plumb; the default is 1:500, about 1 inch in 40 feet. People say the drum device protects the last 3 or 5 wraps, or a full layer; it protects the last 2 wraps. People think the A/D director, a qualified person or a competent person can design the foundation; only the manufacturer or a registered professional engineer designs it. People fix a failed moment limiting device by marking the trolley rope, using the trolley limiter option, or derating; the fix is to get the radius from an indicator or by measuring and give the operator a reliable load weight.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: Tower cranes have supplemental construction rules on top of the general crane rules. These cover how plumb the tower is, foundation design, protecting the last wraps on the hoist drum, and what to do when a limiting device fails. Mobile operators often help erect tower cranes or work beside them, so these terms come up on site.
title: Know tower crane supplemental requirements

exam: This is not on the core exam outline, so treat it as background. Practice items ask for a count, an interval or a day threshold, or describe a permanent installation and ask where the chart goes. Watch whether the item says permanent or temporary.
hard: The default is six equally spaced guys. A different arrangement needs approval and a matching revision to rated capacity. Guy tension is a daily item, while the gudgeon pin and foundation supports are added annual items. The idle trigger is 30 days or more, and the chart posting rule changes between permanent and temporary installations.
mistakes: People accept four guys, or think eight or twelve is the minimum; the default is six equally spaced guys unless an approved variation applies. People check guy tension weekly or monthly; it is a daily item. People treat the gudgeon pin and foundation supports as daily items; those are annual. People use 7, 14 or 60 days as the idle trigger; the specified steps apply at 30 days or more. For a permanent installation, people think a copy in the office, on site or reviewed before the shift is enough; the chart is posted where the people responsible for operation can see it.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: Derricks have their own construction rules on guying, inspections, idle periods and load chart posting. A guy derrick depends on its guys for stability, so the guy count and daily tension checks matter. Whether the installation is permanent or temporary decides where the load chart goes.
title: Know derrick requirements

exam: Barge work is in the core outline under specialty operations, so expect number items (wind, degrees) and scenarios about anti two-block or dive support. Read for crane versus derrick, permanently mounted versus land crane on a barge, and rated capacity.
hard: Several wind speeds appear: load charts consider at least 40 mph, the freeboard stability table uses 60 mph, and the backward stability check with high boom and no load uses 90 mph. List and trim limits are 5 degrees for permanently mounted equipment rated 25 tons or less, 7 degrees above that, and 10 degrees for derricks designed for marine use. Land cranes on barges are capped at 5 degrees. List and trim share the same value in each row.
mistakes: People take 60, 90 or 20 mph as the load chart wind; marine load charts consider at least 40 mph. People give a 40 ton permanently mounted crane 5 or 10 degrees; it gets 7, with 5 for 25 tons or less and land cranes on barges, and 10 only for marine derricks. People think list and trim limits differ; they are the same in each row. People think anti two-block is required on every marine lift, or tied to 25 tons or a vessel alongside; it is required for hoisting personnel and hoisting over an occupied cofferdam or shaft. People release a dive support crane when one diver is back, or let someone approve other lifts; the crane stays dedicated until every diver it serves is out of the water. Line of sight or electronic signals with the tender is a separate requirement, not permission to multitask.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: Cranes on barges and floating platforms have marine rules that change some land crane requirements. Load charts account for wind, list and trim are limited by equipment type, anti two-block devices are required only in certain cases, and diving support gets a dedicated crane. Barge work is listed as a specialty operation, so this is core material.
title: Know floating crane and barge requirements

exam: This is not on the core exam outline, so treat it as background. Practice items ask where the chart goes, who designs the equipment, which date applies, or what triggers a test. Watch the words after versus on or after, and altered versus moved.
hard: The load chart has to be at the operator's control station, not just somewhere on the machine or at the job. Design takes a qualified engineer, which is not the same as a registered professional engineer, who is required for other tasks. The pile driver cutoff is after November 8, 2011, so equipment made on that date is not included. The rated load test applies when equipment is altered or modified.
mistakes: People think an office copy, a copy stored with maintenance papers, or the supervisor's copy is enough; the chart is available at the operator's control station. People think operating or inspection experience qualifies someone to design the equipment; the designer is a qualified engineer. People think every engineering task needs a registered professional engineer; this design provision does not say so. People mix up the pile driver cutoff with the sideboom live boom date, move it a year early, or include the cutoff day; it covers dedicated pile drivers manufactured after November 8, 2011. People think relocation, a new operator or a routine inspection triggers the rated load test; alteration or modification does.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: Sideboom cranes, small cranes and dedicated pile drivers each have short sections that change or add to the general crane rules. Small cranes have specific requirements for load chart location, design qualification and testing. Dedicated pile drivers pick up certain requirements based on manufacture date. Sideboom cranes have their own exceptions, including a live boom date cutoff.
title: Know sideboom, small-crane and pile driver provisions

exam: This is not on the core exam outline, so treat it as background. Practice items ask for a cutoff date, which device qualifies, or whether a delivery scenario is covered. Read for onto a structure versus on the ground, and indicator versus automatic prevention.
hard: There are two cutoff dates for two different devices, and people blend them. The overload rule accepts any of four devices: overload prevention, load weighing, load moment indicator or load moment limiter. The delivery exclusion for placing material onto a structure with a fork or cradle is narrower and needs an automatic overload prevention device. Ground transfer without arranging the material in sequence for hoisting is excluded with no device condition, but prefabricated components are treated differently from sheet goods.
mistakes: People use the overload device date or a general effective date for two-block, or blend the two dates; the two-block cutoff is December 31, 1999. People count anti two-block, a boom angle indicator or outrigger monitoring as one of the overload devices; the list is overload prevention, load weighing, load moment indicator and load moment limiter. People think an indicator, a weight readout or two-block protection meets the onto-structure delivery exclusion; it needs an automatic overload prevention device. People assume every construction site lift is covered, or add the device condition to ground transfers; ground transfer without sequencing is excluded with no device condition. People treat sheet rock as a prefabricated component; it is a sheet good, so ground delivery of it stays excluded.

prov.verifier: crane-content/verify v1 (exact substring of eCFR text, typography repair)

summary: Articulating (knuckle-boom) cranes have their own device requirements and a key exclusion for delivery work. Two-block protection applies to articulating cranes manufactured after December 31, 1999. A separate, later cutoff calls for one of four overload-related devices. Certain deliveries to construction sites are excluded from the standard altogether.
title: Know articulating crane provisions and exclusions
